[Page 116]

**Sūrat al-Isrāʾ (The Night Journey)**

It is Meccan, except for verses 26, 32, 33, 57, and from verse 73 to the end of verse 80, which are Medinan. Its number of verses is 111. It was revealed after Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās that it is Meccan, except for His words ﴿And indeed, they were about to drive you out of the land﴾ [al-Isrāʾ 17:76] up to His words ﴿and grant me from Yourself a supporting authority﴾ [al-Isrāʾ 17:80]. Those verses are Medinan, and they were revealed when the delegation of Thaqīf came.

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque, whose surroundings We have blessed, that We might show him of Our signs. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.﴾

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque, whose surroundings We have blessed, that We might show him of Our signs. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.﴾

**On the verse, there are several issues.**

**The first issue:** The grammarians said: *subḥāna* (Glory be to) is a proper noun used as a verbal noun (*ism ʿalam li-l-tasbīḥ*, a proper noun for the act of glorifying). It is said: *sabbaḥtu Allāh tasbīḥan wa subḥānan*, so *tasbīḥ* is the verbal noun (*maṣdar*). *Subḥān* is a proper noun for *tasbīḥ*, like your saying *kaffartu al-yamīn takfīran wa kufrānan* (I expiated the oath). Its meaning is the declaration of the exaltedness of Allah, the Exalted, above every imperfection.

The author of *al-Naẓm* said: *al-sabḥ* in the language means distance, as His words indicate: ﴿Indeed, for you by day there is extensive occupation﴾ [al-Muzzammil 73:7], meaning a prolonged distance. So the meaning of "Glorify Allah" is: keep Him far away and declare Him free from what is not befitting. The complete rational discussions about the word *tasbīḥ* have been mentioned at the beginning of Sūrat al-Ḥadīd. The word *tasbīḥ* has also come with other meanings:

First: *tasbīḥ* is mentioned in the sense of prayer, as in His words: ﴿Had he not been of those who glorify [Us]﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 37:143], meaning of those who pray. The *subḥa* is the voluntary prayer. The one who prays is called *musabbiḥ* only because he exalts Allah through prayer and declares Him free from what is not befitting.

Second: *tasbīḥ* occurs in the sense of making an exception (*istithnāʾ*) in His words: ﴿The best of them said, "Did I not tell you, 'Why do you not glorify [Allah]?'"﴾ [al-Qalam 68:28], meaning "Why do you not make an exception [by saying *in shāʾ Allāh*]?" Its interpretation also returns to exalting Allah, the Exalted, by making the exception dependent on His will.

Third: It has come in a ḥadīth: "The glories (*subuḥāt*) of His face would burn whatever His sight reaches." It was said: its meaning is the light of His face. It was also said: the glories of His face are the light of His face, which, when the beholder sees it, he says: "Glory be to Allah."

As for His words ﴿asrā﴾ (took by night), the people of language said: *asrā* and *saraā* are two dialects.

As for His words ﴿bi-ʿabdihi﴾ (His servant), the commentators unanimously agreed that the intended one is Muḥammad (ﷺ). I heard the great shaykh, my father ʿUmar ibn al-Ḥusayn, may Allah have mercy on him, say: I heard the great shaykh Abū al-Qāsim Sulaymān al-Anṣārī say: When Muḥammad, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, reached the lofty levels and the elevated ranks in the ascents (*maʿārij*), Allah, the Exalted, revealed to him: "O Muḥammad, with what shall I honor you?" He said: "O Lord, by Your attributing me to Yourself through servanthood." So Allah revealed concerning him: ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant﴾.

As for His words ﴿laylan﴾ (by night), it is in the accusative as an adverb of time (*ẓarf*).

If it is said: The night journey does not happen except at night, so what is the meaning of mentioning the night?

We say: By His words ﴿laylan﴾ in indefinite form, He intended to reduce the duration of the journey, and that He took him by night, in a part of the night, from Mecca to Syria, a distance of forty nights' travel. This is because the indefiniteness in it indicates the meaning of partiality.

They differed about which night it was. Muqātil said: That night was one year before the Hijra. The author of *al-Kashshāf* transmitted from Anas and al-Ḥasan that it was before the prophethood (*baʿtha*).

As for His words ﴿from the Sacred Mosque﴾, they differed about the place from which he was taken. It was said: It is the Sacred Mosque itself, and this is what the apparent wording of the Qur'an indicates. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "While I was in the Sacred Mosque, in al-Ḥijr beside the House, between sleeping and waking, Jibrīl came to me with the Burāq."

It was also said: He was taken from the house of Umm Hāniʾ bint Abī Ṭālib. According to this view, the intended meaning of "the Sacred Mosque" is the Sacred Precinct (*al-Ḥaram*), because it encompasses the mosque and is connected to it. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās: "The entire Ḥaram is a mosque." This is the view of most scholars.

As for His words ﴿to the Farthest Mosque﴾, they agreed that the intended one is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). It was named "the Farthest" because of the great distance between it and the Sacred Mosque.

As for His words ﴿whose surroundings We have blessed﴾, it was said: with fruits and flowers. It was also said: because it is the resting place of the prophets and the descent place of the angels.

Know that the word ﴿ilā﴾ (to) indicates the end of a limit. Therefore, the meaning of His words ﴿to the Farthest Mosque﴾ is that he reached the boundary of that mosque. As for whether he entered that mosque or not, there is no indication in the wording about it.

As for His words ﴿that We might show him of Our signs﴾, it means what he saw on that night of wonders and signs that point to the power of Allah, the Exalted.

If they say: His words ﴿that We might show him of Our signs﴾ indicate that Allah, the Exalted, showed him only some of the signs, because the word ﴿min﴾ (of) indicates partiality. And concerning Ibrāhīm He said: ﴿And thus did We show Ibrāhīm the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Anʿām 6:75]. Then it follows that the ascent (*miʿrāj*) of Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him, was superior to the ascent of Muḥammad (ﷺ).

We say: What Ibrāhīm saw was the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and what Muḥammad (ﷺ) saw was some of the signs of Allah, the Exalted. There is no doubt that the signs of Allah are superior.

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾, meaning: the One who took His servant by night is the All-Hearing of Muḥammad's words, the All-Seeing of his deeds, and knowing that they are refined and sincere, free from the taints of showing off, joined with truthfulness and purity. For this reason, Allah, the Exalted, singled him out with these honors. It was also said: The intended meaning is that He hears what they say to the Messenger about this matter, and sees what they do in this incident.

* * *

**The second issue:** It has been disputed concerning the manner of that night journey. Most of the groups of Muslims agreed that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was taken by night in his body, while a minority said that he was taken only in his spirit.

It is related from Muḥammad ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī in his *Tafsīr*, from Ḥudhayfa, that he said: That was a dream, and the body of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was not lost; rather, he was taken by night in his spirit. This view is also related from ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, and from Muʿāwiya, may Allah be pleased with him.

Know that the discussion on this topic takes place in two stages:

One of them: establishing rational possibility.

The second: the actual occurrence.

As for the first stage, which is establishing rational possibility, we say: A movement reaching this degree of speed is possible in itself. Allah, the Exalted, is capable of all possible things, and this indicates that the occurrence of motion at this degree of speed is not impossible. Here we need to explain two premises.

The first premise: establishing that movement reaching this limit is possible in itself. The following points prove it:

The first point: The greatest sphere (*al-Falak al-Aʿẓam*) moves from the beginning of the night to its end by nearly half a revolution. It has been established in geometry that the ratio of one diameter to the circumference is the ratio of one to three and a seventh. Therefore, the ratio of half a diameter to half a circumference must be the ratio of one to three and a seventh. Supposing it is said that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rose from Mecca to above the greatest sphere, he moved only by the amount of half a diameter. When the movement of half a circumference happened in that amount of time, then the occurrence of movement by the amount of half a diameter is more probable. This is a decisive proof that ascending from Mecca to above the Throne within a third of the night is possible in itself. If that is the case, its occurrence throughout the whole night is even more probable. And Allah knows best.

The second point: It has been established in geometry that the disc of the sun is equal to the Earth a hundred and sixty times or so. Then we observe that the rising of the disc happens in a brief and swift time. This indicates that reaching this degree of speed is possible in itself.

The third point: Just as it is considered unlikely by reason that a dense body should ascend from the center of the world to above the Throne, so also it is considered unlikely that a subtle, spiritual body should descend from above the Throne to the center of the world. If the claim that Muḥammad's ascent (*miʿrāj*) happened in one night is impossible by reason, then the claim that Jibrīl, peace be upon him, descended from the Throne to Mecca in one instant would also be impossible. If we ruled that this impossibility holds, that would be a challenge to the prophethood of all the prophets, peace be upon them. The affirmation of the ascent is a branch of accepting the permissibility of the basic prophethood. So it is established that those who claim the impossibility of such a swift movement to this degree are obliged to claim the impossibility of Jibrīl's descent from the Throne to Mecca in an instant. Since that is false, what they said is also false.

If they say: We do not say that Jibrīl, peace be upon him, is a body that moves from place to place. Rather, we say: what is meant by the descent of Jibrīl, peace be upon him, is the removal of the physical veils from the soul of Muḥammad (ﷺ), so that there appears in his soul some of the unveilings and witnessings that were present and manifest in the essence of Jibrīl, peace be upon him.

We say: Interpreting revelation in this way is the view of the philosophers. As for the majority of Muslims, they affirm that Jibrīl, peace be upon him, is a body, and that his descent means his transfer from the world of the spheres to Mecca. If that is the case, the aforementioned objection is strong.

It was narrated that when he (ﷺ) mentioned the story of the ascent, everyone denied him. They went to Abū Bakr and said: "Your companion says such and such." Abū Bakr said: "If he has said that, then he is truthful." Then he came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the Messenger told him those details. Whenever he mentioned something, Abū Bakr said: "You have spoken the truth." When he finished speaking, Abū Bakr said: "I bear witness that you are truly the Messenger of Allah." The Messenger said to him: "And I bear witness that you are truly the *Ṣiddīq*." The summary of the matter is that Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, was as if saying: Since I have accepted his message, I have already believed him in what is greater than this, so how can I deny him in this?

The fourth point: Most adherents of religions and sects accept the existence of Iblīs, and accept that he is the one who undertakes casting whisperings into the hearts of the children of Adam. They accept that he is able to move from the east to the west in order to cast whisperings into the hearts of the children of Adam. When they accept the permissibility of such swift movement in the case of Iblīs, then it is more fitting that they accept its permissibility in the case of the greatest prophets. This objection is strong against one who holds that Iblīs is a body that moves from place to place. As for those who say that he is one of the evil and wicked spirits, and that he is not a body or corporeal, this objection does not apply to them. However, most adherents of religions and sects agree that he is a subtle moving body.

If they say: Grant that angels and devils may be able to undergo such a swift movement, since they are subtle bodies, and there is no impossibility in such a swift movement in their essence. But the human being is a dense body, so how can such a swift movement be conceived in him?

We say: We argued from the states of the angels and devils only to show that a movement reaching this extent of speed is possible in reality. As for showing that this movement, since it is possible in itself, is also possible to occur in the human bodily frame, that is another stage, whose explanation will come, if Allah, the Exalted, wills.

**The fifth aspect:** The Qur'an states that the winds carried Sulayman (peace be upon him) to distant places in brief periods of time. Concerning the journey of Sulayman (peace be upon him), God the Exalted says: ﴿Its morning journey was a month's travel, and its evening journey was a month's travel﴾ [Saba 34:12]. Moreover, we say: the senses indicate that when winds blow forcefully they move from one place to a far-off place in a single instant. This also indicates that such rapid motion is possible in itself.

**The sixth aspect:** The Qur'an indicates that the one who had knowledge from the Book brought the throne of Bilqis from the farthest part of Yemen to the farthest part of Syria in the blink of an eye. The evidence is God's saying: ﴿The one who had knowledge from the Book said: "I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you"﴾ [al-Naml 27:40]. If this is possible for some people, we know that it is possible in itself.

**The seventh aspect:** Some people say that living creatures see visible things because a ray goes out from their eyes and connects with the object seen. Then, when we open our eyes and look at a man, we see him. According to the view of these people, the ray of the eye moves from our eyes to the man in that subtle instant. This indicates that a motion occurring at this degree of speed is among the possibilities and not among the impossibilities. Thus it is established by these aspects that the occurrence of a motion reaching this degree of speed is a matter that is possible in itself.

[p. 120]

**The second premise:** Explaining that since this motion is possible in itself, its occurrence in the body of Muhammad (ﷺ) cannot be impossible. What shows this is that we have demonstrated by conclusive proofs that bodies are alike in their entire essences. So when such a motion is valid for some bodies, it must be possible for all other bodies. This necessitates the certainty that the occurrence of such a motion in the body of Muhammad (ﷺ) is a matter possible in itself.

Given this, we say: it has been established by proof that the Creator of the world is capable of all possibilities, and it has been established that the occurrence of motion reaching this degree of speed in the body of Muhammad (ﷺ) is possible. Therefore, it is necessary that He, the Exalted, is capable of it. From the totality of these premises it follows that the claim of the established reality of this ascension (mi'raj, the heavenly ascent) is a matter possible in itself.

The most that can be said is that astonishment remains. However, this astonishment is not specific to this station; rather it occurs in all miracles. The turning of the staff into a serpent that swallows seventy thousand ropes and staffs, and then immediately returns to being a small staff as it was, is a wondrous matter! And the emergence of the great she-camel from the solid mountain, and the shading of the great mountain in the air, are wondrous. The same applies to all miracles. If mere astonishment necessitated denial and rejection, it would be necessary to affirm with certainty the falsity of the claim of establishing miracles. But the establishment of miracles is a branch of accepting the principle of prophethood. If mere astonishment does not necessitate denial and refutation, then likewise here. This is the complete discussion explaining that the claim of the ascension is possible and not impossible. And God knows best.

* * *

**The second station:** Concerning the investigation of whether the ascension (mi'raj) actually occurred. The scholars of verification (ahl al-tahqiq) said: what indicates that God carried the spirit and body of Muhammad (ﷺ) from Mecca to the Farthest Mosque (al-Masjid al-Aqsa) is the Qur'an and the report (khabar). As for the Qur'an, it is this verse. The argument's exposition is that "servant" ('abd) is a name for the totality of body and spirit, so the night journey (isra') must have occurred to the totality of body and spirit.

Know that this inference depends on whether the human being is the spirit alone, or the body alone, or the totality of body and spirit. As for those who say the human being is the spirit alone, they have argued for it with several arguments:

The first: The human being is one thing that persists from the beginning of his life to its end, while the bodily parts are in change, transformation and transition, and what persists is not changing. Therefore the human being is distinct from this body.

The second: The human being may know his specific self while being unaware of all his bodily parts, and what is known is distinct from what is unaware of it. Therefore the human being is distinct from this body.

The third: The human being, by the dictate of his sound nature, says "my hand," "my leg," "my brain," "my heart," and likewise for the rest of the organs, so he attributes all of them to his specific self. The thing attributed is other than the thing it is attributed to. Therefore his specific self must be distinct from all these organs.

If they say: Does he not attribute his self to himself, saying "my essence" and "my self"? Then it would follow for you that his self is distinct from his essence, and this is impossible.

We reply: We do not rely on mere wording so as to be bound by what you have mentioned. Rather we rely only on pure reason. Pure reason indicates that the human being is one existent. That one thing takes with the instrument of the hand, sees with the instrument of the eye, and hears with the instrument of the ear. So the human being is one thing, and these organs are instruments for him in these actions. This indicates that the human being is a thing distinct from these organs and instruments. Thus it has been established by these arguments that the human being is a thing distinct from this structure and this body.

Having established this, we say: "Glory be to the One who carried His servant by night" — the meaning of "servant" here is the essence of the spirit. On this explanation, there remains no indication in the verse that the night journey occurred to the body.

If they say: The night journey by the spirit alone is not a matter contrary to custom, so it is not fitting that it be said: "Glory be to the One who carried His servant by night."

We reply: This too is far-fetched, since it is not unlikely to say that there came to his spirit, of types of unveilings and witnessings, what had never come to anyone else at all. Therefore this statement is indeed fitting for him. This is the explanation of the form of the objection to using this verse to prove the ascension with both spirit and body together.

The answer: The word "servant" does not encompass anything except the totality of spirit and body. The proof for this is God's saying: ﴿Have you seen the one who forbids, a servant when he prays?﴾ [al-'Alaq 96:9–10]. There is no doubt that the meaning of "servant" here is the totality of spirit and body. And He also said in Surat al-Jinn: ﴿And when the servant of God stood calling upon Him, they nearly became a crowd around him﴾ [al-Jinn 72:19]. The meaning is the totality of spirit and body, so likewise here.

As for the report, it is the hadith narrated in the Sahih collections, and it is well known. It indicates going from Mecca to Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), then from there to the heavens. Those who deny it argued with several arguments:

The first: By rational arguments, which are three:
The first of them: that motion reaching this degree of speed is not conceivable.
The second: that the ascent of a heavy body to the heavens is not conceivable.
The third: that his ascent to the heavens necessitates the piercing of the spheres, and that is impossible.

The second objection: If this matter were true, it would be greater than all the other miracles, and it would have been necessary for it to appear in the presence of gatherings of people so that they could use it as evidence for the truth of his claim to prophethood. But for it to occur at a time when no one sees it or witnesses it, this would be pointless, and that is not fitting for the Wise.

The third objection: They relied on His saying: ﴿And We did not make the vision which We showed you except as a trial for the people﴾ [al-Isra' 17:60]. That vision is none other than the account of the ascension. It was a trial for people because many who had believed in him, when they heard this statement, denied it and disbelieved in it. So the account of the ascension became a cause of trial for people. Thus it is established that this was a vision he saw in a dream.

The fourth objection: The account of the ascension includes things that are far-fetched. Among them is what is reported about the opening of his chest and its purification with Zamzam water, which is far-fetched, because what can be washed away with water is only material impurities, and this has no effect on purifying the heart from false beliefs and blameworthy character traits. Among them is what is reported about riding the Buraq, which is far-fetched, because when God had transported him from this world to the world of the spheres, what need was there for the Buraq? Among them is what is reported that God obligated fifty prayers, and then Muhammad (ﷺ) kept going back and forth between God the Exalted and Musa until the fifty were reduced to five because of Musa's compassion (peace be upon him). The judge (al-Qadi) said: this necessitates the abrogation (naskh) of a ruling before its time has come, and that it necessitates badaʾ (a change of divine decision based on new knowledge), and that is impossible for God the Exalted. Thus it is established that this hadith includes what cannot be accepted, so it is rejected.

The answer to the rational arguments has already passed, so we will not repeat them.

The answer to the second objection is what God the Exalted mentioned, namely His saying: ﴿That We might show him of Our signs﴾. This is a general statement, and in its detailed explanation and elaboration there are several aspects:

The first: The delights of Paradise are great, and the terrors of the Fire are severe. If he (peace be upon him) had not witnessed them in this world, and then witnessed them at the beginning of the Day of Resurrection, perhaps he would have desired the delights of Paradise or feared the terrors of

[p. 122]

the Fire. But since he witnessed them in this world on the night of the ascension, their impact on his heart on the Day of Resurrection will not be great, and so his heart will not be preoccupied with them, and then he will be free for intercession.

The second: It is not impossible that his witnessing on the night of the ascension of the prophets and the angels became a cause for the perfection of his benefit or their benefit.

The third: It is not unlikely that when he ascended the sphere and witnessed the conditions of the heavens and the Kursi and the Throne, the witnessing of the conditions of this world and its terrors became insignificant in his eyes, so there came to him an increase of strength in the heart, by which he would be more complete in beginning the call to God the Exalted, and his attention to the enemies of God the Exalted would be less. This is clarified by the fact that whoever beholds the power of God the Exalted in this domain, his condition in strength of soul and steadfastness of heart in bearing hardships in jihad and other matters is many times greater than the condition of one who has not beheld it.

Know that His saying: ﴿That We might show him of Our signs﴾ is, as it were, an indication that the benefit of that night journey is specific to him and returns to him in a definite manner.

The answer to the third objection: When we reach the explanation of that verse in this surah, we will show that that vision was a vision of sight and not a vision of dream.

The answer to the fourth objection: There is no objection to God the Exalted in His acts; He does what He wills and decrees what He desires. And God knows best.

**The fourth issue:** As for the ascent to the heavens and to what is above the Throne, this verse does not indicate it. Some have argued for it from the beginning of Surat al-Najm, and some have argued for it from His saying: ﴿You will surely ride from stage to stage﴾ [al-Inshiqaq 84:19]. Their interpretation is mentioned in its proper place. As for the indication of the hadith, it is as has already passed. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verses 2–3:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We gave Moses the Book and made it a guidance for the Children of Israel, [saying], "Do not take other than Me as Disposer of affairs."﴾ ﴿O descendants of those We carried with Noah. Indeed, he was a grateful servant.﴾

Regarding the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that the discourse in the verse preceding this one shifted from the third person to the second person, and from the second person to the third person. For His saying, ﴿Exalted is He who took His servant by night﴾ contains a mention of God in the third person; His saying, ﴿We blessed around it that We might show him of Our signs﴾ contains three expressions indicating the second person; His saying, ﴿Indeed, He is the Hearing, the Seeing﴾ indicates the third person; and His saying, ﴿And We gave Moses the Book,﴾ etc., indicates the second person. The shift of discourse from the third person to the second person, and vice versa, is called the technique of iltifat (shift of grammatical person).

The second issue: God Most High mentioned in the first verse His honouring of Muhammad (ﷺ) by making him travel by night, and He mentioned in this verse that He had honoured Moses (peace be upon him) before him by the Book that He gave him, saying, ﴿And We gave Moses the Book﴾; meaning the Torah. ﴿And We made it﴾

[Page 123]
﴿a guidance﴾, i.e., through that Book He brings them out from the darkness of ignorance and disbelief into the light of knowledge and the true religion. His saying, ﴿Do not take other than Me as Disposer of affairs﴾, and in it there are discussions:

The first discussion: Abu 'Amr recited, "allā yattakhidhū" (with the ya'), as a report about the Children of Israel, while the rest recited with the ta' (tā'), as an address, meaning: We said to them, "Do not take."

The second discussion: Abu 'Ali al-Farisi (d. 377 AH) said: His saying ﴿allā tattakhidhū﴾ has three possible readings:

The first: that "an" (أن) is a particle governing the verb, so the meaning is: "And We made it a guidance so that you would not take."

The second: that "an" has the meaning of "ay" (أي), which is used for explanation, and the discourse shifted from the third person to the second person in the recitation of the majority, just as it shifted from it to the second person and the imperative in His saying, ﴿And the chiefs among them set off, [saying], "Go on"﴾ [Sad: 6]. Likewise, the discourse shifted from the third person to a prohibition in His saying, ﴿allā tattakhidhū﴾.

The third: that "an" is a superfluous particle and "tattakhidhū" is taken as governed by an implied verb of saying, and the estimate is: "And We made it a guidance for the Children of Israel, and We said: Do not take other than Me as Disposer of affairs."

The third discussion: His saying, "wakīlan," meaning: a Lord to whom you entrust your affairs.

I say: The summary of the discourse in the verse is that God Most High mentioned the ennobling of Muhammad (ﷺ) through the night journey, then mentioned immediately after it the ennobling of Moses (peace be upon him) through the sending down of the Torah upon him, then described the Torah as being a guidance, then explained that the Torah was a guidance only because it contains the prohibition of taking other than God as a disposer of affairs, and that is monotheism. Thus the summary of the discourse, after observing these stages, is that there is no higher ascent, no more noble rank, and no greater distinction than that a person should become immersed in the sea of monotheism, and not rely in any matter except upon God. If he speaks, he speaks by mentioning God; if he reflects, he reflects upon the signs of God's transcendence; and if he seeks, he seeks from God. So all of him is for God and through God.

Then He said: ﴿O descendants of those We carried with Noah.﴾ Regarding the accusative case of "dhurriyyata" there are two possibilities:

The first possibility: that it is in the accusative by way of address, meaning: "O descendants of those We carried with Noah." This is the view of Mujahid, for he said: this is an address. Al-Wahidi said: this is only valid according to the reading of the one who reads with the ta', as if it was said to them: "Do not take other than Me as Disposer of affairs, O descendants of those We carried with Noah in the Ark." Qatada said: All people are descendants of Noah, for there were with him in the Ark three sons: Sam, Ham, and Japheth. So all people are of the descendants of those, and His saying, "O descendants of those We carried with Noah," stands in the place of His saying, "O people."

The second possibility: regarding the accusative of "dhurriyyata," that the verb "ittakhadha" (to take) is a verb that transitively takes two objects, as in His saying, ﴿And God took Abraham as a friend﴾ [An-Nisa: 125]. The estimate is: "Do not take the descendants of those We carried with Noah as disposers of affairs other than Me." Then God Most High praised Noah, saying: ﴿Indeed, he was a grateful servant﴾, meaning: he was one who was much grateful. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verses 2–3:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We gave Moses the Book and made it a guidance for the Children of Israel, [saying], "Do not take other than Me as Disposer of affairs."﴾ ﴿O descendants of those We carried with Noah. Indeed, he was a grateful servant.﴾

Regarding the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that the discourse in the verse preceding this one shifted from the third person to the second person, and from the second person to the third person. For His saying, ﴿Exalted is He who took His servant by night﴾ contains a mention of God in the third person; His saying, ﴿We blessed around it that We might show him of Our signs﴾ contains three expressions indicating the second person; His saying, ﴿Indeed, He is the Hearing, the Seeing﴾ indicates the third person; and His saying, ﴿And We gave Moses the Book,﴾ etc., indicates the second person. The shift of discourse from the third person to the second person, and vice versa, is called the technique of iltifat (shift of grammatical person).

The second issue: God Most High mentioned in the first verse His honouring of Muhammad (ﷺ) by making him travel by night, and He mentioned in this verse that He had honoured Moses (peace be upon him) before him by the Book that He gave him, saying, ﴿And We gave Moses the Book﴾; meaning the Torah. ﴿And We made it﴾

[Page 123]
﴿a guidance﴾, i.e., through that Book He brings them out from the darkness of ignorance and disbelief into the light of knowledge and the true religion. His saying, ﴿Do not take other than Me as Disposer of affairs﴾, and in it there are discussions:

The first: that "an" (أن) is a particle governing the verb, so the meaning is: "And We made it a guidance so that you would not take."

The second: that "an" has the meaning of "ay" (أي), which is used for explanation, and the discourse shifted from the third person to the second person in the recitation of the majority, just as it shifted from it to the second person and the imperative in His saying, ﴿And the chiefs among them set off, [saying], "Go on"﴾ [Sad: 6]. Likewise, the discourse shifted from the third person to a prohibition in His saying, ﴿allā tattakhidhū﴾.

The third: that "an" is a superfluous particle and "tattakhidhū" is taken as governed by an implied verb of saying, and the estimate is: "And We made it a guidance for the Children of Israel, and We said: Do not take other than Me as Disposer of affairs."

The third discussion: His saying, "wakīlan," meaning: a Lord to whom you entrust your affairs.

I say: The summary of the discourse in the verse is that God Most High mentioned the ennobling of Muhammad (ﷺ) through the night journey, then mentioned immediately after it the ennobling of Moses (peace be upon him) through the sending down of the Torah upon him, then described the Torah as being a guidance, then explained that the Torah was a guidance only because it contains the prohibition of taking other than God as a disposer of affairs, and that is monotheism. Thus the summary of the discourse, after observing these stages, is that there is no higher ascent, no more noble rank, and no greater distinction than that a person should become immersed in the sea of monotheism, and not rely in any matter except upon God. If he speaks, he speaks by mentioning God; if he reflects, he reflects upon the signs of God's transcendence; and if he seeks, he seeks from God. So all of him is for God and through God.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verses 4–6:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And We decreed for the Children of Israel in the Book: "You will certainly cause corruption on the earth twice, and you will certainly become exceedingly arrogant."﴾ ﴿So when the promise of the first of the two came, We sent against you servants of Ours of great might, and they went through the homes [searching]. And it was a promise fulfilled.﴾ ﴿Then We gave back to you the return [of victory] over them, and We supplied you with wealth and children and made you more numerous in manpower.﴾

Know that when the Exalted mentioned His favour upon the Children of Israel by sending down the Torah to them, and that He made the Torah a guidance for them, He then clarified that they did not take guidance from its guidance, but fell into corruption. So He said: ﴿And We decreed for the Children of Israel in the Book, "You will certainly cause corruption on the earth twice."﴾ In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: qadaa' (decree) in the language is an expression for cutting off matters with firmness, and from it is His saying: ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens﴾ [Fussilat: 12], and the words of the poet:

"And upon them two coats of mail, which Dawud decreed..."

So His saying: ﴿And We decreed﴾ means: We informed them, told them of that, and revealed to them. The word "ila" (to) is a complement for revelation, because the meaning of "qadayna" is "awhayna ilayhim kadha" (We revealed to them thus). His saying: ﴿You will certainly cause corruption﴾ means acts of disobedience and opposition to the rulings of the Torah. His saying: ﴿on the earth﴾ means the land of Egypt. His saying: ﴿and you will certainly become exceedingly arrogant﴾ means that your domination over people will be by other than right, a great domination; because it is said of every tyrant: "he has risen high and magnified himself." Then He said: ﴿So when the promise of the first of the two came﴾, meaning the first of the two times, ﴿We sent against you servants of Ours of great might﴾. The meaning is: when the promise of the wicked came the first time, We sent against you a people of great might, and of valour and severity. Al-ba's means fighting, and from it is His saying: ﴿and at the time of battle﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 177]. The meaning of "ba'athna 'alaykum" is: We sent against you, and We left you and them [to one another], abandoning you. They differed concerning who these servants were. It was said: the Children of Israel exalted themselves, became arrogant, made lawful the forbidden things, killed the prophets and shed blood, and that was the first of the two corruptions. So God empowered Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar) against them, and he killed forty thousand of them who recited the Torah, and took the rest to his own land. They remained there in humiliation until God raised up another king who attacked the people of Babylon, and it happened that he married a woman from the Children of Israel. That woman asked that king to return the Children of Israel to Bayt al-Maqdis, and he did so. After a period, prophets arose among them and they returned to their best condition. This is His saying: ﴿Then We gave back to you the return [of victory] over them.﴾

The second opinion: what is meant by His saying: ﴿We sent against you servants of Ours﴾ is that God empowered Jalut (Goliath) over them until he destroyed and annihilated them, and His saying: ﴿Then We gave back to you the return﴾ is that He strengthened Talut (Saul) until he fought Jalut, and made Dawud (David) victorious until he killed Jalut; that is the return.

The third opinion: His saying: ﴿We sent against you servants of Ours﴾ means that He cast fear of the Children of Israel into the hearts of the Magians; then, when corruption multiplied among them, He removed that fear from the hearts of the Magians, so they targeted them, went to great lengths in killing them, exterminating them and destroying them.

Know that there is little purpose in knowing those peoples by their identities; rather, the intent is that when they increased in disobedience, He empowered over them peoples who killed them and exterminated them.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿So they went through the homes [searching]﴾. Al-Layth said: al-jaws and al-jawasan is roaming through the homes and houses in corruption, and khilal is the space between two things; and ad-diyar: the homes of Bayt al-Maqdis. The expressions of the exegetes differed in explaining "fajasu": from Ibn Abbas: they searched. Abu 'Ubayda said: they sought those within them. Ibn Qutayba said: they spread corruption and caused harm. Al-Zajjaj said: they went around through the homes to see whether anyone was left whom they had not killed. Al-Wahidi said: al-jaws is roaming and seeking, and that is open to all that they said.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And it was a promise fulfilled﴾, meaning: God's decree in that was a decree of certainty, a binding judgment that does not accept annulment or abrogation. Then the Exalted said: ﴿Then We gave back to you the return﴾, meaning: We destroyed your enemies and returned the dynasty and power to you. ﴿And We made you more numerous in manpower.﴾ Nafir: the number of men; its root is from "nafara" (to go forth), when a man goes forth with his clan and people; nafir and nafir are the same, like qadir and qadir. We have mentioned the meaning of "nafara" at His saying: ﴿Why did not a group from each division go forth?﴾ [At-Tawbah: 122], and His saying: ﴿Go forth, light and heavy﴾ [At-Tawbah: 41].

The second issue: Our companions (the Ash'aris) argued with this verse to support their position on the issue of qada' and qadar in several respects:

The first: He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We decreed for the Children of Israel in the Book, "You will certainly cause corruption on the earth twice and you will certainly become exceedingly arrogant."﴾ This qada' at least means a binding judgment and a certain report. Thus it is established that the Exalted informed of them that they would proceed to corruption and disobedience by a certain report that does not accept abrogation, because qada' means a binding judgment as we have explained. Then He emphasized that decree further, saying: ﴿And it was a promise fulfilled.﴾

Once this is established, we say: the non-occurrence of that corruption from them would necessitate the reversal of God's true report into falsehood, the reversal of His binding judgment into nullity, and the reversal of His true knowledge into ignorance, and all of that is impossible. So their not proceeding to that corruption was impossible, and their proceeding to it was necessary, unavoidable, not accepting abrogation or removal; yet they were charged with abandoning it and were cursed for doing it. This indicates our statement: God may command a thing and yet bar from it, and He may forbid a thing and decree its realization. This is one aspect of the argument from this verse.

The second aspect of the argument from this verse: His saying: ﴿We sent against you servants of Ours of great might﴾, meaning those who dominated the Children of Israel through killing, plunder and captivity. God clarified that it was He who sent them against the Children of Israel, and there is no doubt that the killing of the Children of Israel, the plundering of their wealth and the capture of their children involved great injustice and grave disobedience. Then He attributed all of that to Himself by saying: ﴿We sent against you﴾, and this indicates that good and evil, obedience and disobedience, are from God the Exalted.

Al-Jubba'i answered this in two ways:

The first: what is meant by ﴿We sent against you﴾ is that God commanded those peoples to raid the Children of Israel when corruption appeared among them, so that act was attributed to God the Exalted by way of the command.

The second: what is meant is "We left you and them, and We did not cast fear of the Children of Israel into their hearts; the sum of the matter is that the meaning of this sending is leaving and not preventing."

Know that the first answer is weak, because those who intended to destroy Bayt al-Maqdis, burn the Torah and kill the memorizers of the Torah cannot be said to have done that by God's command.

The second answer is also weak, because sending upon an act means strengthening toward it and casting strong motives into the heart, whereas leaving means not preventing; the first is an action, the second is an abandonment, so interpreting "sending" as "leaving" is explaining one of two opposites by the other, and that is not permissible. Thus the correctness of what we have mentioned is established, and God knows best.

We have mentioned the meaning of "nafara" at His saying: ﴿Why did not a group from each division go forth?﴾ [At-Tawbah: 122], and His saying: ﴿Go forth, light and heavy﴾ [At-Tawbah: 41].

The second issue: Our companions (the Ash'aris) argued with this verse to support their position on the issue of qada' and qadar in several respects:

The first: He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We decreed for the Children of Israel in the Book, "You will certainly cause corruption on the earth twice and you will certainly become exceedingly arrogant."﴾ This qada' at least means a binding judgment and a certain report. Thus it is established that the Exalted informed of them that they would proceed to corruption and disobedience by a certain report that does not accept abrogation, because qada' means a binding judgment as we have explained. Then He emphasized that decree further, saying: ﴿And it was a promise fulfilled.﴾

Once this is established, we say: the non-occurrence of that corruption from them would necessitate the reversal of God's true report into falsehood, the reversal of His binding judgment into nullity, and the reversal of His true knowledge into ignorance, and all of that is impossible. So their not proceeding to that corruption was impossible, and their proceeding to it was necessary, unavoidable, not accepting abrogation or removal; yet they were charged with abandoning it and were cursed for doing it. This indicates our statement: God may command a thing and yet bar from it, and He may forbid a thing and decree its realization. This is one aspect of the argument from this verse.

The second aspect of the argument from this verse: His saying: ﴿We sent against you servants of Ours of great might﴾, meaning those who dominated the Children of Israel through killing, plunder and captivity. God clarified that it was He who sent them against the Children of Israel, and there is no doubt that the killing of the Children of Israel, the plundering of their wealth and the capture of their children involved great injustice and grave disobedience. Then He attributed all of that to Himself by saying: ﴿We sent against you﴾, and this indicates that good and evil, obedience and disobedience, are from God the Exalted.

Al-Jubba'i answered this in two ways:

The first: what is meant by ﴿We sent against you﴾ is that God commanded those peoples to raid the Children of Israel when corruption appeared among them, so that act was attributed to God the Exalted by way of the command.

The second: what is meant is "We left you and them, and We did not cast fear of the Children of Israel into their hearts; the sum of the matter is that the meaning of this sending is leaving and not preventing."

Know that the first answer is weak, because those who intended to destroy Bayt al-Maqdis, burn the Torah and kill the memorizers of the Torah cannot be said to have done that by God's command.

The second answer is also weak, because sending upon an act means strengthening toward it and casting strong motives into the heart, whereas leaving means not preventing; the first is an action, the second is an abandonment, so interpreting "sending" as "leaving" is explaining one of two opposites by the other, and that is not permissible. Thus the correctness of what we have mentioned is established, and God knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 17, verse 7:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If you do good, you do good for your own souls; and if you do evil, it is for them. So when the promise of the Hereafter comes, [We will send others] to disfigure your faces and to enter the Temple as they entered it the first time, and to destroy completely whatever they conquered.﴾ ﴿It may be that your Lord will have mercy upon you; but if you return [to sin], We will return [to punishment]. And We have made Hell a prison for the disbelievers.﴾

And in it are several issues:

**The first issue:** Know that Exalted is He related about them that when they disobeyed, He empowered over them peoples who targeted them with killing, plundering and captivity. When they repented, He removed that trial from them and restored their dominion. At that point it became clear that if they obeyed, they had done good to themselves, and if they persisted in disobedience, they had done evil to themselves. It is established in the intellects that doing good to oneself is good and desirable, and that harming oneself is ugly. For this reason Exalted is He said: ﴿If you do good, you do good for your own souls; and if you do evil, it is for them.﴾

**The second issue:** Al-Wahidi said: "There must be an implied element here. The sense is: 'We said: if you do good, you do good for your own souls.' The meaning is: if you do good by performing acts of obedience, you have done good to yourselves, since by the blessing of those acts God opens for you the doors of goodness and blessings. And if you do evil by committing prohibited acts, you have done evil to yourselves, since by the ill omen of those sins God opens for you the doors of punishments."

**Page 127**

**The third issue:** The grammarians said: He said ﴿and if you do evil, it is for them﴾ for the sake of antithesis (*tuqabul*), and the meaning is "to them" or "upon them." This is so even though prepositions may stand in place of one another, as in His saying: ﴿On that Day she will report her news﴾ and ﴿because your Lord has inspired her﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 4–5], meaning "to her."

**The fourth issue:** The people of the allegorical interpretations (*ahl al-isharat*, the esoteric interpreters) said: This verse indicates that God's mercy prevails over His wrath. The evidence is that when He related their good deeds, He repeated it twice, saying: ﴿If you do good, you do good for your own souls﴾. But when He related their evil, He mentioned it only once, saying: ﴿and if you do evil, it is for them﴾. Had the side of mercy not been dominant, it would not have been so.

\* \* \*

Then Exalted is He said: ﴿So when the promise of the Hereafter comes﴾. On this there are issues:

**The first issue:** The exegetes said: its meaning is "the promise of the last time," and this last time is their act of killing Zechariah and John (Yahya), upon them be peace.

Al-Wahidi said: So God sent against them Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar) the Babylonian, the Magian, the most hateful of His creation to Him. He took the Children of Israel captive, killed, and destroyed the Holy Temple (Bayt al-Maqdis).

I say: The histories testify that Bukhtnassar lived many centuries before the time of Jesus, upon him be peace, and John and Zechariah, upon them be peace. It is known that the king who took vengeance upon the Jews on account of these prophets was a king of the Romans called Qustantin (Constantine). God knows best their circumstances. No purpose of the purposes of Qur'anic exegesis depends on knowing the identities of these peoples.

**The second issue:** The answer to His saying ﴿So when [it] comes﴾ is omitted. Its implied sense is: "So when the promise of the Hereafter comes, We sent them to disfigure your faces." This omission is good because of what precedes it, namely His saying ﴿We sent against you servants of Ours﴾ [al-Isra: 5], followed by ﴿to disfigure your faces﴾. Here there are two points:

**The first point:** It is said: *sa'ahu yasu'uhu* means "it grieved him." He attributed the disfigurement to the faces because the effects of the inner psychological states that arise in the heart appear upon the face. If joy arises in the heart, radiance, brightness and illumination appear on the face. If sorrow and fear arise in the heart, gloom, dust and blackness appear on the face. For this reason disfigurement is attributed to the faces in this verse. Similar meanings are numerous in the Qur'an.

**The second point:** The reciters in general (*al-'ammah*) read *li-yasū'ū* in the third person plural form. Al-Wahidi said: this agrees with both the meaning and the wording. As for the meaning, the ones sent are those who actually disfigure them, since they are the ones who kill and take captives. As for the wording, it agrees with His saying ﴿and to enter the Temple﴾. Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr (transmitting from 'Asim) and Hamzah read *li-yasū'a* with the verb ascribed to a singular subject. That singular subject may be one of three things: either it is the name of God, Glorified is He, since what precedes is His saying ﴿then We returned [the turn] to you and aided you﴾, and all of that refers back to God Exalted; or that singular subject is the sending (*al-ba'th*), which is indicated by His saying ﴿We sent﴾, and the preceding verb implies the verbal noun, as in His saying: ﴿And let not those who withhold what God has given them of His bounty think that it is good for them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 180]. Al-Zajjaj said: "*li-yasū'a* [the promise] disfigures your faces." Al-Kisa'i read with the letter *nun* (*li-nasū'a*), which ascribes the verb to God Exalted, like His saying: ﴿We sent against you﴾ and ﴿We aided﴾.

\* \* \*

Then Exalted is He said: ﴿and to destroy completely whatever they conquered﴾. It is said: *tabara al-shay'u tabran* means "the thing perished," and *tabbarahu* means "he destroyed it." Al-Zajjaj said: Whatever you make broken and crushed, you have *tabbartahu*. From this comes the expression *tibr al-zujaj* (broken glass) and *tibr al-dhahab* (gold dust), referring to its broken pieces. From this also is His saying:

**Page 128**

﴿Indeed, these people—what they are in is destroyed, and what they were doing is worthless﴾ [al-A'raf: 139], and His saying: ﴿and do not increase the wrongdoers except in destruction﴾ [Nuh: 28]. As for His saying ﴿what they conquered (*ma 'alaw*)﴾, it may mean what they overpowered and gained victory over, and it may mean "as long as they were dominant," that is, as long as their rule continued over the Children of Israel. As for His saying ﴿destruction (*tatbiran*)﴾, it is a verbal noun mentioned to affirm the report and remove doubt about its truth, like His saying: ﴿and God spoke to Moses with direct speech﴾ [al-Nisa: 164], meaning "truly." The sense is: "and that they would destroy and ruin whatever they had overpowered."

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿It may be that your Lord will have mercy upon you﴾. The meaning is: perhaps your Lord will have mercy on you and pardon you after His retribution against you, O Children of Israel.

* * *
Then He said: ﴿And if you return, We will return﴾. That is, We sent against you whoever We sent, and they did to you what they did as a punishment for you and as an admonition, so that you would benefit from it and be restrained by it from committing sins. Then He showed mercy to you and removed this torment from you. If you return once more to disobedience, We will return to pouring affliction upon you in this world once again.

Al-Qaffal said: We have understood this verse to refer to the punishment of this world because of His exalted saying in Surat al-A'raf, reporting about the Children of Israel: ﴿And when your Lord declared that He would surely send against them until the Day of Resurrection those who would inflict on them a terrible torment﴾ [al-A'raf: 167]. Then He said: ﴿And if you return, We will return﴾. That is: indeed they returned to doing what is not fitting, which is denying Muhammad (ﷺ) and concealing what was revealed in the Torah and the Gospel. So God returned to punishing them at the hands of the Arabs. Thus there befell the Banu al-Nadir, Qurayzah, Banu Qaynuqa' and the Jews of Khaybar what befell them of killing and expulsion. Then the rest of them remained subdued under the jizya (poll tax), having neither dominion nor authority.

* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We have made Hell a confinement (ḥaṣīr) for the disbelievers﴾. The word ḥaṣīr is on the pattern fa'īl, so it may be in the sense of the active participle, meaning: We made Hell confining them. It may also be in the sense of the passive participle, meaning: We made it a place in which they are confined. The meaning is that the torment of this world, though severe and strong, may still allow some people to escape it, and whoever falls into that torment is freed from it either by death or by some other means. As for the torment of the Hereafter, it encloses the human being and surrounds him, with no hope of escape from it. These peoples have, in this world, the torment that we have described, and after that they will have, in the Hereafter, a torment that encompasses them from all directions, from which they will never be freed.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verses 9–10:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright and gives good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a great reward﴾ ﴿And that those who do not believe in the Hereafter – We have prepared for them a painful punishment﴾.

Know that when He, exalted is He, explained what He had done concerning His sincere servants, namely the Night Journey of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the giving of the Book to Musa (peace be upon him), and what He had done concerning the sinners and the rebellious, namely the imposition upon them of various kinds of affliction, this was a reminder that obedience to Allah necessitates every good and honour, and disobedience to Him necessitates every calamity and penalty. Therefore, He praised the Qur'an, saying: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾.

Page 129

Know that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a correct religion, the religion of Ibrahim, a man of pure faith﴾ [al-An'am: 161] indicates that this religion is upright, and His saying in this verse: ﴿that which is most upright﴾ indicates that this religion is more upright than all other religions. I say: Our saying "this thing is more upright than that" is only valid regarding two things that share the meaning of uprightness, where the attainment of the meaning of uprightness in one of the two forms is greater and more complete than its attainment in the second form. This is impossible, because what is meant by its being upright is that it is true and truthful, and the entry of degrees of variation into a thing's being true and truthful is impossible. So describing it as "more upright" is metaphorical, except that the form af'al has come with the meaning of the active participle, as in our saying: "Allah is greater (Allahu akbar)," meaning "Allah is great," and our saying: "al-Ashajj and al-Naqis are the two most just of the Banu Marwan," meaning "the two just ones of the Banu Marwan." Or this word may be taken in its apparent, customary sense. And Allah knows best.

The second discussion: His saying ﴿that which is most upright﴾ is an adjective of an elided noun, and the implied meaning is: "He guides to the religion, or the law, or the path which is the most upright of religions, laws and paths." Such elliptical usage is very frequent in the Qur'an, like His saying: ﴿Repel [evil] with that which is best﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 96], meaning: "with the trait which is best."

As for His saying: ﴿and gives good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a great reward﴾, know that He, exalted is He, described the Qur'an with three types of attributes:

The first attribute: that it guides to that which is most upright, and its explanation has already passed.

The second attribute: that it gives good tidings to those who do righteous deeds of a great reward. This is because the first attribute, since it indicates that the Qur'an is a guide to the most correct belief and the most righteous action, it necessarily follows that this correctness and righteousness must have a visible effect, and that effect is the great reward, because the most upright path must necessarily yield the greatest profit and the greatest benefit.

The third attribute: His saying: ﴿and that those who do not believe in the Hereafter – We have prepared for them a painful punishment﴾. This is because just as the most correct belief and the most righteous action necessitate for their doer the most complete and greatest benefit, so too abandoning them necessitates for their abandoner the greatest and most complete harm.

Know that His saying: ﴿and that those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ is conjoined to His saying: ﴿that they will have a great reward﴾, and the meaning is that He, exalted is He, gave the believers two kinds of good tidings: of their reward and of the punishment of their enemies. A parallel to this is the saying: "I gave Zayd good news that he will be given, and that his enemy will be prevented."

If it is said: How does the word "good tidings" fit with punishment?

We say: It is used in the manner of sarcasm (tahakkum), or it may be said that it is from the usage of naming one of two opposites by the other, like His saying: ﴿and the recompense for an evil deed is an evil deed like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40].

If it is said: This verse was revealed to describe the condition of the Jews, and they did not deny belief in the Hereafter, so how does His saying ﴿and that those who do not believe in the Hereafter – We have prepared for them a painful punishment﴾ fit in this place?

We say: There are two answers to this:

The first: that most Jews deny the reward and punishment of the physical body.

The second: that some of them said: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾ [Al 'Imran: 24], so by this saying they became like those who deny the Hereafter. And Allah knows best.
