Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verse 11:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And man prays for evil as he prays for good, and man has always been hasty.﴾

In the verse there are several discussions:

The first discussion: Know that the connection (wajh al-nazm) of the verse is that man, after Allah has sent down the Qur'an to him and singled him out with this great blessing and perfect honour, may turn away from holding fast to its laws and returning to its clarifications, and may proceed to do what has no benefit in it. So He said: ﴿And man prays for evil as he prays for good﴾.

The second discussion: The scholars have differed regarding the meaning of man's praying for evil, and there are several opinions:

The first opinion: What is meant is al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, when he said: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You﴾ [al-Anfal: 32]. Allah answered his supplication and his neck was struck. Some of them would say: "Bring us the punishment of Allah," and others would say: "When is this promise, if you are truthful?" They did this only out of ignorance and the belief that Muhammad was lying in what he said.

The second opinion: What is meant is that in a time of distress he curses himself, his family, his child and his property; and if he were answered in evil as he is answered in good, he would perish. It was narrated that the Prophet ﷺ handed over a captive to Sawdah bint Zam'ah, and he began to moan at night. She said to him: "What is wrong with you that you moan?" He complained of the pain of the shackle, so she loosened it for him from his shoulders. When she slept, he drew out his hand and fled. When morning came, the Prophet (ﷺ) summoned her and was informed of the matter. He (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, cut off her hand." Sawdah raised her hand, expecting that Allah would cut off her hand. The Prophet ﷺ said: "I asked Allah to make my supplication against those among my family who do not deserve punishment a mercy, because I am a human being; I become angry as you become angry. So let Sawdah return her hand."

The third opinion: I say: It is possible that what is meant is that man may exert himself greatly in supplication seeking something he believes to be good for him, while that thing is actually the source of his harm and damage; and he exerts himself in seeking it out of his ignorance of the reality of that thing. He only undertakes such an act because he is hasty, deceived by the outward appearances of affairs, not scrutinising their realities and secrets.

The fourth discussion: Analogy (al-qiyas): the waw is affirmed in His saying ﴿wa-yadu'u﴾ but it was omitted in the written Mushaf, because it does not appear in pronunciation; however it is not omitted in meaning, because it is in the nominative position. Its counterparts are: ﴿sanad'u al-zabaniyah﴾ [al-'Alaq: 18], ﴿wa-sawfa yu'ti Allahu al-mu'minin﴾ [al-Nisa': 146], ﴿yawma yunadi al-munadi﴾ [Qaf: 41], ﴿fa-ma tughni al-nudhur﴾ [al-Qamar: 5]. Had it been written with a waw and a ya', it would have been correct. This is the statement of al-Farra'. I say: This indicates that He, glorified is He, has preserved this glorious Qur'an from distortion and alteration. The affirmation of the ya' and waw in most words of the Qur'an and their non-affirmation in these few specified places indicates that this Qur'an was transmitted as it was heard, and that no one has altered it according to the extent of his understanding or the strength of his intellect.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and man has always been hasty﴾. Regarding this "man" there are two statements:

The first statement: It is Adam, peace be upon him, because when the soul reached his navel, he looked at his body and was pleased with it, so he tried to stand up but could not. This is His saying: ﴿and man has always been hasty﴾.

The second statement: It is taken to refer to the species, because none of the people is free of haste, and if he were to abandon it, his abandoning it would be better for him in religion and in worldly life. I say: Even assuming that the intended meaning is the first statement, the purpose returns to the second statement, because if we take "man" to be Adam, peace be upon him, the meaning becomes: Adam, who was the origin of mankind, when he was described with this haste, it became necessary that this be an inherent attribute for all; so the purpose returns to the second statement. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verse 12:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs. Then We effaced the sign of the night, and We made the sign of the day to be seeing, that you might seek bounty from your Lord, and that you might know the number of the years and the reckoning. And everything We have detailed with full detail.﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: concerning the arrangement (nazm) of the verse, there are several aspects.

The first aspect: when He, exalted is He, explained in the previous verse the blessings of religion that reached creation, namely the Qur'an, He followed it with an explanation of the blessings of this world that reached them, so He said: ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs﴾. Just as the Qur'an is composed of the decisive (muhkam) and the ambiguous (mutashabih), likewise time is composed of day and night. The muhkam is like the day, and the mutashabih is like the night. And just as the purpose of the obligation (taklif) is not complete except by mentioning the muhkam and the mutashabih, likewise the period and the time are not fully benefited from except through the day and the night.

The second aspect concerning the arrangement: when He, exalted is He, explained in the previous verse that this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright, and that most upright thing is nothing but the mention of the proofs indicating the Oneness of God and prophethood, it therefore followed it with the mention of the proofs of the Oneness of God, which are the wonders of the upper and lower world.

The third aspect: when He described man as being "hasty" (ʿajul), meaning moving from one attribute to another and from one state to another, He explained that all the conditions of this world are likewise, namely moving from light to darkness and vice versa, and the moving of the light of the moon from increase to decrease and vice versa. And God knows best.

The second issue: concerning His saying: ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs﴾, there are two opinions:

The first opinion: that what is meant by the two signs is the night and the day themselves. The meaning is that He made them two indications for creation regarding the interests of religion and the world. As for religion: because each of them is opposed to the other and differs from it, while they alternate continually, they are among the strongest proofs that they do not exist by themselves, but there must be an agent who manages them and determines them with specific measures. As for the world: because the interests of the world are not completed except by night and day; were it not for the night, rest and tranquility would not be achieved, and were it not for the day, earning and活动 in the ways of livelihood would not be achieved.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So We effaced the sign of the night﴾. According to this opinion, the idafa (construct) in "sign of the night" and "sign of the day" is explanatory (li-l-tabyin), and the estimate is: "So We effaced the sign which is the night, and We made the sign which is the day itself to be seeing." Its parallel is our saying: "the very thing and its essence" (nafs al-shay' wa dhatuhu); likewise "the sign of the night" is the night itself. It is also said: "I entered the lands of Khurasan," meaning "I entered the lands which are Khurasan," and so it is here.

The second opinion: that what is meant is: "And We made to see the night and the day as two signs," meaning the sun and the moon. "So We effaced the sign of the night," which is the moon. Regarding the effacing of the moon there are two opinions:

The first opinion: what is meant by it is what appears in the moon of increase and decrease in light; it appears at first in the form of a crescent, then its light continues to increase until it becomes a full moon, then it begins to diminish little by little, and that is the effacing, until it returns to the conjunction (mahaq).

The second opinion: what is meant by the effacing of the moon is the spot (kalaf) which appears on its face. It is related that the sun and the moon were equal in brightness and radiance, so God sent Gabriel, upon him be peace, who passed his wing over the face of the moon and obliterated its light from it. The meaning of "mahw" (effacing) in the language is the removal of a trace; one says: "I erased it (mahawtuhu), I erase it, and it was effaced (inmaha) and was erased (imtaha)" when its trace has gone.

I say: taking the effacing in this verse in the first sense is preferable, because the lam in His saying: ﴿that you might seek bounty from your Lord and that you might know the number of the years and the reckoning﴾ is connected to what is mentioned before it, namely the effacing of the sign of the night. Making the sign of the day to be seeing and the effacing of the sign of the night only have an effect on seeking the bounty of God if we take the effacing to mean the increase and decrease of the moon's light, because the cause of the occurrence of this condition varies with the conditions of the moon's light. The people of experience have explained that the variation in the moon's states of light has a great effect on the conditions and interests of this world, like the states of the seas in ebb and flow, and like the states of experiences as physicians mention in their books. Also, by means of the increase and decrease of the moon's light the months arise, and by the recurrence of the months the Arabic years arise, which are based on the sighting of the crescents, as He said: ﴿and that you might know the number of the years and the reckoning﴾. Thus it is established that taking the effacing as we have mentioned is preferable.

I also say: if we take the effacing to mean the spot which occurs on the face of the moon, it is also a great and overpowering proof of the correctness of the Muslims' position regarding the origin and the return. As for its indication of the correctness of their position regarding the origin: the body of the moon, according to the philosophers, is a simple body, so it must be uniform in its attributes; the occurrence of the different states resulting from the effacing indicates that it is not by the nature of the body, but rather that the choosing agent specified some of its parts with strong light and some of its parts with weak light. This indicates that the manager of the world is a choosing agent, not one who acts necessarily by essence.

The best thing the philosophers mentioned in excusing this is that there were settled in the face of the moon bodies of little light, like the fixing of the stars in the bodies of the spheres. When those bodies were less luminous than the body of the moon, they were therefore seen on the face of the moon like the spot on a man's face. But this does not serve the opponent's purpose, because since the body of the moon is uniform in its parts, why were those dark bodies settled in some parts of the moon and not in the rest of its parts? By the same method one argues concerning the states of the stars: the sphere is a simple body uniform in its parts, so why was it not more fitting for the body of the star to be located in some of its sides rather than in the rest of its sides? This indicates that the specification of that star to that particular determined place of the sphere is due to the specification of the choosing agent. All these proofs are only meant, in their establishment and presentation, to draw attention to the fact that the influence in the world is by a chooser, not by necessity in essence. And God knows best.

As for His saying: ﴿and We made the sign of the day to be seeing﴾, there are two aspects:

The first: that the meaning of its being "seeing" (mubsira) is "illuminating" (mudi'a), because illumination is the cause of the occurrence of sight, so the name of sight was applied to illumination, applying the name of the effect to the cause.

The second: Abu ʿUbayda said: one says "the day has become seeing" (absara al-nahar) when people see in it, like his saying: "a man is corrupt" (mukhbith) when his companions are corrupt, and "a man is weak" (mudh'if) when his offspring are weak. So likewise His saying: "the day is seeing" means its people are sighted (buṣara').

Know that He, exalted is He, mentioned in many verses the benefits of night and day. He said: ﴿And We made the night a covering﴾ ﴿and We made the day for livelihood﴾ [al-Naba' 78:10–11], and He also said: ﴿He has made for you the night and the day that you may rest therein and seek of His bounty﴾ [al-Qasas 28:73].

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿that you might seek bounty from your Lord﴾, meaning: that you might see how you conduct your affairs. ﴿and that you might know the number of the years and the reckoning﴾.

Know that reckoning is built upon four levels: hours, days, months and years. So the counting is for years, and the reckoning is for what is below years, namely months, days and hours. After these four levels, there is nothing but repetition, just as they arranged counting on four levels: units, tens, hundreds and thousands, and after them there is nothing but repetition. And God knows best.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And everything We have detailed with full detail﴾. The meaning is: when He mentioned the states of the two signs, the night and the day, which from one aspect are two decisive proofs of the Oneness of God, and from another aspect are two great blessings from God upon the people of the world, and when God explained their state and detailed what they contain of aspects of proof of the Creator and aspects of great blessings upon creation, that constituted beneficial detail and complete exposition. Therefore He said: ﴿And everything We have detailed with full detail﴾, meaning: everything you need for the interests of your religion and your world, We have detailed and explained. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book﴾ [al-An'am 6:38], and His saying: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an exposition of all things﴾ [al-Nahl 16:89], and His saying: ﴿destroying everything by the command of its Lord﴾ [al-Ahqaf 46:25]. He mentioned the verbal noun, which is His saying "tafsilan" (full detail), for the sake of emphasizing and confirming the speech, as if He said: "and We have detailed it truly, and We have detailed it in the manner beyond which there is no addition." And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verses 13–14 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And every person's omen We have fastened to his neck, and We will bring out for him on the Day of Resurrection a record he will find laid open.﴾ ﴿"Read your record. Your own soul suffices as a reckoner against you this Day."﴾

Know that there are several issues in this verse.

The first issue: concerning the arrangement (nazm) of the verse, there are several aspects.

The first aspect: when He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And everything We have explained in detail﴾, its meaning is that everything needed of the proofs of Tawhid (Divine Oneness), prophethood and the Return (ma'ad) has been mentioned. And everything needed of the explanation of the states of promise and threat, of encouragement and warning, has been mentioned. When this is the case, the excuses have been removed and the pretexts have been cleared. Therefore, everyone who comes to the plain of Resurrection, We have fastened his omen to his neck, and We say to him: ﴿"Read your record. Your own soul suffices as a reckoner against you this Day."﴾

[Page 134]

The second aspect: when He, may He be exalted, explained that He had delivered to creation the kinds of things beneficial to them in religion and in worldly life, such as the two signs of the night and the day and others, He was bestowing upon them the greatest forms of blessing. This requires that they be occupied with serving Him and obeying Him. Therefore, everyone who comes to the plain of Resurrection will be questioned about his deeds and his words.

The third aspect: in the explanation of the arrangement, when He, may He be exalted, explained that He did not create creation except that they should occupy themselves with His worship, as He said: ﴿And I did not create jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56], and then He explained the states of the sun, the moon, the night and the day, the meaning is: I created these things only so that you might benefit from them, and thus become able to occupy yourselves with My obedience and My service. When this is so, I will ask everyone who comes to the plain of Resurrection whether he performed that service and obedience, or rebelled, disobeyed and transgressed. This is the aspect in the explanation of the arrangement.

The second issue: concerning the interpretation of the word "ṭā'ir" (omen, bird), there are two views.

The first view: when the Arabs wanted to undertake one of their actions and wanted to know whether that action would lead them to good or to evil, they would consider the condition of birds: whether it flies on its own or needs to be startled, and when it flies, whether it flies to the right, to the left, upward into the air, or in other conditions which they would consider and by each of which they would infer states of good and evil, fortune and misfortune. When this became frequent among them, good and evil were called "ṭā'ir" (bird), by naming the thing with the name of its concomitant. Its parallel is His saying, may He be exalted, in Surat Ya Sin: ﴿They said, "We augur ill from you"﴾ [Ya Sin: 18], up to His saying: ﴿They said, "Your omen is with you"﴾ [Ya Sin: 19]. So His saying: ﴿And every person's omen We have fastened to his neck﴾ means: every person's deed We have fastened to his neck. The reading of al-Hasan and Mujahid supports the soundness of this view: "alzamnāhu ṭayrahu fī ʿunuqihi" (We have fastened his augury to his neck).

The second view: Abu Ubayda said: the "ṭā'ir" in the Arabs' usage is fortune (al-ḥaẓẓ), which the Persians call bakht (fortune), and on this basis the meaning of "ṭā'ir" may be what has flown to him of good and evil. The verification in this matter is that He, may He be exalted, created creation and assigned to each one of them a specific measure of intellect and knowledge, of lifespan and provision, of happiness and misery. A person cannot exceed that measure or deviate from it; rather, he must reach that measure in quantity and quality. Those predetermined things are as if they fly to him and arrive at him. In this sense, it is not far-fetched to express those predetermined states by the word "ṭā'ir." So His saying: ﴿And every person's omen We have fastened to his neck﴾ is a metaphor (kināya) for the fact that everything that God, may He be exalted, has decreed and that has passed in His knowledge to occur, is necessarily attached to him, reaches him, and does not deviate from him.

Know that this is among the strongest proofs that everything God, may He be exalted, has decreed for a person and judged upon him in His eternal foreknowledge is necessarily to occur and impossible not to occur. Its explanation is from two aspects:

The first aspect: the sense of the verse is: "And every person's deed We have fastened to his neck." He, may He be exalted, explained that this deed is necessarily attached to him. What is necessarily attached to a thing cannot be removed from it, and must occur to it. This is the intended meaning.

The second aspect: He, may He be exalted, attributed this fastening to Himself, because His saying ﴿alzamnāhu﴾ ("We have fastened him") is an explicit statement that this fastening came from Him. Its parallel is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He made them hold fast to the word of piety﴾ [al-Fath: 26]. This verse indicates that nothing appears in eternity except what God has judged in pre-eternity. To this the Prophet (ﷺ) alluded when he said: "The pen has dried up with what is to be until the Day of Resurrection." And God knows best.

[Page 135]

The third issue: His saying ﴿fī ʿunuqihi﴾ ("on his neck") is a metaphor for necessity (al-luzūm), as one says: "I placed this on your neck," meaning: I entrusted you with this task and obligated you to safeguard it. One also says: "I hung (qallad) such-and-such on you and encircled (ṭawwaq) you with such-and-such," meaning: I directed it to you and obligated you to it. From this comes "the sultan entrusted (qallada) him with such-and-such," meaning the authority became necessarily his, in the place of the necklace and the place of the collar. From this one says: "So-and-so imitates (yuqallid) so-and-so," meaning he made that belief like a necklace tied around his neck. The scholars of semantics (ahl al-maʿānī) said: The neck was specifically singled out among the other limbs with this meaning, because what is on it is either good that adorns it or evil that disgraces it. What adorns is like a collar and ornament, and what disgraces is like a shackle. Here, if his deed is among the good works, it is an adornment for him; and if it is among the sins, it is like a shackle on his neck.

* * *

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And We will bring out for him on the Day of Resurrection a record he will find laid open.﴾ Al-Hasan said: "O son of Adam, We have spread out for you a page, and two angels have been appointed over you, one on your right and one on your left. The one on your right records your good deeds, and the one on your left records your bad deeds. When you die, your page is folded and placed with you in your grave until it is brought out for you on the Day of Resurrection." His saying ﴿wa-nukhriju lahu﴾ ("and We will bring out for him"), i.e., from his grave. It may mean: We bring that out for him because he did not see his record in the world; when he is resurrected, it is displayed to him and brought out from concealment. Ya'qub read: "wa-yakhruju lahu yawma al-qiyamati kitaban" ("and there will come forth for him on the Day of Resurrection a record"), meaning: the omen (i.e., his deed) comes forth for him as a written record laid open, like His saying: ﴿And when the pages are spread open﴾ [al-Takwir: 10]. Ibn Umar read: "yulaqqāhu" (he will be made to meet it), from the expression "laqqaytu fulānan al-shayʾa," meaning I made him meet the thing, i.e., I presented it to him. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And He gave them radiance and joy﴾ [al-Insan: 11]. It is transmitted with the doubled form from "laqqaytu al-shayʾa" and "laqqānīhi Zayd" (Zayd made me meet it).

* * *

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Read your record﴾. The implied sense is: it is said to him, and this speaker is God, may He be exalted, through the tongues of the angels: ﴿Read your record.﴾ Al-Hasan said: "He reads it, whether he was unlettered or not." Bakr ibn Abd Allah said: "The believer is brought on the Day of Resurrection with his page, and he reads it, while his good deeds are on its back, and people envy him for them, and his bad deeds are within the page, and he reads them, until when he thinks they will destroy him, God, may He be exalted, says: 'Go, for I have forgiven them for you between Me and you.' So his joy greatly increases, and he becomes one of those about whom He said: ﴿Faces that day will be bright, laughing, rejoicing﴾ [Abasa: 38–39]. Then he says: ﴿Here, read my record!﴾ [al-Haqqah: 19]."

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Your own soul suffices as a reckoner against you this Day﴾, i.e., as one who takes account. Al-Hasan said: "By God, he has been just with you who made you the reckoner of your own soul." Al-Suddi said: "The disbeliever will say on that day: 'You have decreed that You are not unjust to the servants, so let me take account of my own soul.' Then it is said to him: ﴿Read your record. Your own soul suffices as a reckoner against you this Day.﴾" And God knows best.

* * *

The fourth issue: The philosophers of Islam (ḥukamāʾ al-Islām) said: this verse is of the utmost nobility, and in it are wondrous secrets, in several inquiries:

The first inquiry: He, may He be exalted, made the servant's action like the bird that flies to him. This is because He, may He be exalted, decreed for each person in pre-eternity a measure of good and evil. That judgment which passed in His eternal knowledge and His eternal decree must reach him. That judgment is as if it were a bird flying to him from eternity until that time. When that time comes, that bird reaches him with an arrival from which there is absolutely no escape and no deviation from it. When a person knows, in every word, deed, glance and thought, that this was like a bird which God sent flying to him along a specific course and path, and that this bird must reach him, then he realizes that perpetual sufficiency is not complete except through eternal care.

[Page 136]

The second inquiry: these predeterminations were determined by God's binding. That is in the sense that He, may He be exalted, made every occurrence have an occurrence preceding it for the occurrence of the later event. Since the establishment of this chain is from God, all of it is from God. At this point a person imagines birds without end and without a limit to their number, for He, may He be exalted, sent them flying from the nest of eternity and the darkness of the unseen world, and they came and flew in a flight without beginning and without end. Each one of them was directed toward that specific person at the specific time with the specific attribute. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿We have fastened his omen to his neck﴾.

The third inquiry: experience indicates that the repetition of voluntary actions produces the firm psychological disposition (malaka nafsāniyya) in the essence of the soul. Do you not see that whoever persists in repeating one lesson comes to have that lesson memorized, and whoever persists in one action for a long duration makes that action a disposition for himself?

Having known this, we say: since frequent repetition necessitates the attainment of a firm disposition, it must be that each of those actions produces some effect in the essence of the soul. For when we observed that with the successive drops of water upon a stone a hole came to be in the stone, we knew that each of those drops had some effect in producing that hole, even if it was weak and small. And since writing, in the custom of people, is a designation of specific marks which people have agreed to make indicators of specific words, then on this basis the indication of those marks upon those specific meanings is an essential indication, necessarily established and impossible to remove. So the book containing those marks is more deserving of the name "book" than the page containing the marks that indicate by convention and agreement.

Once you understand these two premises, we say: every action that proceeds from a human being, whether much or little, strong or weak, necessarily leaves a specific impression on the substance of the human soul. If that impression draws the essence of the spirit from creation toward the presence of the Truth, it is one of the causes of happiness and honours. If that impression draws the spirit from the presence of the Truth toward preoccupation with creation, it is one of the causes of wretchedness and abandonment. However, these impressions remain hidden as long as the spirit is attached to the body, because the spirit's preoccupation with managing the body prevents these states from being unveiled, manifested and made apparent. When the spirit's attachment to the management of the body ends, then the Resurrection occurs there, in accordance with his saying (peace be upon him): "Whoever dies, his Resurrection has come." The meaning of this state being a Resurrection is that the rational soul (al-nafs al-nāṭiqah) was, as it were, at rest and settled in this lower body. When that attachment is severed, the soul rises and turns upward toward the higher world. This is what is meant by this state being a Resurrection. Then, at the occurrence of the Resurrection in this sense, the covering is removed and the bed-cover is uncovered, and it is said to him: ﴿So We have removed from you your covering, and your sight today is sharp﴾. As for His saying: ﴿And We will bring forth for him on the Day of Resurrection a record which he will find spread open﴾, its meaning is: at the occurrence of this Resurrection, We will bring forth for him from the depths of the dark body a record comprising all those impressions produced by the worldly states. This record will at that time be spread open, because while the spirit was in the body these states were hidden within it, and so they were like something folded up. After the cessation of bodily attachment, these states appear, become clear and are unveiled, so they become like something uncovered and spread out after having been folded, and manifest after having been hidden. At that point the intellectual faculty witnesses all those impressions written by the self-inscription in the substance of the spirit. Then it is said to him in that state: ﴿Read your record﴾, and then it is said to him: ﴿Your own soul suffices against you today as a reckoner﴾. If those impressions are among the causes of happiness, happiness necessarily results, and if they are among the causes of wretchedness, wretchedness necessarily results. This is the interpretation of this verse according to the spiritual states.

[Page 137]

Know that the truth is that the outward states reported in the narrations are true and genuine, with no doubt about them. The verse's capacity to bear these spiritual meanings is also evident. The upright path and the straight way is to affirm all of it. And God knows best the realities of matters.

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Read your record﴾.
