Bakr ibn Abd Allah said: "The believer is brought on the Day of Resurrection with his page, and he reads it, while his good deeds are on its back, and people envy him for them, and his bad deeds are within the page, and he reads them, until when he thinks they will destroy him, God, may He be exalted, says: 'Go, for I have forgiven them for you between Me and you.' So his joy greatly increases, and he becomes one of those about whom He said: ﴿Faces that day will be bright, laughing, rejoicing﴾ [Abasa: 38–39]. Then he says: ﴿Here, read my record!﴾ [al-Haqqah: 19]."

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Your own soul suffices as a reckoner against you this Day﴾, i.e., as one who takes account. Al-Hasan said: "By God, he has been just with you who made you the reckoner of your own soul." Al-Suddi said: "The disbeliever will say on that day: 'You have decreed that You are not unjust to the servants, so let me take account of my own soul.' Then it is said to him: ﴿Read your record. Your own soul suffices as a reckoner against you this Day.﴾" And God knows best.

* * *

The fourth issue: The philosophers of Islam (ḥukamāʾ al-Islām) said: this verse is of the utmost nobility, and in it are wondrous secrets, in several inquiries:

The first inquiry: He, may He be exalted, made the servant's action like the bird that flies to him. This is because He, may He be exalted, decreed for each person in pre-eternity a measure of good and evil. That judgment which passed in His eternal knowledge and His eternal decree must reach him. That judgment is as if it were a bird flying to him from eternity until that time. When that time comes, that bird reaches him with an arrival from which there is absolutely no escape and no deviation from it. When a person knows, in every word, deed, glance and thought, that this was like a bird which God sent flying to him along a specific course and path, and that this bird must reach him, then he realizes that perpetual sufficiency is not complete except through eternal care.

[Page 136]

The second inquiry: these predeterminations were determined by God's binding. That is in the sense that He, may He be exalted, made every occurrence have an occurrence preceding it for the occurrence of the later event. Since the establishment of this chain is from God, all of it is from God. At this point a person imagines birds without end and without a limit to their number, for He, may He be exalted, sent them flying from the nest of eternity and the darkness of the unseen world, and they came and flew in a flight without beginning and without end. Each one of them was directed toward that specific person at the specific time with the specific attribute. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿We have fastened his omen to his neck﴾.

The third inquiry: experience indicates that the repetition of voluntary actions produces the firm psychological disposition (malaka nafsāniyya) in the essence of the soul. Do you not see that whoever persists in repeating one lesson comes to have that lesson memorized, and whoever persists in one action for a long duration makes that action a disposition for himself?

Having known this, we say: since frequent repetition necessitates the attainment of a firm disposition, it must be that each of those actions produces some effect in the essence of the soul. For when we observed that with the successive drops of water upon a stone a hole came to be in the stone, we knew that each of those drops had some effect in producing that hole, even if it was weak and small. And since writing, in the custom of people, is a designation of specific marks which people have agreed to make indicators of specific words, then on this basis the indication of those marks upon those specific meanings is an essential indication, necessarily established and impossible to remove. So the book containing those marks is more deserving of the name "book" than the page containing the marks that indicate by convention and agreement.

Once you understand these two premises, we say: every action that proceeds from a human being, whether much or little, strong or weak, necessarily leaves a specific impression on the substance of the human soul. If that impression draws the essence of the spirit from creation toward the presence of the Truth, it is one of the causes of happiness and honours. If that impression draws the spirit from the presence of the Truth toward preoccupation with creation, it is one of the causes of wretchedness and abandonment. However, these impressions remain hidden as long as the spirit is attached to the body, because the spirit's preoccupation with managing the body prevents these states from being unveiled, manifested and made apparent. When the spirit's attachment to the management of the body ends, then the Resurrection occurs there, in accordance with his saying (peace be upon him): "Whoever dies, his Resurrection has come." The meaning of this state being a Resurrection is that the rational soul (al-nafs al-nāṭiqah) was, as it were, at rest and settled in this lower body. When that attachment is severed, the soul rises and turns upward toward the higher world. This is what is meant by this state being a Resurrection. Then, at the occurrence of the Resurrection in this sense, the covering is removed and the bed-cover is uncovered, and it is said to him: ﴿So We have removed from you your covering, and your sight today is sharp﴾. As for His saying: ﴿And We will bring forth for him on the Day of Resurrection a record which he will find spread open﴾, its meaning is: at the occurrence of this Resurrection, We will bring forth for him from the depths of the dark body a record comprising all those impressions produced by the worldly states. This record will at that time be spread open, because while the spirit was in the body these states were hidden within it, and so they were like something folded up. After the cessation of bodily attachment, these states appear, become clear and are unveiled, so they become like something uncovered and spread out after having been folded, and manifest after having been hidden. At that point the intellectual faculty witnesses all those impressions written by the self-inscription in the substance of the spirit. Then it is said to him in that state: ﴿Read your record﴾, and then it is said to him: ﴿Your own soul suffices against you today as a reckoner﴾. If those impressions are among the causes of happiness, happiness necessarily results, and if they are among the causes of wretchedness, wretchedness necessarily results. This is the interpretation of this verse according to the spiritual states.

[Page 137]

Know that the truth is that the outward states reported in the narrations are true and genuine, with no doubt about them. The verse's capacity to bear these spiritual meanings is also evident. The upright path and the straight way is to affirm all of it. And God knows best the realities of matters.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verse 15:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever is guided, is guided only for his own soul, and whoever goes astray, goes astray only to its detriment. No bearer of burdens bears the burden of another. And We would never punish until We have sent a messenger.﴾

There are several issues concerning this verse.

**The first issue:** When He, exalted is He, said in the previous verse, ﴿And every person's omen We have fastened to his neck﴾, meaning that each person is singularly responsible for his own deeds, He expressed this same meaning in another phrase, one closer to understanding and further from error, saying: ﴿Whoever is guided, is guided only for his own soul, and whoever goes astray, goes astray only to its detriment.﴾ That is, the reward for righteous deeds belongs only to their doer and does not pass from him to another. This is reinforced by His saying: ﴿And that man will have nothing but what he strives for﴾ and ﴿And that his striving will be seen﴾ [al-Najm: 39–40].

Al-Ka'bi said: The verse indicates that the servant has the capacity for good and evil, and that he is not compelled to any particular act at all, because His saying, ﴿Whoever is guided, is guided only for his own soul, and whoever goes astray, goes astray only to its detriment﴾, is fitting only for one who is able to act and has the power to do as he wills. As for one who is compelled to one of two sides and prevented from the other, this is not fitting for him.

* * *

**The second issue:** He, exalted is He, repeated the affirmation that each person is singularly affected in his own self, by His saying: ﴿No bearer of burdens bears the burden of another.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: It is said *wazara yaziru fahuwa wazir*, and *wazara wizran* and *wizra*, and its meaning is *athima ya'thamu ithman* (he sinned, sins, a sin). He said: There are two interpretations of the verse:

The first: The wrongdoer is not held accountable for the sin of another, and likewise, another is not held accountable for his sin; rather, each person is singularly responsible for his own sin.

The second: A person should not commit sin because another committed it, as the unbelievers said: ﴿And thus We did not send before you any warner into a town except that its affluent ones said: "Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion, and we are following in their footsteps."﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 23] — [note: the cited verse in the source is al-Zukhruf: 32; I have rendered the Qur'anic text as quoted in the source].

Know that people have adhered to this verse in establishing many rulings.

**The first ruling:**

Al-Jubba'i said: The verse indicates that He, exalted is He, does not punish children for the disbelief of their fathers; otherwise the child would be held accountable for his father's sin, and that is contrary to the apparent meaning of this verse.

**The second ruling:**

Ibn Umar narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed, the deceased is punished for the weeping of his family." But Aisha (RA) cast doubt on the soundness of this report, and she argued for the soundness of that doubt by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿No bearer of burdens bears the burden of another﴾. For punishing the deceased because of the weeping of his family is taking a person to account for the crime of another, and that is contrary to this verse.

**The third ruling:**

Al-Qadi said: This verse indicates that burden (*wizr*) and sin (*ithm*) are not from the act of God, exalted is He. Its explanation is from several aspects:

The first: If it were so, it would be impossible for the servant to be held accountable for it, just as he is not held accountable for another's burden.

The second: The burden would have to be removed altogether, because one can only be described as a bearer of burden if he is one who chooses and is able to avoid it; for this reason the child is not described with this.

**The fourth ruling:**

A group of early jurists refrained from imposing blood money (*diya*) on the paternal kin ('aqila), and they said: Because that entails holding a person accountable for another's act, and that contradicts this verse.

It was answered that the one who commits an error is not himself held accountable for that act, so how can another become accountable because of that act? Rather, that is an obligation imposed as a starting ruling (*ibtida'*) by God, exalted is He.

* * *

**The third issue:** Our companions said: The obligation of thanking the benefactor is not established by reason but by revelation (*sam'*). The evidence for this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We would never punish until We have sent a messenger.﴾ The manner of inference is that obligation's essence is not established except by the stipulation of punishment for abandoning it, and there is no punishment before the Law (*shar'*), by the ruling of this verse. Therefore, obligation cannot be realized before the Law. They then reinforced this verse by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As messengers bearing good news and warning, so that mankind will have no argument against God after the messengers﴾ [al-Nisa': 165], and by His saying: ﴿And if We had destroyed them with a punishment before it, they would have said: "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger so we could follow Your verses before we were humiliated and disgraced?"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 134].

It may be argued that this inference is weak, and its explanation is from two aspects:

The first: We say: If rational obligation is not established, then legal obligation is not established at all; and this is false, so that (its antecedent) is false. The proof of the implication is from several aspects:

One: When the lawgiver comes and claims that he is a prophet from God, exalted is He, and manifests a miracle, is it obligatory upon the listener to hear his words and reflect on his miracles, or is it not obligatory? If it is not obligatory, then the doctrine of prophethood is refuted. If it is obligatory, then either it is obligatory by reason or by the Law. If it is obligatory by reason, then rational obligation is established. If it is obligatory by the Law, that is false, because that Law is either the claimant himself or someone else. The first is false, because the sum of the statement reverts to the claimant saying: "The proof that it is obligatory to accept my word is that I say it is obligatory to accept my word," and this is establishing a thing by itself. If the lawgiver is someone other than him, the discussion concerning him is the same as in the first case, and it leads either to circularity (*dawr*) or to an infinite regress (*tasalsul*), and both are impossible.

Two: When the Law comes and makes some acts obligatory and forbids others, there is no meaning to obligation and prohibition except that it says: "If you abandon such-and-such and do such-and-such, I will punish you." We then say: Either it is obligatory upon him to guard against punishment or it is not obligatory. If it is not obligatory upon him to guard against punishment, then the meaning of obligation is not established at all; and this is false, so that is false. If it is obligatory upon him to guard against punishment, then either it is obligatory by reason or by revelation (*sam'*). If it is obligatory by reason, then that is the intended conclusion. If it is obligatory by revelation, the meaning of this obligation is not established except by the stipulation of punishment for it, and then the first division returns and an infinite regress is necessary, and that is impossible.

Three: The doctrine of the People of the Sunna is that it is permissible for God, exalted is He, to pardon punishment for abandoning an obligation. If that is so, the essence of obligation exists even without punishment. Nothing remains but to say that the essence of the obligatory is only established through the occurrence of fear of punishment, and this fear is attained by reason alone. Thus it is established that the essence of obligation is only realized through this fear, and it is established that this fear is attained by reason alone; it follows that obligation is attained by reason alone.

If they say: The essence of obligation is only established through the occurrence of fear of blame?

We say: If He, exalted is He, pardons, then blame falls away. Accordingly, the essence of obligation is only established through the occurrence of fear of blame, and that is attained by reason alone. Thus it is established by these aspects that rational obligation cannot be repelled.

Having established this, we say: There are two opinions regarding the verse:

The first: We let the verse stand on its apparent meaning and say: Reason is God's messenger to creation; indeed, it is the messenger without whom the mission of none of the prophets would be established. Reason is thus the original messenger, so the meaning of the verse becomes: "And We would never punish until We have sent the messenger of reason."

The second: We specify the generality of the verse and say: The intended meaning is: "And We would never punish in those acts whose obligation cannot be known except through the Law, until after the coming of the Law." The specification of a general statement, although it is a departure from the apparent meaning, must be resorted to when proofs are established, and we have shown the establishment of the three proofs. Moreover, if we negate rational obligation, it necessarily follows that we negate legal obligation. And God knows best.

Know that what we accept and adhere to is that mere reason is a cause for obligating upon us the doing of what benefits us and the abandoning of what harms us. As for mere reason, it does not indicate that anything is obligatory upon God, exalted is He. This is because we are created disposed to seek benefit and to avoid harm, so reason alone is sufficient for obligation in our case; whereas God, exalted is He, is exempt from seeking benefit and fleeing harm, so it is impossible for reason to rule upon Him concerning the obligation of an act or the abandonment of an act. And God knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 17, verses 16–17:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when We intend to destroy a town, We command its affluent ones, but they defiantly transgress therein; then the word becomes due against it, and We destroy it with complete destruction.﴾ ﴿And how many generations have We destroyed after Noah? And sufficient is your Lord as Knower and Seer of the sins of His servants.﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** His saying, ﴿We command its affluent ones﴾. Regarding the meaning of this "command," there are two opinions.

**The first opinion:** It means a command to act. Then, the wording of the verse does not indicate what He commands them to do. Most scholars said: its meaning is that He commands them to perform acts of obedience and good deeds, but they oppose that command and transgress. The author of *al-Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari) said: The apparent wording indicates that He commands them to commit transgression and they transgress. However, this is a metaphor, and its meaning is that He opened for them the doors of goodness and ease, and at that they became rebellious, insolent, and oppressive. He said: The evidence that the apparent wording requires what we have mentioned is that the object of the command has been omitted because His saying, ﴿they transgressed﴾, indicates it. One says: "I commanded him and he stood up," and "I commanded him and he read," which is not understood unless the object of the command is standing or reading. Likewise here: when He said, ﴿We command its affluent ones, and they transgress therein,﴾ it must be that the meaning is: We commanded them to transgress, and they transgressed. It cannot be said that this is refuted by their saying, "I commanded him and he disobeyed me" or "he opposed me," for this does not mean that I commanded him to disobey or oppose; because we say: disobedience contradicts and negates the command. Likewise, "I commanded him and he transgressed" indicates that the object of the command is something other than transgression, because transgression is an expression for doing the opposite of what was commanded. So, that it is transgression negates that it is commanded, just as that it is disobedience negates that it is commanded. Therefore this wording must indicate that what was commanded is not transgression. This statement is extremely clear, so I do not know why the author of *al-Kashshaf* persisted in his view despite its obvious falsity. Thus it is established that the truth is what everyone has mentioned, namely that the meaning is: We commanded them to perform righteous deeds, which are faith and obedience, but the people opposed that command out of obstinacy and proceeded to transgress.

**The second opinion:** Regarding the interpretation of His saying, ﴿We command its affluent ones﴾, that is: We increased its wicked ones. Al-Wahidi said: The Arabs say "amira al-qawm" when the people increased, and "amarahum Allah" when God increased them, and "amarahum" also with the lengthened vowel (ā). Al-Jarmi narrated from Abu Zayd: "Ammara Allah al-qawm" and "Amara-hum," meaning: He increased them. Abu Ubaydah argued for the soundness of this usage with the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "The best of wealth is a mare that has been multiplied (ma'murah) and a palm-tree that has been fruitful (ma'burah)." The meaning is a mare whose offspring has increased. They say: God multiplied the mare, that is, increased her offspring. Some people denied that "amira" means "increased," and they said: "amira al-qawm" when the people became many, and "amarahum Allah" with the lengthened vowel means He increased them. They interpreted the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying "a mare that has been multiplied" to mean that she was commanded to multiply her offspring, by way of metaphor. As for *al-mutraf*: its meaning in the language is the one who is pampered, whom blessing and abundance of living have made insolent. ﴿They transgressed therein﴾, that is: they went out of what God commanded them. ﴿Then the word becomes due against it﴾, meaning: it deserved punishment. This is like an explanation of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We would not punish until We send a messenger﴾ (Al-Isra 17:15), and His saying: ﴿And your Lord would not destroy the towns until He sends in their mother-town a messenger﴾ (Al-Qasas 28:59), and His saying: ﴿That is because your Lord would not destroy the towns unjustly while their people are unaware﴾ (Al-An'am 6:131). Since He, may He be exalted, has decreed in these verses that He does not destroy a town until they oppose God's command, He therefore mentions here that He commands them, and when they oppose the command, then at that point they deserve destruction, which is expressed by His saying: ﴿the word becomes due against it﴾. And His saying: ﴿So We destroyed it with complete destruction﴾, that is: We destroyed it with destruction of uprooting. *Al-Damar* is destruction in the manner of uprooting.

* * *

**The second issue:** Our companions (the Ash'aris) argued by this verse for the soundness of their doctrine in several ways:

**First:** The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that He intended to inflict harm upon them directly, and then He used that means to destroy them.

**Second:** The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that He specified the affluent ones with that command only because He knew that they would transgress, and this indicates that He intended transgression from them.

**Third:** He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿then the word becomes due against it﴾ with the punishment and disbelief. Whenever the word becomes due against them in this way, it is impossible for faith to proceed from them, because that would necessitate the reversal of God's true report into a lie, and that is impossible, and what leads to an impossibility is impossible.

Al-Ka'bi said: The rest of the verses indicate that He, may He be exalted, does not begin with punishment and destruction, because of His saying: ﴿Indeed, God does not change what is with a people until they change what is in themselves﴾ (Al-Ra'd 13:11), and His saying: ﴿What would God do with your punishment if you are grateful and believe?﴾ (Al-Nisa' 4:147), and His saying: ﴿And We would not be destroyers of the towns unless their people were wrongdoers﴾ (Al-Qasas 28:59). All these verses indicate that He, may He be exalted, does not begin with harm. Also, what precedes this verse indicates this meaning, namely His saying: ﴿Whoever is guided is only guided for [the benefit of] himself, and whoever goes astray only goes astray to its detriment, and no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾. It is impossible that there be contradiction among the verses of the Qur'an. Thus it is established that the verses we have recited are *muhkam* (clear and definitive), and likewise the verse we are interpreting, so this verse must be interpreted in light of those verses. This is what al-Ka'bi said.

Know that the best of people in speech regarding the interpretation of this verse in a way that agrees with the position of the Mu'tazilah is al-Qaffal, for he mentioned two aspects regarding it:

**The first aspect:** He said that God, may He be exalted, informed that He does not punish anyone for what He knows of him before he acts upon it; that is, He does not make His knowledge a proof against one whom He knows, if He commands him, he will disobey. Rather, He commands him, and when his disobedience becomes apparent to the people, then He punishes him. So His saying: ﴿And when We intend to destroy a town, We command its affluent ones﴾ means: when We intend to carry out what has preceded in the decree of destroying a people, We command the pampered, the mighty, who think that their wealth, their children, and their helpers will ward off Our might from them, to believe in Me and act upon the laws of My religion as My messenger conveyed them from Me. Then they transgress, and at that point the prior decree of their destruction becomes due against them because their disobediences have become apparent. Then We destroy them. The sum of the meaning is: when We intend to destroy a town because of Our knowledge that they will only proceed to disobedience, We do not suffice in bringing about that destruction with mere knowledge of that, but We command its affluent ones, and they transgress. When that transgression becomes apparent from them, then We inflict upon them the promised punishment.

**The second aspect** in interpretation is that we say: when We intend to destroy a town because of the appearance of sins from its people, We do not hasten punishment upon them at the first appearance of sins from them, but We command its affluent ones to return from those sins. He specified the affluent ones with that command because *al-mutraf* is the one who is pampered, and whoever has many of God's blessings upon him, his standing in gratitude is more obligatory. So when He commands them to repent and return time after time, while He does not cut off those blessings from them but rather increases them state after state, then at that point their obstinacy, their rebellion, and their distance from returning from falsehood to truth become manifest. Then God pours calamity upon them in abundance.

Then al-Qaffal said: These two interpretations both return to the point that God, may He be exalted, informed His servants that He does not hasten punishment upon an unjust nation until He gives them the utmost warning, by which despair of their faith occurs, as He said about the people of Noah: ﴿And they will not beget except a wicked disbeliever﴾ (Nuh 71:27), and He said: ﴿And it was revealed to Noah that none of your people will believe except those who have already believed﴾ (Hud 11:36), and He said about others: ﴿So they were not to believe in what they had denied before﴾ (Yunus 10:74). Thus He, may He be exalted, first informed that the punishment does not appear except after the sending of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. Then He informed secondly in this verse that when He sends the Messenger too and they deny him, He does not hasten punishment upon them, but continues to send upon them advice and admonitions. If they remain persistent in sins, then there descends upon them the punishment of uprooting. This interpretation which al-Qaffal mentioned, in applying the verse to the Mu'tazilah's position, was not made possible for anyone among the Mu'tazilah shaykhs like him.

Al-Jubba'i responded by saying: The verse does not mean that He, may He be exalted, intends to destroy them before they disobey and deserve it, because that would be injustice, and injustice is impossible for God. Rather, the meaning of "intention" here is the nearness of that state. So the sense is: when the time of destroying a town draws near, We command its affluent ones, and they transgress therein. This is like the saying of one who says: "When the sick person intends to die, his illnesses increase in severity, and when the merchant intends to become poor, losses come upon him from every direction." It does not mean that the sick person wants to die, or that the merchant wants to become poor, but rather they mean that he will become like that. So it is likewise here.

Know that all three aspects we have mentioned in using this verse are undoubtedly deviations from the apparent wording. As for the second and third aspects, they have remained free from criticism. And God knows best.

**The third issue:** The well-known reading among the Seven Readers is ﴿amarna mutrafiha﴾ with a short vowel, without a lengthened alif. It was narrated through a less well-known transmission from Nafi' and Ibn 'Abbas as "a'marna" with lengthening, and from Abu 'Amr as "ammarna" with doubling. The lengthened form is from "amira al-qawm" with a kasra on the mim when they became many, and "amarahumu Allah" with lengthening, meaning God made them many. The doubled form is for empowerment, meaning: We empowered its affluent ones, and its meaning is giving free rein and removing restraint by force. And God knows best.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And how many generations have We destroyed after Noah﴾: know that the meaning is that the path We have mentioned is Our practice with those who transgress and rebel among the earlier generations who came after Noah, namely 'Ad, Thamud, and others. Then He, may He be exalted, addressed His Messenger with something that is addressed to others as well, as a deterrent and warning to all, saying: ﴿And sufficient is your Lord as Knower and Seer of the sins of His servants﴾. And in this there are two discussions:

**The first discussion:** He, may He be exalted, is knowing of all knowable things and seeing of all visible things, so nothing of the states of creation is hidden from Him. It is established that He is capable of all possible things, so He is capable of delivering recompense to each person according to his deserving. Also, He is free from futility and injustice. The combination of these three attributes, namely complete knowledge, perfect power, and freedom from injustice, is a great glad tiding to the people of obedience and a great threat to the people of disbelief and disobedience.

**The second discussion:** Al-Farra' said: If the letter *ba'* (bi) were removed from your saying "bi-rabbika," it would be permissible. The prefixing of *ba'* to a nominative noun is permissible only when its bearer is being praised or blamed, like your saying: "Sufficient is He" (kafāka bihi), "How excellent is he as a man" (akrim bihi rajulan), "Good is your food as food" (ṭāba bi-ṭa'āmika ṭa'āman), and "Generous is your garment as a garment" (jāda bi-thawbika thawban). But if it is not praise or blame, it is not permissible to prefix it. So one may not say "qāma bi-akhīka" meaning "your brother stood." And God knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 17, verses 16–17:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when We intend to destroy a town, We command its affluent ones, but they defiantly transgress therein; then the word becomes due against it, and We destroy it with complete destruction.﴾ ﴿And how many generations have We destroyed after Noah? And sufficient is your Lord as Knower and Seer of the sins of His servants.﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** His saying, ﴿We command its affluent ones﴾. Regarding the meaning of this "command," there are two opinions.

**The first opinion:** It means a command to act. Then, the wording of the verse does not indicate what He commands them to do. Most scholars said: its meaning is that He commands them to perform acts of obedience and good deeds, but they oppose that command and transgress. The author of *al-Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari) said: The apparent wording indicates that He commands them to commit transgression and they transgress. However, this is a metaphor, and its meaning is that He opened for them the doors of goodness and ease, and at that they became rebellious, insolent, and oppressive. He said: The evidence that the apparent wording requires what we have mentioned is that the object of the command has been omitted because His saying, ﴿they transgressed﴾, indicates it. One says: "I commanded him and he stood up," and "I commanded him and he read," which is not understood unless the object of the command is standing or reading. Likewise here: when He said, ﴿We command its affluent ones, and they transgress therein,﴾ it must be that the meaning is: We commanded them to transgress, and they transgressed. It cannot be said that this is refuted by their saying, "I commanded him and he disobeyed me" or "he opposed me," for this does not mean that I commanded him to disobey or oppose; because we say: disobedience contradicts and negates the command. Likewise, "I commanded him and he transgressed" indicates that the object of the command is something other than transgression, because transgression is an expression for doing the opposite of what was commanded. So, that it is transgression negates that it is commanded, just as that it is disobedience negates that it is commanded. Therefore this wording must indicate that what was commanded is not transgression. This statement is extremely clear, so I do not know why the author of *al-Kashshaf* persisted in his view despite its obvious falsity. Thus it is established that the truth is what everyone has mentioned, namely that the meaning is: We commanded them to perform righteous deeds, which are faith and obedience, but the people opposed that command out of obstinacy and proceeded to transgress.

**The second opinion:** Regarding the interpretation of His saying, ﴿We command its affluent ones﴾, that is: We increased its wicked ones. Al-Wahidi said: The Arabs say "amira al-qawm" when the people increased, and "amarahum Allah" when God increased them, and "amarahum" also with the lengthened vowel (ā). Al-Jarmi narrated from Abu Zayd: "Ammara Allah al-qawm" and "Amara-hum," meaning: He increased them. Abu Ubaydah argued for the soundness of this usage with the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "The best of wealth is a mare that has been multiplied (ma'murah) and a palm-tree that has been fruitful (ma'burah)." The meaning is a mare whose offspring has increased. They say: God multiplied the mare, that is, increased her offspring. Some people denied that "amira" means "increased," and they said: "amira al-qawm" when the people became many, and "amarahum Allah" with the lengthened vowel means He increased them. They interpreted the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying "a mare that has been multiplied" to mean that she was commanded to multiply her offspring, by way of metaphor. As for *al-mutraf*: its meaning in the language is the one who is pampered, whom blessing and abundance of living have made insolent. ﴿They transgressed therein﴾, that is: they went out of what God commanded them. ﴿Then the word becomes due against it﴾, meaning: it deserved punishment. This is like an explanation of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We would not punish until We send a messenger﴾ (Al-Isra 17:15), and His saying: ﴿And your Lord would not destroy the towns until He sends in their mother-town a messenger﴾ (Al-Qasas 28:59), and His saying: ﴿That is because your Lord would not destroy the towns unjustly while their people are unaware﴾ (Al-An'am 6:131). Since He, may He be exalted, has decreed in these verses that He does not destroy a town until they oppose God's command, He therefore mentions here that He commands them, and when they oppose the command, then at that point they deserve destruction, which is expressed by His saying: ﴿the word becomes due against it﴾. And His saying: ﴿So We destroyed it with complete destruction﴾, that is: We destroyed it with destruction of uprooting. *Al-Damar* is destruction in the manner of uprooting.

* * *

**The second issue:** Our companions (the Ash'aris) argued by this verse for the soundness of their doctrine in several ways:

**First:** The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that He intended to inflict harm upon them directly, and then He used that means to destroy them.

**Second:** The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that He specified the affluent ones with that command only because He knew that they would transgress, and this indicates that He intended transgression from them.

**Third:** He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿then the word becomes due against it﴾ with the punishment and disbelief. Whenever the word becomes due against them in this way, it is impossible for faith to proceed from them, because that would necessitate the reversal of God's true report into a lie, and that is impossible, and what leads to an impossibility is impossible.

Al-Ka'bi said: The rest of the verses indicate that He, may He be exalted, does not begin with punishment and destruction, because of His saying: ﴿Indeed, God does not change what is with a people until they change what is in themselves﴾ (Al-Ra'd 13:11), and His saying: ﴿What would God do with your punishment if you are grateful and believe?﴾ (Al-Nisa' 4:147), and His saying: ﴿And We would not be destroyers of the towns unless their people were wrongdoers﴾ (Al-Qasas 28:59). All these verses indicate that He, may He be exalted, does not begin with harm. Also, what precedes this verse indicates this meaning, namely His saying: ﴿Whoever is guided is only guided for [the benefit of] himself, and whoever goes astray only goes astray to its detriment, and no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾. It is impossible that there be contradiction among the verses of the Qur'an. Thus it is established that the verses we have recited are *muhkam* (clear and definitive), and likewise the verse we are interpreting, so this verse must be interpreted in light of those verses. This is what al-Ka'bi said.

Know that the best of people in speech regarding the interpretation of this verse in a way that agrees with the position of the Mu'tazilah is al-Qaffal, for he mentioned two aspects regarding it:

**The first aspect:** He said that God, may He be exalted, informed that He does not punish anyone for what He knows of him before he acts upon it; that is, He does not make His knowledge a proof against one whom He knows, if He commands him, he will disobey. Rather, He commands him, and when his disobedience becomes apparent to the people, then He punishes him. So His saying: ﴿And when We intend to destroy a town, We command its affluent ones﴾ means: when We intend to carry out what has preceded in the decree of destroying a people, We command the pampered, the mighty, who think that their wealth, their children, and their helpers will ward off Our might from them, to believe in Me and act upon the laws of My religion as My messenger conveyed them from Me. Then they transgress, and at that point the prior decree of their destruction becomes due against them because their disobediences have become apparent. Then We destroy them. The sum of the meaning is: when We intend to destroy a town because of Our knowledge that they will only proceed to disobedience, We do not suffice in bringing about that destruction with mere knowledge of that, but We command its affluent ones, and they transgress. When that transgression becomes apparent from them, then We inflict upon them the promised punishment.

**The second aspect** in interpretation is that we say: when We intend to destroy a town because of the appearance of sins from its people, We do not hasten punishment upon them at the first appearance of sins from them, but We command its affluent ones to return from those sins. He specified the affluent ones with that command because *al-mutraf* is the one who is pampered, and whoever has many of God's blessings upon him, his standing in gratitude is more obligatory. So when He commands them to repent and return time after time, while He does not cut off those blessings from them but rather increases them state after state, then at that point their obstinacy, their rebellion, and their distance from returning from falsehood to truth become manifest. Then God pours calamity upon them in abundance.

Then al-Qaffal said: These two interpretations both return to the point that God, may He be exalted, informed His servants that He does not hasten punishment upon an unjust nation until He gives them the utmost warning, by which despair of their faith occurs, as He said about the people of Noah: ﴿And they will not beget except a wicked disbeliever﴾ (Nuh 71:27), and He said: ﴿And it was revealed to Noah that none of your people will believe except those who have already believed﴾ (Hud 11:36), and He said about others: ﴿So they were not to believe in what they had denied before﴾ (Yunus 10:74). Thus He, may He be exalted, first informed that the punishment does not appear except after the sending of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. Then He informed secondly in this verse that when He sends the Messenger too and they deny him, He does not hasten punishment upon them, but continues to send upon them advice and admonitions. If they remain persistent in sins, then there descends upon them the punishment of uprooting. This interpretation which al-Qaffal mentioned, in applying the verse to the Mu'tazilah's position, was not made possible for anyone among the Mu'tazilah shaykhs like him.

Al-Jubba'i responded by saying: The verse does not mean that He, may He be exalted, intends to destroy them before they disobey and deserve it, because that would be injustice, and injustice is impossible for God. Rather, the meaning of "intention" here is the nearness of that state. So the sense is: when the time of destroying a town draws near, We command its affluent ones, and they transgress therein. This is like the saying of one who says: "When the sick person intends to die, his illnesses increase in severity, and when the merchant intends to become poor, losses come upon him from every direction." It does not mean that the sick person wants to die, or that the merchant wants to become poor, but rather they mean that he will become like that. So it is likewise here.

Know that all three aspects we have mentioned in using this verse are undoubtedly deviations from the apparent wording. As for the second and third aspects, they have remained free from criticism. And God knows best.

**The third issue:** The well-known reading among the Seven Readers is ﴿amarna mutrafiha﴾ with a short vowel, without a lengthened alif. It was narrated through a less well-known transmission from Nafi' and Ibn 'Abbas as "a'marna" with lengthening, and from Abu 'Amr as "ammarna" with doubling. The lengthened form is from "amira al-qawm" with a kasra on the mim when they became many, and "amarahumu Allah" with lengthening, meaning God made them many. The doubled form is for empowerment, meaning: We empowered its affluent ones, and its meaning is giving free rein and removing restraint by force. And God knows best.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And how many generations have We destroyed after Noah﴾: know that the meaning is that the path We have mentioned is Our practice with those who transgress and rebel among the earlier generations who came after Noah, namely 'Ad, Thamud, and others. Then He, may He be exalted, addressed His Messenger with something that is addressed to others as well, as a deterrent and warning to all, saying: ﴿And sufficient is your Lord as Knower and Seer of the sins of His servants﴾. And in this there are two discussions:

**The first discussion:** He, may He be exalted, is knowing of all knowable things and seeing of all visible things, so nothing of the states of creation is hidden from Him. It is established that He is capable of all possible things, so He is capable of delivering recompense to each person according to his deserving. Also, He is free from futility and injustice. The combination of these three attributes, namely complete knowledge, perfect power, and freedom from injustice, is a great glad tiding to the people of obedience and a great threat to the people of disbelief and disobedience.

**The second discussion:** Al-Farra' said: If the letter *ba'* (bi) were removed from your saying "bi-rabbika," it would be permissible. The prefixing of *ba'* to a nominative noun is permissible only when its bearer is being praised or blamed, like your saying: "Sufficient is He" (kafāka bihi), "How excellent is he as a man" (akrim bihi rajulan), "Good is your food as food" (ṭāba bi-ṭa'āmika ṭa'āman), and "Generous is your garment as a garment" (jāda bi-thawbika thawban). But if it is not praise or blame, it is not permissible to prefix it. So one may not say "qāma bi-akhīka" meaning "your brother stood." And God knows best.

**His words, Exalted is He:** ﴿Whoever desires the fleeting [life], We hasten for him therein what We will, for whomever We wish. Then We appoint for him Hell, where he will burn, censured and banished.﴾ ﴿But whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it as due striving, while being a believer, those are the ones whose striving will be appreciated.﴾ ﴿To each—these and those—We extend from the gift of your Lord, and the gift of your Lord is not withheld.﴾ ﴿See how We have favored some of them over others, and the Hereafter is greater in degrees and greater in favor.﴾

**On this verse there are several issues:**

**The first issue:** Al-Qaffal (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This verse falls under the meaning of His words: ﴿And every person's omen We have fastened to his neck.﴾ Its meaning is that worldly aspiration is of two kinds. Some people intend by their deeds the world, its benefits, and leadership in it. Such a person disdains submitting to the prophets, peace be upon them, and entering into their obedience and answering their call, out of fear that leadership will be taken from him. Such a person has made his own omen a burden, because he is in the grip of Allah the Exalted. Allah gives him from worldly things a measure, not as that person wishes, but as Allah wills. However, his final end is Hell, which he will enter and burn in its heat, censured, blamed, banished, and expelled from the mercy of Allah the Exalted. There are benefits in the wording of this verse.

[p. 143]

**The first benefit:** Punishment is a harm accompanied by humiliation and blame, on condition that it is lasting and free of any admixture of benefit. His words ﴿Then We appoint for him Hell, where he will burn﴾ indicate great harm. ﴿Censured﴾ indicates humiliation and blame. ﴿Banished﴾ indicates distance and expulsion from the mercy of Allah. These indicate that this harm is free of any admixture of benefit or mercy, and they indicate that it is lasting and free of any change into comfort or deliverance.

**The second benefit:** Among the ignorant are those who, when worldly life favors them, are deceived by it and think that this is because of their honor with Allah the Exalted. Allah the Exalted made clear that the world's favoring a person should not be taken as evidence of Allah's pleasure, because worldly favor may be attained while its final outcome is returning to the punishment and humiliation of Allah. Such a person's deeds resemble the bird of ill omen in their clinging to him and in driving him toward the severest punishment.

**The third benefit:** His words ﴿for whomever We wish﴾ indicate that worldly success is not attained by everyone. Rather, many unbelievers and misguided people turn away from religion in pursuit of the world, and then remain deprived of both the world and religion. This is also a great deterrent to those unbelievers and misguided people who abandon religion to seek the world. Often the world escapes them, and they are the greatest losers in deeds, ﴿those whose effort is lost in the life of this world while they think they are doing good work.﴾

**As for the second division,** His words ﴿But whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it as due striving, while being a believer﴾, He, Exalted is He, stipulated three conditions.

**The first condition:** That one intends by one's deed the Hereafter, i.e., its reward. If this intention and this purpose are absent, one does not benefit from that deed, because of His words: ﴿and that man has nothing except what he strives for﴾ [al-Najm: 37], and because of the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "Actions are only by intentions." Also, the purpose of deeds is to illuminate the heart with knowledge and love of Allah the Exalted, and this is not achieved unless one intends by one's deed the worship of Allah the Exalted and seeks His obedience.

**The second condition:** His words ﴿and strives for it as due striving﴾. This means that the deed by which one reaches the success of the Hereafter's reward must be among the deeds through which the Hereafter's reward is gained. It is not so unless it is of the category of drawing near to Allah through acts of devotion and obedience. Many people draw near to Allah the Exalted through false deeds. The unbelievers draw near to Allah the Exalted through worshipping idols, and they have two interpretations (*ta'wil*) of this:

**The first interpretation:** They say: The Lord of the worlds is too exalted and too great for any one of us to be able to display worship and service to Him. We do not have this level or rank. The utmost of our capacity is to occupy ourselves with the worship of some of Allah's closest servants, such as occupying ourselves with worshipping a star or worshipping an angel from among the angels. Then the angel and the star themselves occupy themselves with the worship of Allah the Exalted. These people draw near to Allah the Exalted by this path. However, since it is corrupt in itself, there is no doubt that no benefit is gained from it.

**The second interpretation** of theirs: They said: We have made these images in the forms of the prophets and the saints, and our purpose in worshipping them is that those prophets and saints become intercessors for us before Allah the Exalted. This path is also corrupt. It is also reported about India that they draw near to Allah the Exalted by killing themselves at times and burning themselves at other times, and they exaggerate in glorifying Allah the Exalted.

[p. 144]

However, since the path is corrupt, there is no doubt that no benefit is gained from it. The same applies to all sects of the falsifiers who draw near to Allah the Exalted through their false doctrines, their corrupt sayings, and their deeds deviating from the standard of truth and correctness.

**The third condition:** His words ﴿while being a believer﴾. This condition is binding, because the condition for righteous deeds to bring about reward is the prior existence of faith. When the condition is not present, the conditioned thing is not realized. Then He, Exalted is He, informed that when these conditions are fulfilled, the striving becomes "appreciated" and the deed becomes "accepted."

Know that gratitude (*shukr*) is a combination of three matters: believing that the one who does the favor is a benefactor in those deeds, praising him with speech, and performing actions that show that he is honored by the grateful one. Allah the Exalted treats the obedient with these three matters. He, Exalted is He, knows that they are doing good in those deeds. He praises them with His speech. And He treats them with dealings that indicate they are honored before Allah the Exalted. When all three are present, they are "appreciated" by Allah the Exalted for their acts of obedience.

I have seen in the books of the Mu'tazila (a rationalist school) that Ja'far ibn Harb was present with a man from Ahl al-Sunna (the Sunni community), and he said: The proof that faith came about by the creation of Allah the Exalted is that we thank Allah for faith. If faith were not realized by His bringing it into being, it would be impossible for us to thank Him for it, because praising and thanking a person for what is not his deed is ugly. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and they love to be praised for what they did not do﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 188]. The attendees were unable to answer. Then Thumama ibn al-Ashras entered and said: We only praise Allah the Exalted and thank Him for what He has given us of power and intellect, the sending down of books, and the clarifying of proofs. And Allah the Exalted thanks us for performing faith. He said, Exalted is He: ﴿Then those, their striving was appreciated﴾. He said: Ja'far ibn Harb laughed and said: He made the question difficult, so it became easy.

Know that our statement: "The totality of power together with the motive necessitates the act" is a clear statement, because He, Exalted is He, is the One who gave the complete necessitating cause for the realization of faith. Thus He is the One deserving of gratitude. And when faith was realized for the servant, and faith necessitates complete happiness, the servant also becomes "appreciated," and there is no contradiction between the two matters.

This means that the deed by which one reaches the success of the Hereafter's reward must be among the deeds through which the Hereafter's reward is gained. It is not so unless it is of the category of drawing near to Allah through acts of devotion and obedience. Many people draw near to Allah the Exalted through false deeds. The unbelievers draw near to Allah the Exalted through worshipping idols, and they have two interpretations (*ta'wil*) of this:

**The first interpretation:** They say: The Lord of the worlds is too exalted and too great for any one of us to be able to display worship and service to Him. We do not have this level or rank. The utmost of our capacity is to occupy ourselves with the worship of some of Allah's closest servants, such as occupying ourselves with worshipping a star or worshipping an angel from among the angels. Then the angel and the star themselves occupy themselves with the worship of Allah the Exalted. These people draw near to Allah the Exalted by this path. However, since it is corrupt in itself, there is no doubt that no benefit is gained from it.

**The second interpretation** of theirs: They said: We have made these images in the forms of the prophets and the saints, and our purpose in worshipping them is that those prophets and saints become intercessors for us before Allah the Exalted. This path is also corrupt. It is also reported about India that they draw near to Allah the Exalted by killing themselves at times and burning themselves at other times, and they exaggerate in glorifying Allah the Exalted.

[p. 144]

However, since the path is corrupt, there is no doubt that no benefit is gained from it. The same applies to all sects of the falsifiers who draw near to Allah the Exalted through their false doctrines, their corrupt sayings, and their deeds deviating from the standard of truth and correctness.

**The third condition:** His words ﴿while being a believer﴾. This condition is binding, because the condition for righteous deeds to bring about reward is the prior existence of faith. When the condition is not present, the conditioned thing is not realized. Then He, Exalted is He, informed that when these conditions are fulfilled, the striving becomes "appreciated" and the deed becomes "accepted."

Know that gratitude (*shukr*) is a combination of three matters: believing that the one who does the favor is a benefactor in those deeds, praising him with speech, and performing actions that show that he is honored by the grateful one. Allah the Exalted treats the obedient with these three matters. He, Exalted is He, knows that they are doing good in those deeds. He praises them with His speech. And He treats them with dealings that indicate they are honored before Allah the Exalted. When all three are present, they are "appreciated" by Allah the Exalted for their acts of obedience.

I have seen in the books of the Mu'tazila (a rationalist school) that Ja'far ibn Harb was present with a man from Ahl al-Sunna (the Sunni community), and he said: The proof that faith came about by the creation of Allah the Exalted is that we thank Allah for faith. If faith were not realized by His bringing it into being, it would be impossible for us to thank Him for it, because praising and thanking a person for what is not his deed is ugly. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and they love to be praised for what they did not do﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 188]. The attendees were unable to answer. Then Thumama ibn al-Ashras entered and said: We only praise Allah the Exalted and thank Him for what He has given us of power and intellect, the sending down of books, and the clarifying of proofs. And Allah the Exalted thanks us for performing faith. He said, Exalted is He: ﴿Then those, their striving was appreciated﴾. He said: Ja'far ibn Harb laughed and said: He made the question difficult, so it became easy.

Know that our statement: "The totality of power together with the motive necessitates the act" is a clear statement, because He, Exalted is He, is the One who gave the complete necessitating cause for the realization of faith. Thus He is the One deserving of gratitude. And when faith was realized for the servant, and faith necessitates complete happiness, the servant also becomes "appreciated," and there is no contradiction between the two matters.

**The second issue:** Know that whoever performs an action either intends by it to obtain the good of this world, or the good of the Hereafter, or intends both together, or intends neither of them. This is the correct division. If he intends by it only the good of this world, or only the good of the Hereafter, then Allah the Exalted has mentioned the ruling on these two categories in this verse.

As for the third category, it divides into three sub-categories, because the pursuit of the Hereafter is either dominant or subordinate, or the two pursuits are equal.

As for the first sub-category, where the pursuit of the Hereafter is dominant: is this action accepted by Allah the Exalted? There is a question here. It may be said that it is not accepted, on the basis of what has been related that the Prophet (ﷺ) reported from the Lord of Might that He said: "I am the most self-sufficient of partners. Whoever performs an action in which he associates another with Me, I abandon him and his partner." Also, the seeking of Allah's pleasure is either said to have been an independent cause that moved him to that action and called him to it, or it is said not to have been so. If it was the first, then it is impossible for anything else to have any role in that impulse and call, because when a ruling arises from a complete and perfect cause, it is impossible for anything else to have a share in it. If it was the second, then the thing that moved him to that action and called him to it is that combined whole, and that combined whole is not the seeking of Allah's pleasure, because a whole formed from a thing and something else must be different from each of its two parts. Thus this sub-category joins the category in which the motive was different from the seeking of Allah's pleasure, and so it must be accepted.

It may also be said that since the pursuit of the Hereafter is dominant over the pursuit of this world, the like is opposed by the like, and so the surplus remains as a sincere motive for the pursuit of the Hereafter, and therefore it must be accepted. As for when the pursuit of this world and the pursuit of the Hereafter are equal, or when the pursuit of this world is dominant, then they have agreed that this is not accepted, except that it is in every case better than when the pursuit of this world is completely devoid of the pursuit of the Hereafter.

As for the fourth category, which is that he performed that action without any motive: this depends on whether the proceeding of an action from one who has power requires the presence of a motive or not. Those who say that it requires a motive said: this category is impossible to occur. Those who said that it does not require one said: this action has no effect in the inner reality, and it is forbidden outwardly because it is idle. And Allah knows best.

\* \* \*

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Each﴾, that is, each one of the two groups. The tanwin is a substitute for the omitted word that the noun is annexed to. ﴿We extend to these and to those from the gift of your Lord﴾, that is: He the Exalted extends to both groups with wealth and widens provision for them, such as wealth, children and other causes of honour and adornment in this world. This is because Our gift is not restricted from anyone, whether believer or disbeliever, since all are created in the abode of action. Therefore it is necessary to remove the excuse and eliminate the cause for all, and to deliver the enjoyments of this world to all in the measure that wisdom requires. So He the Exalted made clear that His gift is not forbidden, meaning not prevented. It is said: "he forbade it (yahzuruhu)," and whoever comes between a person and something has forbidden it to him.

\* \* \*

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿See how We have preferred some of them over others﴾, and regarding this there are two statements:

The first statement: the meaning is: look at Our permissible gift to both groups in this world, how We have preferred some of them over others. We delivered it to one believer and withheld it from another believer, and delivered it to a disbeliever and withheld it from another disbeliever. Allah the Exalted has made clear the wisdom in this disparity, saying: ﴿We have apportioned among them their livelihood in the life of this world, and raised some of them above others in degrees, that some of them may take others in service﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 32]. He also said at the end of Surat al-An'am: ﴿And He raised some of you above others in degrees that He may test you through what He has given you﴾ [al-An'am: 165].

\* \* \*

Then He said: ﴿And the Hereafter is greater in degrees and greater in preference﴾. The meaning is: the difference among creatures in the degrees of the benefits of this world is perceptible, so their difference in the degrees of the benefits of the Hereafter is greater and more magnificent. The ratio of the difference in the degrees of the Hereafter to the difference in the degrees of this world is like the ratio of the Hereafter to this world. So if a person's desire is intense in seeking the excellence of this world, then his desire for the excellence of the Hereafter should be all the more intense.

The second statement: the intended meaning is that the Hereafter is greater and more noble than this world. The meaning is that the believers enter Paradise and the disbelievers enter the Fire, so the superiority of the believers over the disbelievers becomes manifest. A parallel to this is His saying the Exalted: ﴿The companions of Paradise on that Day are better in their abode and finer in their resting place﴾ [al-Furqan: 24].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verse 22:

Page 146

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Do not set up with Allah another god, lest you sit down reproached and forsaken.﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: explaining the connection of the discourse (wajh al-nazm). We say: when Allah the Exalted explained that people are of two groups, among them those who intend by their deeds the worldly life alone, and they are the people of punishment and torment, and among them those who intend by it obedience to Allah, and they are the people of reward, He then stipulated three conditions for this:

The first of them: the intention of the Hereafter.

The second: that one perform a deed and strive an effort that is consistent with seeking the Hereafter.

The third: that one be a believer. Accordingly, in this verse He detailed those general matters, beginning first by explaining the reality of faith. The noblest part of faith is monotheism (tawhid) and the negation of partners and rivals, so He said: ﴿Do not set up with Allah another god.﴾ Then He mentioned after it the rest of the deeds, which the one who undertakes them and occupies himself with them is striving an effort befitting the seeking of the Hereafter, and becomes of those whose fortune is blessed, whose lot is good, and whose conditions are perfected.

The second issue: The exegetes said: this is, outwardly, an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), but in meaning it is general to all accountable persons, as in His saying: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women...﴾ [al-Talaq: 1]. It is also possible that the address is to the human being, as if it were said: "O human, do not set up with Allah another god." This possibility is, in my view, more preferable, because He Exalted joined to it His saying: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾ [al-Isra': 23] up to His saying: ﴿If one of them or both of them reach old age with you﴾ [al-Isra': 23], and this is not fitting for the Prophet (peace be upon him), since his parents had not reached old age in his lifetime. So we know that the one addressed by this is the category of humankind.

The third issue: the meaning of the verse is that whoever associates others with Allah is reproached and forsaken. What indicates that the matter is so are several points:

The first: the associator is a liar, and the liar deserves blame and abandonment.

The second: since it is established by proof that there is no god, no governor, and no determiner except the One, the Unique, then on this assumption all blessings are from Allah the Exalted. Whoever associates others with Allah has attributed some of those blessings to other than Allah the Exalted, while the truth is that all of them are from Allah. Then he deserves blame, because the Creator, the Exalted, deserves thanks for bestowing those blessings; when he denies that they are from Allah, he has repaid the kindness of Allah the Exalted with evil, ingratitude and disbelief, and so he deserves blame. We said that he deserves abandonment because, when he affirmed a partner for Allah the Exalted, he deserved that his affair be entrusted to that partner; since that partner is nonexistent, he remains without helper, protector or supporter. And that is the very essence of abandonment.

The third: perfection lies in unity and deficiency lies in multiplicity, so whoever affirms a partner has fallen on the side of deficiency and deserves blame and abandonment. Know that since the wording of the verse indicates that the associator is reproached and forsaken, it necessarily follows by the ruling of the verse that the monotheist is praised and supported. And Allah knows best.

The fourth issue: the "sitting" mentioned in His saying: ﴿lest you sit down reproached and forsaken﴾ has several interpretations:

The first: its meaning is remaining (al-muktht), that is, "lest you remain among people reproached and forsaken." This expression is used in the language of the Arabs and the Persians with this meaning: when a man asks another, "What is so-and-so doing in that town?" the answerer says, "He is sitting in the worst of states," meaning: remaining, whether standing or sitting.

The second: it is the nature of one who is reproached and forsaken to sit regretful and reflecting upon what has escaped from him.

The third: one who is able to obtain the goods strives to obtain them, and striving is only achieved by standing; as for one who is incapable of obtaining them, he does not strive but remains seated, refraining from seeking. Since standing for a man is one of the matters by which success in goods is completed, and sitting and remaining seated are a sign of the lack of that ability and power, standing has therefore been made a metaphor for the capacity to obtain goods, and sitting a metaphor for incapacity and weakness.

Page 147

The fifth issue: al-Wahidi said: His saying ﴿fa-taqʿuda﴾ (then you sit) is in the accusative because it came after the fa' as a response (jawab) to the prohibition (nahy), and its accusative is by the implied "an" (that), as when you say: "Do not cut yourself off from us, lest we shun you" (la tanqati' 'anna fa-najfuwaka). The sense is: let there be no cutting off from you, so that the result is that we shun you. Thus what follows the fa' is connected to the preceding clause by the fa' which is a conjunction. The grammarians called it a response (jawab) because it resembles the conditional (jaza') in that the second is caused by the first. Do you not see that the meaning is: if your estrangement is cut off, then...? Similarly the estimated sense of the verse is: if you set up with Allah another god, you will sit reproached and forsaken.

**His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾.**

Know that when He mentioned in the first verse the greatest pillar of faith, He followed it with mention of what belongs to the rites and conditions of faith, and these are of several kinds.

The first kind: that a person be occupied with the worship of God, exalted is He, and be guarded against worshipping anyone other than God, exalted is He. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾. Concerning it there are two discussions.

The first discussion: *al-qada'* (decree) means a firm, definitive ruling that does not admit of *naskh* (abrogation). The proof for this is that when one of us orders another to do something, it is not said that he "decreed" it upon him. But if he orders him with a firm command and rules upon him with that ruling in a definitive and conclusive manner, then it is said: he decreed it upon him. The word *qada'*, in its basic linguistic sense, refers to the completion and termination of a thing.

Maymun ibn Mihran narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: In this verse the original reading was *"wa-wassa rabbuka"* (and your Lord has enjoined), so one of the two waws joined with the sad, and it was read as *"wa-qada rabbuka"* (and your Lord has decreed). Then he said: Had it been [truly] a matter of *qada'* (decree), no one would ever have disobeyed God, because opposing the decree of God is impossible. Al-Dahhak and Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated this from him in the same way, and it is the reading of 'Ali and 'Abd Allah.

Know that this view is very far-fetched, because it opens the door to the claim that distortion and alteration have entered the Qur'an. If we permitted that, the security of the Qur'an would be lifted, and that would remove it from being a proof. Without doubt, this is a grave attack upon the religion.

The second discussion: We have mentioned that this verse indicates the obligation of worshipping God, exalted is He, and indicates the prohibition of worshipping other than God, exalted is He. This is the truth, because *'ibadah* (worship) is an expression for an act that includes the utmost degree of glorification. The utmost degree of glorification is fitting only for the one from whom the utmost degree of bounty proceeds. The utmost degree of bounty is the bestowal of existence, life, power, desire and intellect. It has been established by proofs that the One who bestows these things is God, exalted is He, and no other. When the One who bestows all blessings is God alone and no other, it follows necessarily that the One deserving worship is God, exalted is He, and no other. Thus the correctness of His saying, ﴿Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾, is established by rational proof.
