**His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And to parents, kindness. Whether one or both of them reach old age with you, do not say to them "uff," nor rebuke them, but speak to them a generous word. And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy, and say: "My Lord, have mercy on them as they raised me when I was small." Your Lord knows best what is in your souls. If you are righteous, then indeed He is ever forgiving to those who turn back [to Him]﴾.**

In the verse there are several issues.

The first issue: Know that He, exalted is He, commanded the worship of Himself, then followed it with the command to show kindness to parents. The explanation of the connection between the command to worship God, exalted is He, and the command to be kind to parents is in several respects.

The first respect: The true cause of a person's existence is the creation and bringing into being by God, exalted is He, while the apparent cause is the two parents. So He commanded the glorification of the true cause, then followed it with the command to glorify the apparent cause.

The second respect: What exists is either eternal or originated. A person's dealings with the eternal God must be with glorification and servitude, and with what is originated must be with the showing of compassion. This is what is meant by his, peace be upon him, saying: "Glorifying the command of God and compassion toward the creatures of God." The most deserving of creatures to whom compassion should be directed are the two parents, because of the abundance of their bounty upon a person. So His saying, ﴿Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾, is an indication of glorifying the command of God, and His saying, ﴿And to parents, kindness﴾, is an indication of compassion toward the creatures of God.

The third respect: Giving thanks to the benefactor is obligatory. The true benefactor is the Creator, glorified and exalted is He. Sometimes one of the created beings is a benefactor to you, and thanking him is also obligatory, due to his, peace be upon him, saying: "Whoever does not thank people has not thanked God." No creature has a bounty upon a person like that of the two parents. Its explanation is in several ways:

One: The child is a part of the parents. He, peace be upon him, said: "Fatimah is a part of me."

Two: The compassion of the parents toward the child is great, and their striving to bring good to the child is like a natural matter, and their avoidance of bringing harm to him is like a natural matter. When the motives to bring good are abundant and the obstacles to it are removed, there is without doubt much bringing of good. Therefore the bounties of the parents upon the child must be more numerous than any bounty that comes from one person to another.

Three: When a person is in the utmost weakness and the extreme of helplessness, he is under the favor of his parents. The kinds of their bounties at that time reach him, and the kinds of the mercy of that child reach the parents at that time. It is known that when a favor occurs in this manner, its position is great.

Four: The bringing of good to another may be for the motive of bringing good to him, and all other motives may mix with this purpose. But the bringing of good to the child is not for this purpose alone. Thus the favor in it is more complete and perfect. It is established that no creature has a bounty upon another like that of the parents upon the child. Therefore God, exalted is He, began with giving thanks for the bounty of the Creator, which is His saying, ﴿Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾, then He followed it with giving thanks for the bounty of the parents, which is His saying, ﴿And to parents, kindness﴾. The reason for this is what we have explained: that the greatest of bounties after the favor of the Creator God is the bounty of the parents.

If it is said: The two parents only sought to obtain pleasure for themselves, so it followed that the child entered existence and came into being in the world of calamities and dangers. What favor then do the parents have upon the child? It is related that one of those known for wisdom used to strike his father and say: "He is the one who brought me into the world of generation and corruption, and exposed me to death, poverty, blindness and affliction." It was said to Abu al-'Ala al-Ma'arri: "What shall we write on your grave?" He said: "Write upon it:"

*This is what my father committed against me, and I committed nothing against anyone.*

And he said regarding abstaining from marriage and children:

*I left my children while they were in the bliss of non-existence, which preceded the delight of the immediate world.*
*Had they been born, they would have endured a severity that casts them into the ruinous things of the hereafter.*

It was said to Alexander: "Is your teacher greater in bounty upon you, or your father?" He said: "The teacher is greater in bounty, because he bore various kinds of hardships and trials in teaching me. He nourished me in the light of knowledge. As for the father, he sought to obtain the pleasure of intercourse for himself, and he brought me out into the calamities of the world of generation and corruption." Among the famous sayings that have been transmitted is: "The best of fathers is the one who teaches you."

The answer: Grant that they at the beginning of the matter sought the pleasure of intercourse. Yet is not the concern with bringing goods and averting calamities from the moment of his entering existence until the time he reaches old age greater than all that can be imagined of the aspects of good and benevolence? Thus these doubts fall away. And God knows best.

The second issue: His saying, ﴿And to parents, kindness﴾. The linguists said: The estimate of the verse is: "Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but God, and that you act kindly," or it is said: "He decreed that you worship none but Him, and be kind to the parents with kindness." Al-Zamakhshari, the author of *al-Kashshaf*, said: The *ba'* in *"wa-bil-walidayni"* (and to the parents) cannot be connected to *al-ihsan* (kindness), because the verbal noun cannot have its complement precede it. He then did not mention any proof that a verbal noun may not have its complement precede it. Al-Wahidi said in *al-Basit*: The *ba'* in *"wa-bil-walidayni"* is part of the complement of *al-ihsan*, and it has been placed before it, as you say: "Bi-Zayd, fa-mrur" (with Zayd, then pass by). This example that al-Wahidi mentioned does not match, because what is required is the placing of the complement of the verbal noun before it, and the example mentioned is not like that.

The third issue: Al-Qaffal said: The term *ihsan* is sometimes connected with the particle *ba'*, and at other times with *ila* (to). Likewise *isa'ah* (wrongdoing): it is said *ahsantu bihi* and *ahsantu ilayhi* (I did well by him/to him), and *asa'tu bihi* and *asa'tu ilayhi* (I did badly by him/to him). God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And He has been good to me﴾ [Yusuf: 100]. And the poet said:

*Treat us badly or treat us well; there is no blame on us, nor are we disliked, if she should turn away.*

I say: The wording of the verse includes many restrictions, each of which requires exaggeration in kindness to the parents:

One: He, exalted is He, said in the previous verse: ﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it with the striving due to it while being a believer, those are the ones whose striving will be appreciated﴾ [al-Isra': 19]. Then He followed it with this verse, which includes the deeds through which success in the happiness of the Hereafter is attained. He mentioned among them righteousness toward parents, and this indicates that this obedience is among the foundational acts of obedience that produce the happiness of the Hereafter.

Two: He, exalted is He, began with mentioning the command to monotheism, repeated with obedience to God, exalted is He, and then a third time with righteousness toward parents. This is a lofty rank and a great emphasis on the glorification of this act of obedience.

Three: He, exalted is He, did not say *"wa-ihsanan bil-walidayni"* but said: ﴿And to parents, kindness﴾. The placing of their mention first indicates the intensity of concern.

Four: He said *"ihsanan"* in indefinite form, and indefiniteness indicates glorification. The meaning is: "Your Lord has decreed that you be kind to the parents with a great, complete kindness." This is because, since their kindness toward you has reached the greatest extent, it is necessary that your kindness toward them be likewise. Then, in all estimations, there is no recompense, because their favor upon you was in the manner of initiation, and in the well-known proverbs it is said: the one who initiates goodness is not repaid.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Whether one or both of them reach old age with you﴾, and in it there are issues.

The first issue: The word *"immā"* is a compound word made of two words: *in* and *ma*. As for *in*, it is a conditional particle. As for *ma*, it is also a conditional particle, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whatever verse We abrogate﴾ [al-Baqarah: 106]. When the two words are combined, they convey emphasis in the sense of conditionality. However, the sign of the jussive did not appear with the *nun* of emphasis (*nun al-tawkid*), because the verb is built (mabni) when it takes the *nun* of emphasis. I say: A questioner may ask: The *nun* of emphasis is only fitting in a place where the appropriate thing is to emphasize that judgment mentioned and to establish it in the strongest manner. But this meaning is not fitting in this place, because when someone says: "The thing is either this or that," what is intended is the alternation of the judgment between those two mentioned things, and this place does not suit emphasis and affirmation. So how is it fitting to combine *immā* with the *nun* of emphasis?

The answer: The meaning is that this judgment, which is firmly established and emphasized, either occurs or does not occur. And God knows best.

The second issue: The majority read: ﴿Whether one of them or both of them reach old age with you﴾, and according to this reading, *"yablughanna"* is a verb whose subject is *"ahaduhuma"* (one of them), and *"aw kilahuma"* (or both of them) is coordinated with it, as in your saying: "Darab Zayd aw 'Amr" (Zayd or 'Amr struck). If the verb *"yablughanna"* were attributed to *"kilahuma"*, it would be permissible because the verb precedes, as you say: "Qala rajulun" (a man said), "Qala rajulani" (two men said), and "Qalat al-rijalu" (the men said). Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *"yablughani"* (they two reach). According to this reading, *"ahaduhuma"* is an apposition (badal) for the *alif* of the pronoun referring to the two parents, and *"kilahuma"* is coordinated with *"ahaduhuma"*, either as the subject or as an apposition.

If it is said: If it were said *"immā yablughāni kilāhumā"* (whether both of them reach old age), then *"kilāhumā"* would be a corroborative (tawkid), not an apposition. So why do you claim it is an apposition?

We reply: Because it is coordinated with something that cannot validly be a corroborative for the dual, so it took its ruling and must be like it in being an apposition.

[Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verse 23 (part 2 of 2)]

If it is asked: why is it not permissible to say that His saying ﴿one of them﴾ is a *badal* (substitute, in apposition), and His saying ﴿or both of them﴾ is a *tawkid* (emphasis), and that this is a *ʿatf* (conjunction) of the emphasis upon the substitute?

We say: *ʿatf* requires sharing, so one of them was made a *badal* and the other a *tawkid*, contrary to the original arrangement. And God knows best.

The third issue: Abu al-Haytham al-Razi, Abu al-Fath al-Mawsili and Abu ʿAli al-Jurjani said: *kilā* (كِلا, "both") is a singular noun that conveys the meaning of duality. Its pattern is *fiʿal*, and its final radical is weak, like the final radical of *ḥijan* and *riḍan*. It is a word established in this form, used to emphasize exactly two, and it never occurs except in construct (mudaf). The proof is that if it were a dual (*tathniyah*), then in the accusative and genitive one would have to say *marartu bi-kilay al-rajulayn* with a kasra on the yāʾ, just as one says *bayna yadayi al-rajul*, *min thulthayi al-layl*, *wa-ya ṣāḥibayi al-sijn*, and *wa-ṭarafayi al-nahār*. Since the matter is not like that, we know that it is not a dual but a singular word established to indicate duality, just as the word *kull* (كُلّ, "all") is a single noun established for the group. Accordingly, you refer to its form as you would refer to a singular, as in His saying: ﴿And each of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone﴾ [Maryam: 95]. Likewise, when you refer to *kilā*, you refer to it as a singular, so you say: "*kilā ikhwatika kāna qāʾiman*" ("both your brothers was standing"). God the Exalted said: ﴿Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce﴾ [al-Kahf: 33], and He did not say "*ātatā*." And God knows best.

Know that when God mentioned this sentence, at this point of the mention He imposed upon the human being five obligations regarding the two parents:

The first type: His saying: ﴿So do not say to them, "Uff"﴾. On this there are several issues:

The first issue: al-Zajjaj said: In it there are seven dialects: the *fāʾ* with a kasra, with a ḍamma, and with a fatḥa, and each of these three is either with *tanwīn* or without *tanwīn*, which makes six. The seventh dialect is *Uffī* with a yāʾ. Al-Akhfash said: It is as if he attributed this utterance to himself, saying "my saying is this." Ibn al-Anbari mentioned three further dialects of this word beyond what al-Zajjaj mentioned: *Iff* with a kasra on the alif and a fatḥa on the fāʾ; *Uffah* with a ḍamma on the alif and with the addition of a hāʾ; and *Uff* with a ḍamma on the alif and a sukun on the fāʾ.

The second issue: Ibn Kathir and Ibn ʿAmir read it with a fatḥa on the fāʾ without *tanwīn*. Nafiʿ and Ḥafṣ read it with a kasra on the fāʾ and with *tanwīn*. The rest read it with a kasra on the fāʾ without *tanwīn*. All of these are dialects. The same difference occurs in surah al-Anbiya: ﴿Uff to you﴾ [al-Anbiya: 67], and in al-Ahqaf: ﴿Uff to both of you﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 17]. I say: the difficult question here is this: since we have transmitted ten kinds of dialects for this word, what is the reason that they left most of those dialects in the recitation of this word and restricted themselves to a few of them?

The third issue: The scholars mentioned several explanations of this word:

The first: al-Farraʾ said: The Arabs say: "So-and-so began to say *tafaffa* (ugh) because of a smell he found," meaning that he kept saying "Uff, uff."

The second: al-Asmaʿi said: *al-Uff* is the ear's wax, and *al-Tuff* is the fingernail's dirt. This is said when something is found disgusting, and then it became widespread until they used it for everything that harms them.

The third: Some said: *Uff* means "little," and it is derived from *al-afīf*, which is a small amount of something. *Tuff* is a follower of it, like their saying: *shayṭān layṭān*, "wicked, corrupt" (*khabīth nabīth*).

The fourth: Thaʿlab related from Ibn al-Aʿrabi: *al-Uff* is annoyance.

The fifth: al-Qutaybi said: The origin of this word is that when dust or ash falls on you, you blow on it to remove it, and the sound produced by that blowing is your saying "*uff*." Then they extended it, mentioning this word at every disliked thing that reaches them.

The sixth: al-Zajjaj said: "*Uff*" means foulness (*nataan*), and this is the view of Mujahid, because he said the meaning of His saying ﴿So do not say to them, "Uff"﴾ is: do not be disgusted by them, just as they were not disgusted by you when you soiled yourself or urinated. In another report from Mujahid: if you find from them an odour that harms you, then do not say to them "Uff."

**[Page 152]**

**Fourth issue:** The saying of the speaker, "Do not say *uff* ("tut") to so-and-so," is a proverb used to forbid every kind of displeasure and harm, however slight or minor. The scholars of legal theory (*usuliyyun*) disagreed over whether the indication of this expression to prohibit all other kinds of harm is a *lafzi* indication (indicated by the wording itself) or an indication understood through *qiyas* (analogical reasoning). Some said it is a *lafzi* indication, because when people of common usage say, "Do not say *uff* to so-and-so," they mean that one should not harass him or cause him any kind of harm or distress. This is like their saying, "So-and-so does not own a *naqir* or a *qitmir*," meaning that by common usage it indicates that he owns nothing at all.

The second view is that this expression indicates the prohibition of all other kinds of harm only through clear analogy (*al-qiyas al-jali*). Its explanation is that when the Law (*al-shar'*) states a ruling explicitly for one case and remains silent about another case, and we wish to attach the silent case to the explicitly stated case, this is of three types:

First: the ruling is more applicable in the silent case than in the explicitly mentioned case. An example is this: the expression prohibits saying *uff*, and striking is more deserving of prohibition than saying *uff*.

Second: the ruling in the silent case is equal to the ruling in the explicitly mentioned case. This is what the scholars of legal theory call *al-qiyas fi ma'na al-asl* (analogy in the meaning of the original case). For this they gave the example of his saying (ﷺ): "Whoever frees his share of a slave, the remainder is valued upon him," since the ruling for the female slave and the male slave is equal.

Third: the ruling in the silent case is less evident than the ruling in the explicitly mentioned case, and this is the strongest type of analogy.

Once you know this, we say: the prohibition of *uff* indicates the prohibition of striking only through clear analogy, which is of the type of deriving the lesser to prove the greater. The evidence for this is that *uff* is other than striking, so the prohibition of *uff* is not in itself a prohibition of striking. Also, the prohibition of *uff* does not logically entail the prohibition of striking, because when a great king captures a mighty king who is his enemy, he may say to the executioner, "Beware lest you belittle him or address him with a hurtful word, but strike his neck." If this is understood in general, we know that the prohibition of *uff* is distinct from the prohibition of striking and does not logically entail the prohibition of striking in general. Yet in this case we know that the purpose of this statement is to emphasize the honouring of the two parents, as shown by His saying: ﴿And speak to them a generous word﴾ ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy﴾. Thus the indication of the prohibition of *uff* on the prohibition of striking is of the type of analogy from the lesser to the greater. And Allah knows best.

**The second type** of the things which Allah the Exalted obligated His servants to do regarding the two parents is His saying: ﴿And do not scold them﴾. It is said: *nahara-hu* and *intahara-hu* when one confronts him with words that rebuke him. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And as for the petitioner, do not scold [him]﴾ [al-Duha: 10].

If it is objected: the prohibition of *uff* indicates the prohibition of scolding by way of priority, so when He first mentioned the prohibition of *uff*, mentioning the prohibition of scolding after it is pointless. But if we suppose He had first mentioned the prohibition of scolding and then followed it with the prohibition of *uff*, it would be useful and fine, because the prohibition of scolding necessarily entails the prohibition of *uff*. So what is the reason for observing this order?

We reply: what is meant by His saying ﴿So do not say to them *uff*﴾ is the prohibition of showing irritation, whether slight or great. And what is meant by His saying ﴿And do not scold them﴾ is the prohibition of showing opposition in speech by way of rejecting and contradicting him.

**The third type** is His saying the Exalted: ﴿And speak to them a generous word﴾. Know that when Allah the Exalted prohibited man, in the preceding verse, from uttering harmful and distressing speech, the prohibition of harmful speech does not amount to a command to speak kindly. Therefore, He followed it with a command to speak good and pleasant words, saying: ﴿And speak to them a generous word﴾. What is meant is that one should address them with speech accompanied by signs of honour and respect. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) said: it is that he says to them, "O my father, O my mother." Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab was asked about the generous word and said: it is the speech of a sinful slave to a harsh master. It is reported from ʿAta' that it means: that you speak with them on condition that you do not raise your voice over them and do not fix your gaze upon them, because these two acts contradict the generous word.

If it is objected: Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was the greatest of people in forbearance, generosity and courtesy. How then did he say to his father—according to the reading of the one who reads (*wa-idh qala Ibrahimu li-abihi Azaru*) with the *damma*—﴿Indeed I see you and your people in manifest error﴾ [al-An'am: 74]? He addressed him by his name, which is harmful, and then attributed him and his people to error, which is the gravest kind of harm.

We reply: the statement of the Exalted, ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you not worship except Him, and to parents, good treatment﴾, indicates that the right of Allah the Exalted takes precedence over the right of the parents. Ibrahim's (peace be upon him) proceeding with that harm was merely giving precedence to the right of Allah the Exalted over the right of the parents.

**The fourth type** is His saying: ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy﴾. What is intended by it is emphasis on humility. Al-Qaffal (may Allah have mercy on him) mentioned two explanations in its interpretation:

[**Page 153**]

The first: when a bird wishes to gather its chick to itself for nurturing, it lowers its wing for it. For this reason, lowering the wing became a metaphor for good upbringing. So it is as if He said to the child: take care of your parents by gathering them to yourself, just as they did with you when you were young.

The second: when a bird wishes to fly and rise up, it spreads its wing; when it wishes to stop flying and stop rising, it lowers its wing. Thus lowering the wing became a metaphor for the act of humility from this aspect.

If it is objected: how did He attribute the wing to humility, when humility has no wing?

We reply: there are two answers:

The first: the wing was attributed to humility as one says *Hatim al-Jud* (Hatim of generosity). Just as there the meaning is "Hatim the generous," so here the meaning is: "lower your humble wing to them," i.e., the wing that is humbled.

The second: the basis of metaphor rests on imagination. So here he imagined a wing for humility and attributed weakness to that wing, to complete the image of this metaphor, as Labid said:

*When she became in the hand of the north wind her reins*

He attributed a hand to the north wind and placed her reins in the hand of the north wind, so likewise here.

His saying ﴿out of mercy﴾ means: let the lowering of your wing to them be due to the abundance of your mercy towards them and your tenderness toward them because of their old age and weakness.

**The fifth type** is His saying: ﴿And say: My Lord, have mercy on them as they brought me up when I was small﴾. In this there are several discussions:

**First discussion:** Al-Qaffal (may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him) said: in teaching righteousness towards parents, He did not limit Himself to teaching words, but added to it teaching actions, namely that one should invoke mercy for them, saying: ﴿My Lord, have mercy on them﴾. The word *mercy* encompasses all good in religion and in this world. Then He says: ﴿as they brought me up when I was small﴾, specifying: "Lord, do with them this kind of goodness as they did goodness to me in raising me." *Tarbiya* (upbringing) is *tanmiya* (development), and it derives from the saying "*raba al-shay'*" when a thing benefits or grows, and from it His saying the Exalted: ﴿But when We send down upon it water, it quivers and swells﴾ [al-Hajj: 5].

**Second discussion:** The exegetes differed concerning this verse in three views:

The first view: it is abrogated by His saying the Exalted: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawbah: 113]. So it is not fitting for a Muslim to seek forgiveness for his parents if they are polytheists, nor to say: "My Lord, have mercy on them."

The second view: this verse is not abrogated, but it is specified (*makhsus*) in the case of polytheists. This is preferable to the first view, because specification is preferable to abrogation (*naskh*).

The third view: there is neither abrogation nor specification, because if the parents are unbelievers, he may invoke for them guidance and right direction, and ask for mercy for them after they attain faith.

**Third discussion:** The apparent meaning of a command is obligation. So His saying: ﴿And say: My Lord, have mercy on them as they brought me up when I was small﴾ is a command, and the apparent meaning of a command does not imply repetition. Therefore, in acting upon the requirement of this verse, it suffices to say this statement once. Sufyan was asked: how many times does a person invoke for his parents? Is it once a day, or once a month, or once a year? He said: we hope that it suffices for him if he invokes for them at the end of the *tashahhud*, just as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O you who believe, send blessings upon him﴾ [al-Ahzab: 56], and they used to consider that the *tashahhud* suffices as the sending of blessings upon the Prophet (ﷺ). And just as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And remember Allah during numbered days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 203], and they repeat it after the prayers.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Your Lord is most knowing of what is in your souls, if you are righteous﴾. The meaning is: We have commanded you in this verse to devote worship sincerely to Allah the Exalted and to do good to the parents. Nothing is hidden from Allah of what you conceal in your souls, whether of sincerity in obedience or of lack of sincerity in it. So know that Allah the Exalted is aware of what is in your souls; indeed He knows those states better than you do, because human knowledge may be mixed with forgetfulness, heedlessness and failure to encompass everything. But the knowledge of Allah is exempt from all of these states. Since the matter is thus, He knows everything in your hearts. The purpose of this is a warning against abandoning sincerity.

\* \* \*

Then He said the Exalted: ﴿if you are righteous﴾, i.e., if you are free from the causes of corruption in the states of your hearts, you are *awwabin*, i.e., those who turn back repeatedly to Allah and devote themselves to Him in all deeds. The custom and judgment of Allah regarding the *awwabin* is that He is Forgiving towards them and expiates their evil deeds for them. The *awwab* is one whose habit and constant practice is returning to the command of Allah the Exalted and seeking refuge in His grace, and he does not seek refuge in the intercession of an intercessor, as the polytheists do when they worship, besides Allah, an inanimate thing, claiming that it will intercede for them. The word *awwab* is of the form *fa''al*, which indicates persistence and abundance, like their saying *qattal* (one who kills much) and *darrab* (one who strikes much).

If that lapse was not for the sake of disobedience but arose from the natural human constitution, it falls under forgiveness. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verse 26–28:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And give to the near of kin his right, and to the needy and the wayfarer, and do not squander wastefully.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the wasteful are brothers of the devils, and ever has Satan been to his Lord ungrateful.﴾ ﴿And if you turn away from them, seeking mercy from your Lord which you expect, then speak to them a gentle word.﴾

Know that this is the fourth kind of good deeds and acts of obedience mentioned in these verses, and in it there are issues:

The first issue: His saying, ﴿And give﴾ — to whom is the address? There are two opinions:

The first opinion: It is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ), so Allah commanded him to give his relatives the rights that were due to them from the fay' (booty without fighting) and the ghanimah (spoils of war). He was also obligated to give the right of the needy and the wayfarer from these two sources.

The second opinion: It is an address to everyone. The evidence for this is that it is joined by conjunction to His saying: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you not worship except Him﴾ [al-Isra' 23]. The meaning is: after you have finished with dutifulness to the two parents, you must busy yourself with dutifulness to the rest of the relatives, the nearest then the nearest, then with improving the conditions of the needy and the wayfarers.

Know that His saying, ﴿And give the near of kin his right﴾, is general (mujmal), and there is no explanation in it of what that right is. According to al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, spending is obligatory only upon children and parents. Some people said: spending upon the unmarriageable kin (mahram) is obligatory to the extent of need. They agreed that whoever is not a mahram, such as paternal cousins, has no right except affection, visiting, good companionship, and friendship in ease and hardship. As for the needy and the wayfarer, their description has already been mentioned in Surat al-Tawbah in the explanation of the verse on zakah. It is obligatory to give the needy what suffices for his sustenance and the sustenance of his dependents, and to give the wayfarer what suffices him of provisions and mount until he reaches his destination.
* * *
Then He said: ﴿And do not squander wastefully.﴾ Tabdhir (squandering) in the language is the corruption of wealth and spending it in extravagance. ʿUthman ibn al-Aswad said: I was circumambulating the Ka'bah with Mujahid in the mosques, and he raised his head toward Abu Qubays and said: "If a man spent the like of this in the obedience of Allah, he would not be among the extravagant; and if he spent one dirham in the disobedience of Allah, he would be among the extravagant." Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verse 26–28:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And give to the near of kin his right, and to the needy and the wayfarer, and do not squander wastefully.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the wasteful are brothers of the devils, and ever has Satan been to his Lord ungrateful.﴾ ﴿And if you turn away from them, seeking mercy from your Lord which you expect, then speak to them a gentle word.﴾

Know that this is the fourth kind of good deeds and acts of obedience mentioned in these verses, and in it there are issues:

The first issue: His saying, ﴿And give﴾ — to whom is the address? There are two opinions:

The first opinion: It is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ), so Allah commanded him to give his relatives the rights that were due to them from the fay' (booty without fighting) and the ghanimah (spoils of war). He was also obligated to give the right of the needy and the wayfarer from these two sources.

The second opinion: It is an address to everyone. The evidence for this is that it is joined by conjunction to His saying: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you not worship except Him﴾ [al-Isra' 23]. The meaning is: after you have finished with dutifulness to the two parents, you must busy yourself with dutifulness to the rest of the relatives, the nearest then the nearest, then with improving the conditions of the needy and the wayfarers.

Know that His saying, ﴿And give the near of kin his right﴾, is general (mujmal), and there is no explanation in it of what that right is. According to al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, spending is obligatory only upon children and parents. Some people said: spending upon the unmarriageable kin (mahram) is obligatory to the extent of need. They agreed that whoever is not a mahram, such as paternal cousins, has no right except affection, visiting, good companionship, and friendship in ease and hardship. As for the needy and the wayfarer, their description has already been mentioned in Surat al-Tawbah in the explanation of the verse on zakah. It is obligatory to give the needy what suffices for his sustenance and the sustenance of his dependents, and to give the wayfarer what suffices him of provisions and mount until he reaches his destination.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verse 29–30:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it fully outstretched, lest you sit reproached and destitute.﴾ ﴿Indeed, your Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts [it]. Indeed, He is ever, of His servants, Acquainted and Seeing.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, commanded him to spend in the previous verse, He taught him in this verse the etiquette of spending. Know also that He, exalted is He, described the spending of His believing servants in Surat al-Furqan, saying: ﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy, but are ever, between that, justly balanced﴾ [al-Furqan: 67]. Here He commanded His Messenger with the like of that description, saying: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾, meaning: do not withhold from spending to the extent that you constrict yourself and your family in the ways of maintaining kinship and the paths of good works. The meaning: do not make your hand, in its contraction, like one that is chained and prevented from extending. ﴿Nor extend it fully outstretched﴾, meaning: do not expand in spending to an excessive degree such that nothing remains in your hand. The summary of the matter: the wise men mentioned in the books of "Ethics" that every moral trait has two extremes, excess and deficiency, and both are blameworthy. Miserliness is excess in withholding, and squandering is excess in spending, and both are blameworthy, while the virtuous trait is justice and the middle, as Almighty God said: ﴿And thus We have made you a justly balanced community﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143].

* * *
Then Almighty God said: ﴿lest you sit reproached and destitute﴾. As for the explanation of "sit" (taqʿuda), it has already been given in the previous verse. As for being "reproached" (malūman), it is because he reproaches himself, and his companions also reproach him for squandering the wealth entirely and leaving his family and children in harm and distress. As for being "destitute" (maḥsūran), al-Farrāʾ said: the Arabs say of a camel, "it is maḥsūr" when its journey has ceased, and "I exhausted the animal" (ḥasartu al-dābba) when I drove it until its journey ceased. From this is the saying of Almighty God: ﴿Your sight will return to you dazed, while it is fatigued﴾ [al-Mulk: 4]. The plural of ḥasīr is ḥasrā, like qatlā and ṣarʿā. Al-Qaffāl said: the intention is to liken the state of one who spends all his wealth and expenses to one who is cut off on his journey because his mount has failed, for that amount of wealth is like a mount that carries a person and brings him to the end of the month or the year, just as that camel carries him and brings him to the end of the stage. When that camel fails, he remains in the middle of the road, helpless and bewildered; likewise, when a person spends the amount he needs for a month, he remains in the middle of that month helpless and bewildered. Whoever does this will incur blame from his family and from those in need of his support, due to his poor management and his neglect of prudence in the affairs of his livelihood.

* * *
Then Almighty God said: ﴿Indeed, your Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts﴾. The intention is that He made His Messenger ﷺ aware that He is a Lord (Rabb). The Lord (al-Rabb) is the One who nurtures the one being nurtured, takes charge of his affairs and meets his needs according to what is right and proper, so He widens provision for some and restricts it for others. The qadr in language means restriction, and from it is the saying of Almighty God: ﴿And whoever has his provision restricted﴾ [al-Talaq: 7], and His saying: ﴿But as for when He tests him and restricts his provision for him﴾ [al-Fajr: 16], meaning: He constricted. He widened it for some only because that is what is good for them. Almighty God said: ﴿And if God extended provision to His servants, they would surely rebel in the earth, but He sends down in measure what He wills﴾ [al-Shura: 27].
* * *
Then Almighty God said: ﴿Indeed, He is ever, of His servants, Acquainted and Seeing﴾, meaning: Almighty God is knowing that the benefit of every person lies in His giving him only that measure. Thus the variation in the provision of His servants is not due to stinginess, but for the sake of attending to their benefits.
