Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verse 31:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty. We provide for them and for you. Indeed, their killing is ever a great sin.﴾

This is the fifth type of obedience mentioned in these verses. There are several issues concerning this verse.

The first issue: concerning the arrangement (nazm) of the verse, there are several aspects.

The first aspect: when He, exalted is He, made clear in the previous verse that He is the One who undertakes the provision of His servants, saying, ﴿Indeed, your Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it﴾, He followed it with His saying, ﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty. We provide for them and for you.﴾

The second aspect: when He, exalted is He, taught the manner of goodness to parents in the preceding verse, He taught in this verse the manner of goodness to children. For this reason some have said: those who are called "the righteous" (al-abrar) were only named so because they were good to both parents and children. The obligation of goodness to parents is in recompense for what they gave of various kinds of goodness to their children. The obligation of goodness to children arises because they are in extreme weakness and have no guardian other than their parents.

The third aspect: the refusal of children to be good to their parents leads to the ruin of the world, because when parents know this, their desire to raise children diminishes, and so the ruin of the world follows from the way we have described. Thus it is established that the flourishing of the world is only achieved when goodness between parents and children is present from both sides.

The fourth aspect: if the killing of children is out of fear of poverty, then it is an evil opinion about God; and if it is for the sake of jealousy over daughters, then it is an effort to ruin the world. The first is contrary to the glorification of God's command, and the second is contrary to compassion for God's creation, and both are blameworthy. And God knows best.

The fifth aspect: the kinship of children is a kinship of part and portion, and it is among the greatest causes of love. So if love is absent, that indicates a severe coarseness of spirit and hardness of heart, and that is among the most blameworthy of characters. Therefore God encouraged kindness to children in order to remove this blameworthy trait.

The second issue: the Arabs used to kill daughters because daughters are unable to earn, while sons are able to do so through their raiding and plundering. Also, they feared that a daughter's poverty would deter her suitable match (kufu') from desiring her, so they would need to marry her off to unsuitable men, and that brings great shame. God therefore said: ﴿And do not kill your children﴾, a term general to males and females. The meaning is that what makes mercy and compassion obligatory is that the child is a child, and this meaning is a quality shared between males and females. As for what is feared of poverty concerning daughters, the same may be feared concerning sons in their infancy, and it may also be feared concerning sons who are incapable of work.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿We provide for them and for you.﴾ That is: provision is in the hand of God, exalted is He. Just as He opened the doors of provision for men, so too He opens the doors of provision for women.

The third issue: the majority read ﴿Indeed, their killing is ever a great sin﴾, meaning a great sin (ithman kabiran). It is said khati'a yakhta'u khi'an, like ya'thama ithman. God said: ﴿Indeed, we were sinners (khati'in)﴾ [Yusuf: 97], meaning sinful (athimin). Ibn 'Amir read (khata'an) with a fatha. It is said: akhta'a yukhti'u ikhta'an and khata'an when one does what is not fitting without intention, and khata' may be a verbal noun. The meaning according to this reading is that their killing is not right. Al-Qaffal, may God have mercy on him, said: Ibn Kathir read "khita'an" with a kasra on the kha' and a long vowel, and perhaps these are two dialects, like daf' and difa', and libs and libas.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verse 32:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not approach fornication. Indeed, it is an abomination and an evil way.﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, commanded the five matters mentioned earlier, the sum of which returns to two things: glorifying the command of Allah and compassion toward the creation of Allah, He followed them with the mention of prohibitions concerning several things.

The first of them: Allah, exalted is He, prohibited fornication, saying: ﴿And do not approach fornication.﴾ Al-Qaffal said: When a person is told "do not approach this," that is more emphatic than saying "do not do it." Then Allah, exalted is He, gave the reason for this prohibition as its being an abomination and an evil way.

Know that people have differed regarding whether, when Allah, exalted is He, commands a thing or prohibits a thing, it is correct to say that He commanded that thing or prohibited it for a reason returning to it or not. Those who affirm the rational goodness and ugliness (of acts) said: The matter is so. Those who deny the rational goodness and ugliness (of acts) said: The matter is not so.

Those who affirm the rational goodness and ugliness (of acts) argued for the soundness of their position with this verse. They said: Allah, exalted is He, prohibited fornication and gave the reason for that prohibition as its being an abomination. It is impossible that its being an abomination should be an expression of its being prohibited, for otherwise it would entail explaining a thing by itself, which is impossible. Therefore it must be said that its being an abomination is an attribute obtained by it in terms of its being fornication. This indicates that things are good or ugly for reasons returning to them in themselves, and it also indicates that Allah's prohibition of them is grounded in their occurrence in themselves upon those aspects. This argument is close, but the better way to put it is: that a thing being in itself a benefit or a harm is a matter established by its own essence and not by the Sharia, for consuming nourishing food is a benefit, and a painful blow is a harm, and that it is so is established by reason and not by the Sharia.

Once this is established, we say: Allah's obligations are in accordance with the benefits of the world in this life and the Hereafter. This is the apparent statement, and in it there are tremendous difficulties and profound inquiries, and we ask Allah for success in reaching the goal regarding them.

Having known this, we say: Fornication includes several kinds of corruption:

The first of them: the confusion and mixing of lineages, so that a person does not know whether the child borne by the fornicating woman is his or someone else's. So he does not take charge of raising him nor continue in his care, and this leads to the loss of children, which leads to the cutting off of progeny and the ruin of the world.

The second: if there is no lawful cause making this man more entitled to this woman than others, then nothing remains for securing that exclusivity except contention and fighting, and this leads to opening the door to chaos, turmoil and battle. How often have we heard of terrible killing caused by the single woman's engaging in fornication.

The third: when a woman engages in fornication and becomes accustomed to it, every sound nature and every upright disposition finds her repugnant, and then affection and love are not achieved, and tranquility and mutual companionship are not complete. For this reason, when a woman becomes known for fornication, the dispositions of most people recoil from associating with her.

The fourth: when the door of fornication is opened, then no man retains exclusive possession of a woman, and every man is able to leap upon any woman who wishes and wills it, and then no difference remains in this respect between the human species and the other animals.

[Page 159]

a difference in this matter.
The fifth: the purpose of a woman is not merely the satisfaction of desire, but that she become a partner to the man in arranging the household and preparing its affairs of food, drink and clothing, that she be the mistress of the house and guardian of the door, and that she be responsible for the affairs of the children and servants. These affairs cannot be completed unless she is single-minded toward this one man, her hope cut off from all other men, and that is not achieved except by prohibiting fornication and closing this door entirely.

The sixth: intercourse entails great humiliation, and the proof of this is that the greatest kinds of insult among people are mentions of the words of sexual intercourse. Had intercourse not entailed humiliation, this would not be so. Also, all sensible people do not undertake intercourse except in concealed places and at times when no one sees them, and all sensible people shrink from mentioning the spouses of their daughters, sisters and mothers, when they would undertake to have intercourse with them. Had intercourse not been humiliation, it would not be so.

Having established this, we say: since intercourse is humiliation, striving to reduce it accords with reason. Confining one woman to one man is striving to reduce that act. Also, the humiliation in it becomes compensated by the benefits obtained in marriage, whereas fornication is opening a door to that base act and is not compensated by any benefit, so it must remain in its original state of prohibition and restriction. Thus it has been established by what we have mentioned that sound minds judge fornication to be ugly.

Having established this, we say: Allah, exalted is He, described fornication with three attributes: that it is an abomination (fāḥisha), hateful (maqt) in another verse, and an evil way (sā'a sabīlan).

As for its being an abomination: it is an indication of its involving the corruption of lineages, which necessitates the ruin of the world, and of its involving fighting and contention over private parts, which also necessitates the ruin of the world.

As for hatefulness: we have mentioned that the fornicating woman becomes detested and disliked, and that entails the absence of tranquility and mutual companionship, and that a person cannot rely on her in any of his affairs and interests.

As for its being an evil way: it is what we have mentioned, that no difference remains between the human being and the animals in the non-exclusiveness of males to females. Also, the humiliation, shame and disgrace of this act remain upon the woman without its being compensated by any benefit. We have mentioned six aspects of the ugliness of fornication, and Allah, exalted is He, mentioned three terms, so we have applied each of these three terms to two of those six aspects. And Allah knows best His intent.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verse 33 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right. And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have certainly given his heir authority, but let him not commit excess in killing; indeed, he is supported.﴾

This is the second category of what Allah has forbidden in this verse, and in it are several issues.

The first issue: One might say that after disbelief in Allah, the greatest of the major sins is killing. So what is the reason that Allah, exalted is He, first mentioned the prohibition of fornication and second mentioned the prohibition of killing?

Its answer: We have explained that opening the door to fornication prevents a human being from entering existence, whereas killing is the nullification of a human being after he has entered existence. His entering existence precedes his destruction and annihilation after his existence. For this reason Allah, exalted is He, mentioned
Page 160
fornication first and then mentioned killing second.

The second issue: Know that the origin regarding killing is severe prohibition, and permissibility is established only by an accidental cause. Since the matter is so, Allah rightly prohibited killing absolutely, based on the ruling of the origin. Then He excepted from it the situation in which the permissibility of killing arises, which is upon the occurrence of accidental causes, saying: ﴿except by right﴾. Here we need to explain that the origin regarding killing is prohibition, and what indicates this are several points:

The first: Killing is harm, and the origin regarding harms is prohibition, due to His saying: ﴿And He has not placed upon you in the religion any difficulty﴾ [al-Hajj: 78], ﴿and Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾, and "There shall be neither harm nor reciprocating harm."

The second: His saying, peace be upon him: "The human being is the building of the Lord; cursed is whoever destroys the building of the Lord."

The third: The human being was created for the occupation of worship, due to His saying: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 56], and His saying, peace be upon him: "The right of Allah over the servants is that they worship Him and not associate anything with Him." And occupation with worship is not complete except in the absence of killing.

The fourth: Killing is corruption, so it must be prohibited, due to His exalted saying: ﴿And do not cause corruption﴾ [al-A'raf: 56].

The fifth: When the evidence for the prohibition of killing and the evidence for its permissibility conflict, they have agreed that the side of prohibition is preponderant; and were it not that the requirement of the origin is prohibition, that would be preference without a preponderating factor, which is impossible.

The sixth: When we do not know in a human being any attribute beyond merely being a rational human, we rule that his killing is prohibited; and when we do not know anything additional to his being human, we do not rule that his blood is permissible. Were it not that the origin of humanity requires the prohibition of killing, it would not be so. Thus it is established by these points that the origin regarding killing is prohibition, and that its permissibility is established only by accidental causes.

And when this is established, we say: Indeed, He, exalted is He, ruled that the origin regarding killing is prohibition, saying: ﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right.﴾ So His saying ﴿And do not kill﴾ is a prohibition and forbiddance, and His saying ﴿which Allah has forbidden﴾ is a repetition of the mention of prohibition by way of emphasis. Then He excepted from it the accidental, conventional causes, saying ﴿except by right.﴾ Then here there are two approaches:

The first approach: The mere saying ﴿except by right﴾ is ambiguous, because there is no explanation in it of what that right is or how it is. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have certainly given his heir authority﴾, i.e., in exacting retaliation from the killer. This statement is suitable to be taken as an explanation of that ambiguity, and its establishment is as if He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right﴾, and that right is that whoever is killed wrongfully, We have certainly given his heir authority in exacting retaliation. And when this is established, it is necessary that the meaning of "right" be this form alone, so the verse's sense becomes: "And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except in retaliation." On this understanding the verse is an explicit text on the prohibition of killing except by this single cause, so it must remain prohibited in every case other than this single form.

The second approach: We say that the Sunnah indicates that this right is one of three matters, namely his saying, peace be upon him: "The blood of a Muslim man is not lawful except by one of three: disbelief after faith, adultery after marriage, or the killing of a soul without right."

Know that this report is of the category of solitary reports (ahad). If we say that His saying ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have certainly given his heir authority﴾ is an explanation of His saying ﴿except by right﴾, then the verse is explicit that killing is lawful only by this single cause, and then this report becomes a specifier of this verse, and that becomes a branch of our position that it is permissible to specify the general wording of the Qur'an by a solitary report. But if we say that His saying ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have certainly given his heir authority﴾ is not an explanation of His saying ﴿except by right﴾, then this report becomes an explanation of the right mentioned in the verse, and on this understanding it does not become a branch of the question of the permissibility of specifying the general wording of the Qur'an by a solitary report. So let this subtle point be known. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: The apparent sense of this verse is that there is no cause for the permissibility of killing except the killing of one wrongfully; and the apparent sense of the report requires adding two other matters to it: apostasy after faith, and adultery after marriage. And another verse indicates a fourth cause, namely His exalted saying: ﴿Indeed, the penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon earth in corruption is that they be killed or crucified﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 33]. Another verse indicates a fifth cause, namely disbelief. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah or in the Last Day﴾ [at-Tawbah: 29], and He said: ﴿And kill them wherever you find them﴾ [an-Nisa': 89].

The jurists have spoken and differed about other matters, among them:

First: Whether one who abandons the prayer is to be killed or not. According to al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, he is to be killed; and from Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, he is not to be killed.

Second: Whether the act of sodomy (liwat) requires killing. According to al-Shafi'i it requires it, and according to Abu Hanifah it does not require it.

Third: If a sorcerer says: "I killed so-and-so by my sorcery," then according to al-Shafi'i this requires killing, and according to Abu Hanifah it does not require it.

Fourth: Whether killing by a blunt instrument requires retaliation. According to al-Shafi'i it requires it, and according to Abu Hanifah it does not require it.

Fifth: Whether refusing to pay zakat requires killing or not. They differed about this in the time of Abu Bakr.

Sixth: Whether bestiality requires killing. According to most jurists it does not require it, and according to some people it does require it.

The argument of those who say that killing is not permissible in these cases is that the verse is explicit in prohibiting killing absolutely, except for one cause, namely the killing of one wrongfully; so in every case other than this one cause, the remaining must be upon the original prohibition. Then they said: This text has been reinforced by many proofs requiring the sanctity of blood absolutely, so abandoning acting upon these proofs can only be due to a counter-consideration, and that counter-consideration is either a mutawatir text, or a solitary text, or analogy. As for a mutawatir text, it is non-existent, otherwise the disagreement would not remain. As for a solitary text, it is outweighed in comparison with these numerous mutawatir texts. As for analogy, it cannot oppose a text. Thus it is established, by the requirement of this strong and overpowering principle, that the origin regarding blood is prohibition, except in the enumerated cases. And Allah knows best.

* * *

The fourth issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have certainly given his heir authority, but let him not commit excess﴾. In it there are two discussions:

The first discussion: This verse indicates that He established an authority for the heir of the blood. As for the explanation of what this authority is established in, there is no indication in His saying ﴿We have certainly given his heir authority﴾. Here there are two approaches:

The first: When He said after it, ﴿but let him not commit excess in killing﴾, it became known that this authority is established in carrying out killing. This is weak, because it is possible that the meaning is: "We have certainly given his heir authority, so the wrongdoer should not commit excess in that killing, because that slain person is supported through the establishment of this authority for his heir."

The second: That this authority is general and then became specified by the verse and the report. As for the verse, it is His saying in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿O you who have believed, retaliation is prescribed for you regarding those murdered﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178], up to His saying: ﴿But whoever is pardoned by his brother [i.e., the victim's heir] of anything, then grant him what is reasonable and pay him with good conduct﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178]. We have explained in the commentary on this verse that it indicates that the obligation is that the responsible person is given the choice between retaliation and blood-money. As for the report, it is his saying, peace be upon him, on the day of the conquest: "Whoever kills a slain person, his family are given the choice between two things: if they wish, they may kill, and if they wish, they may take the blood-money." On this approach, His saying ﴿but let him not commit excess in killing﴾ means: since the authority to carry out retaliation was granted to him if he wishes,
Page 162
and the authority to take blood-money if he wishes, He then said: "but let him not commit excess in killing," meaning that it is better that he not proceed to carry out the killing, and that he be content with taking the blood-money or incline toward pardon. In sum, the particle "fi" (in) is taken to carry the sense of "bi" (by), and the meaning is: he does not become excessive by means of his proceeding to kill; and its meaning becomes an encouragement to pardon and to being content with blood-money, as He said: ﴿And that you pardon is closer to righteousness﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237].

The second discussion: In His saying ﴿whoever is killed wrongfully﴾, He mentioned his being wrongfully killed in indefinite form, and the indefinite form, as is known, indicates completeness. So a slain person who is not complete in the attribute of being wronged does not come under this text. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: We have shown that when a Muslim kills a dhimmi, he does not come under this verse, by the evidence that the dhimmi is a polytheist, and the polytheist's blood is lawful. We say he is a polytheist because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [an-Nisa': 48]. He ruled that whatever is other than polytheism is forgivable for some people; so if the disbelief of the Jew and the Christian were something other than polytheism, it would have to become forgivable for some people by the requirement of this verse. Since it never became forgivable for anyone, this shows that their disbelief is polytheism. Also, He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They have certainly disbelieved who say: Allah is the third of three﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 73]. This trinitarianism that they hold is either a trinity in the attributes, which is false, because that is the truth and is the doctrine of the People of the Sunnah and the Community, so it cannot be made a trinity of disbelief; or it is a trinity in the essences, and that is the truth, and there is no doubt that the one who holds it is a polytheist. Thus it is established that the dhimmi is a polytheist. And we say that the polytheist must be killed, due to His exalted saying: ﴿And fight the polytheists﴾, and the requirement of this evidence is the permissibility of the dhimmi's blood. And if permissibility is not established, then at least a semblance of permissibility arises.

This is the second part of al-Razi's commentary (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verse 33.

Having established this, we say: it has been established that he is not complete in being wronged, so he does not fall under His saying, ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have given his heir authority﴾. As for a free man who kills a slave, he falls under this verse, except that we have shown that His saying, ﴿Retaliation is prescribed for you in the matter of the slain: the free for the free, and the slave for the slave﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:178), indicates the prohibition of killing a free man for a slave in many ways. That verse is more specific (khass) than His saying, ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have given his heir authority﴾, and the specific takes precedence over the general ('amm). Thus it is established that this verse may not be used as evidence in the question that the required penalty for deliberate killing is qisas (retributive justice), nor in the question that a Muslim must be killed for killing a dhimmi (non-Muslim subject), nor in the question that a free man must be killed for killing a slave. And Allah knows best.

As for His saying, ﴿So let him not exceed bounds in killing﴾, there are several discussions concerning it.

The first discussion: there are several views on it.

The first: the intended meaning is that one should not kill both the killer and others besides the killer. This is because when one of them killed a man from a noble tribe, the heirs of that slain man would kill a number of people from the lowly tribe. So Allah the Exalted forbade this and commanded that they limit themselves to killing the killer alone.

The second: it means that one should not be content with killing the killer. The people of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic period) used to target the nobles of the killer's tribe, then kill certain people from among them and leave the killer alone.

The third: it means that one should not be satisfied with killing the killer but should mutilate him and cut off his limbs. Al-Qaffal said: it is not far-fetched to interpret it as covering all of these, since all these meanings share in being excess (israf).

The second discussion: most of the readers recited ﴿فَلا يُسْرِفْ﴾ (fa-la yusrif, with the yā’) and there are two views on it.

The first: the implied meaning is: the guardian (wali) should not exceed bounds in killing.

The second: the pronoun refers originally to the wrongful killer, meaning: that wrongdoer should not exceed bounds, and his exceeding bounds is an expression for his proceeding to that wrongful killing.

Ḥamzah and al-Kisā’ī recited ﴿فَلا تُسْرِفْ﴾ (fa-la tusrif, with the tā’) in the second person. This recitation (qira’ah) may bear two meanings.

The first: the address is to the one who initiated the wrongful killing, as if it were said to him: "Do not exceed bounds, O human." That exceeding bounds is his proceeding to that killing, which is pure injustice. The meaning is: do not do it, for if you kill him wrongfully, he (the heir) will take retaliation from you.

The second: the address is to the guardian, so the implied meaning is: do not exceed bounds in killing, O guardian, that is, be content with exacting retaliation and do not seek more.

* * *

As for His saying, ﴿Indeed, he is ever supported﴾, there are three views on it.

The first: it is as if it were said to the wrongdoer who initiated that killing unjustly: do not do that, for that slain man will be supported in this world and the Hereafter. His support in this world is by the killing of his killer, and in the Hereafter by the abundance of reward for him and the abundance of punishment for his killer.

The second view: this guardian will be supported in killing that wrongful killer, so let him be content with this measure, for he will be supported in it and should not hope for more from it, because whoever is supported by Allah is forbidden to seek more.

The third view: this wrongful killer should be content with exacting retaliation and not seek more.

Know that according to the first and second views, it becomes clear that the slain man and the guardian of his blood are both supported by Allah the Exalted. It is reported from Ibn ‘Abbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: I said to ‘Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib, peace be upon him: "By Allah, Ibn Abī Sufyān will surely prevail over you," because Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have given his heir authority﴾. Al-Ḥasan said: "By Allah, Mu‘āwiyah was not given victory over ‘Alī, peace be upon him, except by the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have given his heir authority﴾." And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verses 34–35:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan, except in the way that is best, until he reaches his maturity (ashudd)﴾.

Know that this is the third category of the things which Allah has forbidden in these verses.

Know that we have mentioned that adultery necessitates the mixing of lineages. That necessitates preventing the concern for raising children, and that necessitates the cutting off of offspring, and that necessitates the prevention of people coming into existence. As for killing, it is the annihilation of people after their coming into existence. So it is established that the prohibition of adultery and the prohibition of killing both ultimately return to the prohibition of destroying souls. When Allah the Exalted mentioned that, He followed it with the prohibition of destroying wealth, because after souls, the most precious things are wealth. The people most deserving of the prohibition against destroying their wealth are orphans, because on account of their youth, their weakness and their complete inability, harm from the destruction of their wealth is greatly magnified. For this reason, Allah the Exalted singled them out in the prohibition against destroying their wealth, saying: ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan, except in the way that is best﴾. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not consume them extravagantly and hastily, fearing that they will grow up. And whoever is wealthy, let him abstain; and whoever is poor, let him eat according to what is reasonable﴾ [an-Nisa': 6]. Regarding the interpretation of His saying ﴿except in the way that is best﴾ there are two views:

The first: except by the disposal that makes it grow and increase.

The second: the intended meaning is that you may eat along with it when you are in need of it. Mujahid narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "If he (the guardian) is in need, he may eat with reasonableness; when he becomes well-off, he repays it; and if he does not become well-off, there is nothing upon him."

Know that the guardianship over the orphan only remains until he reaches his maturity (ashudd), which is the attainment of the age of marriage, as Allah the Exalted explained in another verse, namely His saying: ﴿And test the orphans until they reach marriageable age; then if you perceive in them sound judgment, deliver to them their property﴾ [an-Nisa': 6]. The meaning of ashudd is that he reaches the point where, by means of his intellect and sound judgment, he is able to undertake the affairs of his property, and at that point the guardianship of others over him ceases; and that is the limit of puberty. As for when he reaches puberty without complete intellect, the guardianship over him does not cease. And Allah knows best. The attainment of intellectual maturity is that his intellect and his sensory and motor faculties become complete. And Allah knows best.

* * *

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And fulfil the covenant; indeed, the covenant will be questioned﴾ ﴿And give full measure when you measure, and weigh with a true balance; that is better and more favourable in outcome﴾.

Know that He, exalted is He, first commanded five things, then followed them with the prohibition of three things, namely the prohibition of adultery, of killing except by right, and of approaching the property of the orphan except in the way that is best. Then He followed these three prohibitions with these three commands. The first is His saying: ﴿And fulfil the covenant﴾.

Know that every contract made for the purpose of confirming and affirming a matter is a covenant ('ahd). So His saying ﴿And fulfil the covenant﴾ is parallel to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, fulfil the contracts﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 1]. Thus within His saying ﴿fulfil the contracts﴾ enters every contract among the contracts, such as the contract of sale and partnership, the oath and vow, the contract of reconciliation, and the marriage contract. The summary of the matter is that the requirement of this verse is that every contract and covenant that takes place between two persons makes it obligatory upon both of them to fulfil what that contract and covenant requires, unless a separate proof indicates that fulfilling it is not obligatory. Its ruling therefore is the validity of every sale entered into by mutual consent and the validity of every partnership entered into by mutual consent. This text is reinforced by the other verses indicating fulfilment of covenants and contracts, such as His saying: ﴿And those who, when they make a covenant, are fulfilling of their covenant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177]; His saying: ﴿And those who are, for their trusts and their covenant, observant﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 8]; His saying: ﴿And Allah has permitted trade﴾ [al-Baqarah: 275]; His saying: ﴿Do not consume your properties among yourselves unjustly, except that it be trade by mutual consent among you﴾ [an-Nisa': 29]; His saying: ﴿And take witnesses when you conduct business﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282]; His saying, peace be upon him: "The property of a Muslim man is not lawful except with the good pleasure of his soul." And his saying: "When the two kinds differ, then sell as you wish, hand to hand." And his saying: "Whoever buys a thing he has not seen, he has the option when he sees it." All these verses and reports indicate that the basic principle concerning sales, covenants and contracts is validity and the obligation of adherence.

Having established this, we say: if we find a text more specific than these texts which indicates nullity and invalidity, we judge by it, giving precedence to the specific over the general; otherwise we judge for validity in all cases. As for specifying a text by analogy (qiyas), we have rejected it. By this method, the chapters of transactions, with all their length and detail, become governed and known through this single verse, and the legally responsible person remains at ease in heart and tranquil in soul in acting, because when these texts have indicated their validity, there is no clarification after the clarification of Allah, and the Sharia becomes governed and known.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the covenant will be questioned﴾, and in this there are several views:

The first: that the intended meaning is "the one who made the covenant will be questioned," so the modified noun is omitted and the modifier (the genitive noun) is put in its place, as in His saying: ﴿And ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82].

The second: that the covenant will be questioned, meaning it will be demanded, and it will be demanded of the one bound by it that he not neglect it and that he fulfil it.

The third: that this is a figure of speech, as if it were said to the covenant: "Why were you broken? Would that you had been fulfilled by him," as a rebuke to the one who breaks it, just as it is said to the buried infant girl: ﴿For what sin was she killed?﴾ [at-Takwir: 9], and as in His saying: ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah?"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116]. The address is to Jesus, peace be upon him, while the denunciation is directed at others.

The second category of the commands mentioned in this verse is His saying: ﴿And give full measure when you measure﴾. The intended meaning of it is completing the measure, and the severe warning concerning its deficiency is mentioned in His saying: ﴿Woe to those who give less [than due], who, when they take a measure from people, take in full. But when they measure or weigh for them, they cause loss﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 1–3].

The third category of the commands mentioned in this verse is His saying: ﴿and weigh with a true balance﴾. The preceding verse concerns completing the measure, and this verse concerns completing the weight. A parallel to it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And establish the weight with justice and do not make the balance deficient﴾ [ar-Rahman: 9], and His saying: ﴿And do not deprive people of their things and do not commit abuse on the earth, causing corruption﴾ [Hud: 85].

Know that the discrepancy that results from a deficiency in measure and weight is small, but the warning incurred for it is severe and great, so it is obligatory upon the intelligent person to guard against it. The warning concerning it is great because all people are in need of exchanges, buying and selling, and a person may be heedless and not guided to preserving his property. Therefore the Lawgiver went to great lengths in prohibiting cheating and deficiency, striving to preserve wealth for its owners, and preventing the soul from being stained by stealing that insignificant amount. The qistas has the meaning of the balance, except that in common usage it is larger than it; for this reason it became well known on the tongues of the common people that it is the qabban (steelyard). It has been said that it is in the language of the Romans or the Syriac. The more correct view is that it is the language of the Arabs, and it is derived from qist, which is that in which straightness and balance occur. In sum, its meaning is the balanced one that does not incline to either side. The scholars agreed on the permissibility of both dialects in it: pronouncing the qaf with a damma or with a kasra. The kasra is the reading of Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs from 'Asim, while the rest read it with a damma.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That is better﴾, that is, completing the measure fully and completely is better than the slight cheating, in that a person is delivered through it from bad mention in this world and from severe punishment in the Hereafter: ﴿and more favourable in outcome (ta'wil)﴾. The ta'wil is that to which the matter returns, as He said in another place: ﴿and better in return﴾ [Maryam: 76], ﴿and better in reward﴾ [al-Kahf: 44], ﴿and better in hope﴾ [al-Kahf: 44]. Allah the Exalted judged that the outcome of this matter is the best of outcomes, because in this world, when a person becomes known for abstaining from cheating, people rely upon him and hearts incline toward him, and he attains sufficiency in a short time. How often have we seen poor people, when they became known among people for trustworthiness and abstention from betrayal, hearts turned toward them and great wealth came to them in a brief period. As for the Hereafter, it is success with great reward and deliverance from painful punishment.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verses 34–35:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan, except in the way that is best, until he reaches his maturity (ashudd)﴾.

Know that this is the third category of the things which Allah has forbidden in these verses.

Know that we have mentioned that adultery necessitates the mixing of lineages. That necessitates preventing the concern for raising children, and that necessitates the cutting off of offspring, and that necessitates the prevention of people coming into existence. As for killing, it is the annihilation of people after their coming into existence. So it is established that the prohibition of adultery and the prohibition of killing both ultimately return to the prohibition of destroying souls. When Allah the Exalted mentioned that, He followed it with the prohibition of destroying wealth, because after souls, the most precious things are wealth. The people most deserving of the prohibition against destroying their wealth are orphans, because on account of their youth, their weakness and their complete inability, harm from the destruction of their wealth is greatly magnified. For this reason, Allah the Exalted singled them out in the prohibition against destroying their wealth, saying: ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan, except in the way that is best﴾. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not consume them extravagantly and hastily, fearing that they will grow up. And whoever is wealthy, let him abstain; and whoever is poor, let him eat according to what is reasonable﴾ [an-Nisa': 6]. Regarding the interpretation of His saying ﴿except in the way that is best﴾ there are two views:

The first: except by the disposal that makes it grow and increase.

The second: the intended meaning is that you may eat along with it when you are in need of it. Mujahid narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "If he (the guardian) is in need, he may eat with reasonableness; when he becomes well-off, he repays it; and if he does not become well-off, there is nothing upon him."

Know that the guardianship over the orphan only remains until he reaches his maturity (ashudd), which is the attainment of the age of marriage, as Allah the Exalted explained in another verse, namely His saying: ﴿And test the orphans until they reach marriageable age; then if you perceive in them sound judgment, deliver to them their property﴾ [an-Nisa': 6]. The meaning of ashudd is that he reaches the point where, by means of his intellect and sound judgment, he is able to undertake the affairs of his property, and at that point the guardianship of others over him ceases; and that is the limit of puberty. As for when he reaches puberty without complete intellect, the guardianship over him does not cease. And Allah knows best. The attainment of intellectual maturity is that his intellect and his sensory and motor faculties become complete. And Allah knows best.

* * *

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And fulfil the covenant; indeed, the covenant will be questioned﴾ ﴿And give full measure when you measure, and weigh with a true balance; that is better and more favourable in outcome﴾.

Know that He, exalted is He, first commanded five things, then followed them with the prohibition of three things, namely the prohibition of adultery, of killing except by right, and of approaching the property of the orphan except in the way that is best. Then He followed these three prohibitions with these three commands. The first is His saying: ﴿And fulfil the covenant﴾.

Know that every contract made for the purpose of confirming and affirming a matter is a covenant ('ahd). So His saying ﴿And fulfil the covenant﴾ is parallel to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, fulfil the contracts﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 1]. Thus within His saying ﴿fulfil the contracts﴾ enters every contract among the contracts, such as the contract of sale and partnership, the oath and vow, the contract of reconciliation, and the marriage contract. The summary of the matter is that the requirement of this verse is that every contract and covenant that takes place between two persons makes it obligatory upon both of them to fulfil what that contract and covenant requires, unless a separate proof indicates that fulfilling it is not obligatory. Its ruling therefore is the validity of every sale entered into by mutual consent and the validity of every partnership entered into by mutual consent. This text is reinforced by the other verses indicating fulfilment of covenants and contracts, such as His saying: ﴿And those who, when they make a covenant, are fulfilling of their covenant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177]; His saying: ﴿And those who are, for their trusts and their covenant, observant﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 8]; His saying: ﴿And Allah has permitted trade﴾ [al-Baqarah: 275]; His saying: ﴿Do not consume your properties among yourselves unjustly, except that it be trade by mutual consent among you﴾ [an-Nisa': 29]; His saying: ﴿And take witnesses when you conduct business﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282]; His saying, peace be upon him: "The property of a Muslim man is not lawful except with the good pleasure of his soul." And his saying: "When the two kinds differ, then sell as you wish, hand to hand." And his saying: "Whoever buys a thing he has not seen, he has the option when he sees it." All these verses and reports indicate that the basic principle concerning sales, covenants and contracts is validity and the obligation of adherence.

Having established this, we say: if we find a text more specific than these texts which indicates nullity and invalidity, we judge by it, giving precedence to the specific over the general; otherwise we judge for validity in all cases. As for specifying a text by analogy (qiyas), we have rejected it. By this method, the chapters of transactions, with all their length and detail, become governed and known through this single verse, and the legally responsible person remains at ease in heart and tranquil in soul in acting, because when these texts have indicated their validity, there is no clarification after the clarification of Allah, and the Sharia becomes governed and known.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the covenant will be questioned﴾, and in this there are several views:

The first: that the intended meaning is "the one who made the covenant will be questioned," so the modified noun is omitted and the modifier (the genitive noun) is put in its place, as in His saying: ﴿And ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82].

The second: that the covenant will be questioned, meaning it will be demanded, and it will be demanded of the one bound by it that he not neglect it and that he fulfil it.

The third: that this is a figure of speech, as if it were said to the covenant: "Why were you broken? Would that you had been fulfilled by him," as a rebuke to the one who breaks it, just as it is said to the buried infant girl: ﴿For what sin was she killed?﴾ [at-Takwir: 9], and as in His saying: ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah?"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116]. The address is to Jesus, peace be upon him, while the denunciation is directed at others.

The second category of the commands mentioned in this verse is His saying: ﴿And give full measure when you measure﴾. The intended meaning of it is completing the measure, and the severe warning concerning its deficiency is mentioned in His saying: ﴿Woe to those who give less [than due], who, when they take a measure from people, take in full. [p. 166]

Commentary on his words, exalted is He: ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart — about all of these one will be questioned.﴾

On this verse there are several issues.

The first issue: Know that when Allah, exalted is He, explained the three commands, He returned after them to mention the prohibitions, and He forbade three things.

The first of them is His saying: ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge.﴾ His words ﴿taqfu﴾ (pursue) derive from the expression "qafawtu athar fulan" (I followed the trace of so-and-so), "aqfu qafwan wa qufuwwan," when you follow his trace. The rhyme of a poem is called qafiyah (rhyme) because it follows the verse (bayt). The well-known tribe is called al-Qafah (trackers) because they follow the traces of people's footprints and infer from them the conditions of a person. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then We sent, following in their footsteps, Our messengers﴾ [al-Hadid: 27]. The back of the neck is called qafa because it is the rear part of the human body, as if it were something that follows and trails behind. So His saying ﴿and do not pursue﴾ means: do not follow and do not trace that of which you have no knowledge, whether in speech or in action. Its ultimate meaning returns to the prohibition of judging by what is not known. This is a universal principle under which many kinds fall, and each of the exegetes applied it to one of those kinds. There are several views:

The first view: what is meant is the prohibition of the polytheists from the doctrines they held concerning divinity and prophethood, which they had inherited by blind imitation of their forefathers. Allah attributed these beliefs to their following of desire, saying: ﴿They are nothing but names you have named, you and your fathers, for which Allah has sent down no authority﴾ [al-Najm: 23]. And concerning their denial of resurrection He said: ﴿Rather, their knowledge has failed concerning the Hereafter; rather, they are in doubt about it; rather, they are blind to it﴾ [al-Naml: 66]. It is also reported of them that they said: ﴿We think only a conjecture, and we are not certain﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 32]. He said: ﴿And who is more astray than one who follows his desire without guidance from Allah?﴾ [al-Qasas: 50]. He said: ﴿And do not say, concerning what your tongues describe falsely: "This is lawful and this is unlawful"﴾ [al-Nahl: 116], to the end of the verse. And He said: ﴿Do you have any knowledge that you can bring out to us? You follow nothing but conjecture﴾ [al-An'am: 148].

The second view: it is reported from Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah that what is meant is false testimony. Ibn 'Abbas said: Do not testify except to what your eyes have seen, your ears have heard, and your heart has retained.

The third view: what is meant is the prohibition of slander and of accusing chaste men and women with lies. The Arabs had a custom of this, mentioning it in satire and exaggerating in it.

The fourth view: what is meant is the prohibition of lying. Qatadah said: Do not say "I heard" when you did not hear, or "I saw" when you did not see, or "I know" when you do not know.

The fifth view: that qaf (pursuing) means buhtan (slander/false accusation), and its origin is from qafa (the back of the neck), as if it were a speech said behind a person's back. It has the meaning of backbiting (ghibah), which is mentioning a man in his absence with what would displease him. In some reports: "Whoever slanders a Muslim with what is not in him, Allah will confine him in the mire of al-Khabal (the pus of the Hellfire)." Know that the wording is general and encompasses all of these, so there is no point in restricting it to one. And Allah knows best.

* * *

The second issue: Those who deny qiyas (analogical reasoning) argued from this verse, saying: Qiyas yields only conjecture (zann), and conjecture is different from knowledge (ilm). Therefore, ruling in the religion of Allah by qiyas is ruling by what is not known, and so it must not be permitted, because of His saying: ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge.﴾

They were answered in several ways:

The first: ruling in religion on mere conjecture is permissible by the consensus (ijma') of the community in many cases:

One of them: acting on a fatwa is acting on conjecture, and this is permissible.
Second: acting on testimony is acting on conjecture, and this is permissible.
Third: ijtihad in determining the direction of prayer yields only conjecture, and this is permissible.
Fourth: the valuation of destroyed property and the compensation for injuries can only be reached by conjecture, and this is permissible.
Fifth: bloodletting, cupping, and all other treatments based on conjecture, and this is permissible.
Sixth: that this slaughtered animal is slaughtered by a Muslim is a matter of conjecture, not certainty, and basing a ruling on it is permissible.
Seventh: Allah said: ﴿And if you fear a breach between the two, send an arbiter from his people and an arbiter from her people﴾ [al-Nisa': 35], and the occurrence of that breach is a matter of conjecture, not certainty.
Eighth: ruling that a specific person is a believer is a matter of conjecture, and upon this conjecture we build many rulings, such as the right of inheritance and burial in the graveyards of Muslims, and others.
Ninth: all the actions that are relied upon in worldly affairs, such as travel, seeking profit, transactions up to specified terms, and relying on the friendship of friends and the enmity of enemies, are all conjectural, and building affairs upon those conjectures is permissible.
Tenth: the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "We judge by the outward, and Allah takes charge of the hidden." This is an explicit statement that conjecture is valid in these ten categories, and so the view of one who says that it is not permissible to build a matter upon conjecture is refuted.

The second answer: conjecture is sometimes called knowledge. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿When believing women come to you as emigrants, test them. Allah knows best their faith. If you know them to be believers, do not return them to the disbelievers﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 10]. It is known that knowledge of their faith is possible only on the basis of their affirmation, and that yields only conjecture. Here Allah called conjecture knowledge.

The third answer: since a decisive proof has indicated the obligation to act on qiyas, and that proof is evidence that whenever a conjecture arises that the ruling of Allah in this case equals His ruling in the case of the explicit text, you are obligated to act in accordance with that conjecture. Here the conjecture occurs in the means of arriving at the ruling, while that ruling itself is known and certain.

The opponents of qiyas answered the first question by saying: His saying ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge﴾ is general, and specification (takhsis) has entered into the ten cases mentioned. Therefore this generality remains a valid proof for what lies beyond these cases. Then we say: the difference between these ten cases and the point in dispute is that these ten cases share the feature that those rulings are specific to particular persons at particular times. The event in which a particular person refers to a particular meaning is an event connected to that particular person. The same holds for testimony, for determining the direction of prayer, and for all the other cases. Explicit stipulation regarding the events of particular persons at particular times would amount to explicit stipulation of what has no end, and that is impracticable. For this necessity we have been content with conjecture. As for the rulings established by analogies, they are universal rulings applicable to universal events, and they are limited and few in number, so explicit stipulation of them is possible. That is why the jurists who derived those rulings by way of qiyas recorded them and set them down in their books.

Having understood this, we say: explicit stipulation of rulings in the ten cases you mentioned is not possible, so the Lawgiver was content with conjecture in them. As for matters established by analogical methods, explicit stipulation of them is possible, so it was not permissible to be content with conjecture in them. Thus the difference is clear.

As for the second answer, namely their saying that conjecture is sometimes called knowledge, we say: this is invalid. It is correct to say "this is conjectural and not known," and "this is known and not conjectural," and this indicates that there is a distinction. Moreover, what indicates this is His saying: ﴿Say: "Do you have any knowledge that you can bring out to us? You follow nothing but conjecture"﴾ [al-An'am: 148], which denies knowledge and affirms conjecture, and this indicates the distinction. As for His saying ﴿If you know them to be believers﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 10], the believer is one who affirms, and that affirmation is knowledge.

As for the third answer, it is also weak, because that argument holds only if it is established that qiyas is a valid proof by a decisive argument, and that is false. For that proof is either rational or traditional. The first is false, because qiyas which yields conjecture is not necessarily valid by reason. The evidence for this is that there is no dispute that the Lawgiver may say: "I have forbidden you to resort to qiyas." Had its validity been a purely rational matter, that would be impossible. The second is also false, because the traditional proof for the validity of qiyas would be decisive only if it were transmitted by mass transmission (tawatur), and its implication for this claim were definitive, admitting no contrary. Had such a proof existed, it would have reached everyone, everyone would have known it, and disagreement would have ended. Since this is not the case, we know that no decisive textual proof was found on this question. Thus it is established that no decisive proof at all exists for the validity of qiyas. Your statement therefore fails: "the validity of the ruling established by qiyas is known, not conjectural." This is the full statement of this argument. The best answer that can be given to it is that relying on this verse, which you rely upon, is reliance on a general text that has been specified, and reliance on a general text that has been specified yields only conjecture. So if this verse indicated that relying on conjecture is impermissible, it would indicate that relying on this verse is impermissible. Thus affirming that this verse is a proof leads, if established, to its own negation, and so it is self-contradictory, and the argument from it falls. And Allah knows best. The respondent may answer: we know by the manifest mass transmission from the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ) that relying on the verses of the Qur'an is a proof in the Shari'ah. And this answer may be challenged by saying that the validity of a general text that has been specified is not known by mass transmission. And Allah knows best.

* * *

The third issue: His saying: ﴿Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart — about all of these one will be questioned.﴾ On this there are two discussions.

The first discussion: knowledge is either derived from the senses or from the intellects.

As for the first kind, it is indicated by the mention of hearing and sight, for when a person hears something and sees it, he transmits it and reports it.

As for the second kind, it is knowledge derived from the intellect, and it is of two types: self-evident (badihiyyah) and acquired (kasbiyyah). The mention of the heart (fu'ad) indicates the intellectual sciences.

The second discussion: the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that these organs are questioned, and on this there are several views:

The first view: what is meant is that the owner of the hearing, sight, and heart is the one who is questioned, because questioning is valid only of one who is rational, and these organs are not rational; rather, the rational, understanding being is the human. This is like His saying: ﴿And ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82], where what is meant is its people. It is said to him: Why did you hear what it was not lawful for you to hear? Why did you look at what it was not lawful for you to look at? Why did you resolve upon what it was not lawful for you to resolve upon?

The second view: the meaning of the verse is that all those people will be questioned about their hearing, sight, and heart. It is said to them: Where did you use your hearing? In obedience or in disobedience? The same applies to the rest of the organs. This is because these senses are instruments of the soul, and the soul is like the commander over them, the one who employs them for its interests. If the soul uses them for good, it deserves reward, and if it uses them for sins, it deserves punishment.

The third view: it has been established by the Qur'an that Allah creates life in the organs, and that they then bear witness against the human being. The evidence is His saying: ﴿On the Day when their tongues, their hands, and their feet will testify against them concerning what they used to do﴾ [al-Nur: 24]. Therefore it is not far-fetched that He creates life, reason, and speech in these organs. Then He directs the questioning to them.

"And do not walk upon the earth exultantly; indeed, you will never tear through the earth, nor will you reach the mountains in height." "All that — its evil is hateful in the sight of your Lord."

Know that this is the second category of the things which Allah has forbidden in these verses, and in it there are issues:

The first issue: al-maraḥ (exultation, arrogance in gait) is an intense joy. One says: marija yamraḥu maraḥan, so he is marih. The meaning of the verse is the prohibition against a person walking in a manner that indicates pride and greatness. Al-Zajjaj said: "Do not walk upon the earth haughtily and boastfully." A parallel to this is the words of Allah the Exalted in Surat al-Furqan: "And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility" [al-Furqan: 63]. And He said in Surat Luqman: "And be moderate in your walking and lower your voice" [Luqman: 19]. And He also said in it: "And do not walk upon the earth exultantly. Indeed, Allah does not like everyone self-deluded and boastful" [Luqman: 18].

The second issue: al-Akhfash said: "If it were read 'marihan' with a kasra, it would be better in recitation." Al-Zajjaj said: "Maraḥan is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and marihan is the active participle (ism al-fa'il), and both are permissible, except that the verbal noun is better here and more emphatic. You say: 'Zayd came running (rakḍan)' and 'running (rakiḍan)'; rakḍan is more emphatic because it indicates the emphasis of the verb." Then, He, the Exalted, emphasized the prohibition against vanity and arrogance, saying: "Indeed, you will never tear through the earth, nor will you reach the mountains in height." Here, by "tearing" is meant piercing the earth. Then they mentioned regarding it several aspects:

The first: walking requires rising and lowering, so it is as if it were said: "In your lowering, you cannot pierce the earth and break through it, and in your rising, you cannot reach the peaks of the mountains." The purpose is to alert to his being weak and powerless, so arrogance does not befit him.

The second: the meaning is that beneath you is the earth, which you cannot pierce, and above you are the mountains, which you cannot reach. So you are encompassed from above and below by two kinds of inanimate matter, and you are far weaker than both. The weak and confined one does not deserve arrogance. It is as if it were said to him: "Be humble and do not be arrogant, for you are a weak creature among the creatures of Allah, confined between stone and dust, so do not act like the empowered and mighty."

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: "All that — its evil is hateful in the sight of your Lord." In it there are issues:

The first issue: Most readers read "sayyi'uhu" with a damma on the ha' and the hamza, while Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "sayyi'atan" in the accusative. As for the reading of the majority, its basis is apparent from two aspects:

The first aspect: Al-Hasan said: "Allah mentioned before this things He commanded some of and forbade others. So if He judged all of them to be an evil, it would follow that what was commanded would be an evil, and that is not permissible. But if we read it with the construct form, the meaning is that whatever of those mentioned things is evil, it is hateful in the sight of Allah, and the sentence is sound."

The second aspect: If we judged everything previously mentioned to be an evil, it would necessarily be said that they are hateful, and the matter is not so, because He said: "hatefully (makruhan)". But if we read it in the construct form, the meaning is that the evil of those categories is hateful, and then the sentence is sound. As for the reading of Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr, there are aspects to it:

The first: that the sentence was complete at His saying: "That is better and more excellent in outcome," then He began and said: "And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge," and "And do not walk upon the earth exultantly," then He said: "All that was an evil (sayyi'atan)," and the intended meaning is these last matters which Allah forbade.

The second: that by His saying "All that" is meant: all that Allah forbade in what preceded.

* * *

As for His saying "makruhan," they mentioned in its correction under this reading several aspects:

The first: the estimate is: "All that was an evil and was hateful."

The second: The author of "al-Kashshaf" said: "Evil (sayyi'ah) in the sense of nouns is in the position of sin and wrongdoing; it has lost the rule of adjectives, so its feminine form is not considered, and there is no difference between one who reads sayyi'atan and one who reads sayyi'uhu. Do you not see that you say: 'Adultery is an evil,' just as you say: 'Theft is an evil,' so you do not distinguish between attributing it to a masculine or feminine noun."

The third: there is an inversion, and the estimate is: "All that was hateful and an evil in the sight of your Lord."

The fourth: it is carried to the meaning, because the evil is the sin, and it is masculine.

The second issue: Al-Qadi said: This verse indicates that these actions are hateful to Allah the Exalted, and the hateful cannot be willed by Him, so these actions are not willed by Allah the Exalted. Thus the statement of one who says, "Whatever enters existence is willed by Allah the Exalted," is refuted. And once it is established that they are not by the will of Allah the Exalted, it must follow that they are not created by Him, for if they were created by Allah the Exalted, they would be willed by Him. "And do not walk upon the earth exultantly; indeed, you will never tear through the earth, nor will you reach the mountains in height." "All that — its evil is hateful in the sight of your Lord."

Know that this is the second category of the things which Allah has forbidden in these verses, and in it there are issues:

The first issue: al-maraḥ (exultation, arrogance in gait) is an intense joy. One says: marija yamraḥu maraḥan, so he is marih. The meaning of the verse is the prohibition against a person walking in a manner that indicates pride and greatness. Al-Zajjaj said: "Do not walk upon the earth haughtily and boastfully." A parallel to this is the words of Allah the Exalted in Surat al-Furqan: "And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility" [al-Furqan: 63]. And He said in Surat Luqman: "And be moderate in your walking and lower your voice" [Luqman: 19]. And He also said in it: "And do not walk upon the earth exultantly. Indeed, Allah does not like everyone self-deluded and boastful" [Luqman: 18].

The second issue: al-Akhfash said: "If it were read 'marihan' with a kasra, it would be better in recitation." Al-Zajjaj said: "Maraḥan is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and marihan is the active participle (ism al-fa'il), and both are permissible, except that the verbal noun is better here and more emphatic. You say: 'Zayd came running (rakḍan)' and 'running (rakiḍan)'; rakḍan is more emphatic because it indicates the emphasis of the verb." Then, He, the Exalted, emphasized the prohibition against vanity and arrogance, saying: "Indeed, you will never tear through the earth, nor will you reach the mountains in height." Here, by "tearing" is meant piercing the earth. Then they mentioned regarding it several aspects:

The first: walking requires rising and lowering, so it is as if it were said: "In your lowering, you cannot pierce the earth and break through it, and in your rising, you cannot reach the peaks of the mountains." The purpose is to alert to his being weak and powerless, so arrogance does not befit him.

The second: the meaning is that beneath you is the earth, which you cannot pierce, and above you are the mountains, which you cannot reach. So you are encompassed from above and below by two kinds of inanimate matter, and you are far weaker than both. The weak and confined one does not deserve arrogance. It is as if it were said to him: "Be humble and do not be arrogant, for you are a weak creature among the creatures of Allah, confined between stone and dust, so do not act like the empowered and mighty."

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: "All that — its evil is hateful in the sight of your Lord." In it there are issues:

The first issue: Most readers read "sayyi'uhu" with a damma on the ha' and the hamza, while Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "sayyi'atan" in the accusative. As for the reading of the majority, its basis is apparent from two aspects:

The first aspect: Al-Hasan said: "Allah mentioned before this things He commanded some of and forbade others. So if He judged all of them to be an evil, it would follow that what was commanded would be an evil, and that is not permissible. But if we read it with the construct form, the meaning is that whatever of those mentioned things is evil, it is hateful in the sight of Allah, and the sentence is sound."

The second aspect: If we judged everything previously mentioned to be an evil, it would necessarily be said that they are hateful, and the matter is not so, because He said: "hatefully (makruhan)". But if we read it in the construct form, the meaning is that the evil of those categories is hateful, and then the sentence is sound. As for the reading of Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr, there are aspects to it:

The first: that the sentence was complete at His saying: "That is better and more excellent in outcome," then He began and said: "And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge," and "And do not walk upon the earth exultantly," then He said: "All that was an evil (sayyi'atan)," and the intended meaning is these last matters which Allah forbade.

The second: that by His saying "All that" is meant: all that Allah forbade in what preceded.

* * *

As for His saying "makruhan," they mentioned in its correction under this reading several aspects:

The first: the estimate is: "All that was an evil and was hateful."

Do you not see that you say: 'Adultery is an evil,' just as you say: 'Theft is an evil,' so you do not distinguish between attributing it to a masculine or feminine noun."

The third: there is an inversion, and the estimate is: "All that was hateful and an evil in the sight of your Lord."

The fourth: it is carried to the meaning, because the evil is the sin, and it is masculine.
