Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verse 39–40:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is of what your Lord has revealed to you of wisdom. And do not set up with Allah another deity, lest you be thrown into Hell, blameworthy and expelled.﴾ ﴿Has your Lord then preferred you with sons and taken for Himself from the angels females? Indeed, you say a terrible saying.﴾

Page 171

Know that He, exalted is He, has gathered in this verse twenty-five types of obligations:

The first of them: His saying, ﴿And do not set up with Allah another deity﴾, and His saying, ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you not worship except Him﴾ [al-Isra: 23], comprises two obligations: the command to worship Allah, exalted is He, and the prohibition against worshipping other than Allah. So the total is three. His saying, ﴿and to parents, good treatment﴾ [al-Isra: 23] is the fourth. Then He mentioned, in explaining that goodness, five others, namely: His saying, ﴿So do not say to them, "Uff," and do not repel them, but speak to them a noble word﴾, ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy and say, "My Lord, have mercy on them as they brought me up when I was small"﴾ [al-Isra: 23–24]. So the total becomes nine. Then He said, ﴿And give the relative his right, and the needy, and the traveler﴾, which is three, so the total becomes twelve. Then He said, ﴿And do not squander extravagantly﴾ [al-Isra: 26], so it becomes thirteen. Then He said, ﴿And if you turn away from them, seeking mercy from your Lord which you await, then speak to them a gentle word﴾, which is the fourteenth. Then He said, ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾ [al-Isra: 28–29] to the end of the verse, which is the fifteenth. Then He said, ﴿And do not kill your children﴾ [al-Isra: 31], which is the sixteenth. Then He said, ﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right﴾, which is the seventeenth. Then He said, ﴿And whoever is killed unjustly, We have given his heir authority﴾, which is the eighteenth. Then He said, ﴿So let him not commit excess in killing﴾ [al-Isra: 33], which is the nineteenth. Then He said, ﴿And fulfill the covenant﴾ [al-Isra: 34], which is the twentieth. Then He said, ﴿And give full measure when you measure﴾, which is the twenty-first. Then He said, ﴿And weigh with a true balance﴾ [al-Isra: 35], which is the twenty-second. Then He said, ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge﴾ [al-Isra: 36], which is the twenty-third. Then He said, ﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾ [al-Isra: 37], which is the twenty-fourth. Then He said, ﴿And do not set up with Allah another deity﴾, which is the twenty-fifth. These are twenty-five types of obligations, some of them commands and some of them prohibitions, which Allah, exalted is He, gathered in these verses, and He made their opening His saying: ﴿Do not set up with Allah another deity, lest you sit blameworthy and forsaken﴾ [al-Isra: 22], and their closing His saying: ﴿And do not set up with Allah another deity, lest you be thrown into Hell, blameworthy and expelled.﴾

Having known this, we say: here are some benefits.

The first benefit: His saying, ﴿That﴾ refers to all the obligations mentioned before, and He called them wisdom. He named them by this name for several reasons:

One of them: their substance returns to the command to monotheism, to various kinds of obedience and good deeds, to turning away from this world and turning toward the Hereafter, and reason indicates their soundness. So one who brings a law like this would not be calling to the religion of Satan; rather, the original nature testifies that he calls to the religion of the Most Merciful. The full elaboration of this is what we mention in Surah al-Shu'ara in His saying: ﴿Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend? They descend upon every sinful liar﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 221–222].

Second: the rulings mentioned in these verses are laws obligatory to observe in all religions and creeds, and they do not accept abrogation or nullification; so they were firm (muhkam) and wisdom from this consideration.

Third: wisdom is an expression for knowing the truth for its own sake and the good for the sake of acting upon it. The command to monotheism is an expression for the first category, and the rest of the obligations are an expression for teaching good deeds so that a person persists in them and does not deviate from them. Thus it is established that these things mentioned in these verses are the very essence of wisdom. It is reported from Ibn Abbas that these verses were in the tablets of Musa, peace be upon him:

The first of them: ﴿And do not set up with Allah another deity﴾. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets of everything an admonition and a detailed explanation of all things﴾ [al-A'raf: 145].

The second benefit from the benefits of this verse: He, exalted is He, began these obligations with the command to monotheism and the prohibition of polytheism, and concluded them with this very same meaning. The purpose of this is to alert that the beginning of every deed, saying, thought and remembrance must be the mention of monotheism, and its end must be the mention of monotheism, as an alert that the aim of all obligations is knowledge of monotheism and immersion in it. So this repetition is well placed for this great benefit. Then He, exalted is He, mentioned in the first verse that polytheism makes its doer blameworthy and forsaken, and mentioned in the last verse that polytheism makes its doer thrown into Hell, blameworthy and expelled. So blame and forsaking occur in this world, and being thrown into Hell occurs on the Day of Resurrection. It is incumbent upon us to mention the difference between "blameworthy and forsaken" and "blameworthy and expelled." We say: As for the difference between "mazmum" (blameworthy) and "malum" (blame-deserving), its meaning is that being mazmum means that it is said to him that the act he committed is ugly and reprehensible; this is the meaning of being mazmum. When this is said to him, then it is said to him: Why did you do such an act? What moved you to it? You gained nothing from this deed but harming yourself; and this is blame. Thus it is established that the first stage is that he becomes mazmum, and the last stage is that he becomes malum. As for the difference between "makhdhul" (forsaken) and "mahdur" (expelled), makhdhul is an expression for the weak; it is said: "his limbs became slack" (takhadhalat), i.e., weakened. As for mahdur, it is the one who is driven away, and driving away is an expression for contempt and humiliation. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and he will abide therein in humiliation﴾ [al-Furqan: 69]. So being makhdhul is an expression for withholding help from him and leaving him to himself, and being mahdur is an expression for humiliating him and treating him with contempt. Thus it is established that the first stage is that he becomes makhdhul, and the last stage is that he becomes mahdur. And Allah knows best what He intends.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Has your Lord then preferred you with sons and taken for Himself from the angels females?﴾ know that when He, exalted is He, alerted to the corruption of the way of one who ascribes a partner and equal to Allah, He alerted to the way of one who ascribes offspring to Him, and to the complete ignorance of this group, namely that they believed offspring to be of two kinds: the more noble of the two kinds is sons, and the baser of the two is daughters. Then they ascribed sons to themselves despite knowing their utmost weakness and deficiency, and they ascribed daughters to Allah despite knowing that Allah, exalted is He, is the One described with perfection that has no limit and majesty that has no end. This indicates the utmost ignorance of the one who says this saying. Its parallels are His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Has He daughters and you have sons?﴾ [al-Tur: 39], and His saying: ﴿Is for you the male and for Him the female?﴾ [al-Najm: 21]. As for His saying: ﴿afasfakum﴾, it is said "asfahu bi al-shay'" when one gives preference to someone with something, and the lands which the ruler reserves for his private use are called "al-sawafi." Abu Ubayda said regarding His saying ﴿afasfakum﴾: "Did He single you out?" and al-Mufaddal said: "Did He choose you exclusively?" The grammarians said: this hamza is a hamza indicating denial, in the form of a question, regarding a doctrine of manifest corruption, to which its adherent has no answer except one that contains the greatest disgrace.

* * *

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, you say a terrible saying﴾. The explanation of this magnitude is from two aspects:

The first: that affirming offspring entails that He, exalted is He, is composed of parts and components, and this undermines His being eternal and necessarily existent in His essence. This is a terrible saying and an abhorrent speech.

The second: that even if offspring were established, you would have made the more noble of the two kinds for yourselves and the baser of the two kinds for Allah. This too is a great ignorance.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verses 41–44 (part 1 of 2):

Page 173
His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly varied [the proofs] in this Qur'an that they may be reminded, but it increases them only in aversion﴾ ﴿Say, "If there were with Him other gods, as they say, then they would have sought a way to the Owner of the Throne."﴾ ﴿Exalted is He, and high above what they say, [with] great exaltation.﴾ ﴿The seven heavens and the earth and whatever is in them exalt Him. And there is not a thing except that it exalts [Allah] by His praise, but you do not understand their [way of] exalting. Indeed, He is ever Forbearing and Forgiving.﴾

Know that at-tasrif (variation, turning from one thing to another) in the language means turning a thing from one direction to another, like the turning of the winds and the turning of affairs. This is the original meaning in the language. Then the word tasrif was used as a metaphor for clarification, because whoever attempts to explain something turns his speech from one kind to another and from one example to another, in order to complete the explanation and strengthen the clarity. So His saying, ﴿And We have certainly varied﴾ means: We have clarified. The object of tasrif is omitted, and there are several views on it:

The first: ﴿And We have certainly varied in this Qur'an kinds of every example.﴾

The second: that the particle ﴿fi﴾ (in) is superfluous, as in His saying: ﴿And make righteous for me my offspring﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 15], meaning: make righteous for me my offspring.

As for His saying, ﴿that they may be reminded﴾, there are two issues:

The first issue: The majority read ﴿liyadhdhakaru﴾ with a fatha on the dhal and the kaf and with shaddah on both, and the meaning is liyatadhakkaru (that they may reflect), and the ta' was assimilated into the dhal because their articulation points are close. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿liyadhkuru﴾ with a sukun on the dhal and a damma on the kaf, and in Surat al-Furqan there is similar wording from dhikr. Al-Wahidi said: Here tadhakkur is more fitting than dhikr, because what is meant by it is contemplation and reflection, and what is not meant is the remembrance that occurs after forgetfulness. Then he said: As for the reading of Hamzah and al-Kisa'i, there are two views:

The first: that dhikr has come with the meaning of reflection and contemplation, as in His exalted saying: ﴿Take what We have given you with strength and remember what is in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 63], meaning: understand what is in it.

The second: that the meaning may be: We have varied these proofs in this Qur'an so that they may mention it with their tongues, for remembrance by the tongue may lead to the heart being affected by its meaning.

The second issue: Al-Jubba'i said: His saying, ﴿And We have certainly varied in this Qur'an that they may be reminded﴾, indicates that Allah, exalted is He, only sent down this Qur'an, and only increased in it the mention of proofs, because He, exalted is He, wanted from them understanding of them and faith in them. This indicates that He, exalted is He, does His acts for wise purposes, and it indicates that He, exalted is He, wanted faith from all, whether they believed or disbelieved. And Allah knows best.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿but it increases them only in aversion﴾, and concerning it there are two issues:

The first issue: Al-Asamm said: He likened them to fleeing animals, meaning: they only increased in distance from the truth. This is like His saying: ﴿so it increased them in filth﴾ [at-Tawbah: 125].

The second issue: Our companions (the Ash'aris) used this verse as evidence that Allah, exalted is He, did not will faith from the disbelievers. **Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 17, verses 45–48:**

[Page 177]

*"And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a hidden barrier. And We have placed over their hearts coverings, lest they understand it, and in their ears a deafness. And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an, they turn back on their backs in aversion. We know best what they listen to when they listen to you, and when they confer privately, when the wrongdoers say, 'You follow only a man affected by sorcery.' Look how they strike comparisons for you, so they have gone astray and cannot find a way."*

God Most High, when He spoke in the previous verse about the divine matters, speaks in this verse about what relates to establishing prophethood. The verse contains several issues.

**The first issue:** Regarding His words, *"And when you recite the Qur'an"*, there are two opinions.

The first opinion is that this verse was revealed concerning a people who used to harm the Messenger of God (ﷺ) when he recited the Qur'an to the people. It is narrated that "whenever he (ﷺ) recited the Qur'an, two men from his right and two others from his left, from the descendants of Qusayy, would stand, clapping, whistling, and mixing poetry into his recitation." And it is narrated from Asma' that "the Prophet (ﷺ) was sitting with Abu Bakr when the wife of Abu Lahab came, with a stone in her hand, seeking the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and she was saying:

*"We have come to Mudhammam, we despise his religion,*
*and we disobey his command."*

Abu Bakr said: "O Messenger of God, she has a stone with her, and I fear for you from it." So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited this verse, and she came, but she did not see the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and she said: "Quraysh knows that I am the daughter of its chief, and that your companion has satirized me." Abu Bakr said: "No, by the Lord of this House, he has not satirized you."

Ibn Abbas narrated that "Abu Sufyan, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Abu Jahl and others used to sit with the Prophet (ﷺ) and listen to his speech. One day al-Nadr said: 'I do not know what Muhammad is saying, except that I see his lips moving with something.' Abu Sufyan said: 'I see that some of what he says is true.' Abu Jahl said: 'He is a madman.' Abu Lahab said: 'He is a soothsayer.' And Huwaytib ibn Abd al-Uzza said: 'He is a poet.' Then this verse was revealed." And whenever the Messenger of God (ﷺ) intended to recite the Qur'an, he would recite before it three verses, which are His words in Surah al-Kahf: *"Indeed, We have placed over their hearts coverings lest they understand it, and in their ears a deafness"* [18:57], and in al-Nahl: *"Those are the ones whom God has sealed upon their hearts"* [16:108], and in Ha-Mim al-Jathiyah: *"Have you seen one who takes his own desire as his god?"* [45:23], up to the end of the verse. So God Most High would veil him, by the blessings of these verses, from the eyes of the polytheists. This is what is meant by His words: *"We placed between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a hidden barrier."*

There is a question here: it should have been said *"a concealing barrier"* (ḥijāban sātiran).

The answer to it is in several respects:

**The first respect:** That barrier is a barrier which God Most High creates in their eyes, such that that barrier prevents them from seeing the Prophet (ﷺ), and that barrier is a thing no one sees; thus it is "hidden" in this respect. Our companions (the Ash'arites) argued with this verse for the validity of their view that it is possible for the sense faculty to be sound while the object perceived is present, yet that person does not see it, because God Most High created in his eyes an obstruction preventing him from seeing it. They said by this verse: the Prophet (ﷺ) was present, and the senses of the unbelievers were sound, yet they did not see him. **The first:** *Nufūr* is a verbal noun, and the meaning is "they turned away, being averse, an aversion."

**The second:** That *nufūran* is the plural of *nāfir*, like *shuhūd* and *shāhid*, *rukūʿ* and *rākiʿ*, *sujūd* and *sājid*, *quʿūd* and *qāʿid*.

\* \* \*

Then He said: *"We know best what they listen to when they listen to you."* That is: We know best the manner in which they listen, which is mockery and denial. The *bihi* (with it) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), as you say: "listening with mockery." *"When they listen"* is governed by *aʿlamu* (we know best), meaning: We know best at the time of their listening what they listen with. *"And when they confer privately"*: and what they confer about privately, when they are people who confer privately. *"When the wrongdoers say"* is a substitute for His words *"and when they confer privately, when the wrongdoers say, 'You follow only a man affected by sorcery.'"* In this there are discussions:

**The first:** The exegetes said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) commanded Ali to prepare a meal and invite to it the nobles of Quraysh among the polytheists. Ali did so, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) entered upon them, recited the Qur'an to them, called them to monotheism, and said: 'Say: There is no god but God, so that the Arabs obey you and the non-Arabs submit to you.' But they refused him in that. And when they listened to the Prophet (ﷺ) reciting the Qur'an and calling to God Most High, they would say, conferring among themselves: 'He is a sorcerer,' and 'He is one affected by sorcery,' and what is similar to that of speech." So God Most High informed His Prophet that they say: *"You follow only a man affected by sorcery."*

If it is said: they did not follow the Messenger of God, so how is it correct for them to say *"You follow only a man affected by sorcery"*?

We say: its meaning is that if you follow him, then you have followed a man affected by sorcery. The one affected by sorcery is one who has been bewitched, so his intellect is confused and he has departed from the state of balance. This is the correct view. Some said: the *masḥūr* is one who has been corrupted. One says "food is *masḥūr*" when its making has been corrupted, and "land is *masḥūrah*" when it has received more rain than it should, thus corrupting it. Abu Ubayda said: he means a human being with *siḥr*, meaning possessing a lung (*ri'ah*). Ibn Qutayba said: "I do not know what led him to this objectionable interpretation, when the early generations (*al-salaf*) explained it by clear meanings." Mujahid said: *"masḥūran"* means "deceived," because sorcery is trickery and deception. This is because the polytheists used to say: "Muhammad learns these words from some people, and those people deceive him with these words and these narratives," so they said: "He is *masḥūr*," meaning deceived. Also they used to say: "The Satan appears to him in imagination, so he thinks it is an angel," so they said: "He is deceived by Satan."

\* \* \*

Then He said: *"Look how they strike comparisons for you."* That is: everyone compares you to something else. They said: "He is a soothsayer, a sorcerer, a poet, a teacher, and a madman." So they went astray from the truth and the straight path, and *"they cannot find a way"* to guidance and truth.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 17, verses 45–48:**

[Page 177]

*"And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a hidden barrier. And We have placed over their hearts coverings, lest they understand it, and in their ears a deafness. And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an, they turn back on their backs in aversion. We know best what they listen to when they listen to you, and when they confer privately, when the wrongdoers say, 'You follow only a man affected by sorcery.' Look how they strike comparisons for you, so they have gone astray and cannot find a way."*

God Most High, when He spoke in the previous verse about the divine matters, speaks in this verse about what relates to establishing prophethood. The verse contains several issues.

**The first issue:** Regarding His words, *"And when you recite the Qur'an"*, there are two opinions.

The first opinion is that this verse was revealed concerning a people who used to harm the Messenger of God (ﷺ) when he recited the Qur'an to the people. It is narrated that "whenever he (ﷺ) recited the Qur'an, two men from his right and two others from his left, from the descendants of Qusayy, would stand, clapping, whistling, and mixing poetry into his recitation." And it is narrated from Asma' that "the Prophet (ﷺ) was sitting with Abu Bakr when the wife of Abu Lahab came, with a stone in her hand, seeking the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and she was saying:

*"We have come to Mudhammam, we despise his religion,*
*and we disobey his command."*

Abu Bakr said: "O Messenger of God, she has a stone with her, and I fear for you from it." So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited this verse, and she came, but she did not see the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and she said: "Quraysh knows that I am the daughter of its chief, and that your companion has satirized me." Abu Bakr said: "No, by the Lord of this House, he has not satirized you."

Ibn Abbas narrated that "Abu Sufyan, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Abu Jahl and others used to sit with the Prophet (ﷺ) and listen to his speech. One day al-Nadr said: 'I do not know what Muhammad is saying, except that I see his lips moving with something.' Abu Sufyan said: 'I see that some of what he says is true.' Abu Jahl said: 'He is a madman.' Abu Lahab said: 'He is a soothsayer.' And Huwaytib ibn Abd al-Uzza said: 'He is a poet.' Then this verse was revealed." And whenever the Messenger of God (ﷺ) intended to recite the Qur'an, he would recite before it three verses, which are His words in Surah al-Kahf: *"Indeed, We have placed over their hearts coverings lest they understand it, and in their ears a deafness"* [18:57], and in al-Nahl: *"Those are the ones whom God has sealed upon their hearts"* [16:108], and in Ha-Mim al-Jathiyah: *"Have you seen one who takes his own desire as his god?"* [45:23], up to the end of the verse. So God Most High would veil him, by the blessings of these verses, from the eyes of the polytheists. This is what is meant by His words: *"We placed between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a hidden barrier."*

There is a question here: it should have been said *"a concealing barrier"* (ḥijāban sātiran).

The answer to it is in several respects:

**The first respect:** That barrier is a barrier which God Most High creates in their eyes, such that that barrier prevents them from seeing the Prophet (ﷺ), and that barrier is a thing no one sees; thus it is "hidden" in this respect. Our companions (the Ash'arites) argued with this verse for the validity of their view that it is possible for the sense faculty to be sound while the object perceived is present, yet that person does not see it, because God Most High created in his eyes an obstruction preventing him from seeing it. They said by this verse: the Prophet (ﷺ) was present, and the senses of the unbelievers were sound, yet they did not see him. God Most High informed that this was only because He placed between him and them a hidden barrier. A "hidden barrier" has no meaning except the meaning God created in their eyes, and that meaning was preventing them from seeing and perceiving him.

**The second respect:** It is like saying *lābin* and *tāmir*, meaning *dhū labanin* (possessor of milk) and *dhū tamrin* (possessor of dates). Likewise, it is not far-fetched to say that *"mastūran"* means *dhū sitrin* (possessor of a covering). The evidence for this is the phrase *marṭūb*, meaning *dhū rutūbah* (possessor of moisture), and one does not say *raṭībah*. One says *makānun mahūl*, meaning there is terror in it, and one does not say "I terrified the place" in the sense of "I put terror in it." And one says *jāriyatun maghnūjah*, meaning possessor of coquetry (*ghunj*), and one does not say "I coquetted her."

**The third respect:** Al-Akhfash said: *al-mastūr* here means *al-sātir* (the concealing one), for the active participle may come in the form of the passive participle, as one says: "Indeed you are *mashʾūm* (ill-omened) for us and *maymūn* (blessed)," whereas the correct forms are *shāʾim* and *yāmin*, because it derives from their saying *sha'ammahum* and *yammanahum*. This is al-Akhfash's view, and a group followed him in it, although many of them criticized this view. The truth is the first answer.

**The second opinion:** The meaning of the barrier is the seal (ṭabʿ) upon their hearts, and the seal and the prevention which prevented them from perceiving the subtleties, beauties, and benefits of the Qur'an. So what is meant by the hidden barrier is that seal which God created in their hearts.

\* \* \*

Then He said: *"And We have placed over their hearts coverings lest they understand it, and in their ears a deafness."* This verse is mentioned word for word in Surah al-An'am [6:25], and we mentioned there our companions' argument from it and the objections of the Mu'tazilah (the Rationalist school). It is not objectionable to repeat some of it. Our companions said: this verse indicates that God Most High placed their hearts within coverings. *Akinnah* is the plural of *kinān*, which is that which covers a thing, like the quiver of arrows (*kinān al-nabl*). His words *"lest they understand it"* mean: so that they do not understand it. And He placed in their ears a deafness. It is known that they were intelligent, hearing, and understanding; so we know that what is meant is preventing them from faith and preventing them from hearing the Qur'an in such a way that they do not comprehend its secrets or understand its subtleties and realities.

The Mu'tazilah said: what is meant by the verse is not what you have mentioned, but rather other meanings:

**The first:** Al-Jubba'i said: they used to seek out his place at night in order to reach him and harm him, and they would deduce his place of sleep by hearing his recitation. So God Most High gave him security from their evil, and mentioned to him that He had placed between him and them a barrier, so they could not reach him by it. He explained that He placed in their hearts what would preoccupy them from understanding the Qur'an, and in their ears what would prevent them from hearing his voice. It is possible that this is a preoccupying sickness that prevents them from going to him and devoting themselves to him, not that there actually occurred a covering over the heart and a deafness in the ear.

**The second:** Al-Ka'bi said: because of the intensity of their refusal to accept the proofs of Muhammad (ﷺ), they became as if there had arisen between them and those proofs a barrier that prevents and conceals. God Most High attributed that barrier to Himself, because when He left them with themselves, and did not prevent them from that aversion, that abandonment became as if it were the cause of their falling into that state. This is like a master who does not watch over the conduct of his slave; when his conduct worsens, the master says: "It is I who put you in this state, because I left you with your own opinion and did not watch over your condition."

**The third:** Al-Qaffal said: when He forsook them, meaning He did not perform the favours that would summon them to faith, it became correct to say that He performed the concealing barrier.

Know that these views, together with other statements we mentioned in Surah al-An'am, and answered there, so there is no benefit in repeating them.

\* \* \*

**Al-Razi's commentary (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 17, verses 49–52:**

God Most High says: ﴿They say, "When we have become bones and dust, shall we really be raised up in a new creation?"﴾ ﴿Say, "Be stones or iron,"﴾ ﴿"or a creation of what is greater in your breasts." They will say, "Who will bring us back?" Say, "He who created you the first time." They will shake their heads at you and say, "When will that be?" Say, "Perhaps it is near."﴾ ﴿On the day He calls you, you will respond with His praise, and you will think you stayed only a little while.﴾

Know that when God Most High first spoke about the divine matters (al-ilahiyyat, theology) and then followed that with the doubts they raised concerning prophethood (al-nubuwwat), He mentioned in this verse the doubts of the people in denying the return (al-ma'ad), the resurrection (al-ba'th) and the Resurrection Day (al-qiyamah). We have mentioned many times that the Qur'an revolves around four issues: theology, prophethood, the return, and divine decree and destiny (al-qada' wa'l-qadar). Also, the people described the Messenger of God (ﷺ) as bewitched, of corrupted mind. Among the things they cited as proof of the corruption of his mind was that he claimed that after a human being becomes bones and dust, he returns alive and rational as he was. So they related this statement from him to establish that he was of deranged mind.

Al-Wahidi (may God have mercy on him) said: al-rafat is breaking a thing with your hand. You say: rafatahu, arfituhu, with kasra, as crumbling clay or decayed bone is crumbled. Al-rufat are the crumbled pieces of anything that is broken. It is said: rafata 'izam al-jazur raftan, if he broke the bones of the slaughtered camel. And it is said of figs: al-rufat, because they are fine crumbs of the crop. Al-Akhfash said: rafata raftan, so he is marfut, like hatama hatman, so he is mahtum; and al-rufat and al-hutam are nouns, like al-judhadh, al-rudad and al-futat. This is what relates to the language.

As for the statement of the doubt of the people: when a human dies, his limbs dry out, scatter and disperse around the world, and the parts of his body mix with the other parts of the world. The watery parts of the body mix with the waters of the world; the earthy parts mix with the earth of the world; the airy parts mix with the air of the world; and the fiery parts mix with the fire of the world. When the matter is like this, how is it conceivable that they gather again in their same particular selves? And how is it conceivable that life returns to them in their same particular selves? This is the statement of the doubt.

As for the answer to it: this difficulty is not complete except by impugning the perfection of God's knowledge and the perfection of His power. As for when we grant that He, exalted is He, knows all particulars, then these parts, although they have mixed with the parts of the world, are nevertheless distinct in God's knowledge, Most High. And since we grant that He, Most High, is capable of all possibilities, He is capable of restoring the composition, the assembly and the life and reason to those very parts. Thus it is established that whenever we grant the perfection of God's knowledge and the perfection of His power, this doubt wholly disappears.

As for the statement of God Most High: ﴿Say, "Be stones or iron,"﴾ the meaning is that the people deemed it unlikely that He would return them to the state of life after they had become bones and dust. Although that attribute apparently precludes receiving life, they assumed that these bodies, after death, would end up in another attribute even more incompatible with receiving life than being bones and dust, such as becoming stones or iron. The incompatibility between being stone or iron and receiving life is greater than the incompatibility between being bone and receiving life, because bone had once been part of a living body, whereas stone and iron were never at all described as living. So, supposing that human bodies become described with the attribute of stoniness or ironness after death, God Most High restores life to them and makes them living and rational as they were. The proof of the soundness of this is that those bodies are capable of life and reason, since if this capacity were not present, life and reason would not have come to them in the first place. The God of the world knows all particulars, so the parts of the body of Zayd, the obedient, are not confused for the parts of the body of 'Amr, the disobedient. And He is capable of all possibilities. Since it is established that the return of life to those parts is possible in itself, and it is established that the God of the world knows all knowable things and is capable of all possibilities, the return of life to those parts is necessarily possible, whether they have become bones and dust or have become something further from bone in receiving life, namely stones or iron. This is the statement of this matter with a conclusive rational proof. His saying ﴿Be stones or iron﴾ does not mean a command; rather, the meaning is that even if you were so, you would not make God Most High unable to restore you. This is like the saying of one who says to a man: "Do you hope to get anything from me when I am so-and-so?" and he replies: "Be whoever you want; be the son of the caliph, I will still demand my right from you."

If it is said: what is meant by His saying ﴿or a creation of what is greater in your breasts﴾?

We say: the meaning is that the fact that stone and iron are capable of life is something unlikely. So it was said to them: suppose something else further from receiving life than stone and iron, to the point that your reason finds it unlikely that it could receive life. In this sense, there is no need to specify what that thing is, because the meaning is that human bodies, however far they end up after death, into whatever attribute they are supposed and whatever state they are imagined, even if they are at the extreme of distance from receiving life, God Most High is capable of restoring life to them. And when the meaning of the verse is this, there is no need to specify that thing.

Ibn 'Abbas said: what is meant is death, that is, even if your bodies became death itself, God Most High would restore life to them. Know that this statement is only fitting to mention by way of exaggeration, like saying: "Even if you were the very essence of life, God would make you die; and even if you were the very essence of wealth, God would make you poor." This has been mentioned by way of exaggeration. As for the reality of the matter, it is impossible, because human bodies are substances (ajsam), and death is an accident ('arad), and a substance does not turn into an accident. Then, even supposing it turned into an accident, death would not receive life, because one of two opposites cannot be characterized by the other opposite. Mujahid said: it means the heaven and the earth.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿They will say, "Who will bring us back?" Say, "He who created you the first time."﴾ The meaning is that when He said to them: "Be stones or iron, or something further in receiving life than these two," the restoration of life to it is possible. At that point they said: "Who is this who is able to restore life to it?" God Most High said: Say, O Muhammad, "He who created you the first time." That is, the affirmation of the validity of return is a consequence of granting that the Creator of living beings is God Most High.

Once this is established, we say: those bodies are capable of life and reason, and the God of the world is capable by His essence and knowing by His essence, so His knowledge and power never fail at all. Whoever is capable of initiating is necessarily capable of returning. This is a complete statement and a strong proof.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿They will shake their heads at you﴾. Al-Farra' said: it is said: anghada fulan ra'sahu yunghiduhu inghadan, if he moves it up and down. The ostrich is called naghd because it moves its head. Abu al-Haytham said: it is said of a man who, when told something, shakes his head in denial: "he has nodded his head." So His saying ﴿they will shake their heads at you﴾ means they will move them in a manner of denial and disbelief.

Then God Most High said: ﴿and they say, "When is it?"﴾ Know that this question is corrupt, because they had already judged the impossibility of gathering and resurrection on the basis of the doubt we have related. Then God Most High demonstrated with a dazzling proof that it is possible in itself. So their saying "When is it?" is a statement unconnected to the first inquiry. Since it has been established by rational proof that it is possible in itself, it is obligatory to acknowledge its possibility. As for when it will occur, this cannot be established by reason; rather, it can only be established by transmitted textual evidence (al-dala'il al-sam'iyyah). If God Most High informs of that specific time, it becomes known; otherwise there is no way to know it.

Know that God Most High has made clear in the Qur'an that He does not inform any of creation of its specific time. He said: ﴿Indeed, God has knowledge of the Hour﴾ [Luqman: 34], and He said: ﴿Its knowledge is only with my Lord﴾ [al-A'raf: 187], and He said: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 15]. Therefore, He said: ﴿Say, "Perhaps it is near."﴾ The commentators said: "perhaps" (asa) from God is binding, its meaning being that it is near.

If they say: how can it be near when six hundred years have passed and it has not appeared?

We say: when what has passed is more than what remains, what remains is near and little.

Then God Most High said: ﴿On the day He calls you﴾. In this there are two views:

The first: it is an address to the disbelievers, as evidenced by the fact that everything before this verse is an address to the disbelievers. Then we say that "a day" (yawman) is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for His saying "near." The meaning is: "perhaps the resurrection will be on the day He calls you," that is, with the call that makes you hear, which is the final blast, as He said: ﴿On the day the caller calls from a near place﴾ [Qaf: 41]. It is said that Israfil calls: "O decayed bodies, withered bones and scattered parts, return as you were by the power of God Most High, with His permission and His bringing into being." And God Most High said: ﴿On the day the caller calls to a terrible thing﴾ [al-Qamar: 6]. His saying ﴿you will respond with His praise﴾ means you will answer. Istijabah (response) is conformity with the caller in what he calls to, and it is the same as ijabah (answer), except that istijabah implies seeking conformity, so it is more emphatic than ijabah. As for His saying ﴿with His praise﴾: Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: they will come out of their graves and shake the dust from their heads, and say: "Glory be to You and praise be to You," and this is His saying ﴿you will respond with His praise﴾. Qatadah said: "with knowing Him and obeying Him." The rationale for this view is that when they answered with glorification and praise, that was a recognition and obedience from them, but that will not benefit them on that day. Therefore the commentators said: "they praised when praise will not benefit them." The people of the meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: "you will respond praising Him," that is, you will respond while praising, as one says: "he came in his anger," meaning he came angry, and "the prince rode with his sword," meaning his sword was with him. Al-Zamakhshari, the author of the Kashshaf, said: "with His praise" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from them, that is, praising. This is an intensification of their submission to the resurrection, like your saying to someone you order to do a difficult task: "You will do it while praising and thanking," meaning: you will arrive at a state where you praise God and thank Him that He has been content with that task from you. This is mentioned in the context of threat.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and you will think you stayed only a little while.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: it means between the first and second blasts, for at that time the punishment is removed from them. The evidence for this is His saying in Surah Ya-Sin: ﴿Who has raised us from our sleeping place?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 52], so their thinking that this was a short stay refers to their stay between the two blasts. Al-Hasan said: its meaning is the nearness of the time of resurrection, as if you were in this world not having been, and in the Hereafter not having ceased; this returns to considering the duration of the stay in this world as small. It was also said that what is meant is considering their stay on the plain of the Resurrection as small, because, since the final outcome for them was entry into the Fire, they regarded their stay in the barzakh of the Resurrection as short.

The second view: the speech with the disbelievers ends at His saying ﴿perhaps it is near﴾. As for His saying ﴿On the day He calls you, you will respond with His praise﴾, it is an address to the believers, not to the disbelievers, because this statement is the most fitting for the believers, since they respond to God with His praise and praise Him for His favor toward them. The first view is the well-known one, and the second is more apparent in its possibility.

Also, the people described the Messenger of God (ﷺ) as bewitched, of corrupted mind. Among the things they cited as proof of the corruption of his mind was that he claimed that after a human being becomes bones and dust, he returns alive and rational as he was. So they related this statement from him to establish that he was of deranged mind.

Al-Wahidi (may God have mercy on him) said: al-rafat is breaking a thing with your hand. You say: rafatahu, arfituhu, with kasra, as crumbling clay or decayed bone is crumbled. Al-rufat are the crumbled pieces of anything that is broken. It is said: rafata 'izam al-jazur raftan, if he broke the bones of the slaughtered camel. And it is said of figs: al-rufat, because they are fine crumbs of the crop. Al-Akhfash said: rafata raftan, so he is marfut, like hatama hatman, so he is mahtum; and al-rufat and al-hutam are nouns, like al-judhadh, al-rudad and al-futat. This is what relates to the language.

As for the statement of the doubt of the people: when a human dies, his limbs dry out, scatter and disperse around the world, and the parts of his body mix with the other parts of the world. The watery parts of the body mix with the waters of the world; the earthy parts mix with the earth of the world; the airy parts mix with the air of the world; and the fiery parts mix with the fire of the world. When the matter is like this, how is it conceivable that they gather again in their same particular selves? And how is it conceivable that life returns to them in their same particular selves? This is the statement of the doubt.

As for the answer to it: this difficulty is not complete except by impugning the perfection of God's knowledge and the perfection of His power. As for when we grant that He, exalted is He, knows all particulars, then these parts, although they have mixed with the parts of the world, are nevertheless distinct in God's knowledge, Most High. And since we grant that He, Most High, is capable of all possibilities, He is capable of restoring the composition, the assembly and the life and reason to those very parts. Thus it is established that whenever we grant the perfection of God's knowledge and the perfection of His power, this doubt wholly disappears.

As for the statement of God Most High: ﴿Say, "Be stones or iron,"﴾ the meaning is that the people deemed it unlikely that He would return them to the state of life after they had become bones and dust. Although that attribute apparently precludes receiving life, they assumed that these bodies, after death, would end up in another attribute even more incompatible with receiving life than being bones and dust, such as becoming stones or iron. The incompatibility between being stone or iron and receiving life is greater than the incompatibility between being bone and receiving life, because bone had once been part of a living body, whereas stone and iron were never at all described as living. So, supposing that human bodies become described with the attribute of stoniness or ironness after death, God Most High restores life to them and makes them living and rational as they were. The proof of the soundness of this is that those bodies are capable of life and reason, since if this capacity were not present, life and reason would not have come to them in the first place. The God of the world knows all particulars, so the parts of the body of Zayd, the obedient, are not confused for the parts of the body of 'Amr, the disobedient. And He is capable of all possibilities. Since it is established that the return of life to those parts is possible in itself, and it is established that the God of the world knows all knowable things and is capable of all possibilities, the return of life to those parts is necessarily possible, whether they have become bones and dust or have become something further from bone in receiving life, namely stones or iron. This is the statement of this matter with a conclusive rational proof. His saying ﴿Be stones or iron﴾ does not mean a command; rather, the meaning is that even if you were so, you would not make God Most High unable to restore you. This is like the saying of one who says to a man: "Do you hope to get anything from me when I am so-and-so?" and he replies: "Be whoever you want; be the son of the caliph, I will still demand my right from you."

If it is said: what is meant by His saying ﴿or a creation of what is greater in your breasts﴾?

We say: the meaning is that the fact that stone and iron are capable of life is something unlikely. So it was said to them: suppose something else further from receiving life than stone and iron, to the point that your reason finds it unlikely that it could receive life. In this sense, there is no need to specify what that thing is, because the meaning is that human bodies, however far they end up after death, into whatever attribute they are supposed and whatever state they are imagined, even if they are at the extreme of distance from receiving life, God Most High is capable of restoring life to them. And when the meaning of the verse is this, there is no need to specify that thing.

Ibn 'Abbas said: what is meant is death, that is, even if your bodies became death itself, God Most High would restore life to them. Know that this statement is only fitting to mention by way of exaggeration, like saying: "Even if you were the very essence of life, God would make you die; and even if you were the very essence of wealth, God would make you poor." This has been mentioned by way of exaggeration. As for the reality of the matter, it is impossible, because human bodies are substances (ajsam), and death is an accident ('arad), and a substance does not turn into an accident. Then, even supposing it turned into an accident, death would not receive life, because one of two opposites cannot be characterized by the other opposite. Mujahid said: it means the heaven and the earth.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿They will say, "Who will bring us back?" Say, "He who created you the first time."﴾ The meaning is that when He said to them: "Be stones or iron, or something further in receiving life than these two," the restoration of life to it is possible. At that point they said: "Who is this who is able to restore life to it?" God Most High said: Say, O Muhammad, "He who created you the first time." That is, the affirmation of the validity of return is a consequence of granting that the Creator of living beings is God Most High.

Once this is established, we say: those bodies are capable of life and reason, and the God of the world is capable by His essence and knowing by His essence, so His knowledge and power never fail at all. Whoever is capable of initiating is necessarily capable of returning. This is a complete statement and a strong proof.

* * *

So His saying ﴿they will shake their heads at you﴾ means they will move them in a manner of denial and disbelief.

Since it has been established by rational proof that it is possible in itself, it is obligatory to acknowledge its possibility. This is mentioned in the context of threat.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and you will think you stayed only a little while.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: it means between the first and second blasts, for at that time the punishment is removed from them. The second view: the speech with the disbelievers ends at His saying ﴿perhaps it is near﴾. The first view is the well-known one, and the second is more apparent in its possibility.

We say: the meaning is that the fact that stone and iron are capable of life is something unlikely. So it was said to them: suppose something else further from receiving life than stone and iron, to the point that your reason finds it unlikely that it could receive life. In this sense, there is no need to specify what that thing is, because the meaning is that human bodies, however far they end up after death, into whatever attribute they are supposed and whatever state they are imagined, even if they are at the extreme of distance from receiving life, God Most High is capable of restoring life to them. And when the meaning of the verse is this, there is no need to specify that thing.

Ibn 'Abbas said: what is meant is death, that is, even if your bodies became death itself, God Most High would restore life to them. Know that this statement is only fitting to mention by way of exaggeration, like saying: "Even if you were the very essence of life, God would make you die; and even if you were the very essence of wealth, God would make you poor." This has been mentioned by way of exaggeration. As for the reality of the matter, it is impossible, because human bodies are substances (ajsam), and death is an accident ('arad), and a substance does not turn into an accident. Then, even supposing it turned into an accident, death would not receive life, because one of two opposites cannot be characterized by the other opposite. Mujahid said: it means the heaven and the earth.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿They will say, "Who will bring us back?" Say, "He who created you the first time."﴾ The meaning is that when He said to them: "Be stones or iron, or something further in receiving life than these two," the restoration of life to it is possible. At that point they said: "Who is this who is able to restore life to it?" God Most High said: Say, O Muhammad, "He who created you the first time." That is, the affirmation of the validity of return is a consequence of granting that the Creator of living beings is God Most High.

Once this is established, we say: those bodies are capable of life and reason, and the God of the world is capable by His essence and knowing by His essence, so His knowledge and power never fail at all. Whoever is capable of initiating is necessarily capable of returning. This is a complete statement and a strong proof.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿They will shake their heads at you﴾. Al-Farra' said: it is said: anghada fulan ra'sahu yunghiduhu inghadan, if he moves it up and down. The ostrich is called naghd because it moves its head. Abu al-Haytham said: it is said of a man who, when told something, shakes his head in denial: "he has nodded his head." So His saying ﴿they will shake their heads at you﴾ means they will move them in a manner of denial and disbelief.

Then God Most High said: ﴿and they say, "When is it?"﴾ Know that this question is corrupt, because they had already judged the impossibility of gathering and resurrection on the basis of the doubt we have related. Then God Most High demonstrated with a dazzling proof that it is possible in itself. So their saying "When is it?" is a statement unconnected to the first inquiry. Since it has been established by rational proof that it is possible in itself, it is obligatory to acknowledge its possibility. As for when it will occur, this cannot be established by reason; rather, it can only be established by transmitted textual evidence (al-dala'il al-sam'iyyah). If God Most High informs of that specific time, it becomes known; otherwise there is no way to know it.

Know that God Most High has made clear in the Qur'an that He does not inform any of creation of its specific time. He said: ﴿Indeed, God has knowledge of the Hour﴾ [Luqman: 34], and He said: ﴿Its knowledge is only with my Lord﴾ [al-A'raf: 187], and He said: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 15]. Therefore, He said: ﴿Say, "Perhaps it is near."﴾ The commentators said: "perhaps" (asa) from God is binding, its meaning being that it is near.

If they say: how can it be near when six hundred years have passed and it has not appeared?

We say: when what has passed is more than what remains, what remains is near and little.

Then God Most High said: ﴿On the day He calls you﴾. In this there are two views:

The first: it is an address to the disbelievers, as evidenced by the fact that everything before this verse is an address to the disbelievers. Then we say that "a day" (yawman) is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for His saying "near." The meaning is: "perhaps the resurrection will be on the day He calls you," that is, with the call that makes you hear, which is the final blast, as He said: ﴿On the day the caller calls from a near place﴾ [Qaf: 41]. It is said that Israfil calls: "O decayed bodies, withered bones and scattered parts, return as you were by the power of God Most High, with His permission and His bringing into being." And God Most High said: ﴿On the day the caller calls to a terrible thing﴾ [al-Qamar: 6]. His saying ﴿you will respond with His praise﴾ means you will answer. Istijabah (response) is conformity with the caller in what he calls to, and it is the same as ijabah (answer), except that istijabah implies seeking conformity, so it is more emphatic than ijabah. As for His saying ﴿with His praise﴾: Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: they will come out of their graves and shake the dust from their heads, and say: "Glory be to You and praise be to You," and this is His saying ﴿you will respond with His praise﴾. Qatadah said: "with knowing Him and obeying Him." The rationale for this view is that when they answered with glorification and praise, that was a recognition and obedience from them, but that will not benefit them on that day. Therefore the commentators said: "they praised when praise will not benefit them." The people of the meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: "you will respond praising Him," that is, you will respond while praising, as one says: "he came in his anger," meaning he came angry, and "the prince rode with his sword," meaning his sword was with him. Al-Zamakhshari, the author of the Kashshaf, said: "with His praise" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from them, that is, praising. This is an intensification of their submission to the resurrection, like your saying to someone you order to do a difficult task: "You will do it while praising and thanking," meaning: you will arrive at a state where you praise God and thank Him that He has been content with that task from you. This is mentioned in the context of threat.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and you will think you stayed only a little while.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: it means between the first and second blasts, for at that time the punishment is removed from them. The evidence for this is His saying in Surah Ya-Sin: ﴿Who has raised us from our sleeping place?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 52], so their thinking that this was a short stay refers to their stay between the two blasts. Al-Hasan said: its meaning is the nearness of the time of resurrection, as if you were in this world not having been, and in the Hereafter not having ceased; this returns to considering the duration of the stay in this world as small. It was also said that what is meant is considering their stay on the plain of the Resurrection as small, because, since the final outcome for them was entry into the Fire, they regarded their stay in the barzakh of the Resurrection as short.

The second view: the speech with the disbelievers ends at His saying ﴿perhaps it is near﴾. As for His saying ﴿On the day He calls you, you will respond with His praise﴾, it is an address to the believers, not to the disbelievers, because this statement is the most fitting for the believers, since they respond to God with His praise and praise Him for His favor toward them. The first view is the well-known one, and the second is more apparent in its possibility.

The Exalted said: "And say to My servants that they should say that which is best. Indeed, Satan incites discord among them. Indeed, Satan is to man a clear enemy. Your Lord is most knowing of you. If He wills, He will have mercy upon you, or if He wills, He will punish you. And We have not sent you as a guardian over them. And your Lord is most knowing of whoever is in the heavens and the earth. And We have certainly preferred some of the prophets over others, and We gave David the Zabur."

Know that His saying, "Say to My servants," has two interpretations.

The first interpretation: the intended meaning is the believers, because the word "servants" ('ibad) in most verses of the Qur'an is specific to the believers. The Exalted said: "So give good tidings to My servants, who listen to the word" [az-Zumar: 17-18]. He said: "Enter among My servants" [al-Fajr: 29]. He said: "A spring from which the servants of Allah will drink" [al-Insan: 6].

Having understood this, we say: when He, the Exalted, mentioned the certain proof in refuting polytheism, which is His saying, "If there were in them gods besides Allah, they would have sought a way to the Owner of the Throne" [al-Isra': 42], and mentioned the certain proof concerning the validity of the Return, which is His saying, "Say: He who originated you the first time" [al-Isra': 51], He said in this verse, "And say, O Muhammad, to My servants: when you intend to present the proof to the opponents, mention those proofs in the best manner," that is, that the mention of the proof should not be mixed with insult and abuse. A parallel to this verse is His saying: "Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction" [an-Nahl: 125], and His saying: "And do not argue with the People of the Book except in a way that is best" [al-'Ankabut: 46]. This is because if something of abuse and insult were mixed with the mention of the proof, they would retaliate with its like, as He said: "And do not insult those who call upon other than Allah, lest they insult Allah in enmity without knowledge" [al-An'am: 108]; the anger would increase, the aversion would become complete, and the attainment of the goal would be prevented. But when one confines himself to mentioning the proof in the best manner, free of insult and harm, it has a very strong effect on the heart. This is what is meant by His saying: "And say to My servants that they should say that which is best." Then He, the Exalted, drew attention to the benefit in this method, saying: "Indeed, Satan incites discord among them," encompassing both parties; that is, whenever the proof becomes mixed with vulgarity, it becomes a cause for the eruption of strife.

* * *

Then He said: "Indeed, Satan is to man a clear enemy." The meaning: the enmity existing between Satan and man is an ancient enmity. The Exalted said, relating about him: "Then I will surely come to them from before them and behind them and from their right and from their left" [al-A'raf: 17]. And He said: "Like Satan when he says to man, 'Disbelieve.' But when he disbelieves, [Satan] says, 'Indeed, I am free of you. Indeed, I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds'" [al-Hashr: 16]. And He said: "And when Satan made their deeds appear pleasing to them" [al-Anfal: 48]. And He said: "No one among the people can overcome you today, and indeed I am your protector." Up to His saying: "Indeed, I am free of you" [al-Anfal: 48].

* * *

Then the Exalted said: "Your Lord is most knowing of you. If He wills, He will have mercy upon you, or if He wills, He will punish you." Know that we are speaking now on the assumption that His saying, "Say to My servants," means the believers. On this assumption, His saying, "Your Lord is most knowing of you," is addressed to the believers. The meaning: if He wills, He will have mercy upon you, and the mercy meant is deliverance from the disbelievers of Makkah and their harm; or if He wills, He will punish you by giving them power over you. Then He said: "And We have not sent you, O Muhammad, as a guardian over them," that is, a protector and a guarantor. So occupy yourself with the call, and there is nothing upon you for their disbelief. If Allah wills their guidance, He will guide them; otherwise, not.

The second interpretation: the intended meaning of His saying, "Say to My servants," is the disbelievers. This is because the purpose of these verses is the call, so it is not far-fetched in such a context that they be addressed with good speech, so that this becomes a cause for attracting their hearts and inclining their natures toward accepting the true religion. It is as if He, the Exalted, said: "O Muhammad, say to My servants who have acknowledged that they are My servants: they should say that which is best." This is because before examining the proofs and clear signs, we know by necessity that describing Allah, the Exalted, with unity and freedom from partners and equals is better than affirming partners and equals, and describing Him with the power to resurrect and gather after death is better than describing Him with incapacity for that. He made them aware that it is not befitting for them to persist in those false doctrines out of partisanship for their forefathers, because what drives such partisanship is Satan, and Satan is an enemy, so one should not give heed to him. Then He said to them: "Your Lord is most knowing of you. If He wills, He will have mercy upon you," by enabling you to faith, guidance, and knowledge; "and if He wills, He will cause you to die upon disbelief, and then punish you." Then He said to Muhammad ﷺ: "And We have not sent you over them as a guardian," that is, do not make the matter hard upon them, and do not be harsh to them in speech. The purpose of all these words is to display gentleness and kindness toward them when calling them, for that is what affects the heart and brings about the desired result.

* * *

Then He said: "And your Lord is most knowing of whoever is in the heavens and the earth." The meaning is that since He had said before, "Your Lord is most knowing of you," He said after it, "And your Lord is most knowing of whoever is in the heavens and the earth," meaning that His knowledge is not restricted to you or to your states; rather His knowledge is related to all existents and non-existents, and related to all the essences of the earths and heavens, so He knows the condition of each one and knows what befits him of benefits and harms. For this reason He preferred some prophets over others, gave Musa the Torah, Dawud the Zabur, and 'Isa the Injil. Therefore it is not far-fetched that He should also give Muhammad the Qur'an, and it is not far-fetched that He should prefer him over all creation.

If it is said: what is the reason for specifying Dawud, peace be upon him, by mention in this context?

We say: there are several reasons:

The first reason: He, the Exalted, mentioned that He preferred some prophets over others.

* * *

Then He said: "And We gave David the Zabur." That is, David was a great king; then He did not mention what He gave him of kingship, but mentioned what He gave him of the Book, as an indication that the preference He mentioned before means preference in knowledge and religion, not in wealth.

The second reason: the reason for specifying him by mention is that the Exalted wrote in the Zabur that Muhammad is the seal of the prophets and that his community is the best of communities. The Exalted said: "And We had certainly written in the Zabur after the Reminder that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants" [al-Anbiya': 105], and they are Muhammad and his community.

If it is said: why was it not defined, as in His saying, "And We had certainly written in the Zabur"?

We say: indefiniteness here indicates the magnification of his status, because "zabur" is an expression for "the written," so its meaning was "a book," and the meaning of the indefiniteness is that it is perfect in being a book.

The third reason: the reason for it is that the disbelievers of Quraysh were not people of reflection and disputation; rather they used to refer to the Jews for extracting doubts, and the Jews used to say: there is no prophet after Musa and no book after the Torah. So Allah refuted their words by sending down the Zabur to Dawud. Hamzah recited "Zuburan" with a damma on the zay, and we mentioned the reason for that at the end of Surat an-Nisa'.

The meaning is that since He had said before, "Your Lord is most knowing of you," He said after it, "And your Lord is most knowing of whoever is in the heavens and the earth," meaning that His knowledge is not restricted to you or to your states; rather His knowledge is related to all existents and non-existents, and related to all the essences of the earths and heavens, so He knows the condition of each one and knows what befits him of benefits and harms. For this reason He preferred some prophets over others, gave Musa the Torah, Dawud the Zabur, and 'Isa the Injil. Therefore it is not far-fetched that He should also give Muhammad the Qur'an, and it is not far-fetched that He should prefer him over all creation.

If it is said: what is the reason for specifying Dawud, peace be upon him, by mention in this context?

We say: there are several reasons:

The first reason: He, the Exalted, mentioned that He preferred some prophets over others.

* * *

Then He said: "And We gave David the Zabur." That is, David was a great king; then He did not mention what He gave him of kingship, but mentioned what He gave him of the Book, as an indication that the preference He mentioned before means preference in knowledge and religion, not in wealth.

The second reason: the reason for specifying him by mention is that the Exalted wrote in the Zabur that Muhammad is the seal of the prophets and that his community is the best of communities. The Exalted said: "And We had certainly written in the Zabur after the Reminder that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants" [al-Anbiya': 105], and they are Muhammad and his community.

If it is said: why was it not defined, as in His saying, "And We had certainly written in the Zabur"?

We say: indefiniteness here indicates the magnification of his status, because "zabur" is an expression for "the written," so its meaning was "a book," and the meaning of the indefiniteness is that it is perfect in being a book.

The third reason: the reason for it is that the disbelievers of Quraysh were not people of reflection and disputation; rather they used to refer to the Jews for extracting doubts, and the Jews used to say: there is no prophet after Musa and no book after the Torah. So Allah refuted their words by sending down the Zabur to Dawud. Hamzah recited "Zuburan" with a damma on the zay, and we mentioned the reason for that at the end of Surat an-Nisa'.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verse 56–57:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Call upon those whom you claim besides Him; they have no power to remove the harm from you, nor to change it.﴾ ﴿Those whom they call upon themselves seek the means of access to their Lord, [striving to see] which of them is nearest, and they hope for His mercy and fear His punishment. Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is something to be feared.﴾

Know that the purpose of this verse is to refute the polytheists. We have mentioned that the polytheists used to say: "We are not qualified to occupy ourselves with the worship of God Most High, so we worship some of God's most honored servants, namely the angels." Then they made an image and a likeness of that angel which they worshipped, and occupied themselves with its worship on this interpretation. God Most High argued against the falsity of their claim in this verse, saying: ﴿Say: Call upon those whom you claim besides Him﴾. The intended ones are not idols, because He, exalted is He, said concerning their description: ﴿Those whom they call upon themselves seek the means of access to their Lord﴾, and seeking a means of access to God Most High is absolutely not befitting for idols.

Having established this, we say: a people worshipped the angels, and this verse was revealed concerning them. It is also said that it was revealed concerning those who worshipped the Messiah and Ezra. It is also said that a people worshipped a group of jinn, and then the group of jinn embraced Islam, while those people remained clinging to their worship, so this verse was revealed. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Every place in the Book of God Most High where the word (zaʿama) [claimed] occurs, it means (kadhaba) [lied]."

Then He, exalted is He, argued against the corruption of the doctrine of these people: the God who is worshipped is the One who is able to remove harm and bring about benefit. These things they worship, namely the angels, the jinn, the Messiah and Ezra, are not able to remove harm nor to secure benefit. Therefore it is necessary to affirm with certainty that they are not gods.

One may say: this proof is complete only if you demonstrate that the angels have no power to remove harm nor to secure benefit. What is the proof that the matter is so, so that your argument is complete? If you say: "Because we see that those disbelievers used to entreat them and no answer was obtained," we respond in opposition to that: we also see that the Muslims entreat God Most High and no answer is obtained. The Muslims say that the measure of removing harm and securing benefit that takes place comes only from God Most High, not from the angels, while those disbelievers say that it comes from the angels, not from God Most High. On this assumption, the proof is not complete.

The answer: the proof is complete and perfect, because the disbelievers acknowledged that the angels are servants of God, and that the Creator of the angels, the Creator of the world, must be more capable than the angels, stronger than them, and more perfect in state than them.

Having established this, we say: the perfection of God Most High's power is known and agreed upon, while the perfection of the angels' power is not known nor agreed upon. Rather, what is agreed upon is that their power, in relation to the power of God Most High, is small and insignificant. Since this is so, occupying oneself with the worship of God Most High must be better than occupying oneself with the worship of the angels, because God's being deserving of worship is known, while the angels' being so is unknown, and taking hold of what is known is better.

As for our companions, the theologians of the People of the Sunna and the Community, they have in this matter another method, namely that they establish by rational proof that there is no originator except God Most High, and no one who brings anything out of non-existence into existence except God Most High.

Having established this, it is established that there is no one who harms or benefits except God Most High, and so it is necessary to affirm with certainty that there is no one worshipped except God Most High. This method does not work for the Mu'tazila, because since they permit that the servant is the originator of his own acts, it is impossible for them to argue that the angels have no power over giving life, causing death, and creating bodies. When they are unable to do so, this proof is not complete for them. This is the mention of the decisive proof for the correctness of His saying: ﴿They have no power to remove the harm from you, nor to change it.﴾ And "taḥwīl" (change) is an expression for transfer from one state to another, and from one place to another; it is said: "He changed it, so it changed."

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿Those whom they call upon themselves seek the means of access to their Lord﴾, and concerning it there are two views:

The first: al-Farra' said: His saying ﴿they call upon﴾ is the act of the human worshippers, and His saying ﴿seek﴾ is the act of those who are worshipped, and its meaning is: those who are worshipped themselves seek the means of access to their Lord. There is no dispute that the angels turn to God in seeking benefits and warding off harms, and hope for His mercy and fear His punishment. Since this is so, they are described as needy and incapable, while God Most High is the most self-sufficient of the self-sufficient, so occupying oneself with His worship is better.

If they say: "We do not grant that the angels are in need of God's mercy and fear His punishment," we respond: these angels are either said to be necessarily existent in themselves, or said to be possibly existent in themselves. The first is false, because all the disbelievers acknowledged that the angels are servants of God and in need of Him. The second necessitates saying that the angels are in need of God Most High in their essences and in their perfections, so occupying oneself with the worship of God is better than occupying oneself with the worship of the angels.

The second view: that His saying ﴿Those whom they call upon﴾ refers to the prophets whom God Most High mentioned in His saying: ﴿And We have preferred some of the prophets over others﴾ [al-Isra: 55]. The connection of this statement with what preceded is that those whose station is great, namely the prophets, worship none but God Most High and seek the means of access only to Him, so you are more worthy of following their example, so do not worship other than God Most High. Those who held this view argued for its soundness by saying: the angels do not disobey God, so they do not fear His punishment; therefore it is established that this is not fitting for the angels, and it is fitting only for the prophets.

We say: the angels fear God's punishment should they commit a sin, and the evidence for this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever among them says, "Indeed I am a god besides Him," that one We will recompense with Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya: 29].

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is something to be feared﴾, the meaning is that it is incumbent upon Him that He be feared, and if some people do not fear Him out of ignorance, He does not thereby cease to be such that fear of Him is obligatory.
