**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verse 70 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly honoured the children of Adam, and carried them on the land and the sea, and provided for them of the good things, and preferred them over much of what We have created, with a definite preference.﴾

Know that the purpose of this verse is to mention another great and lofty blessing among the blessings of God Most High upon humankind, namely the qualities by which humankind is preferred over others. In this verse God Most High mentions four kinds:

The first kind is His saying: ﴿We have certainly honoured the children of Adam.﴾ Know that the human being is a substance composed of soul (nafs) and body (badan). The human soul is the most noble of the souls existing in the lower world, and the human body is the most noble of the bodies existing in the lower world. The demonstration of this excellence in the human soul is that the human soul has three original faculties: nutrition (al-ightidha'), growth (al-numuw), and reproduction (al-tawlid). The animal soul has two faculties: sensation, whether outward or inward, and voluntary motion. These five faculties, namely nutrition, growth, reproduction, sensation and motion, are found in the human soul. Moreover, the human soul is distinguished by another faculty, which is the rational faculty (al-quwwa al-'aqliyya) that perceives the realities of things as they are. It is the faculty in which the light of the knowledge of God Most High shines and in which the radiance of His majesty illuminates. It is the faculty that gazes upon the secrets of the two worlds, the world of creation and the world of command, and that comprehends the categories of God's creatures, both spirits and bodies, as they are. This faculty is from the emanation of holy substances and pure divine spirits. This faculty has no comparison in nobility and excellence to those vegetative and animal faculties. Since this is the case, it is clear that the human soul is the noblest of the souls existing in this world. If you wish to know the virtues of the rational faculty and the deficiencies of the bodily faculties, then reflect upon what we have written in this book in the commentary on His saying: ﴿God is the light of the heavens and the earth﴾ (al-Nur: 35), for we mentioned there twenty aspects demonstrating that the rational faculty is greater and higher than the bodily faculty, so there is no benefit in repeating them.

As for the demonstration that the human body is the noblest of the bodies of this world, the commentators have mentioned this kind of excellence in their interpretation of His saying: ﴿We have certainly honoured the children of Adam,﴾ and they have mentioned several things:

The first: Maymun ibn Mihran narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with them both), regarding His saying: ﴿We have certainly honoured the children of Adam,﴾ that he said: "Every creature eats with its mouth except the son of Adam, who eats with his hands." It is also said that al-Rashid had food brought before him and called for spoons, and Abu Yusuf was with him. He said to him: "It has come in the tafsir from your grandfather (ancestor) regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We have certainly honoured the children of Adam,﴾ that 'We made for them fingers with which they eat.'" So he pushed away the spoons and ate with his fingers.

The second: al-Dahhak said: "By speech and discernment." The clarification of this statement is that whoever knows something either cannot make others aware of his knowledge of that thing, or he is able to make this awareness known. As for the first category, it is the condition of all animals other than the human being: when pain or pleasure arises within them, they are unable to convey those states to others in a complete and comprehensive manner. As for the second category, it is the human being, who is able to make others aware of everything he knows, understands and comprehends. His being capable of this kind of communication is what is meant by his being "speaking" (natiq). By this explanation it becomes clear that the mute person is included in this description, because although he is unable to convey what is in his heart by means of speech, he is able to do so by means of gesture, writing and other means. The parrot is not included in it, because although it can make a few utterances, it has no ability to convey all states completely and fully.

The third: 'Ata said: "By the stature of the body (imtidad al-qama)." Know that this statement is incomplete, because trees are taller than the human stature; rather, a condition should be stipulated for it, namely the height of stature together with the perfection of the rational faculty, the sensory faculties, and the motive faculties.

The fourth: Bayan said: "By beauty of form." The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿And He formed you and perfected your forms﴾ (Ghafir: 64). When God Most High mentioned the creation of the human being, He said: ﴿So blessed is God, the best of creators﴾ (al-Mu'minun: 14), and He said: ﴿The dye of God; and who is better than God in dye?﴾ (al-Baqara: 138). And if you wish, reflect upon one single organ of the human being, which is the eye: He created the pupil black, then surrounded that blackness with the whiteness of the eye, then surrounded that whiteness with the blackness of the eyelashes, then surrounded that blackness with the whiteness of the eyelids, then He created above the whiteness of the eyelid the blackness of the eyebrows, then He created above that blackness the whiteness of the forehead, then He created above the whiteness of the forehead the blackness of the hair. Let this single example serve as a model for you in this matter.

The fifth: Some of them said: "Among the honours of the son of Adam is that God gave him writing." The clarification of this matter is that the knowledge a human being can derive by his own effort is small. But when a human being derives a science and deposits it in a book, and a second person comes, makes use of that book, and adds to it other things from his own self, and then they continue to succeed one another, with each later scholar adding many investigations to the knowledge of the earlier ones, the sciences multiply, the virtues and cognitions grow strong, and rational inquiries and legal questions reach the furthest ends and most complete conclusions. It is known that this domain can be achieved only through writing and scribes. And for this complete excellence God Most High said: ﴿Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous﴾ ﴿who taught by the pen﴾ ﴿taught the human being what he did not know﴾ (al-'Alaq: 3).

The sixth: The bodies of this world are either simple or composite. As for the simple ones, they are earth, water, air and fire. The human being benefits from all four of these. As for the earth, it is for us like a nurturing mother. God Most High said: ﴿From it We created you, and into it We return you, and from it We bring you forth once again﴾ (Ta-Ha: 55). God Most High has named it with names in relation to us, namely "bedding" (firash), "cradle" (mahd), and "couch" (mihad). As for water, our benefit from it in drinking, irrigation and tilling is evident. Also, He subjected the sea so that we may eat from it fresh flesh, and extract from it ornaments that we wear, and see ships ploughing through it. As for air, it is the substance of our life, and were it not for the blowing of the winds, the stench would overwhelm this inhabited world. As for fire, by it food and drink are cooked and ripened, and it stands in place of the sun and the moon in dark nights, and it averts the harm of cold, as the poet said:

*Whoever desires fruit in winter, the fire of winter is his fruit.*

As for composite bodies, they are either the celestial phenomena, or minerals and plants. As for animals and the human being, the human being is like one who dominates these categories, benefits from them, and makes all their kinds subservient. So this entire world proceeds like a populated village or a prepared inn, all of whose benefits and interests are directed toward the human being within it, like a ruling master and an obeyed king, while all other animals are in relation to him like slaves. All of this indicates that he has been singled out by God for an abundance of honour and preference. And God knows best.

The seventh: Created beings are divided into four categories: those in whom the rational, wise faculty is present but the appetitive natural faculty is absent, and these are the angels; those for whom the reverse is true, and these are the beasts; those that are free of both categories, namely plants and inanimate things; and those in whom both kinds are present, and this is the human being. There is no doubt that the human being, because he combines the pure holy rational faculty with the bestial appetitive faculties, the irascible and the predatory faculties, is more excellent than the bestial and the predatory. There is also no doubt that he is more excellent than bodies free of both faculties, such as plants, minerals and inanimate things. When this is established, it becomes clear that God Most High has preferred the human being over most categories of created beings. There remains here a investigation as to whether the angel is more excellent or the human being. The meaning is: is the simple essence described by the pure holy rational faculty more excellent, or the human being who combines these two faculties? That is a separate investigation.

The eighth: Existence is either eternal and everlasting together, and this is God, glorified and exalted; or it is neither eternal nor everlasting, and this is the world of this life together with all the minerals, plants and animals within it, and this is the lowest of the categories; or it is eternal but not everlasting, and this is impossible in existence, because whatever's pre-eternity is established, its non-existence is impossible; or it is not eternal but everlasting, and this is the human being and the angel. There is no doubt that this category is nobler than the second and third, and this requires that the human being be nobler than most of God's creatures.

The ninth: The higher world is nobler than the lower world, and the spirit of the human being is of the kind of the higher spirits and holy substances. Therefore, among the existents of the lower world there is nothing in which something of the higher world has come to be, except the human being. So it is necessary that the human being be the noblest of the existents of the lower world.

The tenth: The noblest of existents is God Most High. When this is so, every existent whose nearness to God Most High is more complete must be more noble. But the nearest of the existents of this world to God Most High is the human being, because his heart is illuminated by the knowledge of God Most High, his tongue is honoured by the remembrance of God, and his limbs and organs are made noble by obedience to God Most High. Therefore it is necessary to affirm with certainty that the noblest of the existents of this lower world is the human being. And since it has been established that the human being is a contingent existent in his essence, and a contingent existent in his essence is not brought into being except by the bringing into being of the Necessary Existent in His essence, it is established that every rank of lofty status and noble attribute that the human being attains has come only through God's beneficence and bounty. For this meaning God Most High said: ﴿We have certainly honoured the children of Adam.﴾ And among the completeness of his honour with God Most High is that when He created him at the beginning of the matter, He described Himself as the Most Generous, saying: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ ﴿created the human being from a clinging clot﴾ ﴿Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous﴾ ﴿who taught by the pen﴾ (al-'Alaq: 1). And He described Himself with honour when He nurtured the human being, saying: ﴿We have certainly honoured the children of Adam.﴾ And He described Himself with generosity at the last of the human being's states, saying: ﴿O human being, what has deceived you concerning your generous Lord?﴾ (al-Infitar: 6). This indicates that there is no limit to the generosity, bounty and kindness of God Most High toward the human being. And God knows best.

The eleventh aspect: Some of them said: the meaning of this honouring is that God Most High created Adam with His own hand, and created others by way of "Be, and it is." Whoever is created by the hand of God, the care for him is more complete and perfect, and he is more honoured and more perfect. And since He made us among his descendants, it is necessary that the children of Adam be more honoured and more perfect. And God knows best.

* * *

The second kind of praise mentioned in this verse is His saying: ﴿and carried them on the land and the sea.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: "On the land, upon horses, mules, donkeys and camels; and on the sea, upon ships." This is also among the confirmations of the honour mentioned first, because God Most High subjected these animals to him so that he may ride them, carry loads upon them, wage war, fight, and defend himself. Likewise, God Most High subjected the waters, the ships and other things to him so that he may ride them, transport upon them, and earn a livelihood through them, which belong specially to the son of Adam. All of this indicates that the human being in this world is like the ruling chief who is followed and the king who is obeyed, and all else besides him is his subjects and follows him.

The third kind of praise is His saying: ﴿And We have provided for them of the good things﴾. This is because foods are either animal or vegetable, and a human being eats from both kinds only in their most refined varieties and noblest categories, after thorough cleaning, complete cooking, and full ripening. Such things are attainable only by human beings.

The fourth kind is His saying: ﴿And We have favored them above many of those We have created, with a marked preference﴾. Here there are two discussions.

The first discussion: In the beginning of the verse He said: ﴿And We have certainly honored the children of Adam﴾, and at its end He said: ﴿and We have favored them﴾. There must be a difference between this honoring (takrim) and this favoring (tafdil), otherwise there would be repetition. The closest explanation is that God favored the human being over the rest of the animals with innate, natural, essential qualities such as intellect, speech, writing, a beautiful form, and an upright stature. Then God, through that intellect and understanding, made him able to acquire true beliefs and virtuous character. Thus the first is honoring (takrim), and the second is favoring (tafdil).

The second discussion: He did not say "and We have favored them over all," but rather said:
Page 14
﴿and We have favored them above many of those We have created, with a marked preference﴾. This indicates that among God's creatures there is something over which the human being is not preferred. Everyone who affirmed this category said that it is the angels. It follows that the human being is not more excellent than the angels; rather, the angel is more excellent than the human being. This view is the position of Ibn 'Abbas, and it is the choice of al-Zajjaj, as related by al-Wahidi in al-Basit. Know that this discussion comprises two investigations:

The first investigation: Are the prophets, peace be upon them, more excellent than the angels? This question has already been discussed in detail in Surat al-Baqarah, in the commentary on His saying: ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam"﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:34).

The second investigation: Which is more excellent, the common angels or the common believers? Some said that the believers are more excellent than the angels, and they argued for this with what is related from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: The angels said, "Our Lord, You have given the children of Adam the world, in which they eat and enjoy themselves, and You have not given us that; so give us that in the Hereafter." He said: "By My might and My majesty, I will not make the offspring of those whom I created with My hand like those to whom I said 'Be,' and they were." Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, also said: "The believer is more honored by Allah than the angels who are with Him." This is how al-Wahidi cited it in al-Basit. As for those who hold that the angel is more excellent than the human being absolutely, they relied on this verse. In reality, this is an argument from the implication of the speech (dalil al-khitab), since the way to state the proof is to say: singling out the many for mention indicates that the situation regarding the few is the opposite, and that is an argument from dalil al-khitab. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verses 71–72:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Day We shall call every people with their leader; then whoever is given his record in his right hand, those will read their record, and they will not be wronged the least bit.﴾ ﴿And whoever was blind in this [world] will be blind in the Hereafter, and further astray in the way.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned the kinds of honour bestowed upon man in this world, He mentioned in this verse the states of man's ranks in the Hereafter. In it are several issues:

The first issue: It is read *yad'ū* with a *yā'* and *nūn*, and *yud'ā* (in the passive form) with *kullu unās* (every people). Al-Ḥasan read *yad'ū kullu unās*. Al-Farrā' and the scholars of Arabic (*al-ʿArabiyya*, Arabic grammar and linguistics) said that they do not know any valid grammatical basis for this reading transmitted from al-Ḥasan. Perhaps he read *yud'ā* with a *fatḥa* mixed with a *ḍamma*, so the narrator thought he had read *yad'ū*.

The second issue: His saying *yawma nad'ū* is in the accusative case, governed by an implied verb, *udhkur* (remember). It is not permissible to say that its governing element is His saying *wa-faḍḍalnāhum*, because that is a past-tense verb. It can be answered that the meaning is *wa-nufaḍḍiluhum* (and We shall favour them) by what We give them of honour and reward.

The third issue: His saying ﴿*bi-imāmihim*﴾ (with their leader). Linguistically, *imām* is everyone a people follows, whether they are upon guidance or misguidance. Thus the Prophet is the *imām* of his community, the caliph is the *imām* of his subjects, the Qur'an is the *imām* of the Muslims, and the *imām* of a congregation is the one who is followed in prayer. Regarding the interpretation of *imām* here, scholars have stated several views:

The first view: Their *imām* is their prophet. This is related in a marfūʿ report from Abū Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ). The meaning is that on the Day of Resurrection it will be called out: "O community of Abraham! O community of Moses! O community of Jesus! O community of Muhammad!" Then the people of truth who followed the prophets will stand and take their books in their right hands. Then it will be called out: "O followers of Pharaoh! O followers of Nimrod! O followers of so-and-so and so-and-so, from the leaders of misguidance and the great ones of disbelief!"

On this view, the *bāʾ* in ﴿*bi-imāmihim*﴾ has two possibilities:

First, the implied meaning is: "We shall call every people *with* their *imām*," following and as followers of their *imām*, just as you say, "I call you by your name."

Second, it is connected to an implied element that occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), as if it were said: "We shall call every people while mingled with their *imām*," meaning they will be called while their *imām* is among them, like "a riding party with its troops."

The second view, which is the view of al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn Zayd: *bi-imāmihim* means with their book that was revealed to them. On this view, on the Day of Resurrection it will be called out: "O people of the Qur'an! O people of the Torah! O people of the Gospel!"

The third view: Al-Ḥasan said: with their book in which their deeds are recorded. This is also the view of al-Rabīʿ and Abū al-ʿĀliya. The evidence that this book is called an *imām* is His saying: ﴿And every single thing We have enumerated in a clear *imām*﴾ (Yā-Sīn 36:12). So Allah named this book an *imām*. The *bāʾ* on this view means *maʿa* (with): "We shall call every people and their book with them," like your saying, "Hand it to him with its entire lot" (*bi-rummatihi*), meaning and with him is his lot.

The fourth view: The author of *al-Kashshāf* said: Among the strange (*bidaʿ*) interpretations is that *imām* is the plural of *umm* (mother), and that people will be called on the Day of Resurrection by their mothers. The wisdom in calling by mothers rather than fathers is to preserve the right of Jesus, to show the honour of al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn, and so that the children of fornication are not disgraced. Then the author of *al-Kashshāf* said: "I wonder which of the two is more wondrous: the soundness of its wording or the clarity of its wisdom!"

The fifth view: I say that the wording has another possibility, which is that the kinds of good and bad character are many, and the trait that predominates in each person is one of these kinds. Some people have anger predominating over them; some have the desire for money or for property predominating; some have spite and envy predominating. On the side of good character, some have chastity, courage, generosity, or the seeking of knowledge and asceticism predominating. If you know this, we say: the one who calls to outward actions arising from these inner traits is that inner trait, which is like the *imām* for it, the obeyed king, and the followed leader. On the Day of Resurrection, reward and punishment appear only in accordance with the actions that arise from those traits. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿The Day We shall call every people with their *imām*.﴾ This possibility occurred to me, and Allah knows best what He intends.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then whoever is given his record in his right hand, those will read their record, and they will not be wronged the least bit.﴾ The author of *al-Kashshāf* said: He said *ulāʾika* (those) because *man* (whoever) carries the sense of a plural. *Fatīl* is the thin thread (membrane) in the split of a date-stone. It is named so because when a person tries to extract it, it twists (*yanfatil*). It is used as an example for something small and trivial. Similar are *qiṭmīr* and *naqīr* in such proverbial usage. The meaning is that they will not be reduced in reward by the amount of a *fatīl*. A parallel to it is His saying: ﴿and they will not be wronged anything﴾, and ﴿so he will fear neither injustice nor diminution﴾ (Ṭā-Hā 20:112). Mujāhid narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: *al-fatīl* is the dirt that appears when a person twists his thumb with his index finger. It is *faʿīl* from *fatl* in the sense of *maftūl* (twisted).

If it is asked: why did He single out the people of the right hand for reading their record, when the people of the left hand also read theirs? We say: the difference is that when the people of the left hand look into their record, they find it containing great ruinous acts, complete ugliness, and severe disgrace. Fear and bewilderment take hold of their hearts, their tongues grow heavy, and they are unable to read. As for the people of the right hand, their situation is the opposite. So they read their record in the best and most secure manner. Moreover, they do not suffice with reading it alone; rather, the reader says to the people of the Gathering: ﴿Here, read my record!﴾ (al-Ḥāqqa 69:19). Thus the difference is clear, and Allah knows best.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever was blind in this [world] will be blind in the Hereafter, and further astray in the way.﴾ On this there are two issues:

The first issue: Abū ʿAmr and Abū Bakr (from ʿĀṣim) and Naṣr (from al-Kisāʾī) read *wa-man kāna fī hādhihi aʿmā* with *imāla* (vowel inclination) and *kasra*, and *fa-huwa fī al-ākhirati aʿmā* with *fatḥa*. Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, and Ḥafṣ (from ʿĀṣim) read both with *fatḥa* and *tafkhīm* (full vowels). Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Abū Bakr (from ʿĀṣim, in one narration) read both with *imāla*. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: The correct justification for Abū ʿAmr's reading is that in the first word, *aʿmā* means blind in oneself, and with this meaning the word is complete, so it accepts *imāla*. In the second word, however, *aʿmā* is the elative (*afʿal al-tafḍīl*), meaning "more blind than," and with this meaning the word *aʿmā* is not complete, so it does not accept *imāla*. The conclusion is that applying *imāla* to the first shows that the intended meaning is not the elative, while leaving it unapplied in the second shows that the intended meaning there is the elative. Allah knows best.

The second issue: There is no doubt that His saying ﴿And whoever was blind in this [world] will be blind in the Hereafter﴾ does not mean blindness of sight, but blindness of the heart. As for His saying ﴿he will be blind in the Hereafter﴾, there are two views:

The first view: It also means blindness of the heart. On this view there are several aspects:

First: ʿIkrima said: A group of people from Yemen came to Ibn ʿAbbās, and a man asked him about this verse. He said: "Read what comes before it." He read: ﴿Your Lord is the One who drives the ship for you in the sea﴾ up to His saying ﴿favouring﴾. Ibn ʿAbbās said: Whoever was blind to these blessings that he saw and witnessed, is blind in the matter of the Hereafter, which he did not see or witness, and further astray in the way. On this aspect, *fī hādhihi* (in this) refers to the blessings mentioned in the preceding verses.

Second: Abū Rawq narrated from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: Whoever in the world was blind to what is seen of My power in creating the heavens, the earth, the seas, the mountains, the people, and the animals, is blind regarding the matter of the Hereafter, further astray in the way, and further from attaining knowledge of it. On this aspect, *fī hādhihi* refers to the world. On these two views, the meaning is: whoever was heart-blind in this world to knowing these blessings and proofs, then being heart-blind to knowing the states of the Hereafter is more fitting. So the blindness in both cases occurs in this world.

Third: Al-Ḥasan said: Whoever was astray and a disbeliever in this world, is blind and further astray in the Hereafter, because in this world his repentance is accepted, while in the Hereafter his repentance is not accepted. In this world he can find his way out of the doors of calamities, while in the Hereafter he is not guided to that at all.

Fourth: It is not possible to interpret the second blindness as ignorance of God, because the people of the Hereafter know God by necessity. So what is meant is blindness to the way to Paradise: whoever was blind to knowledge of God in this world is blind to the way to Paradise in the Hereafter.

Fifth: Those in whom heart-blindness arose in this world only came to this state because of their intense greed for acquiring worldly things and their delight in its pleasures and good things. This desire increases in the Hereafter, and their regret over the loss of the world grows greater there, while they have with them none of the lights of knowledge of God Most High. So they remain in intense darkness and great regret. That is what is meant by the blindness.

The second view: The second blindness is to be understood as blindness of the eye and the sight. Whoever was heart-blind in this world will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection blind of eye and sight, as He said: ﴿And We shall gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind﴾, ﴿He will say: My Lord, why have You gathered me blind, when I was seeing?﴾, ﴿He will say: Thus did Our signs come to you and you forgot them, and thus today you are forgotten﴾ (Ṭā-Hā 20:124). And He said: ﴿And We shall gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, mute, and deaf﴾ (al-Isrāʾ 17:97). This blindness is an increase in their punishment. And Allah knows best.

He read: ﴿Your Lord is the One who drives the ship for you in the sea﴾ up to His saying ﴿favouring﴾. Ibn ʿAbbās said: Whoever was blind to these blessings that he saw and witnessed, is blind in the matter of the Hereafter, which he did not see or witness, and further astray in the way. On this aspect, *fī hādhihi* (in this) refers to the blessings mentioned in the preceding verses.

Second: Abū Rawq narrated from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: Whoever in the world was blind to what is seen of My power in creating the heavens, the earth, the seas, the mountains, the people, and the animals, is blind regarding the matter of the Hereafter, further astray in the way, and further from attaining knowledge of it. On this aspect, *fī hādhihi* refers to the world. On these two views, the meaning is: whoever was heart-blind in this world to knowing these blessings and proofs, then being heart-blind to knowing the states of the Hereafter is more fitting. So the blindness in both cases occurs in this world.

Third: Al-Ḥasan said: Whoever was astray and a disbeliever in this world, is blind and further astray in the Hereafter, because in this world his repentance is accepted, while in the Hereafter his repentance is not accepted. In this world he can find his way out of the doors of calamities, while in the Hereafter he is not guided to that at all.

Fourth: It is not possible to interpret the second blindness as ignorance of God, because the people of the Hereafter know God by necessity. So what is meant is blindness to the way to Paradise: whoever was blind to knowledge of God in this world is blind to the way to Paradise in the Hereafter.

Fifth: Those in whom heart-blindness arose in this world only came to this state because of their intense greed for acquiring worldly things and their delight in its pleasures and good things. This desire increases in the Hereafter, and their regret over the loss of the world grows greater there, while they have with them none of the lights of knowledge of God Most High. So they remain in intense darkness and great regret. That is what is meant by the blindness.

The second view: The second blindness is to be understood as blindness of the eye and the sight. Whoever was heart-blind in this world will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection blind of eye and sight, as He said: ﴿And We shall gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind﴾, ﴿He will say: My Lord, why have You gathered me blind, when I was seeing?﴾, ﴿He will say: Thus did Our signs come to you and you forgot them, and thus today you are forgotten﴾ (Ṭā-Hā 20:124). And He said: ﴿And We shall gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, mute, and deaf﴾ (al-Isrāʾ 17:97). This blindness is an increase in their punishment. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verses 73–75:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, they were about to tempt you away from that which We revealed to you, to fabricate against Us other than it; and then they would have taken you as a friend.﴾ ﴿And had We not given you firmness, you would have almost inclined toward them, a little.﴾ ﴿Then We would have made you taste double [punishment] of life and double [punishment] of death; then you would not find for yourself any helper against Us.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, enumerated in the preceding verses the categories of His blessings upon His creation, and followed them with mention of the ranks of creatures in the Hereafter and explained the condition of the blessed, He then added what serves as a warning to the blessed against being deceived by the whisperings of the people of misguidance and against being duped by their speech, which contains deceit and confusion. So He said: ﴿And indeed, they were about to tempt you away from that which We revealed to you﴾. There are several issues concerning this verse:

The first issue: Ibn Abbas said, in the narration of Ata: This verse was revealed concerning "the delegation of Thaqif, who came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and asked him for something excessive. They said: Grant us enjoyment of al-Lat for a year, and make our valley sacred as you made Mecca sacred, its trees, its birds and its wild animals. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) refused that and did not answer them. So they repeated that request, and said: We wish that the Arabs would recognize our superiority over them. If you dislike what we say, and fear that the Arabs will say, 'You gave them what you did not give us,' then say: 'Allah has commanded me to do that.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) held back from them, and greed entered them. Umar shouted at them and said: 'Do you not see that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has withheld from speaking, out of dislike for what you mention?' So Allah revealed this verse." The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) related that they "brought their scribe, who wrote: 'In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. This is a document from Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, to Thaqif: they shall not be taxed, nor shall they be mustered.' They said: 'Nor shall they be made to pay tribute.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) remained silent. Then they said to the scribe: 'Write: nor shall they be made to pay tribute.' The scribe was looking at the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). So Umar ibn al-Khattab stood up, drew his sword, and said: 'O assembly of Quraysh, you have kindled the heart of our Prophet! May Allah kindle your hearts with fire!' They said: 'We are not speaking to you; we are speaking to Muhammad.'" Then this verse was revealed. Know that this story occurred in Medina, and for this reason some said that these verses are Medinan. It is also related that "the Quraysh said to him: 'Make a verse of mercy a verse of punishment, and a verse of punishment a verse of mercy, until we believe in you.'" So this verse was revealed. Al-Hasan said: "The disbelievers seized the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) one night in Mecca before the Hijrah and said: 'Refrain, O Muhammad, from disparaging our gods and reviling them. If that were true, so-and-so and so-and-so would have been more worthy of this matter than you.' So there came into the heart of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he should refrain from reviling their gods." On this interpretation, this verse is Meccan. It is also related from Said ibn Jubayr "that he (peace be upon him) used to touch the Black Stone, and the Quraysh prevented him, saying: 'We will not leave you alone until you touch our gods.' So there came into his soul that he should do that, with reluctance." Then this verse was revealed.

The second issue: Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of the speech is "they were about to tempt you." The particle inna and the lam are for emphasis. Inna here is the lightened form of the heavy inna, and the lam is what distinguishes it from the negating particle. The meaning is: indeed the matter is that they nearly tempted you, i.e., deceived you, being tempters. The origin of fitnah (temptation) is testing: it is said that the goldsmith "fatana the gold" when he puts it in the fire and melts it to distinguish its good from its bad. Then they used it for anyone who removes a thing from its limit and direction, and they said: "fatanahu" (he tempted him). So His saying: ﴿they were about to tempt you away from that which We revealed to you﴾ means: they would turn you aside and divert you from what We revealed to you, meaning the Qur'an. The meaning is: from its ruling. That is because giving them what they asked for would be opposing the ruling of the Qur'an. His saying: ﴿to fabricate against Us other than it﴾ means: other than what We revealed to you, namely their saying: "Say: Allah has commanded me to do that." ﴿And then they would have taken you as a friend﴾ means: if you had done what they wanted, they would have taken you as a friend and made it known to the people that you agree with them in their position and are pleased with their polytheism. Then He said: ﴿And had We not given you firmness﴾, meaning, upon the truth, by Our preserving you. ﴿You would have almost inclined toward them﴾, meaning you would have leaned toward them ﴿a little.﴾ His saying: ﴿a little﴾ is an expression for the verbal noun, meaning a slight inclining. Ibn Abbas said: He means when he remained silent from answering them. Qatadah said: When this verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, do not leave me to myself even for the blink of an eye." Then He threatened him most severely in this matter, saying: ﴿Then We would have made you taste double [punishment] of life and double [punishment] of death﴾, meaning double the punishment of life and double the punishment of death, meaning the punishment of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter. Doubling is an expression for adding to a thing its like. For when a man says to his agent, "Give so-and-so something," and he gives him a dirham, and the man says, "Double it," the meaning is: add to that dirham its like. Knowing this, we say: The mention of punishment was implied in His saying ﴿double [punishment] of life and double [punishment] of death﴾ because the Qur'an has previously described the punishment as doubled, in His saying: ﴿Our Lord, whoever has advanced this for us, then increase him in punishment doubled in the Fire﴾ (Sad: 61), and He said: ﴿For each there is double, but you do not know﴾ (al-A'raf: 38). The summary of the matter is that if you allowed the thoughts of Satan into your heart and fixed your resolve upon inclining toward him, you would deserve by that a doubling of punishment upon you in this world and the Hereafter, and your punishment would become twice the punishment of the polytheist in this world and twice his punishment in the Hereafter. The reason for doubling this punishment is that the categories of Allah's blessings toward the prophets, peace be upon them, are more numerous, so their sins were greater, and the punishment deserved for them was greater. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿O wives of the Prophet, whoever of you commits a clear immorality, her punishment will be doubled twofold﴾ (al-Ahzab: 30). If it is said: He (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever establishes an evil practice, upon him is its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection," then the implication of this hadith is that if he (peace be upon him) had been pleased with what they said, his burden would have been equal to the burden of each one of those disbelievers, and on this reckoning his punishment would exceed doubling. We reply: Establishing doubling does not indicate the negation of what exceeds it, except by building upon the indication of the discourse (dalil al-khitab), and that is a weak proof. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿then you would not find for yourself any helper against Us﴾, meaning: if We made you taste the doubled punishment, you would not find anyone to rescue you from Our punishment and Our retribution. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: Those who object to the infallibility (ismah) of the prophets, peace be upon them, have argued with this verse, saying: This verse indicates that a grave sin proceeded from them, in several respects:

The first: The verse indicates that he (peace be upon him) came close to fabricating against Allah, and fabrication against Allah is among the greatest sins.

The second: It indicates that had Allah not made him firm and preserved him, he would have come close to inclining toward their religion and leaning toward their doctrine.

The third: That there would have been no need to mention this severe threat unless there had been a prior transgression and offense.

The answer to the first: The word kada means "to be near," so the meaning of the verse is that his falling into this temptation was near, and this degree does not indicate that he actually fell into that temptation. For when we say, "The governor almost struck so-and-so," it is not understood from this that he struck him.

The answer to the second: The word lawla indicates the negation of one thing because of the existence of another. You say: "Lawla Ali, Umar would have perished," meaning: the existence of Ali prevented Umar from perishing. Likewise here, His saying: ﴿And had We not given you firmness, you would have almost inclined toward them﴾ means that Allah's giving firmness to Muhammad (ﷺ) occurred, and the occurrence of that firmness prevented the occurrence of that inclination.

The answer to the third: That threat against disobedience does not indicate that he undertook it. The proof of this is verses among which is His saying: ﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings, We would have seized him by the right hand, then We would have severed from him the aorta﴾ (al-Haqqah: 44–46). Among them is His saying: ﴿If you associate others with Allah, your deeds will surely be nullified﴾ (al-Zumar: 65), and among them His saying: ﴿And do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ (al-Ahzab: 1). And Allah knows best.

The fourth issue: Our companions argued for the soundness of their position, that there is no protection from sins except by Allah's granting of success (tawfiq), with His saying: ﴿And had We not given you firmness, you would have almost inclined toward them, a little.﴾ They said: He, exalted is He, made clear that had Allah not given him firmness, he would have turned toward the path of the disbelievers. And there is no doubt that Muhammad (ﷺ) was stronger than others in the strength of religion and the purity of certainty. So when Allah, exalted is He, made clear that his remaining protected from disbelief and misguidance was not achieved except by Allah's help and succor, the attainment of this meaning for others was more fitting. The Mu'tazilah (a theological school) said: What is meant by this firmness is the gracious aids (alutaf) that divert him from that, which are what occurred to his mind of the remembrance of His promise and His threat, and of the remembrance that his being a prophet from Allah, exalted is He, prevents him from that. The answer: There is no doubt that this firmness is an expression for an act performed by Allah that prevents the Messenger from falling into that forbidden deed. We say: If the impetus toward that forbidden deed did not exist in the case of the Messenger, there would be no need for bringing about this preventive factor. And since there was a need to bring about this preventive factor, we know that the impetus had arisen in the case of the Messenger (ﷺ), and that this preventive factor which Allah produced prevented that impetus from acting. This does not hold except if we say that power together with motive necessitates the act, so when a motive arises that opposes the first motive, the effective cause is disturbed and the act is prevented. We only wish to establish this meaning. And Allah knows best.

The fifth issue: Al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: We have mentioned in the occasion of revelation of this verse the aforementioned accounts, and it is also possible to interpret it without restricting it to a specific occasion of revelation, because it is known that the polytheists used to strive to nullify the command of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with all their power. At one time they would say: "If you worship our gods, we will worship your God." So Allah revealed: ﴿Say: O disbelievers, I do not worship what you worship﴾ (al-Kafirun: 1–2), and His saying: ﴿They wish you would compromise, so they would compromise﴾ (al-Qalam: 9). They offered him great wealth and beautiful women so that he would abandon his claim to prophethood, so Allah revealed: ﴿And do not extend your eyes [longingly]﴾ (al-Hijr: 88). They urged him to drive the believers away from himself, so Allah revealed His saying: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord﴾ (al-An'am: 52). So it is possible that these verses were revealed in this category, because they intended to tempt him away from his religion and to remove him from his path. Then He, exalted is He, made clear that He would keep him firm upon the upright religion and the straight path. On this approach, there is no need in the interpretation of these verses for any of those narrations. And Allah knows best.

The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) related that they "brought their scribe, who wrote: 'In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. This is a document from Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, to Thaqif: they shall not be taxed, nor shall they be mustered.' They said: 'Nor shall they be made to pay tribute.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) remained silent. Then they said to the scribe: 'Write: nor shall they be made to pay tribute.' The scribe was looking at the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). So Umar ibn al-Khattab stood up, drew his sword, and said: 'O assembly of Quraysh, you have kindled the heart of our Prophet! May Allah kindle your hearts with fire!' They said: 'We are not speaking to you; we are speaking to Muhammad.'" Then this verse was revealed. Know that this story occurred in Medina, and for this reason some said that these verses are Medinan. It is also related that "the Quraysh said to him: 'Make a verse of mercy a verse of punishment, and a verse of punishment a verse of mercy, until we believe in you.'" So this verse was revealed. Al-Hasan said: "The disbelievers seized the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) one night in Mecca before the Hijrah and said: 'Refrain, O Muhammad, from disparaging our gods and reviling them. If that were true, so-and-so and so-and-so would have been more worthy of this matter than you.' So there came into the heart of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he should refrain from reviling their gods." On this interpretation, this verse is Meccan. It is also related from Said ibn Jubayr "that he (peace be upon him) used to touch the Black Stone, and the Quraysh prevented him, saying: 'We will not leave you alone until you touch our gods.' So there came into his soul that he should do that, with reluctance." Then this verse was revealed.

The second issue: Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of the speech is "they were about to tempt you." The particle inna and the lam are for emphasis. Inna here is the lightened form of the heavy inna, and the lam is what distinguishes it from the negating particle. The meaning is: indeed the matter is that they nearly tempted you, i.e., deceived you, being tempters. The origin of fitnah (temptation) is testing: it is said that the goldsmith "fatana the gold" when he puts it in the fire and melts it to distinguish its good from its bad. Then they used it for anyone who removes a thing from its limit and direction, and they said: "fatanahu" (he tempted him). So His saying: ﴿they were about to tempt you away from that which We revealed to you﴾ means: they would turn you aside and divert you from what We revealed to you, meaning the Qur'an. The meaning is: from its ruling. That is because giving them what they asked for would be opposing the ruling of the Qur'an. His saying: ﴿to fabricate against Us other than it﴾ means: other than what We revealed to you, namely their saying: "Say: Allah has commanded me to do that." ﴿And then they would have taken you as a friend﴾ means: if you had done what they wanted, they would have taken you as a friend and made it known to the people that you agree with them in their position and are pleased with their polytheism. Then He said: ﴿And had We not given you firmness﴾, meaning, upon the truth, by Our preserving you. ﴿You would have almost inclined toward them﴾, meaning you would have leaned toward them ﴿a little.﴾ His saying: ﴿a little﴾ is an expression for the verbal noun, meaning a slight inclining. Ibn Abbas said: He means when he remained silent from answering them. Qatadah said: When this verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, do not leave me to myself even for the blink of an eye." Then He threatened him most severely in this matter, saying: ﴿Then We would have made you taste double [punishment] of life and double [punishment] of death﴾, meaning double the punishment of life and double the punishment of death, meaning the punishment of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter. Doubling is an expression for adding to a thing its like. For when a man says to his agent, "Give so-and-so something," and he gives him a dirham, and the man says, "Double it," the meaning is: add to that dirham its like. Knowing this, we say: The mention of punishment was implied in His saying ﴿double [punishment] of life and double [punishment] of death﴾ because the Qur'an has previously described the punishment as doubled, in His saying: ﴿Our Lord, whoever has advanced this for us, then increase him in punishment doubled in the Fire﴾ (Sad: 61), and He said: ﴿For each there is double, but you do not know﴾ (al-A'raf: 38). The summary of the matter is that if you allowed the thoughts of Satan into your heart and fixed your resolve upon inclining toward him, you would deserve by that a doubling of punishment upon you in this world and the Hereafter, and your punishment would become twice the punishment of the polytheist in this world and twice his punishment in the Hereafter. The reason for doubling this punishment is that the categories of Allah's blessings toward the prophets, peace be upon them, are more numerous, so their sins were greater, and the punishment deserved for them was greater. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿O wives of the Prophet, whoever of you commits a clear immorality, her punishment will be doubled twofold﴾ (al-Ahzab: 30). If it is said: He (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever establishes an evil practice, upon him is its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection," then the implication of this hadith is that if he (peace be upon him) had been pleased with what they said, his burden would have been equal to the burden of each one of those disbelievers, and on this reckoning his punishment would exceed doubling. We reply: Establishing doubling does not indicate the negation of what exceeds it, except by building upon the indication of the discourse (dalil al-khitab), and that is a weak proof. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿then you would not find for yourself any helper against Us﴾, meaning: if We made you taste the doubled punishment, you would not find anyone to rescue you from Our punishment and Our retribution. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: Those who object to the infallibility (ismah) of the prophets, peace be upon them, have argued with this verse, saying: This verse indicates that a grave sin proceeded from them, in several respects:

The first: The verse indicates that he (peace be upon him) came close to fabricating against Allah, and fabrication against Allah is among the greatest sins.

The second: It indicates that had Allah not made him firm and preserved him, he would have come close to inclining toward their religion and leaning toward their doctrine.

The third: That there would have been no need to mention this severe threat unless there had been a prior transgression and offense.

The answer to the first: The word kada means "to be near," so the meaning of the verse is that his falling into this temptation was near, and this degree does not indicate that he actually fell into that temptation. For when we say, "The governor almost struck so-and-so," it is not understood from this that he struck him.

The answer to the second: The word lawla indicates the negation of one thing because of the existence of another. You say: "Lawla Ali, Umar would have perished," meaning: the existence of Ali prevented Umar from perishing. Likewise here, His saying: ﴿And had We not given you firmness, you would have almost inclined toward them﴾ means that Allah's giving firmness to Muhammad (ﷺ) occurred, and the occurrence of that firmness prevented the occurrence of that inclination.

The answer to the third: That threat against disobedience does not indicate that he undertook it. The proof of this is verses among which is His saying: ﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings, We would have seized him by the right hand, then We would have severed from him the aorta﴾ (al-Haqqah: 44–46). Among them is His saying: ﴿If you associate others with Allah, your deeds will surely be nullified﴾ (al-Zumar: 65), and among them His saying: ﴿And do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ (al-Ahzab: 1). And Allah knows best.

The fourth issue: Our companions argued for the soundness of their position, that there is no protection from sins except by Allah's granting of success (tawfiq), with His saying: ﴿And had We not given you firmness, you would have almost inclined toward them, a little.﴾ They said: He, exalted is He, made clear that had Allah not given him firmness, he would have turned toward the path of the disbelievers. And there is no doubt that Muhammad (ﷺ) was stronger than others in the strength of religion and the purity of certainty. So when Allah, exalted is He, made clear that his remaining protected from disbelief and misguidance was not achieved except by Allah's help and succor, the attainment of this meaning for others was more fitting. The Mu'tazilah (a theological school) said: What is meant by this firmness is the gracious aids (alutaf) that divert him from that, which are what occurred to his mind of the remembrance of His promise and His threat, and of the remembrance that his being a prophet from Allah, exalted is He, prevents him from that. The answer: There is no doubt that this firmness is an expression for an act performed by Allah that prevents the Messenger from falling into that forbidden deed. We say: If the impetus toward that forbidden deed did not exist in the case of the Messenger, there would be no need for bringing about this preventive factor. And since there was a need to bring about this preventive factor, we know that the impetus had arisen in the case of the Messenger (ﷺ), and that this preventive factor which Allah produced prevented that impetus from acting. This does not hold except if we say that power together with motive necessitates the act, so when a motive arises that opposes the first motive, the effective cause is disturbed and the act is prevented. We only wish to establish this meaning. And Allah knows best.

The fifth issue: Al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: We have mentioned in the occasion of revelation of this verse the aforementioned accounts, and it is also possible to interpret it without restricting it to a specific occasion of revelation, because it is known that the polytheists used to strive to nullify the command of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with all their power. At one time they would say: "If you worship our gods, we will worship your God." So Allah revealed: ﴿Say: O disbelievers, I do not worship what you worship﴾ (al-Kafirun: 1–2), and His saying: ﴿They wish you would compromise, so they would compromise﴾ (al-Qalam: 9). They offered him great wealth and beautiful women so that he would abandon his claim to prophethood, so Allah revealed: ﴿And do not extend your eyes [longingly]﴾ (al-Hijr: 88). They urged him to drive the believers away from himself, so Allah revealed His saying: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord﴾ (al-An'am: 52). So it is possible that these verses were revealed in this category, because they intended to tempt him away from his religion and to remove him from his path. Then He, exalted is He, made clear that He would keep him firm upon the upright religion and the straight path. On this approach, there is no need in the interpretation of these verses for any of those narrations. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verses 76–77:**

﴿And indeed, they were about to frighten you out of the land to expel you from it; and then they would not have remained after you except for a little.﴾ ﴿[This is] the way of those We sent before you of Our messengers; and you will not find for Our way any alteration.﴾

On this verse there are two opinions:

The first: Qatadah said, "They are the people of Makkah. They intended to expel the Prophet ﷺ from Makkah, and had they done so, they would not have been given respite. But Allah prevented them from expelling him until Allah commanded him to leave. Then their remaining after the Prophet's ﷺ departure from [page 20] Makkah was brief, until Allah sent upon them the slaughter at the Battle of Badr." This is also the view of Mujahid.

The second opinion: Ibn Abbas said, "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ migrated to al-Madinah, the Jews envied him and disliked his nearness to them. They said, 'O Abu al-Qasim, the prophets were sent only to al-Sham, which is a blessed land and was the dwelling of Ibrahim. If you go out to al-Sham, we will believe in you and follow you. We know that nothing prevents you from leaving except fear of the Romans. If you are the Messenger of Allah, then Allah will protect you from them.' So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ encamped a few miles from al-Madinah, said to be at Dhu al-Hulayfah, so that his companions would gather to him and people would see him resolved to set out for al-Sham, out of his eagerness for people to enter the religion of Allah. Then this verse was revealed, and he returned."

The first opinion is the choice of al-Zajjaj and is the more correct view, because the surah is Makki. If the second opinion is sound, then the verse would be Madani. The "land" in His words ﴿from the land﴾ means Makkah according to the first opinion, and al-Madinah according to the second. In the Revelation, mention of "the land" often refers to a specific place, as in His words ﴿or be exiled from the land﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 33), meaning from their places, and His words ﴿I will never leave the land﴾ (Yusuf: 80), meaning the land he had intended in seeking provisions.

If it is said: Allah said ﴿And how many a city, more powerful than your city which has expelled you﴾ (Muhammad: 13), meaning Makkah, and the intended meaning is its people. Thus He mentioned that they expelled him. And in this verse He said ﴿And indeed, they were about to frighten you out of the land to expel you from it﴾. How then can the two be reconciled according to the view of the one who says that "the land" in this verse is Makkah?

We say: They intended to expel him, but he, peace be upon him, did not leave because of their expulsion; he left only by the command of Allah, the Exalted. Thus the contradiction disappears.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And then they would not have remained after you except for a little.﴾ Concerning this there are two issues:

The first issue: Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr, on the authority of 'Asim, read ﴿خَلْفَكَ﴾ (khalfaka) with a fatha on the kha and a sukun on the lam, while the rest read ﴿خِلافَكَ﴾ (khilafaka). Al-Akhfash held that khilafaka has the meaning of khalfaka, and Yunus narrated this from Isa. This is like His words ﴿with their sitting behind (khilaf) the Messenger of Allah﴾ (al-Tawbah: 81).

A poet said:

*"The abodes were effaced after them (khilafahum), as if the palm-leaf weavers had spread a mat between them."*

The author of al-Kashshaf said: it is read ﴿لا يَلْبَثُونَ﴾ (la yalbathuna), and in the reading of Ubayy it is ﴿لا يَلْبَثُوا﴾ (la yalbathu), with idhan operating [in the sense of governing the verb in the subjunctive]. If it is asked: what is the basis of the two readings? We say: As for the first, the verb is conjoined to the verb, and it is in the indicative because it occurs as the predicate of kada (to be about to), and the verb in the predicate of kada occupies the position of a noun. As for the reading of Ubayy, it contains the whole clause by itself, namely His words ﴿And then they would not have remained﴾, conjoined to the clause of His words ﴿And indeed, they were about to frighten you﴾.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿[This is] the way of those We sent before you of Our messengers﴾, meaning that every people who expelled their prophet from among them, the way of Allah was to destroy them. So His words ﴿the way (sunnah)﴾ are in the accusative as an emphatic verbal noun, meaning: We made that a way concerning those We sent before you.

Then He said: ﴿and you will not find for Our way any alteration﴾. The meaning is that what Allah, exalted is He, has put in motion as custom cannot be made possible for anyone to reverse that custom.

The complete discussion of this subject is that the specification of every occurrence with its determined time and its determined attribute is not a matter that belongs to it in itself; otherwise it would follow that it would remain forever in that state, and that a thing would not be distinguished from what is like it in those attributes. Rather, that specification comes about only through the act of a specifier, and that specification is that He, exalted is He, wills its realization at that time. Then His power is related to bringing it about at that time, and then His knowledge is related to its occurrence at that time. Then we say: these three attributes, which are the influences in producing that specification, if they are originated, their origination would require another specification, and it would lead to an infinite regress (tasalsul), which is impossible. And if they are eternal, then the eternal cannot be changed, because what has been established as eternal cannot be non-existent. Since change in those attributes that influence that specification is impossible, change in those determined things is impossible. Thus, by this proof, the truth of His words is established: ﴿and you will not find for Our way any alteration﴾.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verses 78–81 (part 1 of 3)**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun until the darkness of the night, and the recitation of dawn; indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed.﴾ ﴿And from the night, pray with it as a supererogatory act for you; perhaps your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station.﴾ ﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter a sound entrance and to exit a sound exit, and grant me from Yourself a helping authority.﴾ ﴿And say: The truth has come and falsehood has vanished; indeed, falsehood is ever bound to vanish.﴾ In the verse there are several issues:

**The first issue: concerning the arrangement (naẓm) of the verses, there are several aspects.**

The first: When Allah had established the matters of divinity, the Hereafter and prophethood, He followed them with the command to acts of obedience after faith. The most noble of acts of obedience after faith is the prayer, and for this reason He commanded it.

The second: When He said: ﴿And indeed they almost entice you away from the land﴾, He commanded him to devote himself to His worship, so that He would support him against them. It is as if it were said to him: Do not mind their efforts to expel you from your city, and do not turn to them. Occupy yourself with the worship of Allah and persist in performing the prayers, for He will repel their plotting and their evil from you, will make your hand above their hands, and your religion dominant over their religions. A parallel to this is His saying in Surah Ta-Ha: ﴿So be patient over what they say, and glorify the praise of your Lord before the rising of the sun and before its setting, and during the hours of the night glorify Him, and at the ends of the day, that perhaps you may be pleased﴾ (Ṭā-Hā: 130). And He said: ﴿And We know that your breast is constricted by what they say. So glorify the praise of your Lord and be among those who prostrate. And worship your Lord until there comes to you the certainty﴾ (al-Ḥijr: 97–99).

The third aspect in explaining the arrangement: When the Jews said to him, "Go to Syria, for it is the dwelling place of the prophets," he ﷺ resolved to go there. It was as if it were said to him: The worshipped One is one in all lands, and victory and dominion come only through His support and aid. So persist in the prayers, return to your home and residence, and when you enter it and return to it, say: ﴿My Lord, cause me to enter a sound entrance and to exit a sound exit, and grant me from Yourself a helping authority﴾, meaning in this land, a helping authority for establishing Your religion and manifesting Your law. And Allah knows best.

**The second issue:** The lexicographers and exegetes differed over the meaning of ﴿the decline of the sun﴾ (dulūk al-shams), into two views.

The first: its dulūk is its setting. This view is narrated from a group of the Companions. Al-Wāḥidī, in al-Basīṭ, reported from ʿAlī, peace be upon him, that he said: "The dulūk of the sun is its setting." Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh reported that ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd said: "The dulūk of the sun is its setting." Saʿīd ibn Jubayr reported this view from Ibn ʿAbbās. This view is the choice of al-Farrāʾ and, among the later scholars, Ibn Qutayba.

The second view: the dulūk of the sun is its decline (zawāl) from the midst of the sky. This is the choice of most of the Companions and the Successors. Those who held this view argued for its soundness with several arguments:

The first argument: Al-Wāḥidī, in al-Basīṭ, reported from Jābir that he said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his companions ate with me, then they went out when the sun declined, and the Prophet ﷺ said: 'This is the time when the sun declined (dalakat).'"

The second argument: The author of al-Kashshāf reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Jibrīl, peace be upon him, came to me at the dulūk of the sun, when the sun declined, and he led me in the noon prayer."

The third argument: The lexicographers said that the meaning of dulūk in the speech of the Arabs is zawāl (decline). For this reason the sun is called dālika at midday when it has declined, and it is also called dālika when it sets, because in both states it is departing. This is what al-Azharī said. Al-Qaffāl said: The root of dulūk is inclination. One says: the sun inclined for zawāl, and one says: it inclined for ghurūb (setting). Having known this, we say: it is necessary that the intended dulūk here be the decline from the midst of the sky, because He tied the establishment of prayer to the dulūk, and dulūk is an expression for inclination and decline. So it is necessary to say that as soon as inclination and decline first occur, this ruling becomes attached to it. When this meaning occurred at the moment of its inclining from the midst of the sky, the obligation of prayer must become attached to it. That indicates that the intended dulūk in this verse is its inclination from the midst of the sky. This is a strong argument in this matter, which I have deduced from what the lexicographers agreed upon: that dulūk is an expression for inclination and decline. And Allah knows best.

The fourth argument: Al-Azharī said: It is better to interpret dulūk as the decline at midday, and the meaning of ﴿Establish the prayer﴾ is: persist in it from the time of the sun's decline until the darkness of the night. On this interpretation, the Ẓuhr, ʿAṣr, Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ prayers all enter. Then He said: ﴿Establish the prayer﴾. If we take dulūk as decline, the five prayers enter this verse; but if we take it as setting, only three prayers enter it: Maghrib, ʿIshāʾ and Fajr. And taking the words of Allah to what yields more benefit is preferable. Therefore the intended dulūk must be the decline.

Al-Farrāʾ argued for his view that dulūk is setting with the verse of a poet:

"This is the station of the two feet of Rabāḥ, who stood until the sun set, Barāḥ."

Barāḥ is a name of the sun, meaning: until it set.

Ibn Qutayba argued with the words of Dhū al-Rummah:

"Lamps which are not those led by stars, nor are their orbits the dawālik."

Know that this argument is weak. For us, dulūk is an expression for inclination and change, and this meaning is present in setting. So setting is one type of dulūk, and the word dulūk applying to setting does not contradict its applying to decline, just as the word animal applying to a human does not contradict its applying to a horse.

Some also argued for this view, saying that dulūk is derived from dalk (rubbing), because a person rubs his eyes when he looks at the sun, and this applies only at the time when it is possible to look at it. It is known that when the sun is in the midst of the sky it is not possible to look at it, whereas near setting it is possible to look at it, and when a person looks at it at that time he rubs his eyes. So it is established that the word dulūk is specific to setting.

The answer: the need for that clarification is greater when the sun is in the midst of the sky. So what I have mentioned, that dulūk is an expression for decline from the midst of the sky, is preferable. And Allah knows best.

**The third issue:** Al-Wāḥidī said: The lām in ﴿for the decline of the sun﴾ is the lām of time and cause, because the prayer is obligatory only with the decline of the sun. So it is obligatory on the worshipper to establish it because of the sun's decline.

**The fourth issue:** His saying ﴿until the darkness of the night﴾. Ghasaq al-layl is its blackness and darkness. Al-Kisāʾī said: ghasaqa al-layl ghusūqan, and al-ghasaq, with a fatḥa on the sīn, is the noun. Naḍr ibn Shumayl said: ghasaq al-layl is the entry of its beginning. One says: I came to him when ghasaq al-layl, meaning when it mixes and blocks the views.

The root of this word is from flowing. One says: ghasaqat al-ʿayn taghsiqu, which is the flowing of the eye with water. Al-ghāsiq is the flowing thing, and from this is said of what flows from the people of Hell: al-ghassāq. So the meaning of ghasaqa al-layl is that it poured down with its darkness, because darkness seems to pour down over the world.

As for the statements of the exegetes: Ibn Jurayj said: I said to ʿAṭāʾ, "What is ghasaq al-layl?" He said: "Its beginning, when it enters." Nāfiʿ ibn al-Azraq asked Ibn ʿAbbās what al-ghasaq is, and he said: "The entry of the night with its darkness."

Al-Azharī said: Ghasaq al-layl is at the disappearance of the twilight, when darkness accumulates and intensifies. One says: ghasaqat al-ʿayn when it fills with tears, and ghasaqat al-jirāḥa when the wound fills with blood. He said: If we take ghasaq in this sense, the four prayers enter it, namely Ẓuhr, ʿAṣr, Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ. If we take ghasaq as the appearance of the first darkness, only Ẓuhr and Maghrib enter it. So the first is preferable.

Know that from these two views a noble discussion branches out. If we interpret ghasaq as the appearance of the first darkness, then ghasaq is an expression for the beginning of Maghrib. On this basis, what is mentioned in the verse is three times: the time of the decline, the time of the beginning of Maghrib, and the time of Fajr. This requires that the decline be a time for Ẓuhr and ʿAṣr, so this time is shared by these two prayers, and that the beginning of Maghrib be a time for Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ, so this time is also shared by these two prayers. This requires the permissibility of combining Ẓuhr and ʿAṣr, and combining Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ, absolutely. But the evidence indicates that combining while resident, without an excuse, is not permitted. So combining must be permitted with the excuse of travel, rain, or other reasons.

As for if we interpret ghasaq as the accumulated darkness, we say: accumulated darkness occurs only at the disappearance of the white twilight (al-shafaq al-abyaḍ). The word ilā (until) indicates the end of a limit, and a ruling extended up to a limit is legislated before that limit is reached. So it is necessary that the establishment of all the prayers be permitted before the disappearance of the white twilight. This is valid only if we say that they become obligatory at the disappearance of the red twilight. And Allah knows best.

**The fifth issue:** His saying ﴿and the recitation of dawn﴾. They agreed that what is meant is the dawn prayer (ṣalāt al-ṣubḥ). Its being in the accusative is by coordination (ʿaṭf) upon ﴿the prayer﴾ in His saying ﴿Establish the prayer﴾, and the implied sense is: establish the prayer, and establish the recitation of dawn. In this are several benefits:

The first: This verse indicates that the prayer is not complete except with recitation.

The second: He attributed the Qurʾān to dawn, the sense being: establish the recitation of dawn. So the recitation must be tied to the arrival of fajr (dawn). At the first emergence of morning, dawn has come, because fajr was named fajr from the bursting (infijār) of the darkness of the night by the light of morning. The apparent sense of a command is obligation, so the implication of this wording is the obligation to establish the dawn prayer from its first emergence. But we are agreed that this obligation is not present, so it is necessary that recommendation remain. Because obligation is an expression for the preponderance of something that prevents abandonment, when something prevents the realization of the obligation, the prevention from abandonment must be removed, and the basic preponderance remains until the violation of the evidence is established. So it is established that this verse indicates that establishing the dawn prayer at the beginning of its time is better. This indicates the soundness of the school of al-Shāfiʿī that taghlīs (praying early, while it is still dark) is better than tanwīr (praying when it is lit). And Allah knows best.

The third: The jurists explained that the sunnah is for the recitation in this prayer to be longer than the recitation in the other prayers. So the purpose of His saying "and the recitation of dawn" is to urge that lengthening the recitation in this prayer is desired, because specifying it by mention indicates that it is more complete than others.

The fourth: He described the recitation of dawn as ﴿witnessed﴾ (mashhūd). The majority said: its meaning is that the angels of the night and the angels of the day gather at the dawn prayer behind the imam. The angels of the day descend upon them while they are in the dawn prayer, before the angels of the night ascend. When the imam finishes his prayer, the angels of the night ascend and the angels of the day remain. Then, when the angels of the night ascend, they say: "O Lord, we left Your servants praying to You." The angels of the day say: "Our Lord, we came to Your servants while they were praying." Then Allah the Exalted says to the angels: "Bear witness that I have forgiven them."

I say that this too is strong evidence that taghlīs is better than tanwīr. When a person begins it from the first of the morning, the darkness still remains, so the angels of the night are present. Then, when the prayer is prolonged by reciting slowly and at length, the darkness disappears, the light appears, and the angels of the day come. In this way, both the angels of the night and the angels of the day are present in this prayer. But if he begins this prayer at the time of illumination, then there is that which remained.

[Page 22] [Page 23] [Page 24]

...the darkness, so no one from the angels of the night remains at that time, and the stated meaning is not realized. It is established that His saying, ﴿Indeed, it was witnessed﴾, is a strong proof that the *taghlis* (praying the dawn prayer while it is still quite dark, at the very end of the night) is more excellent. However, in my view there is another possibility in interpreting His saying, ﴿Indeed, it was witnessed﴾. This is because whenever the occurring events are greater and more perfect, reasoning from them to the perfection of Allah's power, exalted is He, becomes more perfect. So when a person begins to perform the dawn prayer from the beginning of this time, the intense darkness remains in the world. When the recitation is prolonged during this time, the world turns from darkness to light. Darkness is suitable to death and non-existence, and light is suitable to life and existence. On this assumption, when the person rises from his sleep, it is as if he has passed from death to life and from non-existence to existence. Then, in the course of his prayer, he witnesses the transformation of this entire world from darkness to light, from death to life, from stillness to motion, and from non-existence to existence. This state is a wondrous one, in which intellects and souls testify that none can bring about this turning, changing and transforming except the Creator, who manages with perfect wisdom and infinite power. At that point the intellect is illuminated by the light of this knowledge, and the doors of divine spiritual unveilings (*mukashafat*) open to the intellect and the soul. Thus the prayer, which is a expression for the actions of the limbs, becomes witnessed through these sacred divine unveilings. For this reason, everyone who has a sound disposition and an upright nature, when he rises from his sleep, performs the dawn prayer at the beginning of its time, and considers the changing conditions of the world from the darkness that exists to the light, and from stillness to motion, will find in his heart a spirit, tranquility, an increase in the light of knowledge and strength of certainty. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Indeed, the recitation of dawn was witnessed﴾. It has become clear that this consideration is attained only when the dawn prayer is performed in the manner of *taghlis*. This is what occurred to the mind, and Allah knows best His intended meaning.

There is a third possibility in the verse: that what is meant by His saying, ﴿Indeed, the recitation of dawn was witnessed﴾, is the encouragement to perform this prayer in congregation, and the meaning is that it is witnessed by a large congregation. The further clarification of this is that we have explained that the effect of this prayer in purifying and illuminating the heart is greater than the effect of the other prayers. So when a group of Muslims gathers in the mosque to perform this act of worship, the heart of each one of them is illuminated. Then, through that gathering, it is as if the light of the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, and the light of obedience to Him at that time are reflected from the heart of each one to the heart of the other. Thus their spirits become like shining mirrors facing one another, when the rays of the sun fall upon them, so that the light is reflected from each of those mirrors to the other. Likewise in this case. For this reason, everyone who has a sound disposition and performs this prayer at this time in congregation finds in his heart expansiveness, light and tranquility.

The fifth benefit: His saying, ﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun until the darkness of the night﴾. It may be that the reason it is witnessed is that when a person has slept throughout the night, he becomes like one who is heedless during this period of observing the conditions of the world. So the images of physical events are removed from the tablet of his imagination, his thought and his intellect, and these tablets become like tablets on which corrupt inscriptions were written, and then those inscriptions were washed away and removed from them.
