So at the first moment of rising from sleep, the tablets of his intellect, thought and imagination become purified of the corrupt and false inscriptions. When a person hastens at that time to the worship of Allah, exalted is He, and to the recitation of the words that indicate His transcendence, and to the performance of the acts that indicate the glorification of Allah, exalted is He, these pure and sacred inscriptions are imprinted upon the tablet of his intellect, thought and imagination. Then the occurrence of these inscriptions prevents the corrupt inscriptions from becoming firmly established, namely those inscriptions that arise from the inclination toward the world and its desires. By this route, the inclination toward the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, His love and His obedience seeps in, and the inclination toward the world and its desires weakens. Having understood this, we say: this wisdom is only attained when a person begins the prayer from the moment he rises from sleep, at the *taghlis*, and this indicates the intended meaning. Know that most of the creation has fallen into diseases of the heart, namely love of the world, greed, envy, boasting and rivalry in worldly increase. This world is like the house of the sick when it is filled with the sick, and the prophets are like skilled physicians. The patient, perhaps his illness has grown strong, so he does not return to health except through powerful treatments. Perhaps the patient is ignorant, so he does not submit to the physician and opposes him in most matters. However, if the physician is compassionate and skilled, he strives to remove that illness by every means he is able to. If he cannot remove it, he strives to reduce it and lighten it. Having understood this, we say: the disease of love of the world has overpowered the creation, and there is no cure for it except calling to the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, and serving and obeying Him. This treatment is burdensome to the souls, and few accept it and submit to it. Undoubtedly, the prophets strove to reduce this disease and to bring people to begin obedience and servitude from the first moment of rising from sleep, which benefits in removing this disease in the manner we have established. Therefore it must be prescribed. And Allah knows best the secrets of His speech.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And from the night, perform tahajjud with it as a supererogatory (nafilah) for you﴾. Know that when He, exalted is He, commanded the five prayers by way of allusion and indication, He followed it with the exhortation to the night prayer. There are several discussions concerning it.

The first discussion: *tahajjud* (the night prayer) is an expression for the night prayer. So His saying, *fa-tahajjad bihi*, means "with it," that is, with the Qur'an, as He said: ﴿Stand [in prayer] at night, except a little﴾ (al-Muzzammil: 2), up to His saying: ﴿and recite the Qur'an in measured recitation﴾ (al-Muzzammil: 4).

The second discussion: al-Wahidi said: *al-hujud* in the language is sleep, and it is well known and frequent in poetry. It is said: *ahjadtuhu* and *hajjadtuhu*, meaning I made him sleep. From it is the saying of Labid:

*Hajjidna, fa-qad tala as-sura*
("Let us sleep, for the night journey has grown long.")

It is as if he said: "Let us sleep, for the night journey has lengthened over us until sleep overcame us." Abu Ubayd related from Abu Ubayda: *al-hajid* is the one who sleeps, and *al-hajid* is also the one who prays at night. Tha'lab related from Ibn al-A'rabi a similar statement, as if he said: *hajada ar-rajul* means he prayed during the night, and *hajada* means he slept at night. So according to these scholars, this term is one of the contronyms (words having opposite meanings). As for al-Azhari, he took a middle position in explaining this term and said: the known usage in the speech of the Arabs is that *al-hajid* is the one who sleeps. Then we see that in the Shari'ah, one who rises from sleep to prayer is called *mutahajjid*. Therefore it must be understood that he was called *mutahajjid* because he casts off sleep from himself, just as the worshipper is called *mutahannith*, because he casts off *hinth* from himself, which is sin. It is also said: so-and-so is a man who is *mutaharrij*, *mut'athhim* and *mutahawwib*, meaning he casts off hardship, sin and sinfulness from himself. I say there is another possibility in this: that a person only gives up the pleasure of sleep and bears the hardship of rising for prayer so that his rest and sleep will be pleasant at the time of death. Since his purpose in giving up this sleep is to attain the pleasant sleep at death, this rising is a pursuit of that sleep, so it was called *tahajjud* for this reason.

There is a third aspect: what is related that al-Hajjaj ibn Amr al-Mazini said: "Does one of you think that when he rises at night and prays until morning, he has performed *tahajjud*? *Tahajjud* is only prayer after sleep, then another prayer after another sleep, then another prayer after another sleep. Thus was the prayer of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." Having understood this, we say: whenever a person prays, he seeks sleep and rest, so it is not far-fetched that it was called *tahajjud* for this reason.

The third discussion: the *min* in His saying, ﴿And from the night﴾, must have something it relates to, and the *fa* in His saying, ﴿fa-tahajjad﴾, must have something it is conjoined to. The estimated meaning is: "Rise during part of the night, then perform tahajjud with it." And His saying, *bihi* ("with it"), means with the Qur'an, and what is intended by it is the prayer that includes the Qur'an.

The fourth discussion: the meaning of *nafilah* (supererogatory) in the language is what is an addition beyond the basic obligation. We have mentioned it in His saying: ﴿They ask you about the spoils﴾ (al-Anfal: 1). Its meaning in this verse is also an addition. Regarding how it is an addition, there are two views based on whether the night prayer was obligatory upon the Prophet (ﷺ) or not. Some people said it was obligatory upon him and then it was abrogated (*naskh*, the cancellation of a ruling by later revelation), so it became *nafilah*, meaning voluntary and an addition to the obligatory prayers. Mujahid and al-Suddi mentioned a good explanation of why it is *nafilah*. They said: Allah forgave the Prophet (ﷺ) what preceded and what followed of his sins. So any act of obedience he performs other than the prescribed prayer has no effect at all in expiating sins; rather its effect is in increasing ranks and multiplying reward. The purpose of that worship was increase of reward, so it was called *nafilah* for this reason. Unlike the community, who have sins needing expiations, so they need these acts of obedience to expiate sins and misdeeds. Thus it is established that these acts of obedience are only additions and supererogatory acts with respect to the Prophet (ﷺ), and not with respect to others. For this reason He said: ﴿as a supererogatory for you﴾, meaning they are additions and supererogatory acts in your case and not in the case of others. Its explanation is what we have mentioned. As for those who said that the night prayer was obligatory upon the Prophet (ﷺ), they said that the meaning of its being *nafilah* for him, by way of specification, is that it is an obligation upon you in addition to the five prayers, and you were singled out for it from among your community. This view can be supported by the argument that His saying, ﴿fa-tahajjad﴾, is a command, and the form of a command indicates obligation, so this tahajjud must be obligatory. If we interpret His saying, "as a supererogatory for you," as non-obligatory, a contradiction would arise, and that is contrary to the default. Therefore the meaning of its being a supererogatory for him must be what we have mentioned, namely that its obligation is additional to the obligation of the five prayers. And Allah knows best.

The fifth discussion: His saying, ﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun until the darkness of the night, and the recitation of dawn﴾. Although the apparent address of the command here is specific to the Messenger (ﷺ), it is general in meaning with respect to the community. The evidence for this is that He said: ﴿And from the night, perform tahajjud with it as a supererogatory for you﴾. So He clarified that the command to tahajjud is specific to the Messenger, and this indicates that the command to the five prayers is not specific to the Messenger, peace be upon him. Otherwise, restricting the command to tahajjud by this condition would have no benefit at all. And Allah knows best. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praised station﴾. The exegetes agreed that the word *'asa* ("it may be") from Allah is obligatory. The scholars of meanings (*ahl al-ma'ani*) said: because the word *'asa* conveys raising hope, and whoever raises a person's hope in something and then deprives him of it, it is a disgrace, while Allah, exalted is He, is too generous to raise anyone's hope in something and then not give it to him.

* * *

As for His saying, ﴿a praised station﴾, there are two discussions concerning it.

The first discussion: regarding the accusative (*nasb*) of the word *mahmudan* ("praised"), there are two views. The first: that its accusative is as a circumstantial state (*hal*) of the verb "He raises you", meaning He raises you praised. The second: that it is an adjective (*na't*) for "station", and this is clear.

The second discussion: regarding the interpretation of the praised station, there are several views:

[Page 27]

The first view: it is the intercession (shafa'ah, the Prophet's intercession for sinners on the Day of Judgment). Al-Wahidi said: The commentators have unanimously agreed that it is the station of intercession, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said regarding this verse: "It is the station in which I will intercede for my community." I say: the wording points to this. A person becomes praised only when someone praises him, and praise is given only for a favor. Therefore this praised station must be a station in which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) bestows a favor upon a people, and they praise him for that favor. That favor cannot be the conveying of the religion and the teaching of the Law, because that was already happening at the time. And His saying: ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praised station﴾ is an expression of hope, and to give someone hope regarding something you have already granted him is impossible. So the favor for which he becomes praised must be a favor that he will bestow upon people after this, and that is nothing other than his intercession with God. This shows that the wording of the verse, namely His saying ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praised station﴾, indicates this meaning. Also, the indefiniteness in His saying "a praised station" indicates that the Prophet (ﷺ) will receive in that station a great, complete, and far-reaching praise. It is well known that a person's praise for his efforts in securing deliverance from punishment is greater than his praise for efforts toward an additional reward that he does not need, because a person's need to ward off great pains from himself is greater than his need to obtain additional benefits that he has no need for. Since this is established, the meaning of His saying ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praised station﴾ must be the intercession for the removal of punishment, according to the view of Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah). And since it has been established that the wording of the verse strongly indicates this meaning, and then authentic reports were transmitted confirming this meaning, it is necessary to interpret the wording accordingly. Among what supports this view is the well-known supplication: "And raise him to the praised station that You have promised him, which the first and the last will envy him for." People have agreed that what is meant by it is intercession.

The second view: Hudhayfah said: "People will be gathered in one place, and no soul will speak. The first one called will be Muhammad (ﷺ), and he will say: 'At Your service, and at Your call, and evil is not attributed to You. The one guided is whom You guide. Your servant stands before You. By You and to You. There is no refuge and no escape from You except to You. You are blessed and exalted, Glory be to You, Lord of the House.'" This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praised station﴾. I say: the first view is better, because his effort in intercession leads to people praising him, so he becomes praised. As for the mention of this supplication, it only yields reward, not praise. If they say: Why is it not permissible to say that God praises him for this statement? We reply: Because in language, "praise" (hamd) is specifically the commendation mentioned in return for a favor, and if the word "praise" is used in another sense, it is by way of metaphor.

The third view: what is meant is a station whose outcome is praised. This is also weak, for the reason we mentioned in the second view.

The fourth view: Al-Wahidi said: It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "God will seat Muhammad upon the Throne." And from Mujahid that he said: He will make him sit with Him upon the Throne. Then al-Wahidi said: This is a vile, repugnant, and monstrous view. The text of the Book calls out for the corruption of this interpretation, and several points indicate this:

The first: The opposite of "seating" (ijlas) is said: "I raised (ba'athtu) the one standing and the one sitting, and he rose (in'atha)." And it is said: "God raised (ba'atha) the dead," meaning He brought him up from his grave. So interpreting "ba'th" as "seating" is interpreting an opposite by its opposite, which is invalid.

The second: He, exalted is He, said "a praised station (maqaman mahmudan)" and did not say "a seat (maq'adan)," and "maqam" is the place of standing, not the place of sitting.

The third: If God were sitting upon the Throne in such a way that Muhammad (may the prayers and peace of God be upon him) sat beside Him, then He would be bounded and finite, and whoever is like that is created (muhdath).

The fourth: It is said that his sitting with God upon the Throne contains no great honor, because these ignorant and foolish people say that all the people of Paradise will visit God, exalted is He, and will sit with Him, and that He will ask them about their conditions that they had in the world. If this state is available to all believers, there is no additional distinction or rank in singling out Muhammad (ﷺ) with it.

The fifth: When one says "The sultan sent (ba'atha) so-and-so," it is understood that he sent him to a people to address their affairs, and it is not understood that he seated him with himself. Thus it is established that this view is a vile and worthless statement that only a person of little intellect and no religion would incline toward. And God knows best.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter with a sincere entrance and cause me to exit with a sincere exit﴾. Regarding this there are several discussions:

The first discussion: We mentioned in the interpretation of His saying ﴿And they had almost enticed you away from the land﴾ two views:

One of them: what is meant by it is the effort of the disbelievers of Makkah to expel him from it.

The second: what is meant by it is that the Jews told him: "It would be better for you to leave Madinah for Syria." Then He, exalted is He, said to him: ﴿Establish the prayer﴾, and occupy yourself with the worship of God, exalted is He, and do not pay attention to these ignorant people, for He, exalted is He, is your supporter and helper. Then after this statement He returned to explaining that incident. So if we interpret that verse as meaning that the disbelievers of Makkah wanted to expel him from Makkah, then the meaning of this verse is that He, exalted is He, commanded him to emigrate to Madinah and said to him: ﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter with a sincere entrance﴾, which is Madinah, ﴿and cause me to exit with a sincere exit﴾, which is Makkah. This is the view of al-Hasan and Qatadah. And if we interpret that verse as meaning that the Jews drove him to leave Madinah and go to Syria, so that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) left it, and then God commanded him to return to it, then the meaning is that he (may the prayers and peace of God be upon him), upon returning to Madinah, said: ﴿My Lord, cause me to enter with a sincere entrance﴾, which is Madinah, ﴿and cause me to exit with a sincere exit﴾, meaning: cause me to exit from it to Makkah with a sincere exit, that is, open it for me.

The second view regarding the interpretation of this verse, and it is more complete than what preceded: that what is meant is ﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter﴾ into the prayer, ﴿and cause me to exit﴾ from it, with sincerity, sincere devotion, awareness of Your remembrance, and the fulfillment of the requirements of Your gratitude.

The third view, which is more complete than what preceded: that what is meant is: ﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter﴾ into the carrying out of the duties of conveying Your religion and Your Law, ﴿and cause me to exit﴾ from it after finishing it, an exit that leaves upon me no lingering obligation from it.

The fourth view, which is higher than what preceded: ﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter﴾ into the seas of the proofs of Your oneness, Your transcendence, and Your holiness, and then cause me to exit from occupation with the proof to the light of knowing the thing proven, and from contemplating the traces of the createdness of created things to being absorbed in knowing the One, the Unique, who is free of multiplicities and changes.

The fifth view: "Cause me to enter into everything You cause me to enter, with sincerity in my servanthood and absorption in knowing You, and cause me to exit from everything You cause me to exit from, with sincerity in servanthood, knowledge, and love." The intended meaning is that the sincerity of servanthood should be present in every entering, exiting, movement, and rest.

The sixth view: "Cause me to enter the grave with a sincere entrance, and cause me to exit from it with a sincere exit."

The second discussion: "Mudkhal" with a dammah on the meem is a verbal noun like "idkhal" (entering). It is said: "I caused him to enter (adkhaltuhu) an entrance (mudkhalan)," as He said: ﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to land at a blessed landing place﴾ (al-Mu'minun: 29). The meaning of attributing "mudkhal" and "mukhraj" to "sidq" (sincerity/truthfulness) is to praise them, as if he asked God for a good entrance and a good exit, in which he would see nothing he dislikes. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And grant me from Yourself an authority, a helper﴾, that is, a clear, manifest proof by which You will help me against all who oppose me. In sum, he asked God to grant him strength against those who oppose him, by proof and by power and capability. God, exalted is He, answered his supplication and informed him that He would protect him from people, saying: ﴿And God will protect you from the people﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 67), and He said: ﴿Unquestionably, the party of God are the successful﴾ (al-Mujadilah: 22), and He said: ﴿That He may make it prevail over all religion﴾ (al-Tawbah: 33). When he asked God for victory, God showed him that He had answered his supplication, saying: ﴿And say: The truth has come﴾, which is His religion and His Law, ﴿and falsehood has vanished﴾, which is everything other than it of religions and laws. "Zahaqa" means it was nullified and dissolved, and its origin is from "zahaqat nafsuhu," meaning he perished. It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud: "He entered Makkah on the day of the Conquest, and around the House there were three hundred and sixty idols. He began striking them with a stick in his hand, saying: 'The truth has come and falsehood has vanished,' and the idol would fall on its face." And His saying: ﴿Indeed, falsehood is ever bound to vanish﴾ means that although falsehood may achieve power and dominion, it does not endure, but disappears in the swiftest manner. And God knows best.

[Page 28]

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verses 78–81 (part 1 of 3)**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun until the darkness of the night, and the recitation of dawn; indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed.﴾ ﴿And from the night, pray with it as a supererogatory act for you; perhaps your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station.﴾ ﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter a sound entrance and to exit a sound exit, and grant me from Yourself a helping authority.﴾ ﴿And say: The truth has come and falsehood has vanished; indeed, falsehood is ever bound to vanish.﴾ In the verse there are several issues:

**The first issue: concerning the arrangement (naẓm) of the verses, there are several aspects.**

The first: When Allah had established the matters of divinity, the Hereafter and prophethood, He followed them with the command to acts of obedience after faith. The most noble of acts of obedience after faith is the prayer, and for this reason He commanded it.

The second: When He said: ﴿And indeed they almost entice you away from the land﴾, He commanded him to devote himself to His worship, so that He would support him against them. It is as if it were said to him: Do not mind their efforts to expel you from your city, and do not turn to them. Occupy yourself with the worship of Allah and persist in performing the prayers, for He will repel their plotting and their evil from you, will make your hand above their hands, and your religion dominant over their religions. A parallel to this is His saying in Surah Ta-Ha: ﴿So be patient over what they say, and glorify the praise of your Lord before the rising of the sun and before its setting, and during the hours of the night glorify Him, and at the ends of the day, that perhaps you may be pleased﴾ (Ṭā-Hā: 130). And He said: ﴿And We know that your breast is constricted by what they say. So glorify the praise of your Lord and be among those who prostrate. And worship your Lord until there comes to you the certainty﴾ (al-Ḥijr: 97–99).

The third aspect in explaining the arrangement: When the Jews said to him, "Go to Syria, for it is the dwelling place of the prophets," he ﷺ resolved to go there. It was as if it were said to him: The worshipped One is one in all lands, and victory and dominion come only through His support and aid. So persist in the prayers, return to your home and residence, and when you enter it and return to it, say: ﴿My Lord, cause me to enter a sound entrance and to exit a sound exit, and grant me from Yourself a helping authority﴾, meaning in this land, a helping authority for establishing Your religion and manifesting Your law. And Allah knows best.

**The second issue:** The lexicographers and exegetes differed over the meaning of ﴿the decline of the sun﴾ (dulūk al-shams), into two views.

The first: its dulūk is its setting. This view is narrated from a group of the Companions. Al-Wāḥidī, in al-Basīṭ, reported from ʿAlī, peace be upon him, that he said: "The dulūk of the sun is its setting." Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh reported that ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd said: "The dulūk of the sun is its setting." Saʿīd ibn Jubayr reported this view from Ibn ʿAbbās. This view is the choice of al-Farrāʾ and, among the later scholars, Ibn Qutayba.

The second view: the dulūk of the sun is its decline (zawāl) from the midst of the sky. This is the choice of most of the Companions and the Successors. Those who held this view argued for its soundness with several arguments:

The first argument: Al-Wāḥidī, in al-Basīṭ, reported from Jābir that he said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his companions ate with me, then they went out when the sun declined, and the Prophet ﷺ said: 'This is the time when the sun declined (dalakat).'"

The second argument: The author of al-Kashshāf reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Jibrīl, peace be upon him, came to me at the dulūk of the sun, when the sun declined, and he led me in the noon prayer."

The third argument: The lexicographers said that the meaning of dulūk in the speech of the Arabs is zawāl (decline). For this reason the sun is called dālika at midday when it has declined, and it is also called dālika when it sets, because in both states it is departing. This is what al-Azharī said. Al-Qaffāl said: The root of dulūk is inclination. One says: the sun inclined for zawāl, and one says: it inclined for ghurūb (setting). Having known this, we say: it is necessary that the intended dulūk here be the decline from the midst of the sky, because He tied the establishment of prayer to the dulūk, and dulūk is an expression for inclination and decline. So it is necessary to say that as soon as inclination and decline first occur, this ruling becomes attached to it. When this meaning occurred at the moment of its inclining from the midst of the sky, the obligation of prayer must become attached to it. That indicates that the intended dulūk in this verse is its inclination from the midst of the sky. This is a strong argument in this matter, which I have deduced from what the lexicographers agreed upon: that dulūk is an expression for inclination and decline. And Allah knows best.

The fourth argument: Al-Azharī said: It is better to interpret dulūk as the decline at midday, and the meaning of ﴿Establish the prayer﴾ is: persist in it from the time of the sun's decline until the darkness of the night. On this interpretation, the Ẓuhr, ʿAṣr, Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ prayers all enter. Then He said: ﴿Establish the prayer﴾. If we take dulūk as decline, the five prayers enter this verse; but if we take it as setting, only three prayers enter it: Maghrib, ʿIshāʾ and Fajr. And taking the words of Allah to what yields more benefit is preferable. Therefore the intended dulūk must be the decline.

Al-Farrāʾ argued for his view that dulūk is setting with the verse of a poet:

"This is the station of the two feet of Rabāḥ, who stood until the sun set, Barāḥ."

Barāḥ is a name of the sun, meaning: until it set.

Ibn Qutayba argued with the words of Dhū al-Rummah:

"Lamps which are not those led by stars, nor are their orbits the dawālik."

Know that this argument is weak. For us, dulūk is an expression for inclination and change, and this meaning is present in setting. So setting is one type of dulūk, and the word dulūk applying to setting does not contradict its applying to decline, just as the word animal applying to a human does not contradict its applying to a horse.

Some also argued for this view, saying that dulūk is derived from dalk (rubbing), because a person rubs his eyes when he looks at the sun, and this applies only at the time when it is possible to look at it. It is known that when the sun is in the midst of the sky it is not possible to look at it, whereas near setting it is possible to look at it, and when a person looks at it at that time he rubs his eyes. So it is established that the word dulūk is specific to setting.

The answer: the need for that clarification is greater when the sun is in the midst of the sky. So what I have mentioned, that dulūk is an expression for decline from the midst of the sky, is preferable. And Allah knows best.

**The third issue:** Al-Wāḥidī said: The lām in ﴿for the decline of the sun﴾ is the lām of time and cause, because the prayer is obligatory only with the decline of the sun. So it is obligatory on the worshipper to establish it because of the sun's decline.

**The fourth issue:** His saying ﴿until the darkness of the night﴾. Ghasaq al-layl is its blackness and darkness. Al-Kisāʾī said: ghasaqa al-layl ghusūqan, and al-ghasaq, with a fatḥa on the sīn, is the noun. Naḍr ibn Shumayl said: ghasaq al-layl is the entry of its beginning. One says: I came to him when ghasaq al-layl, meaning when it mixes and blocks the views.

The root of this word is from flowing. One says: ghasaqat al-ʿayn taghsiqu, which is the flowing of the eye with water. Al-ghāsiq is the flowing thing, and from this is said of what flows from the people of Hell: al-ghassāq. So the meaning of ghasaqa al-layl is that it poured down with its darkness, because darkness seems to pour down over the world.

As for the statements of the exegetes: Ibn Jurayj said: I said to ʿAṭāʾ, "What is ghasaq al-layl?" He said: "Its beginning, when it enters." Nāfiʿ ibn al-Azraq asked Ibn ʿAbbās what al-ghasaq is, and he said: "The entry of the night with its darkness."

Al-Azharī said: Ghasaq al-layl is at the disappearance of the twilight, when darkness accumulates and intensifies. One says: ghasaqat al-ʿayn when it fills with tears, and ghasaqat al-jirāḥa when the wound fills with blood. He said: If we take ghasaq in this sense, the four prayers enter it, namely Ẓuhr, ʿAṣr, Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ. If we take ghasaq as the appearance of the first darkness, only Ẓuhr and Maghrib enter it. So the first is preferable.

Know that from these two views a noble discussion branches out. If we interpret ghasaq as the appearance of the first darkness, then ghasaq is an expression for the beginning of Maghrib. On this basis, what is mentioned in the verse is three times: the time of the decline, the time of the beginning of Maghrib, and the time of Fajr. This requires that the decline be a time for Ẓuhr and ʿAṣr, so this time is shared by these two prayers, and that the beginning of Maghrib be a time for Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ, so this time is also shared by these two prayers. This requires the permissibility of combining Ẓuhr and ʿAṣr, and combining Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ, absolutely. But the evidence indicates that combining while resident, without an excuse, is not permitted. So combining must be permitted with the excuse of travel, rain, or other reasons.

As for if we interpret ghasaq as the accumulated darkness, we say: accumulated darkness occurs only at the disappearance of the white twilight (al-shafaq al-abyaḍ). The word ilā (until) indicates the end of a limit, and a ruling extended up to a limit is legislated before that limit is reached. So it is necessary that the establishment of all the prayers be permitted before the disappearance of the white twilight. This is valid only if we say that they become obligatory at the disappearance of the red twilight. And Allah knows best.

**The fifth issue:** His saying ﴿and the recitation of dawn﴾. They agreed that what is meant is the dawn prayer (ṣalāt al-ṣubḥ). Its being in the accusative is by coordination (ʿaṭf) upon ﴿the prayer﴾ in His saying ﴿Establish the prayer﴾, and the implied sense is: establish the prayer, and establish the recitation of dawn. In this are several benefits:

The first: This verse indicates that the prayer is not complete except with recitation.

The second: He attributed the Qurʾān to dawn, the sense being: establish the recitation of dawn. So the recitation must be tied to the arrival of fajr (dawn). At the first emergence of morning, dawn has come, because fajr was named fajr from the bursting (infijār) of the darkness of the night by the light of morning. The apparent sense of a command is obligation, so the implication of this wording is the obligation to establish the dawn prayer from its first emergence. But we are agreed that this obligation is not present, so it is necessary that recommendation remain. Because obligation is an expression for the preponderance of something that prevents abandonment, when something prevents the realization of the obligation, the prevention from abandonment must be removed, and the basic preponderance remains until the violation of the evidence is established. So it is established that this verse indicates that establishing the dawn prayer at the beginning of its time is better. This indicates the soundness of the school of al-Shāfiʿī that taghlīs (praying early, while it is still dark) is better than tanwīr (praying when it is lit). And Allah knows best.

The third: The jurists explained that the sunnah is for the recitation in this prayer to be longer than the recitation in the other prayers. So the purpose of His saying "and the recitation of dawn" is to urge that lengthening the recitation in this prayer is desired, because specifying it by mention indicates that it is more complete than others.

The fourth: He described the recitation of dawn as ﴿witnessed﴾ (mashhūd). The majority said: its meaning is that the angels of the night and the angels of the day gather at the dawn prayer behind the imam. The angels of the day descend upon them while they are in the dawn prayer, before the angels of the night ascend. When the imam finishes his prayer, the angels of the night ascend and the angels of the day remain. Then, when the angels of the night ascend, they say: "O Lord, we left Your servants praying to You." The angels of the day say: "Our Lord, we came to Your servants while they were praying." Then Allah the Exalted says to the angels: "Bear witness that I have forgiven them."

I say that this too is strong evidence that taghlīs is better than tanwīr. When a person begins it from the first of the morning, the darkness still remains, so the angels of the night are present. Then, when the prayer is prolonged by reciting slowly and at length, the darkness disappears, the light appears, and the angels of the day come. In this way, both the angels of the night and the angels of the day are present in this prayer. But if he begins this prayer at the time of illumination, then there is that which remained.

[Page 22] [Page 23] [Page 24]

...the darkness, so no one from the angels of the night remains at that time, and the stated meaning is not realized. It is established that His saying, ﴿Indeed, it was witnessed﴾, is a strong proof that the *taghlis* (praying the dawn prayer while it is still quite dark, at the very end of the night) is more excellent. However, in my view there is another possibility in interpreting His saying, ﴿Indeed, it was witnessed﴾. This is because whenever the occurring events are greater and more perfect, reasoning from them to the perfection of Allah's power, exalted is He, becomes more perfect. So when a person begins to perform the dawn prayer from the beginning of this time, the intense darkness remains in the world. When the recitation is prolonged during this time, the world turns from darkness to light. Darkness is suitable to death and non-existence, and light is suitable to life and existence. On this assumption, when the person rises from his sleep, it is as if he has passed from death to life and from non-existence to existence. Then, in the course of his prayer, he witnesses the transformation of this entire world from darkness to light, from death to life, from stillness to motion, and from non-existence to existence. This state is a wondrous one, in which intellects and souls testify that none can bring about this turning, changing and transforming except the Creator, who manages with perfect wisdom and infinite power. At that point the intellect is illuminated by the light of this knowledge, and the doors of divine spiritual unveilings (*mukashafat*) open to the intellect and the soul. Thus the prayer, which is a expression for the actions of the limbs, becomes witnessed through these sacred divine unveilings. For this reason, everyone who has a sound disposition and an upright nature, when he rises from his sleep, performs the dawn prayer at the beginning of its time, and considers the changing conditions of the world from the darkness that exists to the light, and from stillness to motion, will find in his heart a spirit, tranquility, an increase in the light of knowledge and strength of certainty. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Indeed, the recitation of dawn was witnessed﴾. It has become clear that this consideration is attained only when the dawn prayer is performed in the manner of *taghlis*. This is what occurred to the mind, and Allah knows best His intended meaning.

There is a third possibility in the verse: that what is meant by His saying, ﴿Indeed, the recitation of dawn was witnessed﴾, is the encouragement to perform this prayer in congregation, and the meaning is that it is witnessed by a large congregation. The further clarification of this is that we have explained that the effect of this prayer in purifying and illuminating the heart is greater than the effect of the other prayers. So when a group of Muslims gathers in the mosque to perform this act of worship, the heart of each one of them is illuminated. Then, through that gathering, it is as if the light of the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, and the light of obedience to Him at that time are reflected from the heart of each one to the heart of the other. Thus their spirits become like shining mirrors facing one another, when the rays of the sun fall upon them, so that the light is reflected from each of those mirrors to the other. Likewise in this case. For this reason, everyone who has a sound disposition and performs this prayer at this time in congregation finds in his heart expansiveness, light and tranquility.

The fifth benefit: His saying, ﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun until the darkness of the night﴾. It may be that the reason it is witnessed is that when a person has slept throughout the night, he becomes like one who is heedless during this period of observing the conditions of the world. So the images of physical events are removed from the tablet of his imagination, his thought and his intellect, and these tablets become like tablets on which corrupt inscriptions were written, and then those inscriptions were washed away and removed from them. So at the first moment of rising from sleep, the tablets of his intellect, thought and imagination become purified of the corrupt and false inscriptions. When a person hastens at that time to the worship of Allah, exalted is He, and to the recitation of the words that indicate His transcendence, and to the performance of the acts that indicate the glorification of Allah, exalted is He, these pure and sacred inscriptions are imprinted upon the tablet of his intellect, thought and imagination. Then the occurrence of these inscriptions prevents the corrupt inscriptions from becoming firmly established, namely those inscriptions that arise from the inclination toward the world and its desires. By this route, the inclination toward the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, His love and His obedience seeps in, and the inclination toward the world and its desires weakens. Having understood this, we say: this wisdom is only attained when a person begins the prayer from the moment he rises from sleep, at the *taghlis*, and this indicates the intended meaning. Know that most of the creation has fallen into diseases of the heart, namely love of the world, greed, envy, boasting and rivalry in worldly increase. This world is like the house of the sick when it is filled with the sick, and the prophets are like skilled physicians. The patient, perhaps his illness has grown strong, so he does not return to health except through powerful treatments. Perhaps the patient is ignorant, so he does not submit to the physician and opposes him in most matters. However, if the physician is compassionate and skilled, he strives to remove that illness by every means he is able to. If he cannot remove it, he strives to reduce it and lighten it. Having understood this, we say: the disease of love of the world has overpowered the creation, and there is no cure for it except calling to the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, and serving and obeying Him. This treatment is burdensome to the souls, and few accept it and submit to it. Undoubtedly, the prophets strove to reduce this disease and to bring people to begin obedience and servitude from the first moment of rising from sleep, which benefits in removing this disease in the manner we have established. Therefore it must be prescribed. And Allah knows best the secrets of His speech.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And from the night, perform tahajjud with it as a supererogatory (nafilah) for you﴾. Know that when He, exalted is He, commanded the five prayers by way of allusion and indication, He followed it with the exhortation to the night prayer. There are several discussions concerning it.

The first discussion: *tahajjud* (the night prayer) is an expression for the night prayer. So His saying, *fa-tahajjad bihi*, means "with it," that is, with the Qur'an, as He said: ﴿Stand [in prayer] at night, except a little﴾ (al-Muzzammil: 2), up to His saying: ﴿and recite the Qur'an in measured recitation﴾ (al-Muzzammil: 4).

The second discussion: al-Wahidi said: *al-hujud* in the language is sleep, and it is well known and frequent in poetry. It is said: *ahjadtuhu* and *hajjadtuhu*, meaning I made him sleep. From it is the saying of Labid:

*Hajjidna, fa-qad tala as-sura*
("Let us sleep, for the night journey has grown long.")

It is as if he said: "Let us sleep, for the night journey has lengthened over us until sleep overcame us." Abu Ubayd related from Abu Ubayda: *al-hajid* is the one who sleeps, and *al-hajid* is also the one who prays at night. Tha'lab related from Ibn al-A'rabi a similar statement, as if he said: *hajada ar-rajul* means he prayed during the night, and *hajada* means he slept at night. So according to these scholars, this term is one of the contronyms (words having opposite meanings). As for al-Azhari, he took a middle position in explaining this term and said: the known usage in the speech of the Arabs is that *al-hajid* is the one who sleeps. Then we see that in the Shari'ah, one who rises from sleep to prayer is called *mutahajjid*. Therefore it must be understood that he was called *mutahajjid* because he casts off sleep from himself, just as the worshipper is called *mutahannith*, because he casts off *hinth* from himself, which is sin. It is also said: so-and-so is a man who is *mutaharrij*, *mut'athhim* and *mutahawwib*, meaning he casts off hardship, sin and sinfulness from himself. I say there is another possibility in this: that a person only gives up the pleasure of sleep and bears the hardship of rising for prayer so that his rest and sleep will be pleasant at the time of death. Since his purpose in giving up this sleep is to attain the pleasant sleep at death, this rising is a pursuit of that sleep, so it was called *tahajjud* for this reason.

There is a third aspect: what is related that al-Hajjaj ibn Amr al-Mazini said: "Does one of you think that when he rises at night and prays until morning, he has performed *tahajjud*? *Tahajjud* is only prayer after sleep, then another prayer after another sleep, then another prayer after another sleep. Thus was the prayer of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." Having understood this, we say: whenever a person prays, he seeks sleep and rest, so it is not far-fetched that it was called *tahajjud* for this reason.

The third discussion: the *min* in His saying, ﴿And from the night﴾, must have something it relates to, and the *fa* in His saying, ﴿fa-tahajjad﴾, must have something it is conjoined to. The estimated meaning is: "Rise during part of the night, then perform tahajjud with it." And His saying, *bihi* ("with it"), means with the Qur'an, and what is intended by it is the prayer that includes the Qur'an.

The fourth discussion: the meaning of *nafilah* (supererogatory) in the language is what is an addition beyond the basic obligation. We have mentioned it in His saying: ﴿They ask you about the spoils﴾ (al-Anfal: 1). Its meaning in this verse is also an addition. Regarding how it is an addition, there are two views based on whether the night prayer was obligatory upon the Prophet (ﷺ) or not. Some people said it was obligatory upon him and then it was abrogated (*naskh*, the cancellation of a ruling by later revelation), so it became *nafilah*, meaning voluntary and an addition to the obligatory prayers. Mujahid and al-Suddi mentioned a good explanation of why it is *nafilah*. They said: Allah forgave the Prophet (ﷺ) what preceded and what followed of his sins. So any act of obedience he performs other than the prescribed prayer has no effect at all in expiating sins; rather its effect is in increasing ranks and multiplying reward. The purpose of that worship was increase of reward, so it was called *nafilah* for this reason. Unlike the community, who have sins needing expiations, so they need these acts of obedience to expiate sins and misdeeds. Thus it is established that these acts of obedience are only additions and supererogatory acts with respect to the Prophet (ﷺ), and not with respect to others. For this reason He said: ﴿as a supererogatory for you﴾, meaning they are additions and supererogatory acts in your case and not in the case of others. Its explanation is what we have mentioned. As for those who said that the night prayer was obligatory upon the Prophet (ﷺ), they said that the meaning of its being *nafilah* for him, by way of specification, is that it is an obligation upon you in addition to the five prayers, and you were singled out for it from among your community. This view can be supported by the argument that His saying, ﴿fa-tahajjad﴾, is a command, and the form of a command indicates obligation, so this tahajjud must be obligatory. If we interpret His saying, "as a supererogatory for you," as non-obligatory, a contradiction would arise, and that is contrary to the default. Therefore the meaning of its being a supererogatory for him must be what we have mentioned, namely that its obligation is additional to the obligation of the five prayers. And Allah knows best.

The fifth discussion: His saying, ﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun until the darkness of the night, and the recitation of dawn﴾. Although the apparent address of the command here is specific to the Messenger (ﷺ), it is general in meaning with respect to the community. The evidence for this is that He said: ﴿And from the night, perform tahajjud with it as a supererogatory for you﴾. So He clarified that the command to tahajjud is specific to the Messenger, and this indicates that the command to the five prayers is not specific to the Messenger, peace be upon him. Otherwise, restricting the command to tahajjud by this condition would have no benefit at all. And Allah knows best. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praised station﴾. The exegetes agreed that the word *'asa* ("it may be") from Allah is obligatory. The scholars of meanings (*ahl al-ma'ani*) said: because the word *'asa* conveys raising hope, and whoever raises a person's hope in something and then deprives him of it, it is a disgrace, while Allah, exalted is He, is too generous to raise anyone's hope in something and then not give it to him.

* * *

As for His saying, ﴿a praised station﴾, there are two discussions concerning it.

The first discussion: regarding the accusative (*nasb*) of the word *mahmudan* ("praised"), there are two views. The first: that its accusative is as a circumstantial state (*hal*) of the verb "He raises you", meaning He raises you praised. The second: that it is an adjective (*na't*) for "station", and this is clear.

The second discussion: regarding the interpretation of the praised station, there are several views:

[Page 27]

The first view: it is the intercession (shafa'ah, the Prophet's intercession for sinners on the Day of Judgment). Al-Wahidi said: The commentators have unanimously agreed that it is the station of intercession, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said regarding this verse: "It is the station in which I will intercede for my community." I say: the wording points to this. A person becomes praised only when someone praises him, and praise is given only for a favor. Therefore this praised station must be a station in which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) bestows a favor upon a people, and they praise him for that favor. That favor cannot be the conveying of the religion and the teaching of the Law, because that was already happening at the time. And His saying: ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praised station﴾ is an expression of hope, and to give someone hope regarding something you have already granted him is impossible. So the favor for which he becomes praised must be a favor that he will bestow upon people after this, and that is nothing other than his intercession with God. This shows that the wording of the verse, namely His saying ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praised station﴾, indicates this meaning. Also, the indefiniteness in His saying "a praised station" indicates that the Prophet (ﷺ) will receive in that station a great, complete, and far-reaching praise. It is well known that a person's praise for his efforts in securing deliverance from punishment is greater than his praise for efforts toward an additional reward that he does not need, because a person's need to ward off great pains from himself is greater than his need to obtain additional benefits that he has no need for. Since this is established, the meaning of His saying ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praised station﴾ must be the intercession for the removal of punishment, according to the view of Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah). And since it has been established that the wording of the verse strongly indicates this meaning, and then authentic reports were transmitted confirming this meaning, it is necessary to interpret the wording accordingly. Among what supports this view is the well-known supplication: "And raise him to the praised station that You have promised him, which the first and the last will envy him for." People have agreed that what is meant by it is intercession.

The second view: Hudhayfah said: "People will be gathered in one place, and no soul will speak. The first one called will be Muhammad (ﷺ), and he will say: 'At Your service, and at Your call, and evil is not attributed to You. The one guided is whom You guide. Your servant stands before You. By You and to You. There is no refuge and no escape from You except to You. You are blessed and exalted, Glory be to You, Lord of the House.'" This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praised station﴾. I say: the first view is better, because his effort in intercession leads to people praising him, so he becomes praised. As for the mention of this supplication, it only yields reward, not praise. If they say: Why is it not permissible to say that God praises him for this statement? We reply: Because in language, "praise" (hamd) is specifically the commendation mentioned in return for a favor, and if the word "praise" is used in another sense, it is by way of metaphor.

The third view: what is meant is a station whose outcome is praised. This is also weak, for the reason we mentioned in the second view.

The fourth view: Al-Wahidi said: It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "God will seat Muhammad upon the Throne." And from Mujahid that he said: He will make him sit with Him upon the Throne. Then al-Wahidi said: This is a vile, repugnant, and monstrous view. The text of the Book calls out for the corruption of this interpretation, and several points indicate this:

The first: The opposite of "seating" (ijlas) is said: "I raised (ba'athtu) the one standing and the one sitting, and he rose (in'atha)." And it is said: "God raised (ba'atha) the dead," meaning He brought him up from his grave. So interpreting "ba'th" as "seating" is interpreting an opposite by its opposite, which is invalid.

The second: He, exalted is He, said "a praised station (maqaman mahmudan)" and did not say "a seat (maq'adan)," and "maqam" is the place of standing, not the place of sitting.

The third: If God were sitting upon the Throne in such a way that Muhammad (may the prayers and peace of God be upon him) sat beside Him, then He would be bounded and finite, and whoever is like that is created (muhdath).

The fourth: It is said that his sitting with God upon the Throne contains no great honor, because these ignorant and foolish people say that all the people of Paradise will visit God, exalted is He, and will sit with Him, and that He will ask them about their conditions that they had in the world. If this state is available to all believers, there is no additional distinction or rank in singling out Muhammad (ﷺ) with it.

The fifth: When one says "The sultan sent (ba'atha) so-and-so," it is understood that he sent him to a people to address their affairs, and it is not understood that he seated him with himself. Thus it is established that this view is a vile and worthless statement that only a person of little intellect and no religion would incline toward. And God knows best.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter with a sincere entrance and cause me to exit with a sincere exit﴾. Regarding this there are several discussions:

The first discussion: We mentioned in the interpretation of His saying ﴿And they had almost enticed you away from the land﴾ two views:

One of them: what is meant by it is the effort of the disbelievers of Makkah to expel him from it.

The second: what is meant by it is that the Jews told him: "It would be better for you to leave Madinah for Syria." Then He, exalted is He, said to him: ﴿Establish the prayer﴾, and occupy yourself with the worship of God, exalted is He, and do not pay attention to these ignorant people, for He, exalted is He, is your supporter and helper. Then after this statement He returned to explaining that incident. So if we interpret that verse as meaning that the disbelievers of Makkah wanted to expel him from Makkah, then the meaning of this verse is that He, exalted is He, commanded him to emigrate to Madinah and said to him: ﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter with a sincere entrance﴾, which is Madinah, ﴿and cause me to exit with a sincere exit﴾, which is Makkah. This is the view of al-Hasan and Qatadah. And if we interpret that verse as meaning that the Jews drove him to leave Madinah and go to Syria, so that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) left it, and then God commanded him to return to it, then the meaning is that he (may the prayers and peace of God be upon him), upon returning to Madinah, said: ﴿My Lord, cause me to enter with a sincere entrance﴾, which is Madinah, ﴿and cause me to exit with a sincere exit﴾, meaning: cause me to exit from it to Makkah with a sincere exit, that is, open it for me.

The second view regarding the interpretation of this verse, and it is more complete than what preceded: that what is meant is ﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter﴾ into the prayer, ﴿and cause me to exit﴾ from it, with sincerity, sincere devotion, awareness of Your remembrance, and the fulfillment of the requirements of Your gratitude.

The third view, which is more complete than what preceded: that what is meant is: ﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter﴾ into the carrying out of the duties of conveying Your religion and Your Law, ﴿and cause me to exit﴾ from it after finishing it, an exit that leaves upon me no lingering obligation from it.

The fourth view, which is higher than what preceded: ﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter﴾ into the seas of the proofs of Your oneness, Your transcendence, and Your holiness, and then cause me to exit from occupation with the proof to the light of knowing the thing proven, and from contemplating the traces of the createdness of created things to being absorbed in knowing the One, the Unique, who is free of multiplicities and changes.

The fifth view: "Cause me to enter into everything You cause me to enter, with sincerity in my servanthood and absorption in knowing You, and cause me to exit from everything You cause me to exit from, with sincerity in servanthood, knowledge, and love." The intended meaning is that the sincerity of servanthood should be present in every entering, exiting, movement, and rest.

The sixth view: "Cause me to enter the grave with a sincere entrance, and cause me to exit from it with a sincere exit."

The second discussion: "Mudkhal" with a dammah on the meem is a verbal noun like "idkhal" (entering). It is said: "I caused him to enter (adkhaltuhu) an entrance (mudkhalan)," as He said: ﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to land at a blessed landing place﴾ (al-Mu'minun: 29). The meaning of attributing "mudkhal" and "mukhraj" to "sidq" (sincerity/truthfulness) is to praise them, as if he asked God for a good entrance and a good exit, in which he would see nothing he dislikes. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And grant me from Yourself an authority, a helper﴾, that is, a clear, manifest proof by which You will help me against all who oppose me. In sum, he asked God to grant him strength against those who oppose him, by proof and by power and capability. God, exalted is He, answered his supplication and informed him that He would protect him from people, saying: ﴿And God will protect you from the people﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 67), and He said: ﴿Unquestionably, the party of God are the successful﴾ (al-Mujadilah: 22), and He said: ﴿That He may make it prevail over all religion﴾ (al-Tawbah: 33). When he asked God for victory, God showed him that He had answered his supplication, saying: ﴿And say: The truth has come﴾, which is His religion and His Law, ﴿and falsehood has vanished﴾, which is everything other than it of religions and laws. "Zahaqa" means it was nullified and dissolved, and its origin is from "zahaqat nafsuhu," meaning he perished. It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud: "He entered Makkah on the day of the Conquest, and around the House there were three hundred and sixty idols. He began striking them with a stick in his hand, saying: 'The truth has come and falsehood has vanished,' and the idol would fall on its face." And His saying: ﴿Indeed, falsehood is ever bound to vanish﴾ means that although falsehood may achieve power and dominion, it does not endure, but disappears in the swiftest manner. And God knows best.

[Page 28]

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verses 78–81 (part 1 of 3)**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun until the darkness of the night, and the recitation of dawn; indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed.﴾ ﴿And from the night, pray with it as a supererogatory act for you; perhaps your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station.﴾ ﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter a sound entrance and to exit a sound exit, and grant me from Yourself a helping authority.﴾ ﴿And say: The truth has come and falsehood has vanished; indeed, falsehood is ever bound to vanish.﴾ In the verse there are several issues:

**The first issue: concerning the arrangement (naẓm) of the verses, there are several aspects.**

The first: When Allah had established the matters of divinity, the Hereafter and prophethood, He followed them with the command to acts of obedience after faith. The most noble of acts of obedience after faith is the prayer, and for this reason He commanded it.

The second: When He said: ﴿And indeed they almost entice you away from the land﴾, He commanded him to devote himself to His worship, so that He would support him against them. It is as if it were said to him: Do not mind their efforts to expel you from your city, and do not turn to them. Occupy yourself with the worship of Allah and persist in performing the prayers, for He will repel their plotting and their evil from you, will make your hand above their hands, and your religion dominant over their religions. A parallel to this is His saying in Surah Ta-Ha: ﴿So be patient over what they say, and glorify the praise of your Lord before the rising of the sun and before its setting, and during the hours of the night glorify Him, and at the ends of the day, that perhaps you may be pleased﴾ (Ṭā-Hā: 130). And He said: ﴿And We know that your breast is constricted by what they say. So glorify the praise of your Lord and be among those who prostrate. And worship your Lord until there comes to you the certainty﴾ (al-Ḥijr: 97–99).

The third aspect in explaining the arrangement: When the Jews said to him, "Go to Syria, for it is the dwelling place of the prophets," he ﷺ resolved to go there. It was as if it were said to him: The worshipped One is one in all lands, and victory and dominion come only through His support and aid. So persist in the prayers, return to your home and residence, and when you enter it and return to it, say: ﴿My Lord, cause me to enter a sound entrance and to exit a sound exit, and grant me from Yourself a helping authority﴾, meaning in this land, a helping authority for establishing Your religion and manifesting Your law. And Allah knows best.

**The second issue:** The lexicographers and exegetes differed over the meaning of ﴿the decline of the sun﴾ (dulūk al-shams), into two views.

The first: its dulūk is its setting. This view is narrated from a group of the Companions. Al-Wāḥidī, in al-Basīṭ, reported from ʿAlī, peace be upon him, that he said: "The dulūk of the sun is its setting." Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh reported that ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd said: "The dulūk of the sun is its setting." Saʿīd ibn Jubayr reported this view from Ibn ʿAbbās. This view is the choice of al-Farrāʾ and, among the later scholars, Ibn Qutayba.

The second view: the dulūk of the sun is its decline (zawāl) from the midst of the sky. This is the choice of most of the Companions and the Successors. Those who held this view argued for its soundness with several arguments:

The first argument: Al-Wāḥidī, in al-Basīṭ, reported from Jābir that he said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his companions ate with me, then they went out when the sun declined, and the Prophet ﷺ said: 'This is the time when the sun declined (dalakat).'"

The second argument: The author of al-Kashshāf reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Jibrīl, peace be upon him, came to me at the dulūk of the sun, when the sun declined, and he led me in the noon prayer."

The third argument: The lexicographers said that the meaning of dulūk in the speech of the Arabs is zawāl (decline). For this reason the sun is called dālika at midday when it has declined, and it is also called dālika when it sets, because in both states it is departing. This is what al-Azharī said. Al-Qaffāl said: The root of dulūk is inclination. One says: the sun inclined for zawāl, and one says: it inclined for ghurūb (setting). Having known this, we say: it is necessary that the intended dulūk here be the decline from the midst of the sky, because He tied the establishment of prayer to the dulūk, and dulūk is an expression for inclination and decline. So it is necessary to say that as soon as inclination and decline first occur, this ruling becomes attached to it. When this meaning occurred at the moment of its inclining from the midst of the sky, the obligation of prayer must become attached to it. That indicates that the intended dulūk in this verse is its inclination from the midst of the sky. This is a strong argument in this matter, which I have deduced from what the lexicographers agreed upon: that dulūk is an expression for inclination and decline. And Allah knows best.

The fourth argument: Al-Azharī said: It is better to interpret dulūk as the decline at midday, and the meaning of ﴿Establish the prayer﴾ is: persist in it from the time of the sun's decline until the darkness of the night. On this interpretation, the Ẓuhr, ʿAṣr, Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ prayers all enter. Then He said: ﴿Establish the prayer﴾. If we take dulūk as decline, the five prayers enter this verse; but if we take it as setting, only three prayers enter it: Maghrib, ʿIshāʾ and Fajr. And taking the words of Allah to what yields more benefit is preferable. Therefore the intended dulūk must be the decline.

Al-Farrāʾ argued for his view that dulūk is setting with the verse of a poet:

"This is the station of the two feet of Rabāḥ, who stood until the sun set, Barāḥ."

Barāḥ is a name of the sun, meaning: until it set.

Ibn Qutayba argued with the words of Dhū al-Rummah:

"Lamps which are not those led by stars, nor are their orbits the dawālik."

Know that this argument is weak. For us, dulūk is an expression for inclination and change, and this meaning is present in setting. So setting is one type of dulūk, and the word dulūk applying to setting does not contradict its applying to decline, just as the word animal applying to a human does not contradict its applying to a horse.

Some also argued for this view, saying that dulūk is derived from dalk (rubbing), because a person rubs his eyes when he looks at the sun, and this applies only at the time when it is possible to look at it. It is known that when the sun is in the midst of the sky it is not possible to look at it, whereas near setting it is possible to look at it, and when a person looks at it at that time he rubs his eyes. So it is established that the word dulūk is specific to setting.

The answer: the need for that clarification is greater when the sun is in the midst of the sky. So what I have mentioned, that dulūk is an expression for decline from the midst of the sky, is preferable. And Allah knows best.

**The third issue:** Al-Wāḥidī said: The lām in ﴿for the decline of the sun﴾ is the lām of time and cause, because the prayer is obligatory only with the decline of the sun. So it is obligatory on the worshipper to establish it because of the sun's decline.

**The fourth issue:** His saying ﴿until the darkness of the night﴾. Ghasaq al-layl is its blackness and darkness. Al-Kisāʾī said: ghasaqa al-layl ghusūqan, and al-ghasaq, with a fatḥa on the sīn, is the noun. Naḍr ibn Shumayl said: ghasaq al-layl is the entry of its beginning. One says: I came to him when ghasaq al-layl, meaning when it mixes and blocks the views.

The root of this word is from flowing. One says: ghasaqat al-ʿayn taghsiqu, which is the flowing of the eye with water. Al-ghāsiq is the flowing thing, and from this is said of what flows from the people of Hell: al-ghassāq. So the meaning of ghasaqa al-layl is that it poured down with its darkness, because darkness seems to pour down over the world.

As for the statements of the exegetes: Ibn Jurayj said: I said to ʿAṭāʾ, "What is ghasaq al-layl?" He said: "Its beginning, when it enters." Nāfiʿ ibn al-Azraq asked Ibn ʿAbbās what al-ghasaq is, and he said: "The entry of the night with its darkness."

Al-Azharī said: Ghasaq al-layl is at the disappearance of the twilight, when darkness accumulates and intensifies. One says: ghasaqat al-ʿayn when it fills with tears, and ghasaqat al-jirāḥa when the wound fills with blood. He said: If we take ghasaq in this sense, the four prayers enter it, namely Ẓuhr, ʿAṣr, Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ. If we take ghasaq as the appearance of the first darkness, only Ẓuhr and Maghrib enter it. So the first is preferable.

Know that from these two views a noble discussion branches out. If we interpret ghasaq as the appearance of the first darkness, then ghasaq is an expression for the beginning of Maghrib. On this basis, what is mentioned in the verse is three times: the time of the decline, the time of the beginning of Maghrib, and the time of Fajr. This requires that the decline be a time for Ẓuhr and ʿAṣr, so this time is shared by these two prayers, and that the beginning of Maghrib be a time for Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ, so this time is also shared by these two prayers. This requires the permissibility of combining Ẓuhr and ʿAṣr, and combining Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ, absolutely. But the evidence indicates that combining while resident, without an excuse, is not permitted. So combining must be permitted with the excuse of travel, rain, or other reasons.

As for if we interpret ghasaq as the accumulated darkness, we say: accumulated darkness occurs only at the disappearance of the white twilight (al-shafaq al-abyaḍ). The word ilā (until) indicates the end of a limit, and a ruling extended up to a limit is legislated before that limit is reached. So it is necessary that the establishment of all the prayers be permitted before the disappearance of the white twilight. This is valid only if we say that they become obligatory at the disappearance of the red twilight. And Allah knows best.

**The fifth issue:** His saying ﴿and the recitation of dawn﴾. They agreed that what is meant is the dawn prayer (ṣalāt al-ṣubḥ). Its being in the accusative is by coordination (ʿaṭf) upon ﴿the prayer﴾ in His saying ﴿Establish the prayer﴾, and the implied sense is: establish the prayer, and establish the recitation of dawn. In this are several benefits:

The first: This verse indicates that the prayer is not complete except with recitation.

The second: He attributed the Qurʾān to dawn, the sense being: establish the recitation of dawn. So the recitation must be tied to the arrival of fajr (dawn). At the first emergence of morning, dawn has come, because fajr was named fajr from the bursting (infijār) of the darkness of the night by the light of morning. The apparent sense of a command is obligation, so the implication of this wording is the obligation to establish the dawn prayer from its first emergence. But we are agreed that this obligation is not present, so it is necessary that recommendation remain. Because obligation is an expression for the preponderance of something that prevents abandonment, when something prevents the realization of the obligation, the prevention from abandonment must be removed, and the basic preponderance remains until the violation of the evidence is established. So it is established that this verse indicates that establishing the dawn prayer at the beginning of its time is better. This indicates the soundness of the school of al-Shāfiʿī that taghlīs (praying early, while it is still dark) is better than tanwīr (praying when it is lit). And Allah knows best.

The third: The jurists explained that the sunnah is for the recitation in this prayer to be longer than the recitation in the other prayers. So the purpose of His saying "and the recitation of dawn" is to urge that lengthening the recitation in this prayer is desired, because specifying it by mention indicates that it is more complete than others.

The fourth: He described the recitation of dawn as ﴿witnessed﴾ (mashhūd). The majority said: its meaning is that the angels of the night and the angels of the day gather at the dawn prayer behind the imam. The angels of the day descend upon them while they are in the dawn prayer, before the angels of the night ascend. When the imam finishes his prayer, the angels of the night ascend and the angels of the day remain. Then, when the angels of the night ascend, they say: "O Lord, we left Your servants praying to You." The angels of the day say: "Our Lord, we came to Your servants while they were praying." Then Allah the Exalted says to the angels: "Bear witness that I have forgiven them."

I say that this too is strong evidence that taghlīs is better than tanwīr. When a person begins it from the first of the morning, the darkness still remains, so the angels of the night are present. Then, when the prayer is prolonged by reciting slowly and at length, the darkness disappears, the light appears, and the angels of the day come. In this way, both the angels of the night and the angels of the day are present in this prayer. But if he begins this prayer at the time of illumination, then there is that which remained.

[Page 22] [Page 23] [Page 24]

...the darkness, so no one from the angels of the night remains at that time, and the stated meaning is not realized. It is established that His saying, ﴿Indeed, it was witnessed﴾, is a strong proof that the *taghlis* (praying the dawn prayer while it is still quite dark, at the very end of the night) is more excellent. However, in my view there is another possibility in interpreting His saying, ﴿Indeed, it was witnessed﴾. This is because whenever the occurring events are greater and more perfect, reasoning from them to the perfection of Allah's power, exalted is He, becomes more perfect. So when a person begins to perform the dawn prayer from the beginning of this time, the intense darkness remains in the world. When the recitation is prolonged during this time, the world turns from darkness to light. Darkness is suitable to death and non-existence, and light is suitable to life and existence. On this assumption, when the person rises from his sleep, it is as if he has passed from death to life and from non-existence to existence. Then, in the course of his prayer, he witnesses the transformation of this entire world from darkness to light, from death to life, from stillness to motion, and from non-existence to existence. This state is a wondrous one, in which intellects and souls testify that none can bring about this turning, changing and transforming except the Creator, who manages with perfect wisdom and infinite power. At that point the intellect is illuminated by the light of this knowledge, and the doors of divine spiritual unveilings (*mukashafat*) open to the intellect and the soul. Thus the prayer, which is a expression for the actions of the limbs, becomes witnessed through these sacred divine unveilings. For this reason, everyone who has a sound disposition and an upright nature, when he rises from his sleep, performs the dawn prayer at the beginning of its time, and considers the changing conditions of the world from the darkness that exists to the light, and from stillness to motion, will find in his heart a spirit, tranquility, an increase in the light of knowledge and strength of certainty. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Indeed, the recitation of dawn was witnessed﴾. It has become clear that this consideration is attained only when the dawn prayer is performed in the manner of *taghlis*. This is what occurred to the mind, and Allah knows best His intended meaning.

There is a third possibility in the verse: that what is meant by His saying, ﴿Indeed, the recitation of dawn was witnessed﴾, is the encouragement to perform this prayer in congregation, and the meaning is that it is witnessed by a large congregation. The further clarification of this is that we have explained that the effect of this prayer in purifying and illuminating the heart is greater than the effect of the other prayers. So when a group of Muslims gathers in the mosque to perform this act of worship, the heart of each one of them is illuminated. Then, through that gathering, it is as if the light of the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, and the light of obedience to Him at that time are reflected from the heart of each one to the heart of the other. Thus their spirits become like shining mirrors facing one another, when the rays of the sun fall upon them, so that the light is reflected from each of those mirrors to the other. Likewise in this case. For this reason, everyone who has a sound disposition and performs this prayer at this time in congregation finds in his heart expansiveness, light and tranquility.

The fifth benefit: His saying, ﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun until the darkness of the night﴾. It may be that the reason it is witnessed is that when a person has slept throughout the night, he becomes like one who is heedless during this period of observing the conditions of the world. So the images of physical events are removed from the tablet of his imagination, his thought and his intellect, and these tablets become like tablets on which corrupt inscriptions were written, and then those inscriptions were washed away and removed from them. So at the first moment of rising from sleep, the tablets of his intellect, thought and imagination become purified of the corrupt and false inscriptions. When a person hastens at that time to the worship of Allah, exalted is He, and to the recitation of the words that indicate His transcendence, and to the performance of the acts that indicate the glorification of Allah, exalted is He, these pure and sacred inscriptions are imprinted upon the tablet of his intellect, thought and imagination. Then the occurrence of these inscriptions prevents the corrupt inscriptions from becoming firmly established, namely those inscriptions that arise from the inclination toward the world and its desires. By this route, the inclination toward the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, His love and His obedience seeps in, and the inclination toward the world and its desires weakens. Having understood this, we say: this wisdom is only attained when a person begins the prayer from the moment he rises from sleep, at the *taghlis*, and this indicates the intended meaning. Know that most of the creation has fallen into diseases of the heart, namely love of the world, greed, envy, boasting and rivalry in worldly increase. This world is like the house of the sick when it is filled with the sick, and the prophets are like skilled physicians. The patient, perhaps his illness has grown strong, so he does not return to health except through powerful treatments. Perhaps the patient is ignorant, so he does not submit to the physician and opposes him in most matters. However, if the physician is compassionate and skilled, he strives to remove that illness by every means he is able to. If he cannot remove it, he strives to reduce it and lighten it. Having understood this, we say: the disease of love of the world has overpowered the creation, and there is no cure for it except calling to the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, and serving and obeying Him. This treatment is burdensome to the souls, and few accept it and submit to it. Undoubtedly, the prophets strove to reduce this disease and to bring people to begin obedience and servitude from the first moment of rising from sleep, which benefits in removing this disease in the manner we have established. Therefore it must be prescribed. And Allah knows best the secrets of His speech.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And from the night, perform tahajjud with it as a supererogatory (nafilah) for you﴾. Know that when He, exalted is He, commanded the five prayers by way of allusion and indication, He followed it with the exhortation to the night prayer. There are several discussions concerning it.

The first discussion: *tahajjud* (the night prayer) is an expression for the night prayer. So His saying, *fa-tahajjad bihi*, means "with it," that is, with the Qur'an, as He said: ﴿Stand [in prayer] at night, except a little﴾ (al-Muzzammil: 2), up to His saying: ﴿and recite the Qur'an in measured recitation﴾ (al-Muzzammil: 4).

The second discussion: al-Wahidi said: *al-hujud* in the language is sleep, and it is well known and frequent in poetry. It is said: *ahjadtuhu* and *hajjadtuhu*, meaning I made him sleep. From it is the saying of Labid:

*Hajjidna, fa-qad tala as-sura*
("Let us sleep, for the night journey has grown long.")

It is as if he said: "Let us sleep, for the night journey has lengthened over us until sleep overcame us." Abu Ubayd related from Abu Ubayda: *al-hajid* is the one who sleeps, and *al-hajid* is also the one who prays at night. Tha'lab related from Ibn al-A'rabi a similar statement, as if he said: *hajada ar-rajul* means he prayed during the night, and *hajada* means he slept at night. So according to these scholars, this term is one of the contronyms (words having opposite meanings).
