Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verse 85 (part 1 of 6):

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they ask you about the Spirit. Say, "The Spirit is of the command of my Lord, and you have not been given of knowledge except a little."﴾ Know that when Exalted is He concluded the previous verse with His saying, ﴿Each works according to his manner﴾, and we mentioned that what is meant by it is the conformity of the spirits to the actions issuing from them, it became necessary to investigate here the quiddity and reality of the Spirit, and therefore they asked about the Spirit. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: The exegetes have several opinions about the Spirit mentioned in this verse. The most apparent of them is that what is meant is the Spirit which is the cause of life. It was narrated that the Jews said to the Quraysh: "Ask Muhammad about three things. If he informs you of two and refrains from the third, then he is a prophet. Ask him about the People of the Cave, about Dhu al-Qarnayn, and about the Spirit." So they asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about these three things. He, peace be upon him, said: "Tomorrow I will inform you," and he did not say, "If Allah wills." So revelation was withheld from him for forty days. Then revelation came down after that: ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow,"﴾ ﴿except [with the addition], "If Allah wills."﴾ (Al-Kahf: 23-24). Then he explained to them the story of the People of the Cave and the story of Dhu al-Qarnayn, and he left the story of the Spirit undetailed, and there came down concerning it the saying of Exalted is He: ﴿And they ask you about the Spirit. Say, "The Spirit is of the command of my Lord."﴾ And he made clear that the minds of creation are too limited to know the reality of the Spirit, so He said: ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little.﴾ Some people have criticized this narration on several grounds:

The first: The Spirit is not greater in status or higher in rank than Allah Exalted. If knowledge of Allah Exalted is possible, indeed attained, then what prevents knowledge of the Spirit?

The second: The Jews said, "If he answers about the story of the People of the Cave and the story of Dhu al-Qarnayn but does not answer about the Spirit, then he is a prophet." This is a statement far from reason, because the story of the People of the Cave and the story of Dhu al-Qarnayn are nothing but narratives among narratives, and mentioning a narrative cannot be a proof of prophethood. Moreover, the narrative he relates is either to be considered before knowledge of his prophethood or after knowledge of his prophethood. If it is before knowledge of his prophethood, they would have denied him in it; and if it is after knowledge of his prophethood, then his prophethood would already have been known before that, so there is no benefit in mentioning this narrative. As for his not answering about the reality of the Spirit, it is far-fetched to make this a proof of the validity of prophethood.

The third: The question of the Spirit is known to the lesser philosophers and the base theologians (mutakallimun, practitioners of kalam, scholastic theology). So if the Messenger ﷺ had said, "I do not know it," that would have produced what necessitates belittling and repulsion, for ignorance of such a question diminishes the standing of any person whatsoever, so how much more so the Messenger, who is the most knowledgeable of scholars and the most excellent of the excellent.

The fourth: Exalted is He said concerning him: ﴿The Most Merciful. Taught the Qur'an﴾ (Ar-Rahman: 1-2), ﴿and taught you what you did not know, and ever has the bounty of Allah been upon you Great﴾ (An-Nisa: 113), and said: ﴿And say, "My Lord, increase me in knowledge."﴾ (Ta-Ha: 114). He said concerning the description of the Qur'an: ﴿And no moist or dry thing [is there] but that it is in a clear register﴾ (Al-An'am: 59). And he, peace be upon him, used to say: "Show us things as they are." So how is it fitting for one whose state and description is this to say, "I do not know this question," when it is among the well-known questions mentioned among the majority of creation? Rather, what we choose is that they asked him about the Spirit and that he ﷺ answered it in the best manner. Its explanation is that what is mentioned in the verse is that they asked him about the Spirit, and the question about the Spirit falls under many aspects:

One of them: It may be asked: what is the quiddity of the Spirit? Is it something spatially bounded, or something inhering in what is spatially bounded, or an existent that is neither spatially bounded nor inhering in spatial bounding?

The second: It may be asked: is the Spirit eternal or originated?

The third: It may be asked: do the spirits remain after the death of bodies, or do they perish?

The fourth: It may be asked: what is the reality of the happiness and misery of spirits? In sum, the topics connected with the Spirit are many. His saying, ﴿And they ask you about the Spirit﴾, contains nothing indicating that they asked about these questions or about others, except that He, Exalted is He, mentioned in the answer to this question His saying: ﴿Say, "The Spirit is of the command of my Lord."﴾ This answer is fitting only to two of the questions we have mentioned:

One of them: The question about the quiddity of the Spirit; and the second: about its eternity or origination.

As for the first investigation: They said, "What is the reality and quiddity of the Spirit? Is it an expression for bodies existing within this body, formed from the mixing of temperaments and humours? Or is it an expression for the very mixture and composition? Or is it an expression for another accident subsisting in these bodies? Or is it an expression for an existent that differs from these bodies and accidents?" Allah answered about it by saying that it is an existent differing from these bodies and from these accidents. That is because these bodies are things that come into being from the mixing of humours and elements, whereas the Spirit is not like that, but rather it is a simple, immaterial substance (jawhar, substance) which comes into being only by the command of His saying: ﴿Be, and it is﴾ (An-Nahl: 40).

[Page 32]

They said, "Why is it something differing from these bodies and these accidents?" Allah answered about it by saying that it is an existent which comes into being by the command of Allah, by His bringing it into being, and by its effect in bestowing life on this body. The lack of knowledge of its specific reality does not necessitate its negation, for most realities and quiddities of things are unknown. We know, for instance, that sikanjabin (a vinegar-syrup drink) has a property that requires cutting yellow bile; but if we wish to know the quiddity of that property and its specific reality, that is not known. Thus it is established that most quiddities and realities are unknown, and their being unknown does not necessitate their negation. So it is the same here, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little.﴾

As for the second investigation: It is that the word "command" (amr) has come in the sense of "act." He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And the command of Pharaoh was not rightly guided﴾ (Hud: 97), and He said: ﴿So when Our command came﴾ (Hud: 82), meaning "Our act." So His saying, ﴿The Spirit is of the command of my Lord﴾, means "of the act of my Lord." This answer indicates that they asked him whether the Spirit is eternal or originated, and he said, "Rather, it is originated, and it came into being only by the act of Allah, His bringing it into being and His creating it." Then he argued for the origination of the Spirit by His saying: ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾, meaning that spirits in the beginning of their natural constitution are empty of sciences and cognitions, and then sciences and cognitions come to be in them, so they are constantly moving from one state to another and from deficiency to perfection. Change and transformation are signs of origination. So His saying, ﴿The Spirit is of the command of my Lord﴾, indicates that they asked him whether the Spirit is originated, and he answered that it is originated, occurring by the creation and bringing-into-being of Allah, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿The Spirit is of the command of my Lord.﴾ Then he inferred the origination of spirits from their changing from state to state, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little.﴾ This is what we say on this topic, and Allah knows best.

* * *

The second issue: On mentioning the other opinions stated about the very Spirit mentioned in this verse. Know that people have stated other opinions besides those previously mentioned:

The first opinion: That what is meant by this Spirit is the Qur'an. They said: this is because Exalted is He named the Qur'an "a spirit" in many verses, and what suits the Spirit being asked about in this place is nothing but the Qur'an. So two positions must be established:

The first position: That Allah's naming the Qur'an "spirit" is indicated by His saying: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you a spirit of Our command﴾ (Ash-Shura: 52), and His saying: ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit of His command﴾ (An-Nahl: 2). Also, the reason for naming the Qur'an "the Spirit" is that by the Qur'an the life of spirits and minds is attained, because by it the knowledge of Allah Exalted, the knowledge of His angels, the knowledge of His books and His messengers is attained, and spirits live only by these cognitions. The complete establishment of this point we have mentioned in the commentary on His saying: ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit of His command﴾ (An-Nahl: 2).

As for the explanation of the second position, namely that the Spirit suitable to this place is the Qur'an: it is because what precedes it is His saying: ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers﴾ (Al-Isra: 82), and what follows it is His saying: ﴿And if We willed, We could surely take away that which We revealed to you﴾ (Al-Isra: 86), up to His saying: ﴿Say, "If mankind and the jinn gathered to produce the like of this Qur'an, they would not produce its like, even if some of them were to others assistants."﴾ (Al-Isra: 88). So since what comes before this verse is a description of the Qur'an, and what comes after it is likewise, it is also necessary that what is meant by this Spirit is the Qur'an, so that all the verses of the Qur'an are coherent and harmonious. This is because the people magnified the matter of the Qur'an and asked whether it was of the kind of poetry or of the kind of soothsaying (kahanah). So Allah Exalted answered them that it is not of the kind of human speech, but rather it is speech that appeared by the command of Allah, His revelation and His sending down. So He said: ﴿Say, "The Spirit is of the command of my Lord,"﴾ meaning the Qur'an appeared by the command of my Lord, and is not of the kind of human speech.

The second opinion: That the Spirit asked about in this verse is an angel from among the angels of the heavens, and he is the greatest of them in rank and power, and this is what is meant by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The day the Spirit and the angels stand in rows﴾ (An-Naba: 38). They related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "He is an angel who has seventy thousand faces, for each face seventy thousand mouths, for each mouth seventy thousand tongues, for each tongue seventy thousand languages; he glorifies Allah Exalted in all those languages, and from each glorification Allah creates an angel who flies with the angels until the Day of Resurrection." They said: "Allah Exalted has not created a creation greater than the Spirit, except the Throne; and if He willed to swallow the seven heavens, the seven earths and whoever is in them with one morsel, He would have done it." It may be said that this opinion is weak, and its explanation is in several aspects:

The first: This detail, since 'Ali knew it, the Prophet is more entitled to have known it, so why did he not inform them of it? Also, revelation did not descend upon 'Ali, so this detail he knew only from the Prophet ﷺ; then why did the Prophet ﷺ give that explanation and clarification to 'Ali and not mention it to others?

The second: If that angel were a single living being and a single rational being, there would be no benefit in multiplying those languages; and if the speaker of each one of those languages were a different living being, then that would not be a single angel but rather a collection of angels.

The third: That this is a thing whose existence is unknown, so how can one be asked about it? As for the Spirit which is the cause of life, it is something which the concern of rational people is strongly directed to know, so directing this question to it is more appropriate.

The fourth opinion, which is the opinion of al-Hasan and Qatadah: That this Spirit is Jibril (Gabriel). The evidence for this is that Exalted is He named Jibril "the Spirit" in His saying: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down, upon your heart﴾ (Ash-Shu'ara: 193-194), and in His saying: ﴿Then We sent to her Our Spirit﴾ (Maryam: 17). This is reinforced by the fact that He said: ﴿Say, "The Spirit is of the command of my Lord"﴾ (concerning Jibril), and He said (quoting) Jibril: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾ (Maryam: 64). So they asked the Messenger how Jibril is in himself and how he carries out the conveyance of revelation to him.

The first part of this passage is in the earlier section, so I begin here.

Fifth opinion: Mujahid said, "The spirit is a creation, not from among the angels, in the form of the children of Adam. They eat, and they have hands, feet and heads." Abu Salih said, "They resemble people but are not people." I have not found in the Qur'an or in authentic reports anything that can be relied upon to establish this opinion. Moreover, this is something unknown, so it is far-fetched to direct this question toward it. The summary of what we have mentioned in explaining the spirit mentioned in this verse is these five opinions, and God knows best what is correct.

Question Three: On explaining the views of people concerning the reality of the human being. Know that there is necessary knowledge that there is something to which a person points by saying "I." When a person says, "I knew, I understood, I saw, I heard, I tasted, I smelled, I touched, I became angry," then the thing indicated for everyone by saying "I" is either a body, or an accident, or a composite of body and accident, or something other than the body and accident, or one of these three. This is a rational division.

As for the first part, namely that one says the human being is a body: that body is either this structure itself, or a body within this structure, or a body outside it. Those who say that the human being is this perceptible structure and this perceptible body are the majority of the theologians (mutakallimun). They say: the human being does not need his definition to be explained by a boundary (hadd) or a description (rasm); rather, it is necessary to say: the human being is the body built with this perceptible structure. Know that this view is false in our opinion, and its formulation is that they said: the human being is this perceptible body. So if we refute that the human being is this body, and refute that the human being is perceptible, then their statement collapses entirely. The things that show that the human being cannot be this body are several:

The first proof: There is necessary knowledge that the parts of this body are changing through addition and subtraction, sometimes according to growth and wasting away, and sometimes according to fatness and thinness. There is necessary knowledge that what changes and varies is different from what remains constant. From the combination of these three premises there arises certain knowledge that the human being is not a composite of this body.

The second proof: When a person is occupied in thought, with his attention directed toward a specific matter, he is in that state unaware of all the parts of his body, of its limbs and components, collectively and individually. Yet in that state he is not unaware of his own specific self, as evidenced by the fact that in that state he may say, "I became angry, I desired, I heard your speech, I saw your face," and the "ta" of the pronoun is an allusion to his self. So in that state he knows his specific self while being unaware of the whole of his body and of each of its limbs and components. The known thing is then not the same as what is unknown. Therefore the human being must be different from the whole of this body and from each of its limbs and components.

The third proof: Everyone's reason judges the attribution of each of these limbs to himself, so he says "my head, my eye, my hand, my foot, my tongue, my heart." The attributed is not the same as that to which it is attributed. It follows that the thing which is the human being must be different from the whole of this body and from each of these limbs. If they say: a person may say "my self" and "my essence," attributing self and essence to himself, then it would follow that the thing and its essence are different from itself, which is impossible. We reply: by this may be meant this specific body, and by the self and essence of a thing may be meant the specific reality to which everyone points by saying "I." So when he says "my self" and "my essence," if what is meant is the body, then in our view it is different from the essence of the human being. As for when what is meant by the self and the specific essence is that which is indicated by saying "I," we do not grant that the human being can attribute that thing to his self by saying "my human being," because the very essence of the human being is his own essence, so how could he attribute it once more to his essence?

The fourth proof: Every proof that the human being cannot be a body also shows that he cannot be this body. The formulation of those proofs will come later.

The fifth proof: The human being may be alive while the body is dead, so the human being must be different from this body. The evidence for the correctness of what we have mentioned is the word of God, exalted is He: ﴿And do not think of those who were killed in the way of God as dead; rather, they are alive, with their Lord, being provided for﴾ (Al 'Imran: 169). This text is explicit that those who were killed are alive, while the senses show that this body is dead.

The sixth proof: The word of God, exalted is He: ﴿The Fire; they are exposed to it morning and evening﴾ (Ghafir: 46), and His word: ﴿They were drowned, then they were made to enter a Fire﴾ (Nuh: 25), show that the human being lives after death. Likewise is the word of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "The prophets of God do not die, but they are transferred from one abode to another." Likewise is his word, peace be upon him: "The grave is either a garden from the gardens of Paradise or a pit from the pits of the Fire." Likewise is his word, peace be upon him: "Whoever dies, his resurrection has already occurred." All these texts show that the human being remains after the death of the body. The immediate judgment of reason and of innate nature both testify that this body is dead. If we allowed that it is alive, then the same would be permissible for all inanimate things, and that is pure sophistry. And when it is established that the human being is a thing, and the body is dead, it follows that the human being is a thing other than this body.

The seventh proof: His word, peace be upon him, in a long sermon: "When the dead person is carried on his bier, his spirit hovers above the bier, and it says: 'O my family and my children, let not this world play with you as it played with me. I gathered wealth from lawful and unlawful sources; the enjoyment of it belongs to others, and the consequence falls upon me. So beware of what has befallen me.'" The point of the argument is that the Prophet, peace be upon him, declared that while the body is being carried on the bier, there remains something that calls out and says: "O my family, O my children, I gathered wealth from lawful and unlawful sources." It is known that the one for whom the family was family, and who gathered wealth from both the unlawful and the lawful, and upon whose neck the burden remained, is none other than that human being. This is an explicit statement that at the time when the body was dead and carried, that human being was alive, remaining and understanding. This is an explicit statement that the human being is a thing other than this body and this frame.

The eighth proof: The word of God, exalted is He: ﴿O soul at rest, return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing﴾ (Al-Fajr: 27-28). The address "return" is directed to it at the time of death. This shows that the thing which returns to God after the death of the body is alive, pleased with God, and God is pleased with it. The one who is pleased is none other than the human being. This shows that the human being remained alive after the death of the body, and the living is other than the dead. So the human being is different from this body.

The ninth proof: The word of God, exalted is He: ﴿Until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him, and they do not fail﴾ (Al-An'am: 61), ﴿Then they are returned to God, their true Master﴾ (Al-An'am: 62). This establishes that they are returned to God, who is their Master, at a time when the body is dead. Therefore that which is returned to God must be different from that dead body.

The tenth proof: We see all the groups of the world, from the Indians, the Romans, the Arabs, the non-Arabs, and all the adherents of religions and sects, among Jews, Christians, Magians, Muslims, and the other groups and communities of the world, giving charity on behalf of their dead, praying for them with good, and going to visit them. Were it not that they remain alive after the death of the body, giving charity on their behalf would be futile, praying for them would be futile, and going to visit them would be futile. The consensus upon this charity, this prayer and this visitation shows that their original, sound innate nature testifies that the human being is a thing other than this body, and that this thing does not die, rather it is this body that dies.

The eleventh proof: Many people see their father or son in a dream after his death, and he tells them: "Go to such-and-such a place, for there is gold there that I buried for you." Sometimes he sees him and instructs him to pay off a debt on his behalf. Then, upon waking, when he searches, things are exactly as he saw them in sleep, without any difference. Were it not that the human being remains after death, this would not be so. Since this proof shows that the human being remains after death, and the senses show that the body is dead, the human being must be different from this dead body.

The twelfth proof: If a person loses one of his limbs, such as if his hands or feet are cut off, or his eyes are gouged out, or his ears are cut off, or any other limb, that person finds in his heart and intellect that he is the very same person, and no difference has occurred in the essence of that person. He even says, "I am that person who existed before this, except that they cut off my hand and my foot." That is a certain proof that this person is a thing different from these limbs and components, and this refutes the view of those who say that the human being is a composite of this specific structure.

The thirteenth proof: The Qur'an and the hadiths indicate that a group of Jews were transformed by God and made into the form of apes and swine. We say: did that human being remain during that transformation (maskh, metamorphosis) or did he not remain? If he did not remain, then this would be the killing of that human being and the creation of that swine, and this is not transformation in any sense. If we say that the human being remained during the occurrence of that transformation, then we say on that assumption: that human being remains, and that structure and that frame do not remain. Therefore that human being must be a thing different from that structure.

The fourteenth proof: The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, used to see Gabriel, peace be upon him, in the form of Dihyah al-Kalbi, and he used to see Iblis in the form of the old man of Najd. Here the structure, frame and shape of a human being are present, while the reality of the human being is not present. This shows that the human being is not this structure and this frame. The difference between this proof and the previous one is that the form of this structure was present without this structure and this frame being present.

The fifteenth proof: An adulterer commits adultery with his genitals, and so he is beaten on his back. Therefore the human being must be a thing other than the genitals and other than the back. It is said that this thing uses the genitals for one action and the back for another action, so the one who experiences pleasure and pain is that thing, except that the pleasure is achieved through that organ, and the pain is felt through the beating upon that organ.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verse 85 (part 3 of 6):**

The sixteenth argument: When I speak with Zayd and say to him, "Do such-and-such," or "Do not do such-and-such," the one addressed by this speech, the one commanded and the one forbidden, is not Zayd's forehead, nor his eyeball, nor his nose, nor his mouth, nor any of his particular limbs. Therefore the one commanded, the one forbidden and the one addressed must be something other than these limbs. This shows that the one commanded and forbidden is other than this body. If they say: Why is it not permissible to say that the one commanded and forbidden is the whole of this body, and not any of its limbs or parts? We reply: Imposing obligation (*taklif*) upon the whole is valid only if the whole is understanding and knowing. So we say: If the whole is understanding and knowing, then either a single knowledge subsists in the entire body, or a separate knowledge subsists in each of the body's parts. The first requires an accident (*'arad*) subsisting in many loci, which is impossible. The second requires that each part of the body be knowing, understanding and perceiving independently. We have already shown that necessary knowledge establishes that a specific part of the body is not knowing, understanding and perceiving independently. Thus this objection falls.

The seventeenth argument: The human being must be knowing, and knowledge occurs only in the heart. It follows that the human being is a reality that exists in the heart. Once this is established, the claim that the human being is this frame and this corpse is refuted. We said that the human being must be knowing because he is a free, choosing agent (*fa'il mukhtar*). The free, choosing agent is one who acts through the heart and choice, and these two are conditioned upon knowledge, because what is not intended cannot be aimed at bringing into being. Thus it is established that the human being must be knowing of things. We said that knowledge exists only in the heart on account of proof and the Qur'an. As for proof, we find by necessary knowledge that our sciences come from the direction of the heart. As for the Qur'an, there are verses such as His saying, ﴿They have hearts with which they do not understand﴾ (al-A'raf 7:179), His saying, ﴿He has written faith in their hearts﴾ (al-Mujadila 58:22), and His saying, ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down upon your heart﴾ (al-Shu'ara 26:193-194). Since it is established that the human being must be knowing, and it is established that knowledge is nothing but in the heart or in something connected to the heart, then on either supposition this refutes the view of whoever says: the human being is this body and this frame.

As for the second investigation, which is the demonstration that the human being is not sensible (*mahsus*): the reality of the human being is something distinct from surface, colour, and everything that is visible. It is either surface or colour, and both are two definite premises. This syllogism yields that the reality of the human being is neither visible nor sensible, and this is a certain demonstration.

**The fourth question:** Concerning the explanation of the doctrines of those who hold that the human being is a body existing within the body. Know that the bodies existing in this lower world are either one of the four elements (*'anasir*) or what is generated from their mixture. It is impossible that a pure elemental body should arise in the human body; rather, what arises must necessarily be a body generated from the mixtures of these four. [Page 37] So we say: As for the body in which earthiness predominates, it is the solid, dense organs, such as bone, cartilage, nerve, sinew, ligament, fat, flesh and skin. None of the intelligent people who said that the human being is something distinct from this body has said that it is a particular organ among these organs, because these organs are dense, heavy and dark. Therefore none of the intelligent has said that the human being is one of these organs. As for the body in which wateriness predominates, it is the four humours, and none has said of any of them that it is the human being, except for blood. Some of them said that it is the spirit, on the evidence that when it leaves, death follows. As for the body in which airiness and fieriness predominate, it is the spirits, and these are of two kinds:

The first: bodies of air mixed with innate heat, generated either in the heart or in the brain. They said these are the spirit and that they are the human being. Then they differed. Some say the human being is the spirit that is in the heart. Others say it is an indivisible part in the brain. Others say the spirit is a composite of fiery parts mixed with these heart-spirits and brain-spirits, and those fiery parts, which are called innate heat, are the human being. Some people say the spirit is a composite of luminous, heavenly, subtle bodies, and the substance is of the nature of sunlight. These do not accept dissolution, change, separation or tearing apart. When the body is formed and its preparedness is complete, which is what is meant by His saying, ﴿When I have fashioned him﴾ (al-Hijr 15:29), those noble, heavenly, divine bodies penetrate into the interior of the body's organs, like the penetration of fire into charcoal, the penetration of sesame oil into sesame, and the penetration of rose-water into the substance of a rose. The penetration of those heavenly bodies into the substance of the body is what is meant by His saying, ﴿And I breathed into him of My spirit﴾ (al-Hijr 15:29). Then, as long as the body remains sound and receptive to the penetration of those noble bodies, it remains alive. When thick humours are generated in the body, those thick humours prevent those noble bodies from flowing through it, so they separate from this body, and then death occurs. This is a strong and noble doctrine that must be reflected upon, for it is highly consistent with what has been reported in the divine books concerning the states of life and death. This is the detailed account of the doctrines of those who hold that the human being is a body existing within the body. As for the view that the human being is a body existing outside the body, I know of no one who has held this position.

As for the second division, which is to say that the human being is an accident (*'arad*) inhering in the body: no intelligent person says this, because it is known by necessity that the human being is a substance (*jawhar*), since he is characterized by knowledge, power, management and disposal. Whoever is like this is a substance, and a substance is not an accident. Rather, what every intelligent person can affirm is that the human being requires being characterized by particular accidents. On this supposition, people have several views:

The first view: When the four elements are mixed and the force of each is broken by the force of the other, a balanced quality arises which is temperament (*mizaj*). The degrees of this temperament are unlimited, so some of them are humanness and some are horseness. Humanness is an expression for characterized bodies generated from the mixtures of the parts of the elements in a specific measure. This is the view of the majority of physicians, those who deny the survival of the soul, and the view of Abu al-Husayn al-Basri of the Mu'tazila.

The second view: The human being is an expression for specific bodies on condition that they are characterized by the attribute of life, knowledge and power, and life is an accident subsisting in the body. These people denied the spirit and the soul and said there is nothing here but composite bodies characterized by these particular accidents, namely life, knowledge and power. This is the doctrine of most of the Mu'tazili shaykhs.

The third view: The human being is an expression for bodies characterized by life, knowledge and power. The human being is distinguished from the other animals only by the shape of his body and the configuration of his limbs and parts. However, this is problematic, for the angels sometimes take on the forms of people. Here the form of the human being exists without humanness, and in the case of transformation (*maskh*) the meaning of humanness exists while this form does not exist. Thus the consideration of this shape in the realization of the meaning of humanness has been refuted, both by inclusion and by exclusion.

(As for the third division): which is to say that the human being is an existent that is neither a body nor corporeal. This is the view of most of the divine philosophers (*ilahiyyun min al-falasifa*) who affirm the survival of the soul, who establish for the soul a spiritual return (*ma'ad ruhani*), spiritual reward and punishment, and spiritual reckoning. It was held by a great group of Muslim scholars, such as Shaykh Abu al-Qasim al-Raghib al-Isfahani and Shaykh Abu Hamid al-Ghazali, may God have mercy on both of them. Among the early Mu'tazila was Ma'mar ibn 'Abbad al-Sulami. Among the Shi'a is the one they honour as Shaykh al-Mufid. Among the Karramiyya there is a group. Know that those who affirm the soul are of two groups:

The first: They are the verifiers (*muhaqqiqun*). Some of them say: The human being is an expression for this particular substance and this body. On this supposition, the human being is neither existing within the world nor outside it, neither connected to the world nor separate from it. Rather, he is related to the body by the relation of management and disposal, just as the Lord of the world has no relation to the world except in the manner of disposal and management.

The second group: those who said: When the soul is attached to the body it unites with the body, so the soul becomes the very body and the body becomes the very soul, and the whole of the two together at the time of union is the human being. When the time of death comes, this union is dissolved, the soul remains, and the body decays. This is the sum of the views of people concerning the human being. Thabit ibn Qurra used to affirm the soul and said that it is attached to heavenly, luminous, subtle bodies, not liable to coming into being, corruption, separation or tearing apart, and that these bodies flow through the body. As long as that flowing continues, the soul remains managing the body. When those subtle bodies separate from the substance of the body, the soul's attachment to the body ceases.

**The fifth question:** Concerning the proofs of those who affirm the soul from the side of reason. The people argued with many arguments, some strong and some weak. The strong arguments are partly certain (*qat'iyya*) and partly persuasive (*iqna'iyya*). Let us mention the certain arguments.

The first argument: Without doubt, the human being is a substance. It is either a substance that occupies space (*mutahayyiz*) or one that does not. The first is false, so the second is established. What shows that it is impossible for the human being to be a substance occupying space is that if it were so, then its occupying space would be other than that essence. And if that were so, then everything of which a person knows his particular essence would necessarily be something of which he knows its occupying space with a particular measure. But this is not the case. Therefore the human being must not be a substance occupying space. In establishing this proof we need three premises:

The first premise: If the human being were a substance occupying space, then its occupying space would be identical with its particular essence. The evidence for this is that if its spatial occupation were an attribute subsisting in it, then that locus, considered in itself apart from this attribute, would either be occupying space or not be occupying space. Both of these alternatives are false. Therefore the view that spatial occupation is an attribute subsisting in the locus is refuted. We said that it is impossible that it be the locus of spatial occupation, because this would entail that one and the same thing occupies space twice, and because it would entail the joining of two like things. Also, there is no preference in making one of the two the essence and the other the attribute over the reverse. Also, if the second spatial occupation is the essence, then it is what is intended; and if it is an attribute, it entails an infinite regress, which is impossible. We said that it is impossible for the locus of spatial occupation to be something not occupying space, because the reality of spatial occupation is proceeding in directions and extending in them, and a thing that does not occupy space does not have any relation to directions, and its being present in them is not occupying space, which is impossible. Thus it is established by this that if the human being were a substance occupying space, then its spatial occupation would be other than its particular essence.

**Second premise:** If the specific essence's being spatially located were identical to its specific essence, then whenever a person knows his specific essence, he would know that it is spatially located. The proof is that if his specific essence became known while its spatial location remained unknown, the affirmation and negation would be combined in one thing, and that is impossible.

**Third premise:** We know our own essences while being ignorant of spatial location and of extension in the three dimensions. This is evident upon testing and examination. A person, while occupied with some important matter, may say to his servant: "Why did you do such-and-such? Why did you disobey my command? I will severely discipline and beat you." When he says, "Why did you disobey my command?", he knows his own specific essence. For if he did not know his specific essence, he could not know that this person had disobeyed him, nor could he tell others about himself that he was resolved to discipline and beat him. In this state, he knows his specific essence, even though at that moment the reality of spatial location, extension in dimensions, and occupying a place does not occur to his mind. From what we have mentioned, it is established that if the human essence were a spatially extended substance (*jawhar*), then its spatial location would be identical with its specific essence. And if that were so, then whatever its specific essence is known, its spatial location would be known. But it has been established that this is not so. Therefore it follows that the human essence is not a spatially extended substance, and that is what was to be proven.

If they object that this is countered by the argument that if it were an immaterial substance, then everyone who knows his own essence would know that it is an immaterial substance, and that is not the case, we reply: the difference is clear. Its being immaterial means that it is not spatially located and does not inhere in something spatially located. This negation is not identical with that specific essence, because negation is not identical with affirmation. Given this, it is not unlikely that the specific essence is known while that negation is not known. This contrasts with its being spatially located. We have shown that, on the supposition that the human is a spatially extended substance, its spatial location would be identical with its specific essence. On this supposition, it is impossible that its essence be known while its spatial location remains unknown. Thus the difference is manifest.

**The second argument:** The soul is one, and whenever it is one, it must be distinct from this body and from each of its parts. This argument is built on premises:

**The first premise** is our statement "the soul is one." Here we have two positions: sometimes we claim that knowledge of it is self-evident, and sometimes we establish a proof for its soundness.

As for the first position, the claim of self-evidence: we say that what is meant by "soul" is the thing that each person indicates by his saying "I." And every person knows necessarily that when he points to his specific essence by saying "I," that indicated thing is one, not multiple. If it is objected, "Why could it not be that what is indicated by each person's 'I' is one, yet that one is composed of many things?" we reply: we have no need in this position to answer this objection. Rather, we say that what is indicated by the word "I" is known necessarily to be one thing. As for whether that one is a unity composed of many things, or is one in itself and one in its reality, this is not needed in this position.

As for the second position, the position of inference: What indicates the unity of the soul are several considerations.

**The first argument:** Anger is a psychic state that arises when the intent is to repel what is repugnant, and appetite is a psychic state that arises when seeking what is agreeable, conditioned upon awareness that a thing is agreeable or repugnant. So the irascible faculty, which is the power that repels what is repugnant, if it had no awareness that a thing is repugnant, would be incapable of being moved to repel that repugnant thing deliberately and by choice. For the intention to attract at one time, or to repel at another, is conditioned upon awareness of the thing. Thus a thing described as repelling what is repugnant by choice must necessarily have awareness that it is repugnant. Therefore, whoever becomes angry must necessarily be the very same one who perceives. By this decisive proof, a distinction is established that obtains among distinct essences.

**The second argument:** Suppose we posit two independent substances, each of which is independent in its own specific act. It is impossible that one's occupation with its specific act should prevent the other from occupying itself with its own specific act. Given this, we say: if the locus of perception and thought were one substance, the locus of anger a second substance, and the locus of appetite a third substance, then the occupation of the irascible faculty with its act would not prevent the appetitive faculty from occupying itself with its act, nor vice versa. But the latter is false. For a person's occupation with appetite and his being absorbed in it prevent him from occupying himself with anger and being absorbed in it, and vice versa. So we know that these three matters are not independent principles, but rather are different attributes of one substance. Therefore, the occupation of that substance with one of these acts necessarily hinders it from occupying itself with another act.

**The third argument:** When we perceive things, perception may be the cause of appetite arising, and it may become the cause of anger arising. If the perceived substance were distinct from that which becomes angry and that which desires, then when the perceiving substance perceives the perceived substance, no effect or trace of that perception would occur in the desiring substance. So it would be necessary that neither the arising of appetite nor the arising of anger follow from that perception. But since this sequence and necessary connection do occur, we know that the bearer of perception is identically the bearer of appetite, and identically the bearer of anger.

**The fourth argument:** The reality of the animal is that it is a body with a sensitive soul that moves by will. The soul cannot move by will except when a motive is present, and a motive means nothing but awareness of a good that one desires to attract, or of an evil that one desires to repel. This requires that the thing moving by will be the very same thing that perceives the good and evil, the pleasant and painful, the beneficial and harmful. By what we have mentioned, it is established that the human soul is one thing. And it is established that this thing is the one that sees, hears, smells, tastes, touches, imagines, thinks, remembers, desires, and becomes angry. It is the one described by all perceptions, and the one described by all voluntary acts and volitional movements.

**As for the second premise:** It explains that, since the soul is one thing, the soul must not be in this body, nor be any part of it. The explanation is as follows. As for demonstrating that, when this is the case, it is impossible for the soul to be the whole of this body, and likewise for the faculty of hearing, and likewise all the other faculties such as imagination, remembrance, and thought, then knowing that these faculties do not pervade all the parts of the body is a self-evident knowledge. Indeed, it is among the strongest self-evident truths. As for demonstrating that the soul cannot be a part of this body: we know necessarily that there is no single part of the body that is at once described as seeing, hearing, thinking, and remembering. Rather, what occurs to the mind is that seeing is specific to the eye and not to the other organs, hearing is specific to the ear and not to the other organs, speech is specific to the throat and not to the other organs, and the same holds for all the other perceptions and all the other acts. As for saying that there arose in the body one part described by all these perceptions and all these acts, the necessary knowledge is that the matter is not so. Thus, by what we have mentioned, it is established that the human soul is one thing, described by the entirety of these perceptions and the entirety of these acts. And it is established by self-evidence that the whole body is not so, and it is also established that no part of the body is so. Then certainty arises that the soul is a thing distinct from this body and from each of its parts, and that is what was to be proven.

Let us state this proof in another formulation. We say: we know necessarily that when we see something, we know it; when we know it, we desire it; and when we desire it, we move our bodies toward it. Therefore it is necessary to affirm with certainty that the one who saw is the one who knew, that the one who knew is the one who desired, and that the one who desired is the one who moved toward it. It follows that the one seeing that thing, the one knowing it, the one desiring it, and the one moving toward it are one thing. For if the seer were one thing, the knower a second thing, the desirer a third thing, and the mover a fourth thing, then the one who saw would not have known, the one who knew would not have desired, and the one who desired would not have moved. And it is known that the fact that a thing sees another thing does not entail that another thing becomes aware of that thing. The same applies to all the other stages.

Also, we know necessarily that the one who sees visible things, when he has seen them, has known them; when he has known them, he has desired them; and when he has desired them, he has sought them and moved the limbs toward them. We also know necessarily that the one described by this seeing, this knowing, this desire, and this motion is none other than him. Furthermore, the rational have said: the animal must be sensitive and move by will. For if it does not perceive anything, it does not become aware that something is agreeable or repugnant, and if it is not aware of that, it is impossible for it to will to attract or repel. Thus it is established that the thing that moves by will must necessarily be sensitive. It is established that whatever perceives all perceived objects perceives by all kinds of perception, and that the one who directly performs all voluntary movements is one thing.

Also, when we speak a speech intending to make another understand, we (comprehend) the meanings of those words. Then, when we have comprehended them, we wish to make others understand those meanings. When this will arises in our hearts, we try to bring those letters and sounds into existence, so as to use them to make others understand those meanings. Given that this is established, we say: if the locus of knowledge and will and the locus of those letters and sounds were a single body, it would follow that the locus of knowledge and wills is the throat, the uvula, and the tongue. But it is known that this is not so. If we say the locus of knowledge and wills is the heart, it would also follow that the locus of sound is the heart, and that is also necessarily false. If we say the locus of speech is the throat, the uvula, and the tongue, while the locus of knowledge and wills is the heart, and the locus of power is the nerves, tendons, and muscles, then we would have distributed these matters among these different organs. But we have refuted that, and shown that the one who perceives all perceived objects and moves all the organs in every kind of movement must be one single thing. So nothing remains except to say that, regarding perception and the capacity for moving, [it is] something other than this body and other than the parts of this body, and that these organs function as instruments and tools. Just as a person performs various acts through various instruments, so the soul sees through the eye, hears through the ear, thinks through the brain, and understands through the heart. These organs are the instruments and tools of the soul. The soul is a substance distinct from them, separate from them in essence, and connected to them in the manner of management and direction. This proof is a noble and certain proof for establishing this matter. And God knows best.

[p. 42]

The third premise: If the human being were this body, then either each of its parts would have life, knowledge and power separately, or the totality of its parts would have life, knowledge and power. Both divisions are false, so the claim that the human being is this body is false. As for the falsity of the first division, it requires that each part of the body be a living, knowing, powerful being independently. Then the one human would not be one living being but many living, knowing, powerful beings. In that case there would be no difference between one human being and many persons linked together in a chain. But we know by necessity that this account is false, because I find my self to be one self, not many living beings. Furthermore, if each part of this body were a separate living being, then none of them would have knowledge of the state of its companion. Nothing would prevent one part from wanting to move in this direction while another part wants to move in the opposite direction. Then conflict would occur among the parts of one human body, just as it occurs between two persons. The corruption of this is known immediately. As for the falsity of the second division, it requires that one attribute subsist in many loci, and that is known to be false by necessity. Also, if it were permissible for one attribute to inhere in many loci, it would not be far-fetched for one body to occupy many spaces. Also, if one attribute were to exist in multiple loci, then each of those parts would be a living, knowing being, and the matter would reduce to one corpse being many people. Since the corruption of both divisions has become clear, it is established that the human being is not this corpse.

If they say: Why is it not permissible that one life subsist in one part, and that this life then requires all the parts to become living? We reply: This is false, because life has no meaning except being alive, and knowledge has no meaning except being knowing. Even if we grant that life is a meaning that necessitates being alive, and knowledge is a meaning that necessitates being knowing, we still say: If in the totality of a corpse there occurs one life and one state of knowing, then one attribute has occurred in many loci, which is impossible. And if in each part and in the corpse there occurs a separate life and a separate state of knowing, then we return to what we mentioned, that one human being becomes many humans, which is impossible.

The fourth premise: When we reflected upon the states of the soul, we found its states to be the opposite of the states of the body. This indicates that the soul is not a body. The demonstration of this incompatibility is in several aspects:

The first: Every body in which one form has come to be does not accept another form of the same kind as the first form except after the complete removal of the first form. For example, when the shape of a triangle has come to exist in wax, it is impossible for the shape of a square or a circle to come to exist in it except after the first shape has been removed from it. Yes, we find that the situation regarding the soul's apprehension of intelligible forms is the opposite of this. The soul that has not accepted any intelligible form at all finds it easy to accept some intelligible forms. When it accepts one form, its acceptance of the second form becomes easier. Then the soul continually accepts one form after another without ever becoming weaker. Rather, the more it accepts forms, the easier and quicker its acceptance of the forms that come afterward becomes. For this reason, a human becomes more understanding and more perceptive the more he becomes trained and connected in the sciences. Thus it is established that the soul's acceptance of intelligible forms is contrary to the body's acceptance of form, and this suggests that the soul is not a body.

The second: Constant engagement in subtle thoughts has an effect on the soul and an effect on the body. As for its effect on the soul, it brings the soul from potentiality to actuality in intellections and perceptions. The more the thoughts, the more complete these states become, and that is the ultimate of its perfection and the summit of its nobility and majesty. As for its effect on the body, it causes dryness to dominate the body and wilting to overtake it. If this state persisted, it would lead to melancholia and to the approach of death. Thus it is established from what we have mentioned that these thoughts cause the life and nobility of the soul, and cause the body's deficiency and death. So if the soul were the body, one thing would be the cause of its perfection and its deficiency at once, and of its life and its death at once, and that is impossible.

The third: We observe that sometimes a person's body is weak and emaciated, but when a light of the holy lights shines upon him, and a secret of the secrets of the unseen world is revealed to him, that person acquires great boldness and strong authority. He does not care about the presence of the greatest sultans and gives them no weight. Had the soul not been something other than the body, the matter would not be this way.

The fourth: Practitioners of spiritual exercises (riyada) and struggle (mujahada), the more they overpower the bodily powers and starve the body, the stronger their spiritual powers become, and their secrets are illuminated with divine knowledge. And the more a person indulges in eating, drinking and fulfilling bodily desires, the more he becomes like an animal and remains deprived of the traces of speech, intellect and knowledge. Had the soul not been other than the body, the matter would not be this way.

The fifth: We see that the soul performs its actions through bodily instruments. It sees through the eye, hears through the ear, grasps through the hand, and walks through the foot. But when the matter reaches intellection and comprehension, the soul is independent in itself in this act without the assistance of any of the instruments. For this reason, a person cannot see anything if he closes his eyes, nor hear any sound if he blocks his ears, just as he absolutely cannot remove from his heart the knowledge of what he already knows. So we know that the soul is self-sufficient in its own right in sciences and knowledge, independent of any bodily instruments. These five aspects are strong signs that the soul

[p. 43]

is not a body. Regarding the first issue, many of the arguments of the earlier thinkers are present, which we mentioned in our philosophical books, so there is no benefit in repeating them.

* * *

The sixth issue: Establishing, by the revealed evidences, that the soul is not a body.

The first proof: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not be like those who forgot Allah, so He made them forget themselves﴾ (Al-Hashr: 19). It is known that none of the rational beings forgets this visible frame. This indicates that the soul which a person forgets at the extreme of ignorance is something other than this body.

The second proof: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Bring out your souls﴾ (Al-An'am: 93). This is explicit that the soul is other than the body. We have exhausted the explanation of this verse, so let the reader refer to it.

The third proof: He, exalted is He, mentioned the stages of bodily creation, saying: ﴿And We created man from an extract of clay﴾ ﴿Then We placed him as a drop in a secure lodging﴾ (Al-Mu'minun: 12), up to His saying: ﴿Then We clothed the bones with flesh﴾ (Al-Mu'minun: 14). There is no doubt that all these stages are variations occurring in bodily states. Then, when He, exalted is He, wished to mention the breathing of the spirit, He said: ﴿Then We produced him as another creation﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 14]. This is an explicit statement that what relates to the spirit is a genus different from what was previously mentioned of the changes occurring in bodily states. This indicates that the spirit is something other than the body. If they say: This verse is a proof against you, because He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We created man from an extract of clay﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 12], and the word "min" (from) denotes partitiveness, and this indicates that man is a part of the parts of clay. We reply: The word "min" originally denotes the starting point, like your saying: "I went out from Basra to Kufa." So His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We created man from an extract of clay﴾ requires that the beginning of the creation of man be from this extract. We say in accordance with its meaning, because He, exalted is He, first balances the temperament, then breathes the spirit into it, so the beginning of its creation is from the extract.

The fourth proof: His saying: ﴿So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit﴾ (Al-Hijr: 29). He, exalted is He, distinguished between human formation and the breathing of the spirit. Proportioning refers to the creation of the parts and limbs and the balancing of the temperament and forms. Then, when He distinguished the breathing of the spirit from the proportioning of the limbs, and then attributed the spirit to Himself by saying ﴿of My spirit﴾, this indicates that the essence of the spirit is a meaning different from the essence of the body.

The fifth proof: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And a soul and He who proportioned it﴾ ﴿And inspired it [with an understanding of] its wickedness and its righteousness﴾ (Ash-Shams: 7-8). This verse is explicit about the existence of something characterized by perception and motion in truth, because inspiration (ilham) is an expression for perception, while wickedness and righteousness are acts. This verse is explicit that the human being is one thing, and it is also characterized by perception and motion, and also characterized by the act of wickedness at one time and the act of righteousness at another time. It is known that the totality of the body is not characterized by these two attributes, so there must be the establishment of another essence that is characterized by all these matters.

The sixth proof: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We created man from a drop of mingled fluid that We may try him, and We made him hearing and seeing﴾ (Al-Insan: 2). This is an explicit statement that the human being is one thing, and that thing is the one tested by divine obligations and lordly matters, and it is the one characterized by hearing and sight. The totality of the body is not like this, nor is any single organ of the body like this. So the soul is a thing different from the totality of the body and different from its parts, and it is characterized by all these attributes. Know that the reports

[p. 44]

describing the spirits before their attachment to bodies and after their separation from bodies are numerous, and all of them indicate that the soul is a thing other than this body. It is astonishing that someone reads these many verses and narrates these many reports, and then says: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) died and did not know the spirit. This is among the wonders. And Allah knows best.

* * *

The seventh issue: On the indication of the verse we are explaining for the correctness of what we have mentioned, that if the spirit were a body moving from one state to another and from one attribute to another, it would be equal to the body in being produced from bodies that had become characterized by specific attributes after having been characterized by other attributes. Then, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about the spirit, he would have had to explain that it was a body that was thus and then became thus, until it became a spirit, similar to what was mentioned about how the body is produced: that it was a drop, then a clot, then a lump of flesh. But since he did not say that, but said: ﴿Say, "The spirit is of the affair of my Lord"﴾ [Al-Isra: 85], meaning that it does not come into being or enter existence except because Allah, exalted is He, said to it: ﴿"Be," and it is﴾ (An-Nahl: 40), this indicates that it is a substance that is not of the genus of bodies, but rather a holy, abstract substance. Know that most of the knowers who have unveiling (mukashafa) and the people of spiritual exercises (riyada) and of unveilings and direct witnessing are firm upon this view and certain of this doctrine. Al-Wasiti said: Allah created the spirits from between beauty and splendor, and had He not veiled them, every disbeliever would prostrate to them. As for the explanation that its first attachment is to the heart, and then through it its influence reaches all the limbs, we have explained that in the commentary on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down upon your heart that you may be of the warners﴾ (Ash-Shu'ara: 193-194).

The deniers have argued with several points:

The first: If the spirit were equal to the essence of Allah in not being a body nor an accident, it would be equal to Him in complete quiddity (mahiyya), and that is impossible.

Third point: His saying, "Think not of those who have been killed in the way of Allah as dead. Nay, they are alive, with their Lord, being provided for" (Ali 'Imran: 169), up to His saying, "rejoicing" (Ali 'Imran: 170). This indicates that the soul is a body, because provision and rejoicing are attributes of bodies.

Second point: His saying, "Woe to man! How ungrateful is he! From what thing did He create him? From a drop of sperm He created him and determined him. Then He made the way easy for him. Then He causes him to die and buries him. Then, when He wills, He will resurrect him" ('Abasa: 17-22). This is an explicit statement that man is a created thing from a drop of sperm, that he dies and enters the grave, and then Allah brings him out of the grave. Had man not been this body, the states mentioned in this verse would not be valid.

The answer to the first: equality in not being spatially located (mutahayyiz) and not being an accident inhering in something spatially located is an equality in a negative attribute, and equality in a negative attribute does not necessitate similarity. Know that a group of the ignorant think that since the soul is an existent that is neither spatially located nor inhering in what is spatially located, it must be a likeness of God or a part of God. This is gross ignorance and an ugly error. Its verification is what we have mentioned: that if equality in negations necessitated similarity, it would necessitate the claim that all disparate things are equal, and that any two distinct quiddities must share in negating everything other than themselves. So let this subtle point be known, for it is a great fallacy for the ignorant.

The answer to the second: since man, in common usage and outward appearance, is a designation for this body, the name "man" is applied to it in common usage.

The answer to the third: the provision mentioned in the verse is understood as that which strengthens their state and perfects their perfection, which is knowledge of Allah and love for Him. Indeed, we say this is among the strongest proofs for the validity of our position, because their bodies have decayed under the dust, and Allah, exalted is He, says that their souls dwell in lamps suspended beneath the Throne, and this indicates that the soul is other than the body. Let this be the last of our words on this subject, and let us return to the science of exegesis. Then He, exalted is He, said: "And you have been given of knowledge only a little" (al-Isra': 85). On our view, we have mentioned two possibilities regarding it. As for the exegetes, they said: when the Prophet ﷺ said this to them, they said: "Are we specifically addressed by this address, or are you with us?" He, peace be upon him, said: "Rather, we and you have not been given of knowledge except a little." They said: "How wondrous is your affair, O Muhammad, one moment you say: 'And whoever is given wisdom has been given much good' (al-Baqarah: 269), and another moment you say this." Then the verse was revealed: "And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens..." (Luqman: 27), up to its end. What they mentioned is not necessary, because a thing may be little in relation to one thing and much in relation to another. The knowledge possessed by people is very little in relation to the knowledge of Allah and in relation to the realities of things, but it is much in relation to bodily desires and carnal pleasures.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verses 86–87:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if We willed, We would surely take away what We have revealed to you, then you would not find for yourself any guardian against Us in respect of it. But (it is) a mercy from your Lord. Indeed His bounty toward you has been great.﴾ In this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that when He, exalted is He, explained in the previous verse that He had not given them ﴿of knowledge except a little﴾, He explained in this verse that if He willed to take away from them even that little, He would be able to do so, by erasing its memorization from hearts and its writing from books. Although this is an matter contrary to custom, He, exalted is He, is capable of it.

The second issue: al-Ka'bi (al-Ka'bi, a Mu'tazili theologian) argued from this verse that the Qur'an is created. He said: whatever can be removed and taken away is impossible to be eternal; rather it must be originated. But this argument is weak, because what is meant by this taking away is the removal of knowledge of it from hearts and the removal of the inscriptions indicating it from the codex (mushaf). That does not necessitate that the known, signified thing itself is originated. As for His saying: ﴿then you would not find for yourself any guardian against Us in respect of it﴾, meaning you would not find anyone on whom you could rely to restore any part of it. Then He said: ﴿But (it is) a mercy from your Lord﴾, meaning, except that your Lord has mercy on you and returns it to you. Or it may be an exception of the disjunctive kind, meaning: but the mercy of your Lord has left it not taken away. This is a favor from God by the preservation of the Qur'an. Moreover, He, exalted is He, bestowed upon all scholars two kinds of favor:

The first: facilitating that knowledge for them.

The second: keeping its memorization preserved for them.

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed His bounty toward you has been great﴾, there are two opinions concerning it:

The first: the meaning is that His bounty toward you has been great by reason of preserving knowledge and the Qur'an for you.

The second: the meaning is that His bounty toward you has been great by reason of His making you the master of the sons of Adam, sealing the prophets with you, and granting you the Praised Station. Since this is so, He surely also bestowed upon you the favor of preserving knowledge and the Qur'an for you.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verse 88:**

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Say: If mankind and the jinn were to gather together to produce the like of this Qur'an, they would not produce its like, even if they were to help one another.﴾ There are several issues concerning the verse.

**The first issue:** Know that in Surat al-Baqarah, in commenting on His words, exalted is He: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant, then produce a surah like it﴾ (2:23), we explained at length the inimitability (i'jaz) of the Qur'an. People have two views on it. Some say the Qur'an is inimitable in itself. Others say it is not inimitable in itself, but that when God diverted their motives from attempting to match it, although those motives were strong, this diversion (al-sarfah) became the miracle. The position we choose in this matter is that we say: the Qur'an in itself is either inimitable or it is not. If it is inimitable, then the goal is achieved. If it is not inimitable, but they were capable of producing a counterpart to it, their motives were strongly directed toward producing this counterpart, and nothing turned them away or prevented them, then under this assumption producing a counterpart would have been obligatory and necessary. Therefore, their failure to produce this counterpart, given the aforementioned assumptions, would constitute a breach of the normal course of things, and so it would be a miracle. This is the method we choose in this matter.

**The second issue:** One may say: Suppose it has become clear that humans are unable to match it. How do you know that the jinn are unable to match it? Also, why is it not possible to say that this speech is the composition of the jinn, who threw it at Muhammad (ﷺ) and devoted it to him as a means of striving to mislead people? On this view, you only know the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ) when you know that Muhammad (ﷺ) is truthful in his claim that it is not the speech of the jinn but is in fact the speech of God, exalted is He. Then a circular argument arises. And no one may say: How can it be conceived that this is the speech of the jinn? For we say: this verse indicates that the challenge was addressed to the jinn as well, and such a challenge is appropriate only if they were eloquent and skilled in speech. And once this is the case, the aforementioned possibility remains.

The scholars answered the first point: the inability of humans to match it is sufficient to establish that it is a miracle.

As for the second point: if that had occurred, then by God's wisdom it would have been necessary for Him to reveal that deception. Since it was not revealed, this indicates that it did not occur. And God, exalted is He, has already answered this question with sufficient and conclusive answers at the end of Surat al-Shu'ara', in His words: ﴿Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend? They descend upon every lying sinner﴾ (26:221–222). We have explained these answers there, so there is no benefit in repeating them.

**The third issue:** The Mu'tazilah (the Mu'tazilites) said: the verse indicates that the Qur'an is created, because the challenge is made with the eternal (al-qadim), and this issue we have also discussed in full detail in Surat al-Baqarah, so there is no benefit in repeating it.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We have certainly diversified for the people in this Qur'an from every example﴾

This statement admits of several interpretations:

The first: The challenge (al-tahaddi) was issued with the entire Qur'an, as in this verse. The challenge was also issued with ten surahs of it, as in His saying: ﴿Then bring ten surahs like it, fabricated﴾ (Hud: 13). And the challenge was issued with a single surah, as in His saying: ﴿Then bring a surah like it﴾ (al-Baqarah: 23). And the challenge was issued with a passage (kalam) from a single surah, as in His saying: ﴿Then let them bring a statement like it﴾ (al-Tur: 34). So His saying: ﴿And We have certainly diversified for the people in this Qur'an from every example﴾ may mean the challenge, as we have explained. Then, despite the clear evidence of their inability at all these levels, they persisted in their disbelief.

The second: What is meant by His saying: ﴿And We have certainly diversified for the people in this Qur'an from every example﴾ is that We informed them that those who persisted in disbelief, like the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud, how He afflicted them with various kinds of trials. We have explained this method repeatedly and in various ways. Yet these peoples—meaning the people of Makkah—did not benefit from this explanation, but persisted in disbelief.

Then these disbelievers did not benefit from hearing them, but persisted in polytheism and denial of prophethood.

﴿But most of the people refused except disbelief﴾

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿But most of the people refused except disbelief﴾. "Refused" (abā) means most of the people of Makkah. ﴿Except disbelief﴾, i.e., denial of the truth, because they rejected what did not need to be made manifest. If it is asked: how is ﴿But most of the people refused except disbelief﴾ permissible, when it is not permissible to say "I struck except Zayd"? We reply: the verb abā (refused) carries the sense of negation, as if it were said: "they were not pleased except with disbelief."

The first of them is their saying: ﴿until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth﴾. Whoever reads with shaddah intends the abundance of flowing from the spring, and although it is singular, because of the abundance of gushing from it, it is appropriate to read it with shaddah, just as you say "daraba Zayd" when the striking from him is frequent, so that his action becomes intensified even though the agent is one. The first: 'Ikrimah said: as you claimed, O Muhammad, that you are a prophet, then cause the sky to fall upon us.

The second: others said: as you claimed that your Lord, if He wills, does so.

The third: it is possible that what is meant is what God, exalted is He, mentioned in this surah in His saying: ﴿Do you feel secure that He will not cause the earth to swallow you on the side of the land, or send against you a sandstorm?﴾ (al-Isra': 68).
