The sixth: their saying: ﴿or you ascend into the sky﴾. Al-Farra' said: it is said raqaytu, and I ascend ruqan and ruqiyyan, and he recited:

"You are the one who burdened me with the ruqa of the stairway, with weariness, grey hair and limping."

His saying fi al-sama' means: in the ascents of the sky, so the modifier is omitted; it is said raqa al-muslim and ruqiya al-darajah. Then they said: ﴿and we will not believe in your ascent (liruqiyyika)﴾, that is, we will not believe for the sake of your ascent, ﴿until you send down to us a book that we may read﴾, in which there is confirmation of you. 'Abd Allah ibn Umayyah said: ﴿and we will not believe﴾ until you place a ladder against the sky and climb it while I look on, until you reach it, then come to us with you bringing an open document with four angels with it who testify for you that the matter is as you say. When God, exalted is He, related the disbelievers' proposal of these miracles, He said to Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿Say: Glory be to my Lord! Am I anything but a human messenger?﴾ and there are discussions regarding this:

The first discussion: He, exalted is He, related from the disbelievers' speech their saying: ﴿We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Say: Glory be to my Lord﴾. All of this is the people's speech, and we do not find any difference in the arrangement of those words from the rest of the verses of the Qur'an. Thus the disbelievers' statement is shown to be valid: "If we willed, we would say the like of this." The answer: this Qur'an is short, and there does not appear in it a difference between levels of eloquence and rhetoric, so this objection is removed.

The second discussion: these verses are among the strongest proofs that coming and going are impossible for God, because the word subhan is for declaring Him free from what is unfitting. His saying subhana rabbi is a declaration of God, exalted is He, free from anything unbefitting Him, or attributed to Him from what was previously mentioned. And there is nothing in what was previously mentioned that is unbefitting God except their saying: "or you bring God." This indicates that His saying: ﴿Glory be to my Lord﴾ is a declaration of God's freedom from coming and going, and that indicates the corruption of the view of the anthropomorphists (mushabbihah) that God comes and goes. If they say: why is it not permissible that what is meant is to declare God free from being subjected to the dictates of those who dictate proposals of things? We say: the people did not dictate to God; they only said to the Messenger (ﷺ): if you are a truthful prophet, ask God to honor you with these miracles. So the people dictated to the Messenger, and did not dictate to God. Therefore it is not appropriate to take His saying "Glory be to my Lord" in this sense, and it is necessary to take it in reference to their saying "or you bring God."

The third discussion: the explanation of this answer is that it may be said: either what you intend by this proposal is that you demanded that I bring these things from myself, or that you demanded that I ask God, exalted is He, to manifest them through me so that they would show that I am a true messenger from God. The first is false, because I am a human, and a human has no power over these things. The second is also false, because I have already brought you one miracle, which is the Qur'an, and the indication that it is a miracle. So demanding these miracles is demanding what is not needed and not necessary; thus their demand is like obstinacy and dictation. I am a servant commanded; it is not for me to dictate to God. So this question falls away. Thus it is established that His saying: ﴿Say: Glory be to my Lord! Am I anything but a human messenger?﴾ is a sufficient answer in this matter. The sum of the matter is that He, glory be to Him, showed by His saying: ﴿Glory be to my Lord! Am I anything but a human messenger?﴾ that they were in error regarding divinity (ilahiyyat) and regarding prophethood (nubuwwat). As for divinity, their error is indicated by His saying "Glory be to my Lord," that is, He is glorified above having coming, going, or departing. As for prophethood, their error is indicated by His saying: ﴿Am I anything but a human messenger?﴾, and its explanation is what we have mentioned.

When God, exalted is He, related the disbelievers' proposal of these miracles, He said to Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿Say: Glory be to my Lord! Am I anything but a human messenger?﴾ and there are discussions regarding this:

The first discussion: He, exalted is He, related from the disbelievers' speech their saying: ﴿We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Say: Glory be to my Lord﴾. All of this is the people's speech, and we do not find any difference in the arrangement of those words from the rest of the verses of the Qur'an. Thus the disbelievers' statement is shown to be valid: "If we willed, we would say the like of this." The answer: this Qur'an is short, and there does not appear in it a difference between levels of eloquence and rhetoric, so this objection is removed.

The second discussion: these verses are among the strongest proofs that coming and going are impossible for God, because the word subhan is for declaring Him free from what is unfitting. His saying subhana rabbi is a declaration of God, exalted is He, free from anything unbefitting Him, or attributed to Him from what was previously mentioned. And there is nothing in what was previously mentioned that is unbefitting God except their saying: "or you bring God." This indicates that His saying: ﴿Glory be to my Lord﴾ is a declaration of God's freedom from coming and going, and that indicates the corruption of the view of the anthropomorphists (mushabbihah) that God comes and goes. If they say: why is it not permissible that what is meant is to declare God free from being subjected to the dictates of those who dictate proposals of things? We say: the people did not dictate to God; they only said to the Messenger (ﷺ): if you are a truthful prophet, ask God to honor you with these miracles. So the people dictated to the Messenger, and did not dictate to God. Therefore it is not appropriate to take His saying "Glory be to my Lord" in this sense, and it is necessary to take it in reference to their saying "or you bring God."

The third discussion: the explanation of this answer is that it may be said: either what you intend by this proposal is that you demanded that I bring these things from myself, or that you demanded that I ask God, exalted is He, to manifest them through me so that they would show that I am a true messenger from God. The first is false, because I am a human, and a human has no power over these things. The second is also false, because I have already brought you one miracle, which is the Qur'an, and the indication that it is a miracle. So demanding these miracles is demanding what is not needed and not necessary; thus their demand is like obstinacy and dictation. I am a servant commanded; it is not for me to dictate to God. So this question falls away. Thus it is established that His saying: ﴿Say: Glory be to my Lord! Am I anything but a human messenger?﴾ is a sufficient answer in this matter. The sum of the matter is that He, glory be to Him, showed by His saying: ﴿Glory be to my Lord! Am I anything but a human messenger?﴾ that they were in error regarding divinity (ilahiyyat) and regarding prophethood (nubuwwat). As for divinity, their error is indicated by His saying "Glory be to my Lord," that is, He is glorified above having coming, going, or departing. As for prophethood, their error is indicated by His saying: ﴿Am I anything but a human messenger?﴾, and its explanation is what we have mentioned.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verse 94–96:

﴿And nothing prevented the people from believing when the guidance came to them, except that they said: "Has God sent a mere human as a messenger?"﴾ ﴿Say: "If there were angels walking calmly on the earth, We would have sent down to them from the heaven an angel as a messenger."﴾ ﴿Say: "God suffices as a witness between me and you. Indeed, He is ever Acquainted with His servants, Seeing."﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, related the doubt of the people concerning their demand for additional miracles and answered it, He related another doubt of theirs, namely that the people deemed it improbable that God would send to creation a messenger from among humans. Rather, they believed that if God, exalted is He, were to send a messenger to creation, that messenger would have to be from among the angels. So God, exalted is He, answered this doubt in several ways:

The first: His saying: ﴿And nothing prevented the people from believing when the guidance came to them﴾. The explanation of this answer is that, supposing God were to send an angel as a messenger to creation, people would believe in his being a messenger from God only because of the presence of a miracle that indicates his truthfulness. That miracle is what guides them to recognizing that angel's claim to being the messenger of God. Therefore, what is meant by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿when the guidance came to them﴾ is the miracle alone. This miracle, whether it appears at the hand of an angel or at the hand of a human, makes it obligatory to acknowledge his messengerhood. Thus it is established that their claim that the messenger must necessarily be from the angels is an arbitrary judgment and baseless obstinacy.

The second: Among the answers that God mentioned in this verse to this doubt is that if the people of the earth were angels, their messenger would necessarily have to be from the angels, because a kind is more inclined toward its own kind. But if the people of the earth are humans, their messenger must necessarily be from humans. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿If there were angels walking calmly on the earth, We would have sent down to them from the heaven an angel as a messenger.﴾

The third: Among the answers mentioned in this verse is His saying: ﴿Say: "God suffices as a witness between me and you."﴾ Its explanation is that when God, exalted is He, manifested the miracle in accordance with my claim, that was a testimony from God, exalted is He, that I am truthful. Whoever God testifies to his truthfulness is truthful. After this, the claim of the one who says that the messenger must be an angel and not a human is a baseless arbitrary judgment that deserves no attention. When God, exalted is He, mentioned these three answers, He followed them with what amounts to a threat and warning, saying: ﴿Indeed, He is ever Acquainted with His servants, Seeing.﴾ That is, He knows their outward and inward states, and He knows from their hearts that they mention these doubts only out of pure envy, love of leadership, and disdain for submitting to the truth.

[p. 51]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whomever Allah guides, he is the one who is guided; and whomever He leads astray, you will not find for them any protectors besides Him. And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, mute, and deaf. Their refuge is Hell; whenever it subsides, We increase it for them in blaze.﴾ ﴿That is their recompense, because they disbelieved in Our signs.﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, had answered the doubts of the people concerning their denial of prophethood, and followed this with a general threat, which is His saying, ﴿Indeed He is ever, of His servants, All-Aware, All-Seeing﴾, He then mentioned the severe threat in detail. As for His saying, ﴿Whomever Allah guides, he is the one who is guided; and whomever He leads astray, you will not find for them any protectors besides Him﴾, its purpose is to console the Messenger. The meaning is that those for whom Allah's decree of faith and guidance has preceded must become believers, and those for whom Allah's decree of misguidance and ignorance has preceded cannot turn away from that misguidance, and it is impossible that anyone should exist who could turn them away from that misguidance. Our companions (the Ash'ariyyah) have used this verse as evidence for the correctness of their position regarding guidance and misguidance. The Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school that held human free will and divine justice as central principles) interpreted this misguidance at times as leading astray from the path to Paradise, at times as withholding the divine kindnesses (al-alṭāf), and at times as leaving them to themselves and not interfering to prevent it. These discussions we have mentioned many times, so there is no benefit in repeating them.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, mute, and deaf﴾, if it is asked, how is it possible for them to walk upon their faces? We answer: the answer is in two respects.

The first: they will be dragged upon their faces. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The Day they are dragged into the Fire upon their faces﴾ (al-Qamar: 48).

The second: Abu Hurayrah narrated: "It was said: O Messenger of Allah, how will they walk upon their faces? He said: 'Indeed, He who makes them walk upon their feet is able to make them walk upon their faces.'" The sages of Islam said: the souls of the disbelievers are strongly attached to this world and its pleasures, and have no attachment to the world of the righteous or to the presence of the Divine, glorified and exalted is He. Since the faces of their hearts and souls are turned toward this world, it is inevitable that their gathering will be upon their faces.

As for His saying, ﴿blind, mute, and deaf﴾, know that a man said to Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him: Does He not say: ﴿And the criminals will see the Fire﴾ (al-Kahf: 53), and He said: ﴿They will hear its raging and roaring﴾ (al-Furqan: 12), and He said: ﴿There they will call for destruction﴾ (al-Furqan: 13), and He said: ﴿The Day every soul will come pleading for itself﴾ (al-Nahl: 111), and He said, relating of the disbelievers: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ (al-An'am: 23). So through these verses it is established that they see, hear, and speak. How then does He say here: ﴿blind, mute, and deaf﴾? Ibn Abbas and his students answered this in several respects:

The first: Ibn Abbas said: "Blind, they see nothing that would please them; deaf, they hear nothing that would please them; mute, they utter no argument."

The second: he said in the narration of Ata: "Blind to looking at what Allah has prepared for His friends; mute from addressing Allah and addressing the angels brought near; deaf to the praise of Allah, exalted is He, for His friends."

The third: Muqatil said: "When it is said to them: ﴿Be silent in it, and do not speak to Me﴾ (al-Mu'minun: 108), they become blind, mute, and deaf. Before that, they see, hear, and speak."

The fourth: they will be seeing, hearing, and speaking in the place of standing (on the Day of Judgment), for otherwise they would not be able to read their books or to hear the establishing of Allah's proof against them. Only when they begin to go from the place of standing to the Fire does Allah make them blind, mute, and deaf. The answer is that the preceding verses indicate that in the Fire they see, hear, and cry out.

As for His saying, ﴿Their refuge is Hell﴾, it is clear. As for His saying, ﴿whenever it subsides, We increase it for them in blaze﴾, there are several discussions concerning it:

The first discussion: al-Wahidi said: "al-khabw is the subsiding of the fire. It is said: the fire subsided (khabat), it subsides (takhbū), when its flame calms. The meaning of khabat is it calmed and was extinguished. It is said of its verbal noun al-khabw, and al-mukhabbi' extinguished it, ikhbā'an, meaning he put it out." Then he said: ﴿We increase it for them in blaze﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: "We increase them in blaze," meaning in blazing.

The second discussion: One might say that He, exalted is He, does not lighten the punishment for them, and His saying ﴿whenever it subsides﴾ indicates that the punishment lessens at that time. We reply: "whenever it subsides" implies the calming of the flame of the fire, but this does not indicate that the punishment lessens at that time.

[p. 52]
The third discussion: His saying, ﴿whenever it subsides, We increase it for them in blaze﴾, apparently requires that the second state be greater than the first state, and if that is so, the first state would be a lightening in comparison with the second. The answer is: the increase that occurs in the first state is lighter than its occurrence in the second state, so the punishment is severe. It is also possible to say that when the punishment becomes great, the variation occurring in its times becomes imperceptible. We seek refuge in Allah from it. And when the Exalted mentioned the kinds of this threat, He said: ﴿That is their recompense, because they disbelieved﴾. The "bi" in His saying "bi-annahum kafarū" is the bā' of causation, and it is evidence for the one who says: deeds are the cause of recompense. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verses 98–100:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they say, "When we have become bones and crumbled dust, shall we truly be resurrected in a new creation?"﴾ ﴿Do they not see that Allah, who created the heavens and the earth, is able to create their likenesses? And He has appointed for them a term, about which there is no doubt. But the wrongdoers refuse except to be ungrateful.﴾ ﴿Say, "If you possessed the treasuries of the mercy of my Lord, you would surely withhold them for fear of spending. And man is ever stingy."﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had answered the doubts of those who denied prophethood, He returned to relating the doubt of those who denied the Gathering and the Resurrection, in order to answer it. That doubt is that man, after becoming dust and decayed bones, is far-fetched to return as he was. Allah, exalted is He, answered it by saying that whoever is able to create the heavens and the earth is not far from being able to restore them in their own selves. Regarding His saying ﴿is able to create their likenesses﴾ there are two opinions:

The first: the meaning is that He is able to create them a second time, and He expressed their second creation with the word "likeness," just as the theologians (mutakallimun, scholastic theologians) say that the restoration is the likeness of the origination.

The second opinion: the intended meaning is that He is able to create other servants who will affirm His oneness, acknowledge the perfection of His wisdom and power, and abandon the mention of these corrupt doubts. According to this interpretation, it is like His saying: ﴿and bring a new creation﴾ (Ibrahim: 19), and His saying: ﴿and replace you with another people﴾ (al-Tawbah: 39). Al-Wahidi said: The first opinion is the correct one, because it better fits what precedes it.

When Allah, exalted is He, demonstrated by the aforementioned proof that the resurrection and the Last Day are a matter possible in themselves, He followed it by stating that their occurrence and entry into existence has a time known to Allah, which is His saying: ﴿and He has appointed for them a term, about which there is no doubt.﴾ Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿But the wrongdoers refuse except to be ungrateful﴾, meaning: after these manifest proofs, they refused except disbelief, aversion and denial.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "If you possessed the treasuries of the mercy of my Lord, you would surely withhold them for fear of spending. And man is ever stingy."﴾ In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: when the disbelievers said: ﴿We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth﴾, they requested the flowing of rivers and springs in their land so that their wealth would increase and their livelihood would be broadened. So Allah, exalted is He, informed them that if they possessed the treasuries of Allah's mercy, they would remain upon their miserliness and stinginess, and would not proceed to bestow benefit upon anyone. On this assumption, there is no benefit in granting them this request which they sought. This is the discourse on the aspect of the arrangement (naẓm) of the verse, and Allah knows best.

The second issue: His saying ﴿if you﴾ contains a discussion related to grammar and another discussion related to the science of eloquence (ʿilm al-bayan). As for the grammatical discussion: the word "law" (لَوْ) is by nature specific to the verb, because "law" indicates the negation of one thing due to the negation of another, and the noun indicates essences, whereas the verb is what indicates effects and states. What is negated are the states and effects, not the essences. Thus it is established that "law" is specific to verbs. They cited the verse of al-Mutalammis:

*"Had any but my maternal uncles intended to belittle me, I would have raised for them a mourning-tent above the noblest of noses."*

The meaning is: had anyone other than my maternal uncles intended. As for the discussion related to the science of eloquence: placing a word first indicates specificity, so His saying ﴿you possess﴾ is an indication that they are the ones specifically characterized by this base state and complete stinginess.

The third issue: the treasuries of Allah's bounty and mercy are infinite. So the meaning is that if you possessed treasuries of goodness and blessings without end, you would remain in stinginess. This is a great exaggeration in describing them with this trait. Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And man is ever stingy﴾, meaning, miserly. It is said: qatara yaqtiru qatran, and aqtara iqtaran, and qattara taqtiran, when one falls short in spending. If it is said: the generous and noble man is also included in "man," the answer is in several respects:

First: the original state of man is stinginess, because he was created needy, and the one in need must love that by which he removes his need and must withhold it for himself. However, he may give it out of external causes. Thus it is established that the original state of man is stinginess.

Second: man gives only to seek praise and commendation, and to discharge an obligation. Thus, in reality, he spends only to receive a return, and so in reality he is stingy.

Third: the intended "man" here is the one previously mentioned: those who said ﴿We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth.﴾

[p. 53]

The first: the meaning is that He is able to create them a second time, and He expressed their second creation with the word "likeness," just as the theologians (mutakallimun, scholastic theologians) say that the restoration is the likeness of the origination.

The second opinion: the intended meaning is that He is able to create other servants who will affirm His oneness, acknowledge the perfection of His wisdom and power, and abandon the mention of these corrupt doubts. According to this interpretation, it is like His saying: ﴿and bring a new creation﴾ (Ibrahim: 19), and His saying: ﴿and replace you with another people﴾ (al-Tawbah: 39). Al-Wahidi said: The first opinion is the correct one, because it better fits what precedes it.

When Allah, exalted is He, demonstrated by the aforementioned proof that the resurrection and the Last Day are a matter possible in themselves, He followed it by stating that their occurrence and entry into existence has a time known to Allah, which is His saying: ﴿and He has appointed for them a term, about which there is no doubt.﴾ Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿But the wrongdoers refuse except to be ungrateful﴾, meaning: after these manifest proofs, they refused except disbelief, aversion and denial.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "If you possessed the treasuries of the mercy of my Lord, you would surely withhold them for fear of spending. And man is ever stingy."﴾ In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: when the disbelievers said: ﴿We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth﴾, they requested the flowing of rivers and springs in their land so that their wealth would increase and their livelihood would be broadened. So Allah, exalted is He, informed them that if they possessed the treasuries of Allah's mercy, they would remain upon their miserliness and stinginess, and would not proceed to bestow benefit upon anyone. On this assumption, there is no benefit in granting them this request which they sought. This is the discourse on the aspect of the arrangement (naẓm) of the verse, and Allah knows best.

The second issue: His saying ﴿if you﴾ contains a discussion related to grammar and another discussion related to the science of eloquence (ʿilm al-bayan). As for the grammatical discussion: the word "law" (لَوْ) is by nature specific to the verb, because "law" indicates the negation of one thing due to the negation of another, and the noun indicates essences, whereas the verb is what indicates effects and states. What is negated are the states and effects, not the essences. Thus it is established that "law" is specific to verbs. They cited the verse of al-Mutalammis:

*"Had any but my maternal uncles intended to belittle me, I would have raised for them a mourning-tent above the noblest of noses."*

The meaning is: had anyone other than my maternal uncles intended. As for the discussion related to the science of eloquence: placing a word first indicates specificity, so His saying ﴿you possess﴾ is an indication that they are the ones specifically characterized by this base state and complete stinginess.

The third issue: the treasuries of Allah's bounty and mercy are infinite. So the meaning is that if you possessed treasuries of goodness and blessings without end, you would remain in stinginess. This is a great exaggeration in describing them with this trait. Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And man is ever stingy﴾, meaning, miserly. It is said: qatara yaqtiru qatran, and aqtara iqtaran, and qattara taqtiran, when one falls short in spending. If it is said: the generous and noble man is also included in "man," the answer is in several respects:

First: the original state of man is stinginess, because he was created needy, and the one in need must love that by which he removes his need and must withhold it for himself. However, he may give it out of external causes. Thus it is established that the original state of man is stinginess.

Second: man gives only to seek praise and commendation, and to discharge an obligation. Thus, in reality, he spends only to receive a return, and so in reality he is stingy.

Third: the intended "man" here is the one previously mentioned: those who said ﴿We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth.﴾

[p. 53]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 17, verses 101–104:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And We had certainly given Moses nine clear signs. So ask the Children of Israel, when he came to them, and Pharaoh said to him, "Indeed, I think you, O Moses, are bewitched."﴾ ﴿He said, "You have certainly known that these have not sent down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as evidence, and indeed, I think you, O Pharaoh, are doomed."﴾ ﴿So he intended to expel them from the land, but We drowned him and those with him, all together.﴾ ﴿And We said after him to the Children of Israel, "Dwell in the land, and when the promise of the Hereafter comes, We will bring you forth as a mixed multitude."﴾ In the verse there are several issues:

[Page 54]

The first issue: Know that the purpose of this speech is also to answer their saying: ﴿We will not believe you until you bring us [such] a compelling miracle,﴾ so Allah, exalted is He, said: (We gave Moses the Book), with miracles equal to these things you have asked for, rather, stronger and greater than them. Had it been known to Us that bringing them in your time would be beneficial, We would have done so, just as We did for Moses. This indicates that We did not bring them in your time because We know there is no benefit in doing so.

The second issue: Know that He, exalted is He, mentioned in the Qur'an many of the miracles of Moses, peace be upon him:

The first of them: that Allah, exalted is He, removed the knot from his tongue. It has been said in the tafsir (exegesis) that the non-Arabic quality (al-'ujmah) disappeared and he became eloquent.

The second: the staff turning into a serpent.

The third: the serpent swallowing their ropes and staffs despite their large number.

The fourth: the white hand.

And five others, which are: the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the blood.

The tenth: the splitting of the sea, which is His saying: ﴿And when We parted the sea for you﴾ (al-Baqarah: 50).

The eleventh: the rock, which is His saying: ﴿Strike the rock with your staff﴾ (al-A'raf: 160).

The twelfth: the mountain being raised over them, which is the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And when We lifted the mountain over them as if it were a canopy﴾ [al-A'raf: 171].

The thirteenth: the sending down of manna and quails upon him and his people.

The fourteenth and fifteenth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly seized the people of Pharaoh with years [of drought] and a shortage of fruits﴾ (al-A'raf: 130).

The sixteenth: the obliteration of their wealth, of honey, flour, foodstuffs, dirhams, and dinars. It is narrated that 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz asked Muhammad ibn Ka'b about His saying: ﴿nine clear signs﴾. Muhammad ibn Ka'b mentioned, regarding the nine: the untying of the knot of the tongue and the obliteration. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said: "This is how the jurist (faqih) should be." Then he said: "O boy, bring out that saddlebag." He brought it out and shook it, and in it were eggs broken in two, walnuts broken, fava beans, chickpeas, and lentils, all of which were stones. When you know this, we say that He, exalted is He, mentioned in the Qur'an these sixteen miracles of Moses, peace be upon him, and said in this verse: ﴿And We had certainly given Moses nine clear signs.﴾ The specifying of the nine by mention does not harm the matter, the existence of additional ones beyond them, because we have explained in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) that specifying a number by mention does not indicate the negation of what is beyond it. Rather, we say that this verse is only used in this issue as a proof. Then we say: As for these nine, they agreed upon seven of them: the staff, the hand, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the blood, and two remained, and each of the exegetes has another opinion regarding them. Since those circumstances were not based on a speculative proof, let alone a certain proof, those narrations were therefore abandoned. Regarding the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿nine clear signs,﴾ there are opinions, the best of which is what Safwan ibn 'Assal narrated, that he said: "A Jew said to his companion, 'Come, let us go to this Prophet and ask him about nine signs.' So they went to the Prophet ﷺ and asked him about them. He said: 'They are: that you do not associate anything with Allah, do not steal, do not commit adultery, do not kill, do not practice sorcery, do not consume usury, do not slander chaste women, do not flee on the day of battle, and upon you, specifically the Jews, is to be just regarding the Sabbath.' Then the two Jews stood up, kissed his hands and feet, and said: 'We testify that you are a Prophet. If not for fear of being killed, we would follow you.'"

The third issue: His saying: ﴿So ask the Children of Israel, when he came to them﴾ has several discussions:

The first discussion: There are several aspects:

The first aspect: It is a parenthetical interjection that entered the speech, and the implied meaning is: ﴿And We had certainly given Moses nine clear signs﴾ – when he came to the Children of Israel, so ask them. According to this interpretation, the aim of asking the Children of Israel is not that you learn this knowledge from them. Rather, the intention is that the truth of what the Messenger said becomes manifest to the common Jews and their scholars, so this question is a question of seeking testimony.

The second aspect: that His saying "so ask the Children of Israel" means: ask them about Pharaoh, and say to him: "Send the Children of Israel with me."

The third aspect: "Ask the Children of Israel," meaning: ask them to agree with you, and seek from them righteous faith. According to this interpretation, the implied meaning is: So We said to him, "Ask them to support you, and let their hearts and hands be with you."

The second discussion: He commanded the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to ask the Children of Israel. Its meaning: those who were present in the time of the Prophet ﷺ. And those to whom Moses, peace be upon him, came were those who were in his time. However, since those who were in the time of Muhammad ﷺ were the children of those who were in the time of Moses, this expression was apt. Then Allah, exalted is He, informed that Pharaoh said to Moses: ﴿Indeed, I think you, O Moses, are bewitched.﴾ Regarding the word "bewitched" (mash'ur), there are several meanings:

The first: al-Farra' said: it means "one who practices sorcery" (sahir), like "ill-omened" (mash'um) and "blessed" (maymun). We mentioned this in His saying: ﴿a hidden barrier﴾ [al-Isra': 45].

The second: that it is a passive participle from sorcery (sihr), meaning that people have bewitched you and confused you, so you say these words for this reason.

The third: Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: its meaning is "you have been given the knowledge of sorcery, so these wonders you bring are from that sorcery." Then Moses, peace be upon him, answered him with his saying: ﴿You have certainly known that these have not sent down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth.﴾ Regarding this there are discussions:

The first discussion: al-Kisa'i recited "'alimtu" with a dammah on the tā' (i.e., "I have known"), meaning: "I have known that they are from the knowledge of Allah; so if you know and acknowledge, [well], otherwise you will perish." The rest recited it with a fatha (i.e., "you have known"). The dammah is the reading of 'Ali, and the fatha is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas. 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, used to say: "By Allah, the enemy of Allah did not know, but Moses is the one who knew." This reached Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and he argued with His saying: ﴿And they denied them while their souls were convinced of them﴾ (al-Naml: 14), to show that Pharaoh and his people had recognized the truth of Moses' matter, peace be upon him. Al-Zajjaj said: The better reading is the fatha, because Pharaoh's knowledge that these were signs sent down from Allah is stronger as proof. Therefore, Moses' argument against Pharaoh based on Pharaoh's own knowledge is stronger than arguing based on his own knowledge. Those who support the reading of 'Ali, peace be upon him, responded to the evidence of Ibn 'Abbas, saying: His saying: ﴿And they denied them while their souls were convinced of them﴾ indicates that they were certain of something, but as for their being certain that these signs were sent down from Allah, there is nothing in the verse that indicates it.

They answered the second aspect by saying that Pharaoh said: ﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is a madman﴾ (al-Shu'ara': 27). Moses said: ﴿You have certainly known,﴾ as if he negated that, and said: "You have certainly known the truth of what I have brought with a true knowledge, the knowledge of the intelligent. Know that these signs are from Allah, and do not doubt that, because of your foolishness."

The second discussion: The implied meaning is "what these have sent down, the signs," and its parallel is the poet's saying: "And life after those peoples [is nothing]."

His saying "clear signs" (basa'ir), meaning: clear proofs, as if they were insights of the intellects. The precise statement is that a miracle is an act that breaks customary norms, performed by its doer for the purpose of confirming the claim. The miracles of Moses, peace be upon him, were described by these two attributes, since they were acts breaking customary norms. Pure intellects testify that turning a staff into a serpent is a great miracle that no one can accomplish except Allah. Then that serpent swallowed the ropes and staffs of the sorcerers despite their large number, and then it returned to being a staff as it was. Therefore, the kinds of these acts can be performed by no one except Allah. The same applies to the splitting of the sea and the raising of the mountain. Thus it is established that these things were not sent down except by the Lord of the heavens.

The second attribute: that He, exalted is He, created them only to show the truth of Moses in his claim to prophethood. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿These have not sent down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth,﴾ while they are "clear signs," i.e., indicating the truth of Moses in his claim. These subtleties cannot be understood from the Qur'an except after mastering the science of the principles (usul al-din or usul al-fiqh, as they put it). I say: It is far-fetched that any rational science of principles should become dominant in interpreting the words of Allah, exalted is He. Then Allah, exalted is He, related that Moses said to Pharaoh: ﴿And indeed, I think you, O Pharaoh, are doomed.﴾ Know that Pharaoh

[Page 56]

said to Moses: ﴿Indeed, I think you, O Moses, are bewitched,﴾ so Moses countered him and said to him: ﴿And indeed, I think you, O Pharaoh, are doomed.﴾ Al-Farra' said: "al-mathbur" is the cursed, the one restrained from good. The Arabs say: "What has held you back from this?" meaning: what prevented you from it and turned you away. Abu Zayd said: "One says: 'I held so-and-so back from the thing (thabartu fulanan 'an al-shay'), I hold him back (athburuhu),' meaning: I turned him away from it." Mujahid and Qatadah said: "Destroyed." Al-Zajjaj said: "It is said: 'The man was made doomed (thubira al-rajul), so he is mathbur,' if he perished. And ruin (thubur) is destruction." It is a well-known expression: "So-and-so calls out 'woe and ruin' (wayl wa-thubur) when a calamity befalls him." Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿There they will call for destruction﴾ and ﴿Do not call out today for one destruction, but call for many destructions﴾ (al-Furqan: 14). Know that when Pharaoh described Moses as bewitched, Moses answered him, "You are doomed," meaning: these signs are manifest, these miracles are overpowering, and no intelligent person doubts that they are from Allah, and that He, exalted is He, displayed them only to confirm me, while you deny them. Nothing drives you to this denial except envy, obstinacy, deviation, ignorance, and love of this world. Whoever is like this, his end is ruin and destruction. Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So he intended to expel them from the land,﴾ meaning: Pharaoh intended to drive them out, that is, Moses and his people, the Children of Israel. The meaning of "istifzaz" (driving out) has been explained earlier in this surah. ﴿From the land,﴾ meaning the land of Egypt. Al-Zajjaj said: It is not far-fetched that the intended meaning of driving them out is expelling them from it by killing or by removing them. Then He said: ﴿But We drowned him and those with him, all together.﴾ The meaning is what Allah, exalted is He, mentioned in His saying: ﴿And the evil plot does not encompass anyone except its own people﴾ (Fatir: 43). Pharaoh intended to expel Moses from the land of Egypt so that the land would be his alone, but Allah, exalted is He, destroyed Pharaoh and made the kingdom of Egypt exclusively for Moses and his people. He said to the Children of Israel: "Dwell in the land exclusively for you, free from your enemy." Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when the promise of the Hereafter comes,﴾ meaning the Resurrection, ﴿We will bring you forth as a mixed multitude,﴾ from here and from there. Al-laffif is a great gathering of diverse mixtures: noble and base, obedient and disobedient, strong and weak. Everything you mix with something else has been "laffaftahu" (you have mixed it). From this it is said: "I mixed the armies (laffaftu al-juyush)" when you strike some of them against others. And His saying: "The ranks came together (iltaffati al-zuhuf)," and from it: "The leg was wrapped with the leg (iltaffa al-saq bi-al-saq)." The meaning is: We will bring you from your graves to the place of assembly as mixed groups, meaning all of creation, the Muslim and the disbeliever, the righteous and the wicked.

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when the promise of the Hereafter comes,﴾ meaning the Resurrection, ﴿We will bring you forth as a mixed multitude,﴾ from here and from there. From this it is said: "I mixed the armies (laffaftu al-juyush)" when you strike some of them against others. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 17, verses 101–104:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And We had certainly given Moses nine clear signs. So ask the Children of Israel, when he came to them, and Pharaoh said to him, "Indeed, I think you, O Moses, are bewitched."﴾ ﴿He said, "You have certainly known that these have not sent down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as evidence, and indeed, I think you, O Pharaoh, are doomed."﴾ ﴿So he intended to expel them from the land, but We drowned him and those with him, all together.﴾ ﴿And We said after him to the Children of Israel, "Dwell in the land, and when the promise of the Hereafter comes, We will bring you forth as a mixed multitude."﴾ In the verse there are several issues:

[Page 54]

The first issue: Know that the purpose of this speech is also to answer their saying: ﴿We will not believe you until you bring us [such] a compelling miracle,﴾ so Allah, exalted is He, said: (We gave Moses the Book), with miracles equal to these things you have asked for, rather, stronger and greater than them. Had it been known to Us that bringing them in your time would be beneficial, We would have done so, just as We did for Moses. This indicates that We did not bring them in your time because We know there is no benefit in doing so.

The second issue: Know that He, exalted is He, mentioned in the Qur'an many of the miracles of Moses, peace be upon him:

The first of them: that Allah, exalted is He, removed the knot from his tongue. It has been said in the tafsir (exegesis) that the non-Arabic quality (al-'ujmah) disappeared and he became eloquent.

The second: the staff turning into a serpent.

The third: the serpent swallowing their ropes and staffs despite their large number.

The fourth: the white hand.

And five others, which are: the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the blood.

The tenth: the splitting of the sea, which is His saying: ﴿And when We parted the sea for you﴾ (al-Baqarah: 50).

The eleventh: the rock, which is His saying: ﴿Strike the rock with your staff﴾ (al-A'raf: 160).

The twelfth: the mountain being raised over them, which is the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And when We lifted the mountain over them as if it were a canopy﴾ [al-A'raf: 171].

The thirteenth: the sending down of manna and quails upon him and his people.

The fourteenth and fifteenth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly seized the people of Pharaoh with years [of drought] and a shortage of fruits﴾ (al-A'raf: 130).

The sixteenth: the obliteration of their wealth, of honey, flour, foodstuffs, dirhams, and dinars. It is narrated that 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz asked Muhammad ibn Ka'b about His saying: ﴿nine clear signs﴾. Muhammad ibn Ka'b mentioned, regarding the nine: the untying of the knot of the tongue and the obliteration. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said: "This is how the jurist (faqih) should be." Then he said: "O boy, bring out that saddlebag." He brought it out and shook it, and in it were eggs broken in two, walnuts broken, fava beans, chickpeas, and lentils, all of which were stones. When you know this, we say that He, exalted is He, mentioned in the Qur'an these sixteen miracles of Moses, peace be upon him, and said in this verse: ﴿And We had certainly given Moses nine clear signs.﴾ The specifying of the nine by mention does not harm the matter, the existence of additional ones beyond them, because we have explained in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) that specifying a number by mention does not indicate the negation of what is beyond it. Rather, we say that this verse is only used in this issue as a proof. Then we say: As for these nine, they agreed upon seven of them: the staff, the hand, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the blood, and two remained, and each of the exegetes has another opinion regarding them. Since those circumstances were not based on a speculative proof, let alone a certain proof, those narrations were therefore abandoned. Regarding the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿nine clear signs,﴾ there are opinions, the best of which is what Safwan ibn 'Assal narrated, that he said: "A Jew said to his companion, 'Come, let us go to this Prophet and ask him about nine signs.' So they went to the Prophet ﷺ and asked him about them. He said: 'They are: that you do not associate anything with Allah, do not steal, do not commit adultery, do not kill, do not practice sorcery, do not consume usury, do not slander chaste women, do not flee on the day of battle, and upon you, specifically the Jews, is to be just regarding the Sabbath.' Then the two Jews stood up, kissed his hands and feet, and said: 'We testify that you are a Prophet. If not for fear of being killed, we would follow you.'"

The third issue: His saying: ﴿So ask the Children of Israel, when he came to them﴾ has several discussions:

The first discussion: There are several aspects:

The first aspect: It is a parenthetical interjection that entered the speech, and the implied meaning is: ﴿And We had certainly given Moses nine clear signs﴾ – when he came to the Children of Israel, so ask them. According to this interpretation, the aim of asking the Children of Israel is not that you learn this knowledge from them. Rather, the intention is that the truth of what the Messenger said becomes manifest to the common Jews and their scholars, so this question is a question of seeking testimony.

The second aspect: that His saying "so ask the Children of Israel" means: ask them about Pharaoh, and say to him: "Send the Children of Israel with me."

The third aspect: "Ask the Children of Israel," meaning: ask them to agree with you, and seek from them righteous faith. According to this interpretation, the implied meaning is: So We said to him, "Ask them to support you, and let their hearts and hands be with you."

The second discussion: He commanded the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to ask the Children of Israel. Its meaning: those who were present in the time of the Prophet ﷺ. And those to whom Moses, peace be upon him, came were those who were in his time. However, since those who were in the time of Muhammad ﷺ were the children of those who were in the time of Moses, this expression was apt. Then Allah, exalted is He, informed that Pharaoh said to Moses: ﴿Indeed, I think you, O Moses, are bewitched.﴾ Regarding the word "bewitched" (mash'ur), there are several meanings:

The first: al-Farra' said: it means "one who practices sorcery" (sahir), like "ill-omened" (mash'um) and "blessed" (maymun). We mentioned this in His saying: ﴿a hidden barrier﴾ [al-Isra': 45].

The second: that it is a passive participle from sorcery (sihr), meaning that people have bewitched you and confused you, so you say these words for this reason.

The third: Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: its meaning is "you have been given the knowledge of sorcery, so these wonders you bring are from that sorcery." Then Moses, peace be upon him, answered him with his saying: ﴿You have certainly known that these have not sent down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth.﴾ Regarding this there are discussions:

The first discussion: al-Kisa'i recited "'alimtu" with a dammah on the tā' (i.e., "I have known"), meaning: "I have known that they are from the knowledge of Allah; so if you know and acknowledge, [well], otherwise you will perish." 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, used to say: "By Allah, the enemy of Allah did not know, but Moses is the one who knew." This reached Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and he argued with His saying: ﴿And they denied them while their souls were convinced of them﴾ (al-Naml: 14), to show that Pharaoh and his people had recognized the truth of Moses' matter, peace be upon him. Al-Zajjaj said: The better reading is the fatha, because Pharaoh's knowledge that these were signs sent down from Allah is stronger as proof. Therefore, Moses' argument against Pharaoh based on Pharaoh's own knowledge is stronger than arguing based on his own knowledge. Those who support the reading of 'Ali, peace be upon him, responded to the evidence of Ibn 'Abbas, saying: His saying: ﴿And they denied them while their souls were convinced of them﴾ indicates that they were certain of something, but as for their being certain that these signs were sent down from Allah, there is nothing in the verse that indicates it.

They answered the second aspect by saying that Pharaoh said: ﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is a madman﴾ (al-Shu'ara': 27). Moses said: ﴿You have certainly known,﴾ as if he negated that, and said: "You have certainly known the truth of what I have brought with a true knowledge, the knowledge of the intelligent. The second discussion: The implied meaning is "what these have sent down, the signs," and its parallel is the poet's saying: "And life after those peoples [is nothing]."

His saying "clear signs" (basa'ir), meaning: clear proofs, as if they were insights of the intellects. The precise statement is that a miracle is an act that breaks customary norms, performed by its doer for the purpose of confirming the claim. Therefore, the kinds of these acts can be performed by no one except Allah. The same applies to the splitting of the sea and the raising of the mountain. **Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verses 105–109:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And with the truth We have sent it down, and with the truth it has descended, and We have not sent you except as a bearer of good news and a warner.﴾ ﴿And a Qur'an which We have separated, that you might recite it to the people over a period, and We have sent it down in stages.﴾ ﴿Say: "Believe in it or do not believe. Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it, when it is recited to them, fall down on their faces in prostration.﴾ ﴿And they say, "Glory be to our Lord! Indeed, the promise of our Lord has been fulfilled."﴾ ﴿And they fall down on their faces weeping, and it increases them in humility.﴾

Know that when He, Exalted is He, explained that the Qur'an is a miracle, overpowering and indicative of the truthfulness [of the Prophet], in His saying: ﴿Say: "If mankind and the jinn gathered together..."﴾ (al-Isra': 88), then He related that the disbelievers were not satisfied with this miracle, but demanded all other miracles. Then God answered them that there is no need to manifest all the other miracles, and He explained this with many arguments. Among them: the people of Musa (peace be upon him) were given by God nine clear signs, and when they denied them, God destroyed them. So it is here as well. Furthermore, if He gave the people of Muhammad those miracles they proposed and then they disbelieved in them, the punishment of annihilation would necessarily descend upon them. That is not permissible in wisdom, since God knows that among them are those who will believe, and that from the offspring of the unbelievers there will emerge those who become believers. When this answer was complete, He returned to magnifying the state of the Qur'an and the exaltedness of its rank, and so He said: ﴿And with the truth We have sent it down, and with the truth it has descended.﴾ The meaning is that We did not intend by its sending down anything except the establishment of truth and truthfulness, and just as We intended this meaning, so this meaning was realized and achieved. In this verse there are several benefits:

The first benefit: Truth (al-haqq) is that which is firm and does not vanish, just as falsehood (al-batil) is that which passes away and departs. This noble Book contains matters that do not cease, because it includes the proofs of Divine Oneness, the attributes of majesty and generosity, the honouring of the angels, the establishment of the prophethood of the prophets, and the affirmation of resurrection, gathering and the Last Day. All of these are matters that do not admit cessation. It also contains a law that remains, which is not open to abrogation (naskh, the cancelling of a ruling by a later revelation), invalidation, or distortion (tahrif, altering the text or meaning). Moreover, this Book is one which God has undertaken to preserve from the distortion of the deviant and the alteration of the ignorant, as He said: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian.﴾ (al-Hijr: 9). Thus this Book is true in every respect.

The second benefit: His saying: ﴿And with the truth We have sent it down﴾ implies restriction (al-hasr), and its meaning is that it was not sent down for any purpose other than the manifestation of the truth. The Mu'tazilites (the Mu'tazila, a rationalist school of theology) said: This indicates that He did not intend by its sending down to lead any of creation astray, nor to mislead them, nor to prevent them from the religion of God.

The third benefit: His saying: ﴿And with the truth We have sent it down, and with the truth it has descended﴾ indicates that sending down (al-inzal) is other than descending (al-nuzul). Accordingly, it follows that the creating (al-khalq) is other than the created (al-makhluq), and that the bringing into being (al-takwin) is other than the thing brought into being, according to what a group has held.

The fourth benefit: Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: The letter ba' (بِ) in His saying ﴿And with the truth We have sent it down﴾ means "with" (ma'a), as you say "he descended with his equipment" and "he went out with his weapon." The meaning is: We sent down the Qur'an together with the truth. As for His saying ﴿And with the truth it has descended﴾, it has two possibilities:

The first: that the meaning is "it descended by means of the truth," as you say "I alighted at Zayd," and according to this interpretation, "the truth" is Muhammad (ﷺ), because the Qur'an descended by means of him, that is, upon him.

The second: that it means "with" (ma'a), as we have said regarding His saying ﴿And with the truth We have sent it down﴾. Then Exalted is He said: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a bearer of good news and a warner.﴾ The intended meaning is that these ignorant people who propose these miracles to you and rebel against accepting your religion, there is nothing on you for their disbelief. For I did not send you except as a bearer of good news to the obedient and a warner to the deniers. If they accept the true religion, they will benefit from it; otherwise, there is nothing on you for their disbelief.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And a Qur'an which We have separated, that you might recite it to the people over a period﴾, and concerning this there are several discussions:

The first discussion: The people said: Suppose this Qur'an is a miracle, yet, even assuming that the matter is so, it was necessary that God send it down to you all at once, so that the aspect of its inimitability would be manifest in it. So they made the Messenger's bringing of this Qur'an in separate parts a ground for doubt, claiming that he contemplates each section and recites it to the people. God answered them that He only separated it so that its memorisation would be easier, and so that comprehension of its subtleties and realities and standing upon them would be easier.

The second discussion: Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: The whole Qur'an descended on the Night of Power (laylat al-qadr) from the uppermost heaven to the lowest heaven, and then it was detailed in the years in which it descended. Qatadah said: Between its beginning and its end there were twenty years. The meaning is: We divided it verse by verse and surah by surah, and We did not send it down all at once, ﴿that you might recite it to the people over a period﴾ — with the fath and the damm (the vowel on the kaf of مُكْثٍ: fatha or damma) — meaning at leisure and deliberately, that is, not in haste. Al-Farra' said: It is said makatha and makuthu yamkuthu (both forms of the verb "to remain"), and the fath is the reading of 'Asim in His saying: ﴿So he remained not long﴾ (al-Naml: 22).

The third discussion: The preferred reading among the Imams is faraqnahu with the light (takhfif) form of the verb, and Abu 'Amr interpreted it as "We made it clear" (bayyannahu). Abu 'Ubayd said: The light form is more pleasing to me, because its explanation is "We made it clear." As for the one who reads it with the intensive form (tashdid, farraqnahu), it has no meaning except that it was sent down in separate parts; so separation (al-farq) includes clarification (al-tabyin). This is confirmed by what Tha'lab related from Ibn al-A'rabi, that he said: "I separate (faraqtu ufarriq) between speech, and I separate between bodies." It is also indicated by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The two sellers have the option (of cancelling the sale) as long as they have not separated (lam yatafarraqa)," and he did not say "as long as they have not parted (yaftariqa)." The verb tafarruq is the intransitive (mutawa') form of tafriq, and iftiraq is the intransitive form of farq.

Then He said: ﴿And We have sent it down in stages﴾, that is, according to the limit mentioned and the description mentioned.

Then He said: ﴿Say: "Believe in it or do not believe"﴾, addressing those who proposed those great miracles, in a manner of threat and denial. That is: God has made the clear signs and proofs manifest and removed excuses, so choose what you wish.

Then Exalted is He said: ﴿Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it﴾, that is, before the revelation of the Qur'an. Mujahid said: They are people from the People of the Book, who, when they heard what was sent down upon Muhammad (ﷺ), fell down in prostration. Among them were Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl, Waraqah ibn Nawfal, and 'Abd Allah ibn Salam. Then He said: ﴿They fall down on their faces in prostration﴾, and concerning this there are several opinions:

The first opinion: Al-Zajjaj said: The dhaqan (chin) is the meeting place of the two jaws. Whenever a person begins to fall down into prostration, the nearest thing to the forehead to the ground is the chin.

The second opinion: That al-adhqan (the chins) is a metonym for the beards. When a person, in prostration, goes to great lengths in humility and reverence, he perhaps rubs his beard on the dust, for the beard is one that is greatly cleaned; so when a person covers it with dust, he has reached the utmost in magnifying God.

The third opinion: When the fear of God Exalted overcomes a person, he may fall to the ground in the posture of prostration like one who has lost consciousness, and when this is the case, his falling upon the chin is in the place of prostration. So His saying ﴿they fall down upon their chins﴾ is a metonym for the extreme of his rapture, fear, and awe. Then two questions remain concerning the verse:

The first question: Why did He say ﴿they fall down upon their chins in prostration﴾ and not "they prostrate"? The answer: The purpose of mentioning this expression is their haste toward that, to the extent that they fall down.

The second question: Why did He say ﴿they fall down upon their chins﴾ and not "upon the chins"? The answer: The Arabs say, when a man falls and lands on his face, "he fell down upon the chin (kharra lil-dhaqan)." And God knows best.

Then Exalted is He said: ﴿And they say, "Glory be to our Lord! Indeed, the promise of our Lord has been fulfilled."﴾ The meaning is that they say in their prostration: ﴿Glory be to our Lord﴾, that is, they declare Him far above imperfection and magnify Him. ﴿Indeed, the promise of our Lord has been fulfilled﴾, that is, by the sending down of the Qur'an and the sending of Muhammad. This indicates that these people were from the People of the Book, because the promise of the mission of Muhammad had preceded in their Book; so they were awaiting the fulfilment of that promise. Then He said: ﴿And they fall down upon their chins weeping﴾. The benefit of this repetition is the difference of the two states: their falling for prostration, and their being in a state of weeping upon hearing the Qur'an. This is indicated by His saying ﴿and it increases them in humility﴾. It is also possible that the repetition of the statement indicates the repetition of the act on their part. His saying ﴿weeping﴾ means the circumstantial state (hal). ﴿And it increases them in humility﴾, that is, in lowliness (tawadu'). Know that the purpose of this verse is to establish their contemptibility, the disdain of their position, the disregard for them and for their faith, and their refusal of it; and that although they did not believe in it, there has believed in it one who is better than them.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 17, verses 105–109:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And with the truth We have sent it down, and with the truth it has descended, and We have not sent you except as a bearer of good news and a warner.﴾ ﴿And a Qur'an which We have separated, that you might recite it to the people over a period, and We have sent it down in stages.﴾ ﴿Say: "Believe in it or do not believe. Indeed, the promise of our Lord has been fulfilled."﴾ ﴿And they fall down on their faces weeping, and it increases them in humility.﴾

Know that when He, Exalted is He, explained that the Qur'an is a miracle, overpowering and indicative of the truthfulness [of the Prophet], in His saying: ﴿Say: "If mankind and the jinn gathered together..."﴾ (al-Isra': 88), then He related that the disbelievers were not satisfied with this miracle, but demanded all other miracles. Then God answered them that there is no need to manifest all the other miracles, and He explained this with many arguments. Among them: the people of Musa (peace be upon him) were given by God nine clear signs, and when they denied them, God destroyed them. So it is here as well. Furthermore, if He gave the people of Muhammad those miracles they proposed and then they disbelieved in them, the punishment of annihilation would necessarily descend upon them. That is not permissible in wisdom, since God knows that among them are those who will believe, and that from the offspring of the unbelievers there will emerge those who become believers. When this answer was complete, He returned to magnifying the state of the Qur'an and the exaltedness of its rank, and so He said: ﴿And with the truth We have sent it down, and with the truth it has descended.﴾ The meaning is that We did not intend by its sending down anything except the establishment of truth and truthfulness, and just as We intended this meaning, so this meaning was realized and achieved. In this verse there are several benefits:

The first benefit: Truth (al-haqq) is that which is firm and does not vanish, just as falsehood (al-batil) is that which passes away and departs. This noble Book contains matters that do not cease, because it includes the proofs of Divine Oneness, the attributes of majesty and generosity, the honouring of the angels, the establishment of the prophethood of the prophets, and the affirmation of resurrection, gathering and the Last Day. All of these are matters that do not admit cessation. It also contains a law that remains, which is not open to abrogation (naskh, the cancelling of a ruling by a later revelation), invalidation, or distortion (tahrif, altering the text or meaning). **The Words of the Exalted:** ﴿Say: Call upon Allah, or call upon the Most Merciful; whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names. And do not recite your prayer aloud, nor recite it in a whisper, but seek between that a middle way﴾ ﴿And say: Praise belongs to Allah, who has not taken a son, and has not had a partner in the dominion, and has not had any protector out of weakness. And glorify Him with great glorification﴾

The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: "What is meant by the two names is the name and not the named (the referent). The *waw* (in *aw*) is for choice, meaning: ﴿Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Merciful﴾, that is: name Him by this name or by that, or mention Him, either this or that. The tanwin in *ayyan* is a substitute for the genitive noun that is omitted. The *ma* is an added element (*silah*) that emphasizes the indefiniteness contained in *ayy*. The implied meaning is: whichever of these two names you name and mention. ﴿So to Him belong the most beautiful names﴾. The pronoun in His saying ﴿to Him﴾ does not refer to either of the two mentioned names, but to what they name, which is His Essence, may He be glorified and exalted. The meaning is: ﴿whichever you call upon﴾, it is good, so He placed in its position His saying ﴿to Him belong the most beautiful names﴾, because if His names are beautiful, then these two names are beautiful, since they are among them. The meaning of the beauty of Allah's names is that they convey the meanings of praise and sanctity. The thorough discussion of this topic has already been presented at the end of Surat al-A'raf, in the commentary on His saying: ﴿And to Allah belong the most beautiful names﴾ [al-A'raf: 180], so call upon Him by them."

Al-Jubba'i used this verse as an argument, saying: "If the Exalted were the creator of injustice and oppression, it would be correct to say, 'O Unjust One!' and then what is established in this verse, that all His names are beautiful, would be invalidated." The answer: We do not concede that if He were the creator of the actions of the servants, it would be correct to describe Him as unjust and oppressive, just as it does not follow from His being the creator of motion and stillness, blackness and whiteness, that one should say, 'O Moving One! O Still One! O Black One! O White One!' If they say: "Then it would be necessary to permit saying, 'O Creator of injustice and oppression!'" we reply: "Then it would be necessary for you to say, 'O Creator of filth, worms and beetles!' Then the Exalted said: ﴿And do not recite your prayer aloud, nor recite it in a whisper﴾. Concerning this there are discussions:

**The First Discussion:** As for His saying ﴿do not recite your prayer aloud﴾, there are several opinions:

The first: Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning this verse that he said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to raise his voice in recitation. When the polytheists heard it, they would revile him and revile the one who brought it. So Allah the Exalted revealed to him: ﴿do not recite your prayer aloud﴾, so that the polytheists would not hear and then revile Allah out of enmity without knowledge. ﴿Nor recite it in a whisper﴾, so that your companions do not hear you. ﴿And seek between that a middle way﴾."

The second opinion: "It is narrated that the Prophet ﷺ went around at night to the houses of the Companions. Abu Bakr used to lower his voice in recitation during his prayer, and 'Umar used to raise his voice. When morning came and Abu Bakr and 'Umar came, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to Abu Bakr, 'Why do you lower your voice?' He said, 'I am conversing with my Lord, and He knows my need.' He said to 'Umar, 'Why do you raise your voice?' He said, 'I drive away the devil and wake the sleeper.' So the Prophet ﷺ commanded Abu Bakr to raise his voice a little, and commanded 'Umar to lower his voice a little."

The third opinion: Its meaning is: ﴿do not recite your prayer aloud﴾ in its entirety, ﴿nor recite it in a whisper﴾ in its entirety, and ﴿seek between that a middle way﴾, by reciting aloud in the night prayer and reciting quietly in the day prayer.

The fourth opinion: That what is meant by "prayer" (*salah*) is supplication (*du'a'*). This is the view of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, Abu Hurayrah and Mujahid. 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "It concerns supplication." It is also narrated in a marfu' report that the Prophet ﷺ said concerning this verse: "It is only about supplication and asking. Do not raise your voice, lest you mention your sins and they are heard, and you are reproached for them." So raising the voice in supplication is forbidden, and exaggeration in silence is not permissible, and the recommended course in this is moderation, which is that one should make oneself hear, as it is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "He who makes his ears hear has not been silent."

The fifth opinion: al-Hasan said: "Do not show off with its public aspect, and do not do evil with its private aspect."

**The Second Discussion:** *Salah* is an expression for the totality of actions and remembrances, while loudness and softness are accidental qualities of the voice. So what is meant here by "prayers" is a part of the reality of the prayer, namely the remembrances and the Qur'an, and this is of the type of naming the whole to intend a part.

**The Third Discussion:** It is said: "His voice became faint (*khafata*), it fades (*yakhfitu*), a fading (*khaftan*) and a subsiding (*khufuwan*), when it weakens and becomes still." And "a faint voice" means a low voice. From this derives the saying about a man when he dies: "He has faded," meaning his speech has ceased. And "the crop faded" when it withered. And "the man faded in his recitation" when he did not clarify his recitation by raising his voice. And "the people whispered (*takhafatu*)" when they spoke secretly among themselves.

I say: It is established in the books of ethics that both extremes of matters are blameworthy, and justice is observing the middle. For this meaning Allah praised this nation by His saying: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. He also said in praise of the believers: ﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy, but are between that, a balance﴾ [al-Furqan: 67]. And Allah commanded His Messenger, saying: ﴿Do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it completely outstretched﴾ [al-Isra': 29]. So likewise here, He forbade the two extremes, which are loudness and softness, and commanded the middle between them, saying: ﴿and seek between that a middle way﴾. Some have said that the verse is abrogated by His saying: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly﴾ [al-A'raf: 55], but this is far-fetched.

Know that when the Exalted commanded that He not be mentioned nor called upon except by His most beautiful names, He taught him the manner of praising Him, saying: ﴿Say: Praise belongs to Allah, who has not taken a son, and has not had a partner in the dominion, and has not had any protector out of weakness﴾. So He mentioned here attributes of transcendence and majesty, which are negative attributes, in three types:

The first type of attributes: that He has not taken a son. The reasons for this are several:

The first: A son is something produced from a part of another thing. Everyone who has a son is composed of parts, and the composite is originated, and the originated is in need, and cannot achieve perfect bestowal, so he does not deserve perfect praise.

The second: Everyone who has a son withholds all blessings for his son. So if He had no son, He would pour out all those blessings upon His servants.

The third: A son is the one who takes the place of the father after his passing and death. So if He had a son, He would be subject to passing away, and whoever is like that is not able to achieve perfect bestowal at all times, and therefore he must not deserve praise absolutely.

The second type of negative attributes is His saying: ﴿and has not had a partner in the dominion﴾. The reason for considering this attribute is that if He had a partner, then it would not be known that He is deserving of praise and gratitude.

The third type is His saying: ﴿and has not had any protector out of weakness﴾. The reason for considering this attribute is that if it were permissible for Him to have a protector out of weakness, then His gratitude would not be obligatory, since it would be possible that someone else compelled Him to that bestowal or prevented Him from it. But when He is free from a son and from a partner, and free from having a protector who manages His affair, He is deserving of the greatest kinds of praise and worthy of the most exalted kinds of gratitude.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And glorify Him with great glorification﴾. Its meaning is that praise must be accompanied by glorification (*takbir*), and it admits of several meanings:

The first of these: glorifying Him in His essence, which is to believe that He is necessary of existence in Himself, and that He is independent of everything other than Himself.

The second: glorifying Him in His attributes, and this is in three aspects:

The first of them: to believe that everything which is an attribute of His is one of the attributes of majesty, might, greatness and perfection, and that He is free from every attribute of deficiency.

The third of them: to believe that each of those attributes is connected to an endless number of known things, and His power is connected to an endless number of capable and possible things.

The fourth of them: to believe that just as His essence is sanctified from origination and exalted above change, decay, transformation and movement, so likewise His attributes are eternal, ancient, everlasting, free from change, decay, transformation and movement.

The third type of glorifying Allah is glorifying Him in His acts. Here the people of compulsion (*jabr*) and of destiny (*qadar*) differ. The Ahl al-Sunna (Sunni scholars) said: "We praise Allah, glorify Him and magnify Him, above that anything should occur in His dominion not in accordance with His judgment and will. Everything occurs by the decree of Allah, His power, His will and His volition." The Mu'tazila (a theological school) said: "We glorify Allah and magnify Him above being the doer of these ugly and shameful acts, but rather we believe that His wisdom requires that He be exalted and sanctified above them and above willing them." I heard that the Ustadh Abu Ishaq al-Isfara'ini was sitting in the house of al-Sahib ibn 'Abbad, when the Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar ibn Ahmad al-Hamdani entered. When he saw him he said: "Glory be to the One who is exalted above indecency." The Ustadh Abu Ishaq said: "Glory be to the One who does not allow in His dominion anything except what He wills."

The fourth type: glorifying Allah in His commands, which is to believe that He is a King who is obeyed, and that to Him belong command, prohibition, elevation and abasement, and that no one has any objection against Him regarding any of His judgments. He honors whom He wills and humiliates whom He wills.

The fifth type: glorifying Allah in His names, which is that He is not mentioned except by His most beautiful names, and not described except by His sanctified, exalted and transcendent attributes.

The sixth type of glorification is that a person, after exerting himself in magnifying, glorifying, transcending and sanctifying Him to the extent of his intellect, understanding and imagination, acknowledges that his intellect and understanding do not suffice to know the majesty of Allah, his tongue does not suffice to thank Him, and his limbs and members do not suffice to serve Him. So he glorifies Allah beyond that his glorification should be adequate to the reality of His glory and might. This is the utmost that the weak servant can achieve of glorification and magnification. We ask Allah the Exalted for mercy before death, at death and after death. Indeed He is the Generous, the Merciful. And from Allah comes protection and success, and Allah is sufficient for us and He is the best Disposer of affairs.

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "The tafsir (exegesis) of this surah was completed on Tuesday, between the noon and afternoon prayers, on the twentieth day of the month of Muharram, in the town of Ghazni, in the year six hundred and one (601 AH). And praise belongs to Allah, and blessings upon His Prophet Muhammad, his family, his Companions, and may He grant them abundant peace."
